entries.title: Abaddon
entries.content:
Meaning in the original: destruction or place of destruction; In the vision, the name of the angel of the bottomless pit is accompanied by the Greek equivalent Ἀπολλύων, “the destroyer.” 

Key Evidence: Job 26:6; 28:22; 31:12; Proverbs 15:11; 27:20; Revelation 9:11.

Place and context: the world of the dead in the language of Hebrew wisdom, and Hades in the symbolic vision of the Book of Revelation.

People associated with the text: Job, the wise men of Israel, John the Revelator.

Theological study: Abaddon is not the name of an independent god in the books of wisdom, but rather a word juxtaposed with Sheol and death to describe the hidden realm of destruction before God. In Job and Proverbs, the cognitive limit of man is highlighted: even the world of death is exposed to the Lord and is not possessed by humans. As for Revelation 9:11, it transfers the word to an apocalyptic scene, and identifies it with its Greek equivalent, “Apollyon.” The difference in genre is crucial here; The reader does not have the right to transform the image of the vision into a detailed map of the unseen world. The entry links God's sovereignty over death with the hope of judgment, and preserves the difference between using a poetic term in wisdom and using a personal name within the end-time vision.

references.author: Ludwig Koehler and Walter Baumgartner
references.title: The Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, Brill, 1994-2000, s.v. אבדון

references.author: David E. Aune
references.title: Revelation 6-16, Word Biblical Commentary 52B, Word Books, 1998

originalLanguage.language: Hebrew אֲבַדּוֹן ('abaddon), from the root אבד meaning to destroy or destroy; The Greek Ἀβαδδών in Revelation 9:11 is a transliteration of the Hebrew name.
originalLanguage.meaning: Perdition or place of perdition; In the vision, the name of the angel of the bottomless pit is accompanied by the Greek equivalent Ἀπολλύων, “the destroyer.”

entries.title: Abram
entries.content:
Originally meaning: a high-ranking father or an honorable father; The interpretation of Genesis 17 for the new name Abraham is “father of a multitude of nations.” 

Key Evidence: Genesis 11:27-32; 12:1-9; 13:1-18; 15:1-6; 17:1-8; Romans 4:1-12.

Place and context: Ur of the Chaldeans and Haran in the family background, then Shechem, Bethel, the Negev, and Canaan.

People associated with the text: Terah, Sarai, Lot, Melchizedek, Hagar.

Theological study: Abram is the name of Abraham before the renewal of the covenant in Genesis 17, and therefore it is read within the advocacy movement, not as a separate character. The narrative begins with the emergence from the network of family and place into a land promised by God, then hunger, conflict, and fear reveal that obedience is not a path of victory without fragility. In Genesis 13 Abram relinquishes the right of choice to Lot, and in Genesis 15 the delayed promise places the question of faith before God. The covenant promise does not excuse his treatment of Hagar or his mistakes in Egypt; Rather, the text reveals the difference between God’s initiative and man’s attempts to secure the promise through his means. Paul reuses Abraham's faith in Romans 4 in his argument for grace and promise to the nations, without eliminating the Genesis story or its moral complexity.

references.author: Ludwig Koehler and Walter Baumgartner
references.title: The Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, Brill, 1994-2000, s.v. אברם

references.author: Gordon J. Wenham
references.title: Genesis 1-15, Word Biblical Commentary 1, Word Books, 1987

originalLanguage.language: Hebrew אַבְרָם ('avram). The name is usually understood as "honourable father" from אָב "father" and ־רוּם "high", with the pre-text history of the name remaining unresolved.
originalLanguage.meaning: A high-ranking or honored father; The interpretation of Genesis 17 for the new name Abraham is “father of a multitude of nations.”

entries.title: Ibrahim
entries.content:
Meaning in the original: Biblical interpretation of the name: Father of a multitude of nations. 

Key Evidence: Genesis 12:1-3; 15:1-6; 17:1-8; 21:1-7; 22:1-19; Isaiah 51:1-2; Romans 4; Galatians 3:6-9.

Place and context: Canaan, Hebron, Beersheba, and Mount Moriah in the context of Genesis 22.

People associated with the text: Sarah, Lot, Hagar, Ishmael, Isaac, Melchizedek.

Theological Study: The Book of Genesis presents Abraham as a recipient of the promise of land, descendants, and blessing to the nations, not as the founder of his own religious project. The progression of the covenant from the call to cutting and then circumcision shows that the promise is a divine initiative that requires a response of faith and obedience. The narrative prevents the deification of the hero: his fear in Egypt and Gerar, the crisis of Hagar and Ishmael, and the test of Isaac remain within the story and may not be deleted. Isaiah reads Abraham into the memory of the hope of the exiles, and Paul makes his faith central to his argument for the blessing that comes to the nations. This apostolic usage does not replace the meaning of Genesis, but rather expands the effect of the promise within the canonical reading of the book.

references.author: Nahum M. Sarna
references.title: Genesis, JPS Torah Commentary, Jewish Publication Society, 1989

references.author: Paul R. Williamson
references.title: Abraham, Israel and the Nations, Sheffield Academic Press, 2000

originalLanguage.language: Hebrew אַבְרָהָם ('avraham). Genesis 5:17 explains the name within the narrative: “father of a multitude of nations”; The exact historical derivation behind this interpretation is a matter of linguistic debate.
originalLanguage.meaning: Biblical interpretation of the name: Father of a multitude of nations.

entries.title: Abraham and Isaac
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 1:21-21; 22:1-19; 24:1-9; Hebrews 11:17-19.

Place and context: Beersheba, the land of Moriah, and Canaan.

People associated with the text: Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Ishmael, the angel of the Lord.

Theological study: Abraham's relationship with Isaac is linked to the continuation of the promise, because Isaac is born after a long wait as Sarah's son. The narrative culminates in Genesis 22 when God commands Abraham to take his son up to the land of Moriah. The text does not describe a human sacrifice performed; The Lord stops the action and provides a ram instead of Isaac, separating the story from the practices of human sacrifice that the biblical tradition rejects. Hebrews reads Abraham's obedience in light of his trust in God's power, but it does not erase the narrative's tension or the son's relatively silent voice. The introduction puts the promise, the test, and the provision of an alternative in balance, and refuses to use the story to justify harm to children or blind obedience to authority.

references.author: Jon D. Levenson
references.title: The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son, Yale University Press, 1993

references.author: Gordon J. Wenham
references.title: Genesis 16-50, Word Biblical Commentary 2, Word Books, 1994

entries.title: Abraham and the covenant
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 12:1-3; 15:1-21; 17:1-27; 22:15-18; Romans 4:1-25; Galatians 6:3-18.

Place and context: Shechem, Hebron, and Canaan, then the Romans and Galatians in Paul’s reading.

People associated with the text: Abraham, Sarah, Ishmael, Isaac, Paul.

Theological Study: Abraham's covenant progresses in Genesis from an invitation promising seed, land, and blessing to the nations to the cutting scene in Genesis 15 and the sign of circumcision in Genesis 17. These units are not treated as one identical legal formula; Each highlights an aspect of God's initiative and Abraham's response. Paul links Genesis 15:6 with his question about faith and blessing for the nations, while the sign of the covenant and family history remain part of the textual text and not a detail that can be overlooked. The introduction rejects the reduction of the covenant to the possession of land or to a closed identity, because the promise of blessing addresses all the clans of the earth and demands practical fidelity to God.

references.author: Paul R. Williamson
references.title: Sealed with an Oath: Covenant in God's Unfolding Purpose, IVP Academic, 2007

entries.title: Abraham and Lot
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 1:13-18; 14:1-24; 18:16-33; 19:1-29; 2 Peter 2:6-8.

Place and context: Canaan, the Jordan Plain, Sodom and Gomorrah.

People associated with the text: Abraham, Lot, Melchizedek, angels of the Lord, inhabitants of Sodom.

Theological Study: The story of Abraham and Lot begins with a peaceful separation due to the lack of land for their livestock, but Lot's choice of the Jordan Plain brings him closer to Sodom and puts him on a path of escalating danger. Abraham rescues him after the War of the Kings, then Abraham intercedes when the Lord announces the judgment of Sodom. Intercession does not provide a guarantee that divine justice ignores evil, but it opens the question of the destruction of the righteous with the wicked within a bold dialogue with God. Lot's salvation does not turn his choices into wisdom, just as his description in 2 Peter does not negate the criticism of Genesis. The introduction calls for a reading of kinship, responsibility, intercession, and judgment without simplifying the character of Lot or the inhabitants of the cities.

references.author: Gordon J. Wenham
references.title: Genesis 16-50, Word Biblical Commentary 2, Word Books, 1994

references.author: Robert Alter
references.title: The Five Books of Moses, W. W. Norton, 2004

entries.title: Apple converted
entries.content:
Meaning originally: name of a place, often “changed meadow/pasture”; The suggestion of derivation must not be converted into geographical certainty.

Key Evidence: Judges 7:22; 1 Kings 4:12; 19:16-21.

Place and context: The Jordan Valley, and textual evidence places it near or south of Beit Shean; The exact archaeological identification is inconclusive.

People associated with the text: Elijah, Elisha son of Shaphat, Gideon, residents of the area.

Theological study: Abel Meholah is a place that appears on the route of the flight of the Midianites in Judges 7, then in the division of Solomon’s administration, and most famously in the call of Elisha. Elijah finds Elisha in the field with twelve acres of cows, and the narrative makes agricultural labor a realistic backdrop to the transition of prophetic ministry. Throwing on a robe is not just a personal gesture; It proclaims the continuity of God's Word after Elijah's exhaustion at Horeb. The text does not allow for an adequate description of the city's economy or boundaries, so a distinction must be made between the connotation of place in the narrative and attempts to map it. The introduction links the call to obedience and abandonment of what is familiar, without turning the event into a rule against work or family ties.

references.author: Anson F. Rainey and R. Steven Notley
references.title: The Sacred Bridge: Carta's Atlas of the Biblical World, Carta, 2006

references.author: Iain Provan
references.title: 1 and 2 Kings, New International Biblical Commentary, Hendrickson, 1995

originalLanguage.language: Hebrew אָבֵל מְחוֹלָה ('avel meholah). Apple often means “meadow or pasture,” and the second part is the name of a place that may be associated with dancing or twirling, the etymology of which is not conclusively proven.
originalLanguage.meaning: The name of a place, often “a converted meadow/pasture”; The suggestion of derivation must not be converted into geographical certainty.

entries.title: Dad Ngo
entries.content:
Meaning in the original: Abdnego/Nebo in the Babylonian name; In contrast to the Hebrew name Azariah, “the Lord has helped.” 

Key Evidence: Daniel 6:1-7; 2:17-18; 3:1-30.

Place and context: Babylon in the court of Nebuchadnezzar and the Plain of Dura, where the statue was erected.

People associated with the text: Daniel, Hananiah, Michael, Nebuchadnezzar.

Theological Study: Abi-Nego is the Babylonian name for Azariah in Daniel's account, and the story places him within an imperial policy that renames young men, educates them, and demands their loyalty. He appears in the third chapter with Shadrach and Meshach when they refuse to bow down to the statue. The force of their answer is not a promise of guaranteed deliverance: God is able to save, “or else” they would not worship the king’s idol. Therefore, the scene is a testimony against the deification of authority, not a promise that the believer will always be exempt from danger. The presence of the fourth person in the furnace declares the sovereignty of God in the face of the fire and the emperor, while the narrative and apocalyptic style of Daniel prevents the construction of a detailed doctrine of the identity of this fourth person.

references.author: Ludwig Koehler and Walter Baumgartner
references.title: The Aramaic Lexicon in The Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, Brill, 1994-2000, s.v. עבד נגו

originalLanguage.language: Aramaic עֲבֵד־נְגוֹ ('aved-nego), Babylonian name given to Azariah. The first part means “slave,” while the word Nego is linked to a Babylonian god in the text, and the details of its setting between Nebo and Nego are subject to debate.
originalLanguage.meaning: Abd Nego/Nebo in the Babylonian name; In contrast to the Hebrew name Azariah, “the Lord has helped.”

entries.title: Appiah
entries.content:
Meaning in the original: Jehovah is my father or my father is Jehovah.

Key Evidence: 1 Kings 1:14-18; 15:1-8; 2 Chronicles 13:1-22.

Place and context: Tirzah in the Northern Kingdom, Jerusalem, and Mount Samaraim in Judah.

People associated with the text: Jeroboam, Ahijah the Shilonite, Rehoboam, Jeroboam son of Nebat.

Theological study: Abijah is a frequent name, and its most important bearers are the son of Jeroboam and the king of Judah, the son of Rehoboam. Therefore, the entry does not read as one artificial biography. In 1 Kings 14, the story of Jeroboam’s son is connected to Ahijah’s word about the judgment of the house, while 1 Kings 15 briefly introduces the king of Judah. 2 Chronicles 13 expands the image of the king and his speech against Jeroboam, focusing on the covenant of David, the temple, and the priesthood. The difference in presentation makes clear that the chronicler is rereading the memory of the kingdom in light of the worship in Jerusalem. This does not justify sectarian rhetoric, but rather reveals that the claim of religious legitimacy is tested by fidelity to the covenant and justice.

references.author: Ludwig Koehler and Walter Baumgartner
references.title: The Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, Brill, 1994-2000, s.v. אביה

references.author: Sara Japhet
references.title: I & II Chronicles, Old Testament Library, Westminster John Knox, 1993

originalLanguage.language: Hebrew אֲבִיָּה/אֲבִיָּהוּ ('aviyyah/'aviyyahu), from אָב "Father" and the divine name Yahweh.
originalLanguage.meaning: Jehovah my father or father is Jehovah.

entries.title: Abigail
entries.content:
Meaning in the original: Father of joy or source of joy.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 1:25-44; 2 Samuel 2:2-3; 3:3.

Place and context: Carmel in Judah, the wilderness of Paran, and Hebron.

People associated with the text: Nabal, David, Nabal's servants, David's men.

Theological Study: Abigail appears in 1 Samuel 25 in the midst of an economic dispute that could turn into bloodshed. Nabal rudely rejects David's request, and David chooses revenge, so Abigail moves in, carrying supplies and a letter reminding him of the Lord's promise and the danger of bearing the guilt of wild blood. The narrative does not make her wisdom a justification for a violent system or a responsibility imposed on women to right men's wrongs; Rather, it reveals how the rational word interrupts the cycle of insult and revenge. Nabal's death and her marriage to David do not erase the previous tension, but the story links the legitimacy of the next king to the control of power and the acceptance of advice.

references.author: Ludwig Koehler and Walter Baumgartner
references.title: The Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, Brill, 1994-2000, s.v. אביגיל

references.author: David G. Firth
references.title: 1 & 2 Samuel, Apollos Old Testament Commentary, IVP Academic, 2009

originalLanguage.language: Hebrew אֲבִיגַיִל ('avigayil), from אָב "father" and ־גִּיל "joy or rejoicing".
originalLanguage.meaning: My father is a joy or a source of joy.

entries.title: Abishai
entries.content:
Meaning in the original: Abi Attiya or the gift of my father.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 26:5-12; 2 Samuel 2:18-24; 16:5-14; 21:15-17; 23:18-19.

Place and context: Saul's camp in the Wilderness of Ziph, Jerusalem, and the battlefields against the Philistines.

People associated with the text: David, Joab, Asael, Saul, Shimei, Abishai the Gishtite.

Theological study: Abishai, son of Zeruiah and brother of Joab and Asael, and the narrative combines in his person military loyalty and dangerous impulse. In Saul's camp, killing the king is a legitimate opportunity, but David refuses to extend his hand to the Lord's anointed. Then Abishai appears ready to kill Shimei, and participates in the wars of the Bene Raphah. The novels do not describe him as a traitor, but they reveal that loyalty and courage are not enough to create faithful leadership unless they are controlled by the limits of the covenant. Therefore, his character does not serve as a model to justify political revenge or religious violence. Rather, it calls for a distinction between the ability to act and the legitimacy of the act.

references.author: Ludwig Koehler and Walter Baumgartner
references.title: The Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, Brill, 1994-2000, s.v. אבישי

originalLanguage.language: Hebrew אֲבִישַׁי ('avishay), from אָב "father" and ־שַׁי "gift or gift".
originalLanguage.meaning: Abi Attia or Attiya Abi.

entries.title: Abishag
entries.content:
Key Evidence: 1 Kings 1:1-4; 2:13-25.

Place and context: Shunem and Jerusalem in David's palace.

People associated with the text: David, Adonijah, Bathsheba, Solomon.

Theological study: Abishag the Shunammite is a young woman who is brought to David in his old age to serve him and warm him, and the text stresses that he did not know her. After David's death, Adonijah asks to marry her through Bathsheba, and Solomon understands the request within the succession struggle, not just as a private marriage issue. In ancient palace codes, an association with a woman of the late king's household may have the meaning of claiming political right, as the example of Absalom in 2 Samuel 16 demonstrates. Yet the text does not present Abishag's voice or choice, and she must not be reduced to an instrument in the struggle of men. The entry reveals the fragility of women within court politics, and the complexity of the transition of rule from David to Solomon.

references.author: Tikva Frymer-Kensky
references.title: Reading the Women of the Bible, Schocken, 2002

entries.title: Abimelech
entries.content:
Meaning in the original: My father is a king; The name may be a royal title or a personal name, depending on the context.

Key Evidence: Genesis 1:20-18; 21:22-34; 26:1-33; Judges 8:31-9:57.

Place and context: Gerar in southern Canaan, Shechem, and the land of Ephraim.

People associated with the text: Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Gideon, Jotham, the people of Shechem.

Theological study: The name Abimelech carries more than one personality, and it is not permissible to combine them into one identity. In Genesis 20 and 26, the king of Gerar is linked to the protection of the patriarchs’ wives and to the covenants of wells and peace; The text does not definitively specify whether the name is a nickname for a dynasty or two separate individuals. As for Abimelech the son of Gideon in Judges 9, he builds his kingdom on killing his brothers and wooing Shechem with money and lineage. He, like Jotham, reveals an authority that promises protection and then burns those around it. The two narratives put authority under the test of justice and limits, and prevent the use of similarity in name to obscure the radical difference in personality and context.

references.author: Ludwig Koehler and Walter Baumgartner
references.title: The Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, Brill, 1994-2000, s.v. אבימלך

references.author: Daniel I. Block
references.title: Judges, Ruth, New American Commentary, B&H, 1999

originalLanguage.language: Hebrew אֲבִימֶלֶךְ ('avimelekh), from אָב "father" and ־מֶלֶךְ "king".
originalLanguage.meaning: My father is a king; The name may be a royal title or a personal name, depending on the context.

entries.title: Abinadab
entries.content:
Meaning in the original: Abi Karim or Abi Nabil.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 7:1-2; 2 Samuel 3:6-7; 1 Chronicles 13:7-10.

Place and context: Kirjath-jearim, then the road to Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: Eliezer, Uzzah, Ahio, David.

Theological study: The Ark of the Covenant was preserved in the house of Abinadab in Kirjath Jearim after its return from the Philistines, and Eliezer was sanctified to guard it. Years later, David transports the ark on a new cart from the house of Abinadab, and Uzzah dies when he holds it. The narrative does not make the house guilty or explain the responsibility of everyone in it; Rather, he places the enthusiasm for transporting the ark before the holiness of the Lord and the method of carrying it determined by the Torah. 1 reads the news of the event in light of the Levites' responsibility. Therefore, the scene is not used to intimidate believers, but rather to understand that worship is not reduced to sincere intention when the limits of the text and the preservation of life are neglected.

references.author: Ludwig Koehler and Walter Baumgartner
references.title: The Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, Brill, 1994-2000, s.v. אבינדב

originalLanguage.language: Hebrew אֲבִינָדָב ('avinadav), from אָב "father" and ־נָדִיב "noble or generous".
originalLanguage.meaning: My father is generous or my father is noble.

entries.title: Ararat
entries.content:
Originally meaning: the name of a mountainous region in historical Armenia, not the name of a single specific peak.

Key Evidence: Genesis 4:8; 2 Kings 19:37; Isaiah 37:38; Jeremiah 51:27.

Place and context: Urartu highlands around Lake Van in eastern Anatolia; The text does not designate a specific mountaintop.

People associated with the text: Noah and his family, Sennacherib, Sennacherib's sons.

Theological study: Ararat appears in Genesis in the plural form “Mountains of Ararat,” which prevents the text from being directly equated with one mountain in the modern tradition. The function of place in the story of the flood is the transfer of the ark from the waters of judgment to a land on which a new life could begin, before Noah’s covenant with all flesh. In 2 Kings and Isaiah, Sennacherib's killers flee to the land of Ararat, while Jeremiah mentions the kingdoms of Ararat, Mni, and Ashkenaz in the context of the alliance against Babylon. These places reveal that the name is geographical and political, and that the Assyrian evidence helps define the region without proving every narrative or archaeological detail in the story of the ark.

references.author: Ludwig Koehler and Walter Baumgartner
references.title: The Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, Brill, 1994-2000, s.v. אררט

references.author: Gordon J. Wenham
references.title: Genesis 1-15, Word Biblical Commentary 1, Word Books, 1987

originalLanguage.language: Akkadian Urartu, the name of the region known in Assyrian sources; The Hebrew word אֲרָרָט is used to refer to the region.
originalLanguage.meaning: The name of a mountainous region in historical Armenia, not the name of one specific peak.

entries.title: Arnon
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Numbers 21:13-15; Deuteronomy 2:24-36; Joshua 12:1-2; Judges 11:13-28; Isaiah 16:2.

Place and context: A deep valley that empties into the Dead Sea, and formed a border between Moab and the Amorites in the biblical accounts.

People associated with the text: Moses, Sihon, Jephthah, the elders of Ammon and Moab.

Theological study: Arnon is a border landmark in Transjordan, and its importance appears when Israel moves from the land of Moab to the land of Sihon. In Numbers 21, the ancient poem preserves the memory of the valley, while Deuteronomy and Joshua define the border of the Amorite kingdom that Israel defeated. Jephthah uses the same memory in his debate with the Ammonites, which reveals that the borders in the biblical narrative are carried by history and political argument, not by maps alone. In Isaiah, the valley becomes part of the image of the refugee Moab. The name does not prove modern political ownership or boundaries; His job is to understand the terrain of Transjordan and the movement of peoples within the text.

references.author: Anson F. Rainey and R. Steven Notley
references.title: The Sacred Bridge: Carta's Atlas of the Biblical World, Carta, 2006

references.author: Jacob Milgrom
references.title: Numbers, JPS Torah Commentary, Jewish Publication Society, 1990

entries.title: A statement
entries.content:
Key Evidence: 2 Kings 1:5-14.

Place and context: Damascus in Aram; The name is associated with one of its rivers, and the modern designation is debated between Aberdey and another river.

People associated with the text: Naaman, Elisha, Naaman's maid, Gehazi.

Theological study: His statement does not occur except in Naaman’s objection to Elisha’s order to wash in the Jordan. The Aramean leader compares the waters of Damascus to the waters of Israel, and the narrative reveals how national and military prestige collide over a simple prophetic command. The Jordan in the story is not a magical water, just as the Abana is not a reprehensible river. Healing comes when Naaman abandons his own conditions and obeys God's Word. The young Israelite maid initiates the chain of events, and Gehazi later reveals the danger of turning grace into gain. Therefore, geography here serves to criticize pride and the extension of God's mercy to a person from outside Israel.

references.author: Anson F. Rainey and R. Steven Notley
references.title: The Sacred Bridge: Carta's Atlas of the Biblical World, Carta, 2006

entries.title: Efrat
entries.content:
Originally meaning: the name of the Euphrates River; The Hebrew text does not provide a etymology of its meaning.

Key Evidence: Genesis 2:14; 15:18; Deuteronomy 1:7; 2 Samuel 8:3; Jeremiah 46:2-10; Revelation 9:14; 16:12.

Place and context: The Euphrates River in Mesopotamia, from Anatolia to the Gulf; A northeastern border in images of the biblical world.

People associated with the text: Abraham, David, Nebuchadnezzar, John the Revelator.

Theological study: The Euphrates is a major historical river in the geography of the Near East. It is mentioned in Genesis 2 among the rivers of Eden and in Genesis 15 in describing the extent of the promise to Abraham. The description does not mean that every age witnessed political possession corresponding to these limits; The books distinguish between the promise and the changing historical reality. In Samuel the river is associated with David's campaigns north, and in Jeremiah with its confrontation with Egypt and Babylon near Carchemish. The vision uses the Euphrates in a symbolic scene of judgment, so the historical river does not dissolve into the symbol and the symbol is not treated as a contemporary war map. The introduction shows how geography moves from promise and history to apocalyptic literature.

references.author: Ludwig Koehler and Walter Baumgartner
references.title: The Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, Brill, 1994-2000, s.v. פרת

references.author: Richard Bauckham
references.title: The Theology of the Book of Revelation, Cambridge University Press, 1993

originalLanguage.language: Hebrew פְּרָת (perat), corresponding to the Akkadian name Purattu and the Greek Εὐφράτης.
originalLanguage.meaning: The name of the Euphrates River; The Hebrew text does not provide a etymology of its meaning.

entries.title: Jericho
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Joshua 1:2-24; 6:1-27; 2 Kings 4:2-22; Luke 10:30-37; 18:35-43; 19:1-10.

Place and context: The Jordan Valley north of the Dead Sea, as the road ascends to the Jerusalem Heights.

People associated with the text: Joshua, Rahab, Elisha, Jesus, Bartimaeus, Zacchaeus.

Theological study: Jericho is a strategic oasis city at the entrance to the road from the Jordan Valley to the highlands. In Joshua, it is linked to crossing the land and saving Rahab and her family, and the war narrative should not be transformed into a model of contemporary religious violence. In 2 Kings, Elisha treats the city’s water, bringing the place into a different prophetic memory. As for the Gospels, they turn Jericho into a place of healing for the blind man and a pure encounter, and like the road to the city, so the place of the borders turns into a space of mercy and restoration. The archaeological layers of Jericho remain the subject of specialized debate, and no single study confirms every detail in the story. Therefore, the introduction distinguishes between the history of the site and its theological function in each book.

references.author: Richard S. Hess
references.title: Joshua, Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries, IVP Academic, 1996

references.author: James K. Hoffmeier
references.title: The Archaeology of the Bible, Lion Hudson, 2008

entries.title: Ur
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 11:27-32; 12:1-9; Nehemiah 9:7; Acts 7:2-4; Hebrews 11:8-10.

Place and context: Southern Mesopotamia according to the traditional definition of Sumerian Ur; The family's travel begins from there before Haran and Canaan.

People associated with the text: Terah, Abram, Sarai, Lot, Stephen.

Theological Study: Ur of the Chaldeans appears as a starting point for Terah's family in Genesis 11, from where the journey goes to Haran and then Canaan. Nehemiah links Abraham's choice to his exodus from Ur, while Stephen reads the call within a broader movement before settling in the land. The association of the name with the Chaldeans, a people historically later than the time of the fathers according to some histories, opens a question about the language of the narrator and the modernization of the names of the sites, not a contradiction that can be resolved by a quick assumption. The archaeologically known Sumerian city of Ur helps understand the Mesopotamian environment, but does not provide details of Abram's story. The theological meaning remains in the call to follow God's promise without fully owning the future.

references.author: Nahum M. Sarna
references.title: Genesis, JPS Torah Commentary, Jewish Publication Society, 1989

entries.title: Edom
entries.content:
Originally meaning: red; It is the name of Esau, his people, and his land in the southeast of the Dead Sea.

Key Evidence: Genesis 25:29-34; 36:1-43; Numbers 20:14-21; Obadiah 1-21; Malachi 2:1-5.

Place and context: The highlands located southeast of the Dead Sea, approximately between Moab and the Gulf of Aqaba.

People associated with the text: Esau, Jacob, Moses, King of Edom, Obadiah.

Theological study: Edom is the name of Esau, his descendants, and their land, and therefore his relationship with Israel begins from a bond of brotherhood, not from abstract enmity. The king of Edom refuses Israel's passage in number, and the relationship develops into political conflicts in the time of the kings. Obadiah condemns Edom for his participation or gloating at the fall of Jerusalem, so the prophetic judgment is not a permanent racial condemnation but an accountability for a specific historical act against a brother. Malachi reuses Edom to confirm Jacob's choice in the post-exilic controversy. The introduction distinguishes between historical Edom and later prophetic images, and warns against using texts to legitimize modern hostility.

references.author: Ludwig Koehler and Walter Baumgartner
references.title: The Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, Brill, 1994-2000, s.v. אדם

references.author: John R. Bartlett
references.title: Edom and the Edomites, Sheffield Academic Press, 1989

originalLanguage.language: Hebrew אֱדוֹם ('edom), from אָדֹם "red"; Genesis 25:30 links the name to Esau's request for red food.
originalLanguage.meaning: red; It is the name of Esau, his people, and his land in the southeast of the Dead Sea.

entries.title: Athens
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Acts 16:17-34; 1 Thessalonians 3:1.

Place and context: Athens in the Attica region of Greece, its complex, square and Areopagus.

People associated with the text: Paul, Epicureans, Stoics, Dionysius, Damers.

Theological Study: Athens appears in Acts 17 as a city filled with idols and a center for philosophical dialogue, but Luke does not depict it merely as a museum of thought. Paul begins from the altar of “an unknown God” and from Greek poets to speak in an understandable language. Then he proclaims God the Creator who does not live in made-up temples and does not need human service. This approach does not dissolve the Gospel into the culture of the city; The speech reaches repentance, judgment, and resurrection, which is the point on which the listeners were divided. The entry provides an example of communication that respects the audience and confronts its assumptions, not one that compromises the message or disdains the culture.

references.author: Craig S. Keener
references.title: Acts: An Exegetical Commentary, Volume 3, Baker Academic, 2014

references.author: Ben Witherington III
references.title: The Acts of the Apostles: A Socio-Rhetorical Commentary, Eerdmans, 1998

entries.title: Areopagus
entries.content:
Meaning in the original: Hill of Aris; The name was also used for a judicial council or meeting place depending on the context.

Key Evidence: Acts 19:17-34.

Place and context: Areopagus hill near the Acropolis in Athens; The text may refer to the council as much as it refers to the place.

People associated with the text: Paul, Athenian philosophers, Dionysius the Areopagite, Damers.

Theological study: The Athenians lead Paul to the Areopagus after hearing his teaching, but the Greek phrase refers to the familiar council or hill itself. The Book of Acts does not resolve this detail in a way that makes geography more important than rhetoric. Paul declares there that God, the Creator of humans and nations, is close to them even though he is not surrounded by temples, and he concludes with a call to repentance due to resurrection and judgment. The reference to a Greek poet does not mean that Paul agrees with all Greek philosophy, nor does the reaction of the listeners mean that the speech fails; The text mentions those who believe. The entrance links the place with the judiciary, public dialogue, and testimony about the Resurrection.

references.author: Frederick W. Danker
references.title: A Greek-English Lexicon of the New Testament and Other Early Christian Literature, University of Chicago Press, 2000, s.v. Ἄρειος Πάγος

references.author: Craig S. Keener
references.title: Acts: An Exegetical Commentary, Volume 3, Baker Academic, 2014

originalLanguage.language: Greek Ἄρειος Πάγος (Areios Pagos), “Hill of Arees,” meaning the hill attributed to Ares, the god of war in Greek religion.
originalLanguage.meaning: Tel Ares; The name was also used for a judicial council or meeting place depending on the context.

entries.title: Ephesians
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Acts 19:18-21; 19:1-41; 20:17-38; Ephesians 1:1; Revelation 2:1-7.

Place and context: A major port city in the Roman province of Asia, on the western coast of Asia Minor.

People associated with the text: Paul, Priscilla, Aquila, Apollos, Timothy, Demetrius, elders of Ephesus.

Theological study: Ephesus is an important urban, commercial, and religious center, and Acts 19 reveals that the proclamation of Christ reached the city's economy and the cult of Artemis, not an isolated private conviction. Luke does not describe all the inhabitants of the city with one description; Rather, it narrates a debate between magicians, merchants, audiences, and messengers. Paul stays there for a long time, then bids farewell to its elders in Miletus, calling on them to guard the flock and serve the weak. The vision addresses the Church of Ephesus, warning against abandoning first love. Therefore, the entrance combines the historic city, the diversity of its groups, and the Church’s call to fidelity that is not subject to the worship of profit or status.

references.author: Craig S. Keener
references.title: Acts: An Exegetical Commentary, Volume 3, Baker Academic, 2014

references.author: Clinton E. Arnold
references.title: Ephesians, Zondervan Exegetical Commentary on the New Testament, Zondervan, 2010

entries.title: Antioch
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Acts 19:11-30; 13:1-3; 14:26-28; 15:22-35; Galatians 2:11-14.

Place and context: Syrian Antioch on the Orontes River, a major Roman regional center.

People associated with the text: Barnabas, Saul, Agabus, Peter, Judas Barsabas, Silas.

Theological study: In the Acts of the Apostles, Antioch becomes a community that receives Jews and Greeks and calls the disciples “Christians” first. Sent by the Holy Spirit, Barnabas and Saul, she then receives news of serving the Gentiles and participates in the discussion of circumcision in Acts 15. This history does not depict an ideal church without tension; Galatians 2 mentions the disagreement between Paul and Peter around the table, which confirms that the unity of the group is not achieved by hiding differences. Antioch reveals how worship, fasting, mission, giving, and theological accountability intertwine in a multicultural, urban church.

references.author: Wayne A. Meeks
references.title: The First Urban Christians, Yale University Press, 2003

references.author: F. F. Bruce
references.title: The Book of the Acts, New International Commentary on the New Testament, Eerdmans, 1988

entries.title: Ashdod
entries.content: Ashdod was one of the main cities in the Philistine region, and it was a coastal city of commercial and military importance. It appears in the story of the Ark of the Covenant in 1 Samuel 5, when the Philistines take it and place it in the House of Dagon in Ashdod, and then events begin that end with the return of the Ark. The story reveals a conflict between the symbols of Palestinian political and religious power and the holiness of God. The Ark of the Covenant does not become a spoils belonging to the victor, but rather its presence leads to a series of crises within Palestinian cities. Ashdod also appears in historical and prophetic texts within the conflict between Israel and the Palestinians. In Acts 8:40, Philip arrives there after his meeting with the Ethiopian eunuch, and then continues to preach in the cities until Caesarea. Thus, the presence of the city extends from the Old Testament to the New Testament. Its coastal location helps understand its importance in trade and military routes, and its relationship with other Philistine cities reveals a broader regional political network.

references.author: Trude Dothan and Seymour Gitin
references.title: Ekron of the Philistines, Israel Exploration Society, 1997

references.author: K. Lawson Younger Jr.
references.title: The Old Testament in Its World, 2002

entries.title: Arad
entries.content: Arad is a Canaanite city in the Negev region that is linked in Numbers 21 to Israel’s conflict during its march toward the Promised Land. The text mentions the king of Arad who heard of the coming of Israel and fought them. Then Israel vowed to the Lord and the confrontation took place that ended in their victory. The site also appears in historical and archaeological studies because of what excavations have revealed about settlement, fortifications, economics, and worship in the southern region. However, archaeological data must be separated from interpreting each layer as a direct correspondence with the biblical event. Arad's geographical importance stems from its location on the southern roads that connect the Negev regions, the entrances to Sinai, and the highlands. Therefore, it is included in the study of the movement of tribes, armies, and desert roads. Its mention in the Book of Numbers also reveals that Israel’s advance towards the land was not a path devoid of resistance, but was interspersed with confrontations with local entities. The introduction then combines military geography, history, settlement, and Israel's march toward the Promised Land.

references.author: James K. Hoffmeier
references.title: Ancient Israel in Sinai, Oxford University Press, 2005

entries.title: Ashkelon
entries.content: Ashkelon is an ancient Palestinian port city, and was one of the main cities associated with the Philistines. Its name appears in contexts of the conflict between Israel and the Palestinians, and is then repeated in prophecies dealing with coastal cities. Ashkelon's coastal location gave it strategic and commercial importance, as it was linked to sea trade networks and land routes that passed along the Mediterranean coast. Control of the city was therefore part of the struggle over the coastal passes. In the prophetic texts, Ashkelon appears with Gaza, Ashdod, and Ekron within the judgment discourses, which reflects the transition of the name from being a geographical landmark to an element in the prophetic message about the fall of political powers. Studying Ashkelon helps understand the world of the Philistines, the coastal cities, and the relationship between geography, trade, and war. The prophecies also reveal that political power is no guarantee of continuity, and that cities that appear historically well-established can become objects of judgment.

references.author: John F. Wilson
references.title: The New Encyclopedia of Archaeological Excavations in the Holy Land, Israel Exploration Society, 1993

entries.title: Alabaster
entries.content: Alabaster is a stone material that was associated in the ancient world with the manufacture of small containers to store perfumes and precious oils, and therefore it appears in the study of the Gospels that talk about pouring perfume on Jesus. In Matthew 26 and Mark 14, the story of the woman who broke the flask of ointment and poured it on Christ’s head is mentioned, while Luke 7 presents the story of a sinful woman who anointed Jesus’ feet, and John 12 mentions Mary who used the very expensive ointment of valerian. Not all novels should be combined in a way that eliminates the narrative differences between them, but the theme of the bottle, perfume, value, and dedication can be studied as common elements in some novels. The importance of the bowl is that it holds a valuable substance, and when the substance is spilled it cannot be retrieved. Therefore, the act becomes an image of complete dedication and dedication. Historically, one should be careful not to assume that every perfume vessel in the ancient world was made in the same way or from the same material. Studying the alabaster helps understand ancient economy, perfumes, worship, hospitality, and dignity, and then examines the way the Bible uses material things to communicate theological meanings.

entries.title: Purple
entries.content: Purple is a color and dye that in the ancient world was associated with luxury, power, property, and social status. It appears in descriptions of the fabrics of the Tabernacle and the clothing of the priests, as well as in contexts relating to kings and the rich, and then takes on an ironic and tragic connotation in the story of the Passion of Christ when the soldiers dress him in a purple robe and mock him as a king. In Exodus 25-28 and Exodus 35, purple is included among the official items of worship, indicating the value of dyeing and the quality of the fabric. In the Gospels, color becomes part of literary irony. The soldiers are meant to mock Jesus' kingship, while the Christian narrative reveals that Jesus is the true king. Therefore, the meaning of power, luxury, holiness and sarcasm can be combined in color. Historically, some types of purple dye were very expensive and associated with marine dyes, so they were a status symbol. Study of Purple reveals how the Bible uses material objects within a system of religious, social, and royal symbols.

references.author: Philip J. King and Lawrence E. Stager
references.title: Life in Biblical Israel, Westminster John Knox, 2001

entries.title: Rice
entries.content: Cedar, especially the cedar of Lebanon, is one of the most important woods mentioned in the Bible. It was associated with royal and structural architecture, especially in the time of Solomon, when wood was imported from Lebanon as part of the temple and palace construction project. In 1 Kings 5-7 and 2 Chronicles cedar appears as part of an economic and political network between Israel, Tire, and Lebanon. Therefore, the material reveals the existence of trade, craft expertise, and regional contacts during the time of the kingdom. Rice is not limited to its structural function; In biblical poetry, it is used as an image of strength, elevation, and prosperity, and in some prophetic texts it can become a symbol of pride that rises and then falls. This transformation from building material to poetic image is very important in understanding the biblical language. Studying rice also helps understand the region's natural resources, ancient trade networks, architecture, and poetic symbolism. Methodologically, a distinction must be made between the historical use of rice and the symbolic meaning it takes on in each text.

references.author: John H. Walton
references.title: Ancient Near Eastern Thought and the Old Testament, Baker Academic, 2006

entries.title: I will
entries.content: Aswuf is a plant associated in a number of biblical texts with spraying and purification. In Exodus 12, the apron is used to place the blood of the Passover lamb on the two doorposts and the lintel, and in Leviticus and Numbers it appears within the rituals of purification, and in Psalm 51 David uses the image of the apron in the prayer of repentance and purification. In John 19:29, the name appears in the context of the scene of the cross. Therefore, a strong relationship arose between Asuf and the concepts of blood, purification, and the transition from a state of impurity to purity. But careful study requires not assuming that every use of the plant carries one fixed symbol; His function in the Easter ritual is different from his function in the purification rituals, and different from his poetic image in the Psalm. Caution should also be exercised when trying to definitively identify a modern plant that matches an ancient term. The introduction reveals the importance of plants in ancient worship and in the language of purification. It also allows for a study of the relationship between ritual legislation, poetry, and the Bible.

entries.title: Inks
entries.content: Inks are an essential element in the ancient world of writing, and studying them helps understand the physical environment in which written documents and texts originated. Writing was done on different materials such as papyrus, leather, boards or other surfaces depending on the region and time, and ink was part of the document production process. Many references to the book, the scribe, the book, the seal, and the letters appear in the Bible, reflecting the existence of a developed writing culture. In Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and elsewhere, writing appears in prophetic contexts, while the Book of Revelation uses the images of the book, the scroll, the seal, and writing within an apocalyptic structure. Therefore, the study of ink is not only related to a chemical substance, but rather to the history of writing, documents, scribes, and the transmission of texts. Archaeological studies can investigate the remains of ancient inks and their components, but every archaeological discovery must not be turned into direct proof of a specific written version. The introduction helps link biblical studies to the history of manuscripts and writing in the Near East and the Greco-Roman world.

references.author: Emanuel Tov
references.title: Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, Fortress Press, 2012

entries.title: Bronze tools
entries.content: Bronze is an important metal in the ancient world, and appears in the Bible as part of the manufacture of worship tools, weapons, utensils, and some elements of architecture. In the Tabernacle and Temple metals appear in a graded system including gold, silver, copper, and other materials, while 1 Kings 7 gives an extensive description of Hiram of Tyre's work in making metal tools for the Temple. Items associated with the metal include the copper sea, columns, utensils, and parts used in service. These texts reveal an advanced level of craftsmanship and the existence of economic and technical relations between Israel and neighboring regions, especially Tyre. Bronze was also used in tools and weapons, making it part of the study of military and civil technology. But the metal should not be considered sacred in itself; Holiness is linked to the function God gave the tool and the place of its use within worship. Therefore, the introduction helps to understand metallurgy, architecture, economics, and worship in the biblical world.

references.author: Philip J. King and Lawrence E. Stager
references.title: Life in Biblical Israel, Westminster John Knox, 2001

entries.title: Atyab
entries.content: Spices, perfumes, and aromatic oils appear in the Bible in worship, ownership, hospitality, bodily care, and funerary honors. In Exodus 30 the recipe for sacred anointing oil and incense appears, and the text sets clear limits on the use of these sacred formulations. In the Gospels, perfumes appear in the stories of pouring perfume on Jesus and in preparing the body for burial. Therefore, perfume was not just a cosmetic item, but rather a part of religious and social culture. The value of some perfumes was high, so offering them became an expensive act that could carry a meaning of devotion and love. In the story of the woman who poured perfume on Jesus, the precious thing turns into an act of worship that has a meaning that goes beyond its material value. Studying spices also helps to understand ancient trade routes, because many materials came from distant regions. It is important to distinguish between essential oils used in everyday life and formulations designated for use in worship, because texts sometimes set strict boundaries between the sacred and the ordinary.

references.author: Joan E. Taylor
references.title: The Essenes, the Scrolls, and the Dead Sea, Oxford University Press, 2012

entries.title: Noah
entries.content:
Noah is a central character in Genesis 5-9, and the narrative places him at a transition between a world that he describes as corruption and violence and a new world that begins after the waters recede. The text describes him as righteous and perfect in his generations and walking with God, but the conclusion reminds of the fragility of man after salvation. Salvation begins with God's initiative, and faith is demonstrated in obedience before the result is seen. The covenant of Genesis 9 includes all flesh, and links judgment to the preservation of creation and the sanctity of the blood. There are literary connections with the traditions of Atrahasis and Gilgamesh, but the similarity does not prove a correspondence or a single source. The New Testament books read him as an example of faith and warning, while the Mishnah and Talmud discuss the responsibility of the sons of Noah within a later reception history.

Key Evidence: Genesis 5-9; Matthew 24:37-39; Hebrews 11:7.

The modern interpretation reads Noah within a tension between the judgment of violence and the preservation of creation. The astronomy is not just an individual survival story; The covenant in Genesis 9 includes all flesh, and places the sanctity of blood and the responsibility of man before life. Studies compare the Book of Genesis with ancient flood literature while rejecting the equality of the texts. In the Jewish tradition, the responsibility of the sons of Noah expands, while the New Testament reads Noah as an example of faith and warning. Spiritually, survival does not end with getting out of the water, but rather begins with building a just life.

references.author: Gordon J. Wenham, Genesis 1-15, Word Biblical Commentary 1
Nahum M. Sarna, Genesis, JPS Torah Commentary

entries.title: Nineveh
entries.content:
Nineveh is a major Assyrian city that becomes, in Greece, a test for extending mercy to a national enemy, and in Nahum, an image of an empire held accountable by God for violence. Its description in Greece does not provide a simple urban analogy, and excavations do not corroborate every narrative detail. Historically, it is located near modern Mosul and flourished in the Neo-Assyrian era, then fell in 612 BC within the framework known to ancient sources. A distinction should be made between the historical city, the city within the plot and the prophetic symbol. Josephus witnesses a later Jewish reception, there is no alternative to the Hebrew text or Assyrian inscriptions.

Basic evidence: Jonah 1-4; Nahum 1-3; 2 Kings 19:36.

Nineveh in Greece is an enemy city that becomes a test of the extent of God’s mercy, and in Nahum an empire that God holds accountable for violence. This tension prevents the two books from being combined into one simplified message. Historically, Nineveh was a major Assyrian center, but the literary image goes beyond the urban description to the question of the repentance of power. The entry distinguishes between the historical city and the prophetic symbol, and rejects the use of religion to justify hatred of peoples.

references.author: Douglas Stuart, Hosea-Jonah, Word Biblical Commentary 31
T. Desmond Alexander, Obadiah, Jonah and Micah, TOTC

entries.title: Nehemiah
entries.content:
Nehemiah is a leading figure in Persian Judah, and his narrative combines prayer of confession, imperial administration, the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem, and the reform of the post-exilic community. The project begins with fasting and confession before planning, then the narrative balances the division of labor, guarding, and prayer. Chapter Five reveals that construction is not reform if it maintains the exploitation of the poor, while reading Sharia and renewing the covenant makes religious reform collectivistic. Modern scholarship discusses the history of the mission, the Ezra-Nehemiah synthesis, and Nehemiah's memoirs, and mentioning Josephus is not sufficient to close these questions. Marriage and identity restrictions should be read in the context of a small group under foreign rule and not transformed into contemporary ethnic provisions.

Key Evidence: Nehemiah 1-13; Ezra 7-10.

Nehemiah combines prayer, administration, rebuilding the wall, and reforming the economy. The narration of the fifth chapter reveals that religious reform is not complete if the rich exploit the poor, and that the Surah is not salvation in itself. His memoirs overlap with the Ezra-Nehemiah formulation, so the studies present issues of date and authorship with caution. Spiritually, faithful leadership listens to complaints and links worship to public justice.

references.author: H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah, Word Biblical Commentary 16
Joseph Blenkinsopp, Ezra-Nehemiah, Old Testament Library

entries.title: Nicodemus
entries.content:
Nicodemus is a Pharisee and a leader of the Jews, and he appears in the Gospel of John through three scenes, not through a complete biography. The dialogue begins at night with the signs and the teacher, and then Jesus moves the discussion to the birth from above and the work of the Spirit that is not subject to human control. The text does not state that night means fear alone. In John 7 Nicodemus advocates hearing a person before judging him, and in John 19 he participates in Jesus' burial. The arrangement allows for a reading of a narrative development, but it does not justify the invention of unmentioned turning details. The word Pharisee should not be used as an insult; The Jewish context in the first century is essential for interpretation.

Key Evidence: John 1:3-21; 7:45-52; 19:38-42.

John presents Nicodemus through three interviews: a nightly question about signs, a legal defense of hearing, and participation in Jesus' burial. The text does not state that night is fear, nor does it establish a complete tradition about its transformation. His Pharisee background is important for understanding the dialogue within first-century Judaism, not for stigmatizing the Pharisees. Spiritually, faith moves from question to practical witness without erasing complexity.

references.author: Raymond E. Brown, The Gospel According to John I-XII, Anchor Bible 29
Craig S. Keener, The Gospel of John, Hendrickson

entries.title: Nahum
entries.content:
The Book of Nahum is a poetic prophetic text announcing the fall of Nineveh and placing the violence of the empire before the justice of the Lord. He opens by declaring that God is slow to anger and does not acquit the guilty, and then uses the language of war, personification, and sarcasm to chart the collapse of the city. Many researchers believe that the final context is closer to the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC, although there is still debate about the date of the passages and the composition of the book. Comparison with Jonah does not eliminate either of them: Jonah highlights the possibility of repentance, and Nahum highlights the reckoning of injustice. The book does not give a contemporary congregation a mandate to carry out God's judgment or justify racial hatred.

Key Evidence: Nahum 1-3; Jonah 3-4.

Nahum is a poetic book that announces the fall of Nineveh, and combines God's justice with the hope of the oppressed. It is not right to truncate the language of war to justify contemporary violence. It is a speech of judgment for a specific empire. The study compares Nahum and Jonah: the mercy of repentance in one and the reckoning of violence in the other. The proposed date for the book remains close to the fall of Nineveh, although there is critical debate about its composition.

references.author: O. Palmer Robertson, The Books of Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah, NICOT
Duane L. Christensen, Nahum, Anchor Bible 24F
Adele Berlin, Poetics and Interpretation of Biblical Narrative

entries.title: Naboth
entries.content:
Naboth the Jezreelite is an example of the conflict between the right to property and the authority of the king. His account reveals that the usurpation of land was not a private dispute, but an assault on the covenant structure that made land a gift and a liability rather than an absolute commodity. The use of perjury and judicial power demonstrates how the institution can be used to produce injustice that appears lawful. Historically, the story reflects the reality of kingship and power in the Northern Kingdom, while Elijah interprets the event as a religious and moral crime. It is not correct to turn the novel into a direct political slogan. Rather, it is studied as part of the criticism of the king’s prophecy when he places desire above covenant and justice.

Basic evidence: 1 Kings 21; 2 Kings 9:26.

Naboth the Jezreelite refuses to sell the inheritance of his fathers, revealing the conflict between ownership of land as a covenantal gift and the king’s desire for expansion. The usurpation of the field is not carried out by force alone, but rather through false testimony and a judicial institution, which exposes the corruption of the regime. Elijah's confrontation with Ahab links prophecy to economic justice. Spiritually, legitimacy is not measured by the ruler's ability to make injustice legal.

references.author: Walter Brueggemann, First and Second Kings, Smyth & Helwys
J. Maxwell Miller and John H. Hayes, A History of Ancient Israel and Judah, Westminster John Knox

entries.title: Nabal
entries.content:
Nabal is a complex character in David's narrative; His name, which indicates stupidity, is consistent with his behavior, but the story does not justify reducing the character to an individual insult. His refusal to receive hospitality and acknowledge David's status puts the community in danger of revenge, so Abigail intervenes to prevent David from shedding blood. The text highlights the difference between armed force and the wisdom that preserves moral legitimacy. Nabal's death occurs within the framework of God's judgment, not as a call for personal revenge. Studying pastoral economics and hospitality is useful in understanding the scale of demand and its context, while it is necessary not to project personality descriptions onto contemporary groups.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 25.

Nabal in the story of David and Abigail embodies the danger of wealth without generosity and armed protection without control. His refusal of hospitality threatens to turn an economic dispute into a massacre, so Abigail stops David from seeking revenge. His death does not provide a license for revenge, but rather places David with the responsibility of not becoming a blood king. Spiritually, wisdom preserves life when authority fails to control anger.

references.author: David G. Firth, 1 & 2 Samuel, Apollos Old Testament Commentary
Robert Alter, The David Story, W. W. Norton

entries.title: Nadab
entries.content:
Nadab, the son of Aaron, appears in two different contexts that must be distinguished: the priest who died with Abihu after offering strange fire, and the king of Israel, the son of Jeroboam. In Leviticus 10, the text does not explain the nature of the violation in detail, so one should avoid asserting details that are not mentioned. The novel places the sanctity of worship and the responsibility of the priest before a human initiative that goes beyond divine command. As for the king, it represents the continuation of the crisis in the house of Jeroboam and the worship of the two calves. The comparison reveals that a single name is not enough to define a character, and that lineage and literary context are necessary.

Key Evidence: Exodus 6:23; Leviticus 10:1-7; 1 Kings 14:20.

Nadab the priest appears in Leviticus 10, and appears as king in 1 Kings 14, and one name does not mean one person. The text does not explain the nature of the strange fire in detail, so the study refuses to confirm what the source did not mention. King Nadab enters into a crisis in the house of Jeroboam and the worship of the two calves. The introduction teaches the necessity of distinguishing between lineage and context before constructing doctrine.

references.author: Jacob Milgrom, Leviticus 1-16, Anchor Bible 3, Doubleday
Baruch Halpern, The First Historians, Pennsylvania State University Press

entries.title: Nathan
entries.content:
Nathan the Prophet plays multiple roles in the history of David: he confronts the king with the story of the lamb, conveys the promise of the Davidic house, and intervenes in the transfer of power to Solomon. These roles reveal that the prophet's job is neither to automatically justify nor oppose the king, but to place his authority under the word of God. In 2 Samuel 7 the promise interacts with the correction of an earlier revelation, teaching the researcher to be wary of reading prophecy as a rigid political program. In 2 Samuel 12, the narrative rhetoric turns into a moral trial for the king. As for the news of the transfer of the throne, it highlights the role of advice and legitimacy.

Key Evidence: 2 Samuel 7; 12; 1 Kings 1.

Nathan the Prophet announces the promise of the Davidic house and then confronts David with his sin, revealing that prophecy is neither a device of justification for the king nor a mechanical opposition to him. The story of the pregnancy transfers the crime from the language of authority to the conscience of the judge, and then Nathan announces its results without canceling the promise. Its events take place in Jerusalem and the palace, and its contemporaries are David, Bathsheba, and Solomon. Spiritually, the True Word protects the covenant from the worship of the ruler.

references.author: A. A. Anderson, 2 Samuel, Word Biblical Commentary 11
Walter Brueggemann, First and Second Samuel, Westminster John Knox

entries.title: Nahash
entries.content:
Nahash is a name associated with the kings of Ammon in various narratives, and therefore all references should not be combined into one character without clues. In 1 Samuel 11 the threat of Jabesh-gilead leads to the emergence of Saul as a saving leader, while the narratives of 2 Samuel 10 and Chronicles display strained relations between Ammon and the House of David. These texts help in the study of diplomacy, shame, and war in the Near East, but they do not give a comprehensive account of Ammonite history. The use of the name remains an area for comparison between historical texts, not for constructing a connected biography without evidence.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 11; 2 Samuel 10; 1 News 19.

Nahash is a name associated with the kings of Ammon in various accounts, and the characters should not be combined without clues. The threat of Jabesh-gilead places Saul with the responsibility of protecting the community, while the accounts of David and Ammon reveal the complexity of diplomacy, shame, and war. The political background in Transjordan helps understand the events, but it does not confirm every detail. Spiritually, reading war does not turn into national hatred.

references.author: K. Lawson Younger Jr., Ancient Conquest Accounts, Sheffield Academic Press
Daniel C. Snell, The Ancient Near East, Blackwell

entries.title: Nahor
entries.content:
Nahor appears in Terah's genealogy and in Abraham's family background, and the city of Nahor is also linked to northern Mesopotamia in some texts. The literary function of the name is to link Abraham's calling to a family and geographical network, not to present a broad independent biography. Genealogies reveal memory, identity, alliance, and marriage, and a distinction must be made between a person's name and the name of the city or group to which he is attributed. Phonetic similarity is not enough to prove an archaeological identity, so texts are compared with geographical data without converting probability into certainty.

Key Evidence: Genesis 11:22-32; 22:20-24; 24:10.

references.author: Nahum M. Sarna, Genesis, JPS Torah Commentary
Gordon J. Wenham, Genesis 1-15, Word Biblical Commentary 1

entries.title: Nahshon
entries.content:
Nahshon the son of Amminadab, the leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness, and his lineage is linked to Ruth and to the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew. The Book of Numbers places it within the group organization and tribal leadership, while Ruth and Matthew use it to construct the memory of royal and messianic lineage. The text does not provide many personal details, so the gaps should not be filled in by later tales without marking them as imitations. Its theological importance comes from the way the name is transformed into a knot linking the Exodus, the kingdom, and the messianic hope.

Key Evidence: Exodus 6:23; Numbers 1:7; 2:3; Ruth 4:20; Matthew 1:4.

references.author: Jacob Milgrom, Numbers, JPS Torah Commentary
R. T. France, The Gospel of Matthew, NICNT

entries.title: Noman
entries.content:
Naaman, an Aramaic leader. The text narrates his recovery from leprosy after obeying Elisha’s order to wash in the Jordan. The story deliberately subverts expectations of power: a leader is healed neither by military distinction nor by a ritual of his choosing, but by a prophetic word and a humble act. The unknown girl, Elisha, and Gehazi reveal the multiple centers of testimony and responsibility. The story also draws a line between God's gift and greed for money, as the narrative condemns Gehazi's attempt to turn grace into gain. Historically, the story reflects the relations of Israel and Aram, and should not be used to provide a comprehensive medical explanation for ancient leprosy.

Basic evidence: 2 Kings 5.

references.author: Iain Provan, 1 and 2 Kings, New International Biblical Commentary
Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor, II Kings, Anchor Bible 11

entries.title: Nebuchadnezzar
entries.content:
Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon appears in the Bible as an imperial tool in the fall of Jerusalem, and then as a king learning the limits of power before God's sovereignty in the Book of Daniel. A distinction must be made between the historical Nebuchadnezzar, known from Babylonian records and his urban projects, and the literary and theological construction in Daniel. Calling him a servant of divine justice does not mean exonerating his empire from violence; The prophetic texts hold Babylon accountable later. Later Jewish literature discusses the king's pride and downfall in a cautionary vein, while Christian interpretations examine Daniel's statues and dreams in the context of the Kingdom of God. It is not correct to equate every translation of a name with one form when searching.

Key Evidence: 2 Kings 24-25; Daniel 1-4; Jeremiah 25; 52.

references.author: John F. Goldingay, Daniel, Word Biblical Commentary 30
Carol A. Newsom, Daniel, Old Testament Library

entries.title: Naphtali
entries.content:
Naphtali, one of Jacob's sons, appears in the texts as a tribe with a land and a place within the history of Israel. The image of the tribe differs between the Birkat of Jacob and the Birkat of Moses and the geographical division in Joshua, which makes it possible to study the development of tribal memory. The Naftali region is connected to the Upper Galilee and to the northern roads, and therefore gained political and military importance. Matthew mentions Galilee and Naphtali in a messianic reading of Jesus' ministry, but this later usage does not negate the original geographical meaning. A distinction should be made between poetic genealogies and administrative data and Biblical rereading.

Key Evidence: Genesis 30:8; 49:21; Numbers 1:43; Joshua 19.

references.author: Richard S. Hess, Joshua, Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries
Nahum M. Sarna, Genesis, JPS Torah Commentary

entries.title: Nathanael
entries.category: Disciples and the Gospel of John
entries.content:
Nathaniel is a disciple presented in the Gospel of John in a scene of invitation based on testimony, dialogue, and the transition from doubt to confession. John does not explicitly mention this title of the Twelve in the first chapter, and the relationship between Nathanael and Bartholomew remains an interpretive tradition that is not stated in the text. The story reveals that knowledge of Christ grows through Philip's invitation, Nathanael's question, Jesus' hidden knowledge, and then the promise of seeing something greater. Accurate interpretation depends on the Johannine narrative and not on incorporating all later traditions indiscriminately.

Key Evidence: John 1:45-51; 21:2.

references.author: Raymond E. Brown, The Gospel According to John I-XII, Anchor Bible 29
Craig S. Keener, The Gospel of John, Hendrickson

entries.title: Nethania
entries.category: Priests and the return of captivity
entries.content:
Nethaniah is a name that appears in the lists of the post-exilic community, and the reading varies according to the identification of the person and the textual context. The priestly and family lists reveal that the reorganization of worship after the exile relied on memory, lineage, and function, not just abstract theological discourse. The brevity of the reference does not allow for the construction of an extensive biography, so this study provides a methodological introduction to reading names in lists: comparing texts, examining differences in transmission, and not equating a repeated name with a single person. Its importance lies in the history of the religious institution and the legitimacy of service after the return.

Key Evidence: Ezra 10:22; Nehemiah 12:21.

references.author: H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah, Word Biblical Commentary 16
Joseph Blenkinsopp, Ezra-Nehemiah, Old Testament Library

entries.title: Nebuzaradan
entries.content:
Nebuzaradan, the chief of police or commander of the Babylonian guard in the accounts of the fall of Jerusalem, appears as an implementer of the policy of burning and transportation, and then an instrument in Jeremiah's release. The texts combine the imperial decision with the theological consequence of the captivity, so as not to explain the catastrophe solely militarily. Comparison of 2 Kings and Jeremiah allows for a study of difference in wording and order, while the Babylonian records help place the event within Babylonian history without proving every biblical detail. The spelling of the name must be corrected when comparing translations.

Key Evidence: 2 Kings 8:25-20; Jeremiah 39:9-14; 52:12-27.

references.author: Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor, II Kings, Anchor Bible 11

entries.title: Naomi
entries.content:
Naomi is the center of the narrative in the Book of Ruth; Her presence begins with the loss of her husband and two sons, then she returns to Bethlehem and interprets her life through bitterness. The book does not make her grief a simple lack of faith, but rather gives her a voice to name the pain, and then displays the transformation of hope through the faithfulness of Ruth and Boaz and childbirth. Naomi is associated with the reintegration of the widow, family, and land within the structure of kinship and redemption, but the term “redeemer” requires a social and legal reading, not a direct Christian projection. The genealogies conclude the story by linking the verse to the memory of David, so bitterness becomes part of the history of hope without erasing the previous pain.

Key Evidence: Ruth 1-4.

references.author: Robert L. Hubbard Jr., The Book of Ruth, NICOT
Adele Berlin, Ruth, JPS Bible Commentary

entries.title: Ntinim
entries.content:
The Netinim are a service group associated with the Temple in the lists of return from captivity. The name denotes people dedicated or given to service, but the origin of the group and the development of its social status are discussed in the study. They should not be reduced to one class throughout all ages; The lists and later texts reflect different stages of the organization of worship. Study of the name helps understand non-priestly work, communal identity, and how the post-exilic community maintained temple continuity. A distinction must be made between textual description and historical inference about their origin.

Key Evidence: Ezra 2:43-58; 8:20; Nehemiah 3:26.

references.author: Joseph Blenkinsopp, Ezra-Nehemiah, Old Testament Library

entries.title: Harbinger
entries.content:
A Nazirite is a person or child who is separated by a special vow, and the number 6 provides provisions for abstaining from alcohol, cutting hair, and avoiding the impurity of the dead. The vow does not mean that a person possesses personal holiness, but rather places his life under a temporary or extended system of worship. The story of Samson reveals a difference between the description of the vow and its narrative application, while Hannah's request links Samuel to a personal vow. The Mishnah discusses the provisions of vows in מסכת נזיר, and is useful in the study of halakhic reception, but it is not a direct explanation of the text of Numbers. A distinction must be made between the Christian monk and the Christian monk and the popular uses of the word.

Key Evidence: Numbers 6:1-21; Judges 13:5; 1 Samuel 1:11.

references.author: Jacob Milgrom, Numbers, JPS Torah Commentary

entries.title: Nazareth
entries.content:
Nazareth is the village of Galilee associated with Jesus' childhood and early ministry, and Nathaniel's contempt for her appears in John as part of the expectations of the place and the Messiah. Matthew's statement does not require that there be a single direct quotation with the name Nazareth; It may combine prophetic traditions about Christ being a despiser or a warner, which is a controversial issue. Historical excavations and geographical clues help to map out a small first-century Jewish village, but they do not prove every biblical detail. A distinction must be made between historical Nazareth and the textual title Nazareth, while keeping the form “Nazareth” as a common name in research.

Key Evidence: Matthew 2:23; Mark 1:9; Luke 1:26; John 1:46.

references.author: Craig S. Keener, The Gospel of Matthew, Eerdmans
James D. G. Dunn, Jesus Remembered, Eerdmans

entries.title: Warner of God
entries.content:
Samson's description as a Nazirite to God from the womb links the personal calling with a divine intent to save Israel from the Philistines. But the narrative creates a paradox between the external sign of the vow and Samson's disturbed behavior, and does not allow long hair alone to be transformed into evidence of fidelity. The story requires consideration of the vow in verse 6, the tension between calling and moral choice, and the way strength and weakness are presented in the book of Judges. Later Jewish tradition expands the discussion of harbinger rulings, but they should be labeled as a later interpretation.

Key Evidence: Judges 13:5-7; 16:17.

references.author: Barry G. Webb, The Book of Judges, NICOT

entries.title: Valerian
entries.content:
Valerian is a precious perfume that appears in Hebrew poetry and accounts of the anointing of Jesus. The texts allow for the study of economics, hospitality, the body, dignity, and worship, but not every poetic mention may be equated with a single commercial prescription. In the Gospels, spending perfume turns into a sign of love and devotion, and the details of the narratives differ in a way that deserves comparative reading, not mechanical integration. Ancient sources help understand the value of perfumes and trade routes, while the exact identity of the plant remains a subject of linguistic and historical research.

Key Evidence: Song of Songs 1:12; 4:13-14; Mark 3:14; John 12:3.

references.author: Marvin H. Pope, Song of Songs, Anchor Bible 7C
Craig S. Keener, The Gospel of John, Hendrickson

entries.title: Harbinger/crown
entries.content:
The Hebrew root associated with consecration or crown opens a field for studying the relationship between holiness and power. The Nizar appears in the turban of the high priest, and related words appear in people’s vows or consecration. Not every linguistic usage should be combined into a single meaning; The context determines whether what is meant is a sign of royalty, priesthood, or sacred separation. Comparing the priesthood texts and the prophets is helpful in understanding how physical symbols are used to construct a perception of the authority under God's holiness.

Key Evidence: Exodus 29:6; Leviticus 8:9; Zechariah 6:11-14.

references.author: Mark J. Boda, The Book of Zechariah, NICOT

entries.title: Mosquitoes
entries.content:
Law is a common translation of the Torah or Sharia, but its meaning changes depending on the context and does not always equal an abstract list of laws. In the Psalms he shows teaching, joy, and contemplation, while Paul discusses his relationship to sin, promise, and faith within first-century polemics.
