Doctrine should not be built on a superficial comparison between law and grace, but on reading each message and its Jewish context. The Mishnah and Talmud are useful for studying the history of Torah interpretation and application, but they do not automatically explain all Pauline usage. Translating the term into law may hide some of its educational and covenantal dimensions.

Key Evidence: Psalm 2:1; 19:7; Romans 2:12; Galatians 3.

references.author: E. P. Sanders, Paul and Palestinian Judaism, Fortress Press

entries.title: Breath
entries.content:
The soul in the Bible is not always a separate entity in the modern philosophical sense; It may refer to life, person, desire, or living being, depending on the Hebrew and Greek context. Genesis 2:7 describes man as a living soul after the breath of life, and does not simply say that he has a soul within a body. In Leviticus, the soul is associated with blood and life, while the uses of the word vary in the Psalms and the Gospels. Linguistic analysis should be separated from later dogmatic theology, drawing on but not equating Jewish and Hellenistic literature.

Key Evidence: Genesis 2:7; Leviticus 17:11; Psalm 42; Matthew 10:28.

references.author: Joel B. Green, Body, Soul, and Human Life, Baker Academic
Nahum M. Sarna, Genesis, JPS Torah Commentary

entries.title: Blessing
entries.content:
Grace in the Bible is not a single abstract idea; It is an acceptance or favor in the context of a relationship, a covenantal mercy, and a saving gift. Genesis 6:8 places Noah's blessing within the story of judgment, while Exodus 33 links grace to God's presence and Moses' request. In the New Testament letters, grace appears in justification, calling, and new life. Grace should not be separated from truth and holiness or reduced to moral indulgence. A distinction must also be made between the common Arabic uses of חן, חסד, and between Paul's theological formulation and the Old Testament contexts.

Key Evidence: Genesis 6:8; Exodus 33:12-17; Romans 3:24; Ephesians 2:8.

references.author: John M. G. Barclay, Paul and the Gift, Eerdmans
Nahum M. Sarna, Genesis, JPS Torah Commentary

entries.title: Fire
entries.content:
Fire is a sign with multiple connotations: a divine presence in the bush, a covenantal passage in Genesis 15, the acceptance of a sacrifice, and it may be an instrument of judgment or purification. Not every fire can be interpreted as a single symbol; The context determines whether it is an appearance, a rule, a ritual, or a poetic image. Leviticus associates fire with the holiness of worship, while the New Testament reuses images of fire in spirit and judgment. Comparisons with Near Eastern rituals are historically useful, but they do not negate the specificity of biblical theology.

Key Evidence: Genesis 15:17; Exodus 3:2; Leviticus 9:24; Acts 2:3.

references.author: Richard B. Hays, Reading Backwards, Baylor University Press

entries.title: Light
entries.content:
Light is one of the central images in the Bible. It begins with the separation of light from darkness in creation, and then moves to protection, guidance, proclamation, and salvation. This does not mean that all uses of light are identical; The psalm uses the language of trust, Isaiah places the image in historical hope, and John links it to life and the word. The study requires comparing poetry with narrative and the Bible, and not turning the symbol into physical proof. The Jewish background of Creation, the Temple, and the Lights also helps to understand the transition of the image to Christian theology.

Key Evidence: Genesis 3:1-5; Psalm 27:1; Isaiah 9:2; John 1:4-9.

references.author: Gordon J. Wenham, Genesis 1-15, Word Biblical Commentary 1
Marianne Meye Thompson, John, New Testament Library

entries.title: River
entries.content:
Rivers in the Bible are life resources, borders, trade routes, and images of abundant blessing or danger. The River of Eden in Genesis 2 links geography with creation, the Nile in the story of Moses enters into the structure of empire, death, and salvation, and the River of Life in Revelation 22 restores the image of Paradise within the horizon of the new creation. A single geographical identity should not be imposed on each symbolic river, nor should maps become a substitute for literary analysis. The study of ancient rivers is useful in understanding agriculture, power, and urbanization.

Key Evidence: Genesis 2:10-14; Exodus 2:3; Psalm 46:4; Revelation 22:1.

references.author: Richard Bauckham, The Theology of the Book of Revelation, Cambridge University Press

entries.title: Offspring
entries.content:
Offspring is a central concept in the Genesis promise, and depending on the context, it refers to offspring, a group, or the continuation of a covenant. It should not be limited to a biological meaning, nor should a Pauline reading be imposed on every Genesis text before understanding its context. The promises develop from Abraham's lineage to Israel and the king, and then Galatians 3 rereads the singular into a Christian debate about Christ. The study requires attention to the plural and singular in Hebrew and Greek and to the difference between historical meaning and legal interpretation. Jewish literature is useful in studying lineage and identity, with the biblical text remaining the primary reference.

Key Evidence: Genesis 3:15; 12:7; 15:5; Galatians 3:16.

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic
Nahum M. Sarna, Genesis, JPS Torah Commentary

entries.title: Impurity
entries.content:
Impurity in the Torah is a ritual and social classification that does not automatically equal moral sin. Leviticus distinguishes between impurity and purity and links them to the possibility of approaching the sacred, while the Gospels and Acts re-negotiate the boundaries of food, the body, and community in new contexts. It is not correct to describe the ritual system as mere hygiene, nor to read Mark as a comprehensive abolition of every Jewish tradition without studying the text. The Mishnah discusses the chapters on purity in great detail, and is useful for reception history rather than as a sole explanation of Leviticus.

Key Evidence: Leviticus 11-15; Mark 1:7-23; Acts 10.

entries.title: Purity
entries.content:
Purity may refer to the heart, behavior, or ritual state, and it is not correct to combine them into one definition. Psalm 24 links the ascent to the mountain of the Lord with purity of hands and heart, while Psalm 51 asks for a clean heart after sin. In the Beatitudes, purity appears within the vision of God, not as a claim to self-perfection. The comparison between Wisdom, the Psalms and the Gospels allows us to follow the transition of the concept from ritual to morality and the interior without eliminating ritual. Contextual differences should be documented rather than providing a general, non-specific theology.

Key Evidence: Psalm 24:4; 51:10; Proverbs 20:9; Matthew 5:8.

references.author: Willem A. VanGemeren, Psalms, Expositor's Bible Commentary

entries.title: Vow
entries.content:
A vow is a voluntary commitment pronounced before God, and the texts present its power and danger. Numbers 30 shows the impact of the vow within the family and society, while the story of Jephthah reveals the tragedy of a hasty promise and controversial interpretations of what happened to his daughter. The story should not be used as a direct legislative basis, but rather its relationship to narrative criticism and the sanctity of speech should be studied. The Mishnah and Talmud discuss the chapters on vows in detail, and help to understand the history of Jewish application while remaining differences between later law and the biblical text.

Key Evidence: Genesis 28:20-22; Number 30; Judges 11:30-40.

references.author: Jacob Milgrom, Numbers, JPS Torah Commentary

entries.title: Noob
entries.content:
Nob is the city of the priests, which is linked to Ahimelech feeding David and killing the priests of the Lord on the orders of Saul. The story reveals a tension between the protection of life and ritual, and the madness and violence of power, and is cited by Jesus in the discussion of the Sabbath in the Gospels. Readings differ about the limits of David's action and the priest's responsibility, and therefore the disagreement must be presented, not obscured. Historically, the location of Nob cannot be determined with complete certainty, but the account posits a priestly network near Jerusalem. The rabbinic literature re-discusses the Holy Bread and David, a material of reception rather than a substitute for narrative.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 21-22.

entries.title: Weep
entries.content:
Nobah occurs in short geographical and military references, and may refer to a person or place depending on the context. The shortness of the material requires caution against creating a complete biography based on the similarity of the name. In Numbers 21 it is linked to the control of the Transjordan region, while Judges 8 mentions Nobah in the context of Gideon's campaign. These references reveal the difficulty of reading place names in texts with different layers and traditions, and require comparison of manuscripts, translations and historical maps. Nobah should not be equated with a modern city without evidence.

Basic evidence: Numbers 21:30; Judges 8:11.

references.author: Jacob Milgrom, Numbers, JPS Torah Commentary
Richard S. Hess, Judges, Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries

entries.title: Nimrim
entries.content:
Nimrim, the place of Moab, appears in prophecies of judgment on Moab, and his image is associated with dry waters and desolation. The text does not provide coordinates that allow for a definitive identification, so a distinction must be made between geographical suggestions and textual certainty. Water functions here on two levels: a geographical resource and a carrier of the image of collapse. The study of Moab and its connections with Israel helps in understanding the political background of the prophecies, while literary interpretation remains necessary so that the poem does not turn into a topographical report.

Key Evidence: Isaiah 15:6; Jeremiah 48:34.

references.author: J. A. Thompson, The Book of Jeremiah, NICOT
Christopher B. Hays, Hidden Riches, Westminster John Knox

entries.title: Nimrod
entries.content:
Nimrod in the Table of Nations is a mighty man, a hunter, and the founder of kingdoms, and the narrative links power, civilization, and empire. The text does not describe all aspects of his personality, so his image in later Jewish and Christian traditions is more expansive than the textual material. Some researchers link his name to the memories of Mesopotamian kings, but etymological suggestions alone do not amount to historical proof. The story reveals how Genesis organizes people's memory and power after the Flood, without necessarily making every city evil.

Key Evidence: Genesis 8:10-12; 1 Chronicles 1:10.

references.author: Nahum M. Sarna, Genesis, JPS Torah Commentary
Gordon J. Wenham, Genesis 1-15, Word Biblical Commentary 1

entries.title: We walk
entries.content:
Namshi, Yahoo's grandfather, and his lineage appears in the context of Yahoo's survey and his role in the Northern Kingdom's coup. The text does not present an independent Namshi character with actions, but rather the name functions as a marker of lineage and narrative legitimacy. Therefore, we should not fabricate information about his life, but rather study the function of genealogy in royal history and how it links political violence to the word of the Prophet. Jehu's reversal illustrates the complexity of implementing judgment; The announced reform may produce a new violent regime, and this is an issue that requires critical reading and not mechanical glorification.

Key Evidence: 1 Kings 19:16; 2 Kings 2:9-20.

references.author: Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor, II Kings, Anchor Bible 11
Walter Brueggemann, First and Second Kings

entries.title: Abner
entries.content:
Abner, son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, then became a pivotal factor in the transfer of power to David. His story reveals that royal legitimacy in Samuel is not understood by weapons alone; Military force can prolong the conflict, but it does not create a divine promise. His move from supporting Ish-bosheth to negotiating with David reveals the intersection of political conviction, interest, and personal dignity. The text ends with his killing at the hands of Joab, thus drawing a tragic line between the project of reconciliation and the logic of revenge. The spiritual reading does not exonerate Abner or condemn his every move, but rather examines the fragility of authority when it is separated from the control of anger and justice.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 14:50-52; 2 Samuel 2-3.

entries.title: Emmanuel
entries.content:
Immanuel is a Hebrew expression meaning that God is with us, and it comes in Isaiah within a real political crisis concerning Ahaz and the threat to Aram and Israel. It is not right to extract the name from its historical context and immediately turn it into a doctrinal definition without going through its function in the message of Isaiah. In Matthew, the text is reused within the interpretation of the birth of Jesus, and the relationship between the historical meaning and the biblical rereading emerges. The issue is not abolishing the first level, but rather understanding how the Christian community sees the completion of the pattern of divine presence in Christ. Therefore, the introduction combines translation, prophetic context, and messianic reading.

Key Evidence: Isaiah 7:14; 8:8-10; Matthew 1:22-23.

references.author: John N. Oswalt, The Book of Isaiah 1-39, NICOT
R. T. France, The Gospel of Matthew, NICNT

entries.title: Othniel
entries.content:
Othniel is the first judge mentioned in the Book of Judges after the cycle of the fall, the cry, and salvation. The narrative links the Spirit of the Lord with the leader's ability to save Israel, but it does not present a military model separate from the critique of Baalim and Astarte worship. The importance of character is literary; It sets the pattern in which the judges' stories will be repeated with different results. The phrase “The Spirit of the Lord” must not be turned into a permanent justification for violence, but rather read within the story of the liberation of an oppressed group. The marriage in Aksah between Othniel and Caleb also links military leadership to the structure of the land and family.

Key Evidence: Joshua 15:17; Judges 3:7-11.

references.author: Barry G. Webb, The Book of Judges, NICOT
Yairah Amit, The Book of Judges, Sheffield Academic Press

entries.title: Ajloun
entries.content:
Eglon is the name of the king of Moab and the name of a Canaanite city in two different places, and therefore it is not permissible to combine the person with the place. In Judges 3, the king represents a political force that imposes tribute on Israel, and then the story of Ehud comes as a narrative of resistance to occupation, not a general recipe for assassination. As for Ajloun, the city is included in the geography of the alliance of the kings of the south. The comparison reveals the impact of the name on two problems: indexing Arabic, and reading violence within historical and theological texts. The event should be viewed in its ancient context while refusing to dismiss it as a contemporary license for political murder.

Key Evidence: Joshua 3:10-27; Judges 3:12-30.

references.author: Richard S. Hess, Judges, Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries
Daniel I. Block, Judges, Ruth, New American Commentary

entries.title: Ekron
entries.content:
Ekron is one of the cities of the Philistines and appears in the stories of the Ark of the Covenant and in the context of the worship of Beelzebub. The book not only presents the city as a neutral background, but also places its gods and institutions before the sovereignty of God. However, one should avoid reducing the Palestinians to a single religious image, as archaeological and epigraphic sources reveal diverse cities and political networks. Ekron is useful for studying coastal borders, economics, warfare, and the exchange of religious symbols. Determining the location and archaeological layers remains an area for comparison, not for forcing the text into definitive matches.

Key Evidence: Joshua 13:3; 1 Samuel 5-6; 2 Kings 1:2-3.

references.author: Trude Dothan and Seymour Gitin, Ekron of the Philistines, Israel Exploration Society
K. Lawson Younger Jr., The Old Testament in Its World

entries.title: Amalek
entries.content:
Amalek appears in biblical memory as an enemy attacking the weak and backward people of the Exodus group, and then his presence develops in the narratives of Saul and David. The difficulty of the entry is moral and theological: it is not permissible to transfer ancient war texts into hatred of a contemporary group or justification for genocide. Amalek as an enemy in a specific narrative must be distinguished from his later symbolic use in Jewish literature. Memory, trauma, and divine justice should also be studied while recognizing the tension of the texts. Christian reading is required to maintain historical distance and moral criticism rather than simplification.

Key Evidence: Exodus 8:17-16; Deuteronomy 25:17-19; 1 Samuel 15.

references.author: Jacob Milgrom, Numbers, JPS Torah Commentary

entries.title: Amnon
entries.content:
The story of Amnon and Tamar is one of the most harsh texts in the book in exposing the abuse of power and desire. The narrative begins with a distorted desire, which then turns into hatred after the attack, while David fails to deal with the crime in a way that maintains justice. The text should not be read as a romantic story or as a justification for family silence; It exposes the impact of violence on the victim, the family and the state. Absalom's revenge does not provide a sound solution, but rather expands the circle of blood. Spiritually, the entry reveals that royal inheritance and religious privilege do not confer moral immunity.

Key Evidence: 2 Samuel 13.

entries.title: Anathoth
entries.content:
Anathoth is a priestly city in the land of Benjamin and the homeland of Jeremiah, and therefore the history of the priesthood and the history of prophecy meet in it. Abiathar's exile to it in 1 Kings reflects a struggle for priestly authority, while Jeremiah makes it a starting point for a prophet opposing both his city and authority. Knowing the site is not enough to understand the entrance; Place acts as a social memory, an identity, and a source of tension. The plot of the men of Anathoth reveals that the prophet's word may collide with his closest group. Anathoth's study balances the geography and political and social layers of the text.

Key Evidence: Joshua 21:18; 1 Kings 2:26; Jeremiah 1:1; 11:21-23.

entries.title: Crooked
entries.content:
Og, king of Bashan, appears in Israelite memory as a great opponent who was defeated before entering the land. Deuteronomy mentions his great bed, an image that serves a memorial function and should not automatically be transformed into an accurate archaeological measurement of his body. The novel focuses on the fact that fear of the opponent's power does not undermine God's promise, but it does not cancel out the reality of war and its consequences on peoples. The presence of Og in the Psalms shows how worship preserves the memory of salvation and victory. Responsible reading distinguishes between historiography, literary exaggeration, and commemorative theology.

Key Evidence: Numbers 21:33-35; Deuteronomy 3:1-11; Psalm 135:11.

references.author: Jacob Milgrom, Numbers, JPS Torah Commentary

entries.title: Obadiah
entries.content:
Obadiah is the name of a minor prophet and traveler, and the name of a palace employee in the story of Elijah, and the text does not prove that they are the same person. The Book of Obadiah focuses on the judgment of Edom due to its position on the fall of Jerusalem, linking historical kinship with moral responsibility. The prophecy reveals that not participating directly in the crime does not excuse complicity, gloating, and exploiting a brother’s weakness. As for Ahab's employee, he presents a different picture of a God-fearing man inside a hostile royal palace. The distinction between the two names is an example of the necessity of adjusting the context before building a biography.

Basic evidence: The Book of Obadiah; 1 Kings 3:18-16.

references.author: Paul R. Raabe, Obadiah, Anchor Bible 24D
Ehud Ben Zvi, A Historical-Critical Study of the Book of Obadiah, de Gruyter

entries.title: Ofer
entries.content:
Ofer is a place known in texts for its abundance of gold, but its geographical location has not been definitively decided. Its association with Solomon's ships places it within the economy of maritime trade and Red Sea networks, while the poetic references make it a symbol of rare wealth. It is not possible to turn every geographical proposition into reality, nor to use gold to sanctify commercial expansion. Ofer's study reveals the tension between the wisdom of the kingdom and the dangers of wealth accumulation. It is a window into the ancient economy and the book’s criticism of reliance on metal and kingship instead of God.

Key Evidence: 1 Kings 9:26-28; 10:11; Job 22:24.

references.author: K. A. Kitchen, On the Reliability of the Old Testament, Eerdmans

entries.title: Esau
entries.content:
Esau is Jacob's brother and the origin of the Israeli memory of Edom. Therefore, the entry combines a family story with the history of a people. Genesis presents him as a hunter and a carnal man, but these traits do not justify hatred of a race or a people. The conflict of blessing and birth reveals the effect of preference and deception within the family, and then the reconciliation of Jacob and Esau opens the door to a reading that goes beyond hostility. Malachi uses language of election and judgment within a later argument, which should not be separated from its prophetic context. Jewish and Christian scholarship is required not to turn Esau into a moral caricature.

Key Evidence: Genesis 19:25-36; 27; 32-36; Malachi 2:1-5.

references.author: Nahum M. Sarna, Genesis, JPS Torah Commentary
Gordon J. Wenham, Genesis 16-50, Word Biblical Commentary 2

entries.title: Elijah
entries.content:
Elijah, the prophet of the covenant, confronts the crisis of Baal worship, but his story is not limited to the victory of Mount Carmel. After the confrontation, the Prophet collapses and asks for death, so God meets him with food and rest, and then with a calm voice, he returns him to the mission. The story reveals that spiritual zeal does not eliminate the fragility of the servant, and that God's presence is not reduced to loud phenomena. Elijah confronts Ahab and Jezebel regarding Naboth's case, linking prophecy to justice and kingship. He appears in the New Testament with Moses in the transfiguration, making the reception of the character part of the study of messianism and hope.

Basic evidence: 1 Kings 17-19; 21; 2 Kings 1-2.

references.author: Walter Brueggemann, First and Second Kings, Smyth & Helwys
Iain Provan, 1 and 2 Kings, New International Biblical Commentary

entries.title: Elisha
entries.content:
Elisha succeeds Elijah and appears in stories of miracles affecting widows, strangers, soldiers, and kings. The abundance of miracles does not make the book a book of wonders separated from reality. It reveals the economy of weakness, the danger of hunger, and the community’s need for the Word of God. Naaman's healing places an Aramean leader within grace that transcends boundaries, while the story of Gehazi exposes the danger of turning grace into gain. Elisha's tone is different from Elijah's, but both place the king under the word of the Lord. Spiritual reading balances confidence in the miracle with the responsibility not to invent medical or historical details.

Key Evidence: 1 Kings 16:19-21; 2 Kings 2-13.

references.author: Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor, II Kings, Anchor Bible 11
Iain Provan, 1 and 2 Kings, New International Biblical Commentary

entries.title: Elam
entries.content:
Elam is a historical entity in eastern Mesopotamia that appears in the Bible in warfare, prophecy, and imperial geography. Genesis 14 places it within an ancient network of kings, while the prophecies announce its judgment and then open in Jeremiah the horizon of returning the captivity. The name should not be equated with all of Persian history, as political periods and regional identity differ. Inscriptions and monuments are useful in understanding Susa and Elam, but they do not eliminate the literary function of the text. The introduction reveals that God in prophecy is not only the God of Israel's borders, but rather the Lord of history and nations.

Key Evidence: Genesis 14:1; Isaiah 11:11; Jeremiah 49:34-39; Daniel 8:2.

references.author: John D. W. Watts, Isaiah 1-33, Word Biblical Commentary 24
Lester L. Grabbe, A History of the Jews and Judaism in the Second Temple Period, T&T Clark

entries.title: My dear
entries.content:
Eli, a priest in Shiloh, meets in his story the weakness of the religious leadership with the corruption of his sons Hophni and Phinehas. The text does not describe him as corrupt in the same way, but it condemns him for his delay in controlling the home and institution. The prayer of Hannah and the ascension of Samuel open an alternative path to leadership, and then the fall of the Ark of the Covenant and the death of Eli signify the collapse of the priestly house. The novel reveals that a person's proximity to the sacred does not protect the institution from judgment. It is a deep study of the responsibility of the father and leader, and of the transmission of the word from one house to another.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 1-4.

references.author: P. Kyle McCarter Jr., I Samuel, Anchor Bible 8

entries.title: Eleazar
entries.content:
Eleazar, son of Aaron, represents the transfer of the priesthood after the death of his father and two brothers, and then he participates with Moses at the moment of the transfer of leadership to the new generation. The texts of the number place him within the sanctity of the job and its limits, so that the priest does not become a king nor the prophet a substitute for the community. His death and burial in Gibeah of Phinehas link the priesthood to continuity and memory. His character makes it possible to study institutional succession after crises, and how the legal tradition is preserved without claiming that continuity means infallibility. The Jewish comparison is useful in following the development of the concepts of priesthood and sacrifices.

Key Evidence: Exodus 6:23; Leviticus 10; Numbers 20:22-29; Joshua 24:33.

references.author: Jacob Milgrom, Numbers, JPS Torah Commentary

entries.title: Elisha son of Shaphat
entries.content:
Elisha's call reveals that prophecy is neither a spiritual hobby nor a family inheritance, but rather a response to a call to break with the previous way of life. Burning plowing tools and offering oxen is a symbolic act of abandoning the old source of livelihood, but it does not mean despising agricultural work. Elijah lays hands on him, and then Elisha learns the ministry before assuming the prophetic role. The story allows for an examination of the cost of calling, obedience, and the teacher-disciple relationship. An entire biography should not be built from the invitation scene alone, but rather linked to what appears later in Elisha’s ministry.

Key Evidence: 1 Kings 16:19-21.

references.author: Walter Brueggemann, First and Second Kings, Smyth & Helwys
Iain Provan, 1 and 2 Kings, New International Biblical Commentary

entries.title: Azariah
entries.content:
Azariah, called Uzziah in other places, is the king of Judah who begins with a successful rule and then collides with the limits of authority when he enters the temple to burn incense. The difference in name does not mean a difference in personality, but rather requires a textual comparison between the Book of Kings and Chronicles. The Book of Chronicles links leprosy with transgression into the priestly realm, thus drawing a line between the king and the priest. The story does not read as a disdain for the king, but rather as a warning against turning success into a right in every job. His end in isolation displays the price of pride, with the necessity of reading illness within ancient notions of purity and not within the stigmatization of today's patients.

Key Evidence: 2 Kings 15:1-7; 2 News 26.

references.author: Sara Japhet, I & II Chronicles, Old Testament Library

entries.title: Azariah the priest
entries.content:
The name Azariah occurs frequently in the priestly records, so not every character bearing the name should be combined. In the Chronicles a priest appears associated with organizing gifts in the temple, while other names appear in genealogical lists. This type of approach is important because it teaches reading lists as institutional memory rather than marginal material. The lists reveal how the legitimacy of ministry is built after crises, and how the economy relates to worship. It is necessary to examine the lineage, context, and transcription before attributing one verb to each Azariah.

Key Evidence: 2 Chronicles 31:10; Ezra 7:1-5.

references.author: Sara Japhet, I & II Chronicles, Old Testament Library
H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah, Word Biblical Commentary 16

entries.title: Athaliah
entries.content:
Athaliah, Queen of Judah, in a coup novel that combines dynastic conflict, violence against the heirs to the throne, and the rearrangement of worship. She cannot be reduced to being an evil woman; The text discusses a political network that includes the house of Ahab, the priesthood, the palace guards, and the child Joash. Jehoash's hiding in the temple reveals the role of the religious institution in preserving the Davidic lineage. Then comes Jehoiada's coup as both a political and religious act. The story needs a critical reading of royal violence, not the glorification of each victorious party. The importance of women in the transition of power is also highlighted, even when the narrative describes them from the perspective of their opponents.

Basic evidence: 2 Kings 11; 2 Chronicles 22-23.

references.author: Athalia Brenner, The Israelite Woman, JSOT Press

entries.title: Azza
entries.content:
The death of Uzzah upon touching the Ark of the Covenant is one of the texts that raises questions about holiness and good faith. Samuel's account presents the event as a shock that reveals that the sanctuary is not subject to improvisation, while Chronicles provides a clearer context for the carrying of the ark according to the law. This does not mean that Uzzah was evil or that God punishes every attempt to help, but rather that worship has order and responsibility. The first fear leads David to relearn, and then the transfer turns into controlled joy. The introduction balances the awe of holiness and God's mercy with the necessity of reforming the practice.

Key Evidence: 2 Samuel 6; 1 News 13; 15.

references.author: P. Kyle McCarter Jr., II Samuel, Anchor Bible 9
Sara Japhet, I & II Chronicles, Old Testament Library

entries.title: Azika
entries.content:
Azekah is a place in the Shephelah that occurs in the context of Joshua's war and the site of the confrontation between David and Goliath. The name combines the geography of the battle and the memory of the conflict with the Palestinians, but the similarity of the location does not prove that all the narratives took place in the same place in the modern sense. Studying the Shephelah helps understand the transitional zone between the coast and the highlands, where roads and armies intersect. The introduction also reveals that geography in the biblical narrative performs a theological function: place places fear and hope within realistic terrain. Archaeological evidence should be presented with scientific probability, not legal certainty.

Key Evidence: Joshua 10:10-11; 1 Samuel 17:1.

references.author: Richard S. Hess, Joshua, Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries
James K. Hoffmeier, The Archaeology of the Bible, Lion Hudson

entries.title: Wagon
entries.content:
The Arabah is a geographical name for the valley of the collapse extending south from the Sea of Galilee, and it appears in the description of the wilderness, the roads, and the scene of the fall of Jerusalem. The Arabah should not be confused with every desert valley in translations, as the context determines the location and meaning. Geography helps understand the crossing of kingdoms, the movement of armies, and the borders between Edom, Moab, and Israel. In prophecies, the valley may turn into an image of devastation or the course of life. The entry combines maps, Hebrew text, and prophetic allegory without reducing one to the other.

Key Evidence: Deuteronomy 1:1; 2 Kings 25:4; Ezekiel 47:8.

references.author: Anson F. Rainey and R. Steven Notley, The Sacred Bridge, Carta
John H. Walton, Ancient Near Eastern Thought and the Old Testament, Baker Academic

entries.title: Howled
entries.content:
The Awis appear in the list of peoples of the coast and the south as part of the description of the land that remained unpossessed. The brevity of the reference makes the identity and position of the group a subject of debate, and therefore a detailed national history should not be made from a single verse. The introduction reveals the function of lists in drawing the boundaries of the promise and the boundaries of reality at the same time: the land is a gift, but it was not a complete reality. Comparison between translations is useful in determining the name, because the difference in drawing may obscure its connection with other names. The spiritual value here is in respecting the promise without denying historical complexity.

Key Evidence: Joshua 13:3-4.

references.author: Richard S. Hess, Joshua, Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries
A. S. van der Woude, The Peoples of the Old Testament

entries.title: Uzziah
entries.content:
Uzziah, King of Judah, whose death is linked to the beginning of Isaiah's vision of the Lord sitting on the throne. The text creates a strong theological contrast between the throne of a human king shaking because of leprosy and a stable divine throne that fills the temple with glory. The king's success in war and construction does not protect him from exceeding the limits of the priesthood, and therefore his end becomes a warning against pride. Isaiah's vision does not escape the crisis of politics, but rather rearranges it under the holiness of God. The research distinguishes between Uzziah and Azariah as two versions of the same person in two textual traditions.

Key Evidence: 2 Kings 15:1-7; 2 News 26; Isaiah 6:1.

references.author: John N. Oswalt, The Book of Isaiah 1-39, NICOT
Sara Japhet, I & II Chronicles, Old Testament Library

entries.title: Uz
entries.content:
The land of Uz in the opening of the Book of Job is an open literary and geographical location, so mentioning it alone does not prove a single location or final ethnic identity. Job's position outside the Land of Israel allows the book to raise the question of suffering and righteousness before an audience broader than the confines of the community. The book does not present the problem of evil merely as a theoretical issue; It tests the limits of quick explanations that blame the sufferer. Uz is also associated with Edom or eastern territories in some texts, but comparisons remain likely. The entrance teaches humility in the face of geographical ambiguity, and the necessity of not reducing pain to direct punishment.

Key Evidence: Job 1:1; Lamentations 4:21; Jeremiah 25:20.

references.author: Carol A. Newsom, The Book of Job, Norton Critical Edition
David J. A. Clines, Job 1-20, Word Biblical Commentary 17

entries.title: Ohhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhh
entries.category: Jewish tradition and the Feast of Tabernacles
entries.content:
Oshezin is an Aramaic expression in the Jewish tradition for the symbolic guests received in the sukkah during the Feast of Tabernacles, including Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Joseph, and David. The term itself does not appear in the Torah, and therefore it must be presented as a later interpretive and liturgical development rather than as a direct biblical ruling. The tradition reveals how the memory of the fathers and the exodus turns into a practice of hospitality, so that welcoming the poor and the stranger becomes a test of sincerity of joy. His study helps to understand the relationship between text, interpretation, and Jewish liturgy. Christian dialogue can learn from it the centrality of memory and hospitality without erasing the specificity of the Jewish holiday.

Key Evidence: Leviticus 23:33-43; Nehemiah 8:14-18.

references.author: Howard Eilberg-Schwartz, The Savage in Judaism, Indiana University Press

entries.title: Astarte
entries.content:
Astarte is the name of a goddess or religious title associated with Canaanite and Phoenician cults, and appears in the Bible as part of the crisis of monotheism and loyalty. Every archaeological image or every relative's name should not be equated with a single cult without distinction of time and geography. The Book of Judges links the worship of Astarte to the cycle of abandonment from God, while the story of Samuel reveals that repentance includes removing symbols and redirecting the heart. Ugaritic and Phoenician texts are useful as background, but they do not make the book a mere copy of neighborhood mythology. Deep study balances the history of religions with Covenant criticism of rival cults.

Key Evidence: Judges 2:13; 1 Samuel 7:3-4; 1 Kings 11:5.

references.author: John Day, Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan, Sheffield Academic Press
Mark S. Smith, The Early History of God, Eerdmans

entries.title: Asaph
entries.content:
Asaph is the name of a praise leader in the temple and a reference to a collection of psalms, not just an isolated poet. His psalms confront the question of evil and the success of the wicked, moving from confusion to entering the sanctuary and restoring the covenant perspective. Therefore, worship is not reduced to feelings of victory; It has room for complaint, protest and remembrance. The attribution of the Psalms to Asaph allows for the study of liturgical memory and composition, while acknowledging that the title of the psalm does not resolve the entire history of composition. In the Jewish and Christian tradition, Asaph's voice becomes a model for communal prayer in the midst of injustice.

Key Evidence: 1 Chronicles 6:31-32; 16:5-7; Psalms 50; 73-83.

references.author: William P. Brown, The Oxford Handbook of the Psalms, Oxford University Press

entries.title: Achor
entries.content:
The Valley of Achor is linked in Joshua to the sin of Achan and to the shift from disorder to consolidation of the group. The name itself carries the meaning of distress or turmoil, but prophecies repurpose it as a door of hope, so the memory of fate turns into the possibility of a new beginning. It is not right to use the story of Achan to justify collective punishment outside of its narrative and historical context. The comparison reveals that the Bible does not leave the place captive to its first meaning, but rather reinterprets it in the light of mercy. The entrance combines collective responsibility, the sanctity of the group, and the hope of recovering the devastation.

Key Evidence: Joshua 7:24-26; Hosea 2:15; Isaiah 65:10.

references.author: Richard S. Hess, Joshua, Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries
Francis I. Andersen and David Noel Freedman, Hosea, Anchor Bible 24

entries.title: Achan
entries.content:
Achan is a central character in the story of defeat before Ai, as the narrative links individual transgression to group disorder. The text takes betrayal seriously because it occurred in a consecrated context, but an ethical reading needs to respect the difference of the ancient world from modern justice systems. Achan does not offer a lesson in searching people or making subjective judgments, but rather reveals how greed threatens trust and covenant. The association of his name with the Valley of Achor makes geographical memory a carrier of the tension of guilt and hope. The novel should be read within the structure of Joshua, recognizing its difficult questions about punishment and collective representation.

Key Evidence: Joshua 7.

references.author: Richard S. Hess, Joshua, Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries
Yairah Amit, Reading Biblical Narratives, Fortress Press

entries.title: Asa
entries.content:
King Asa of Judah presents a complex model of reform: he eliminates some aspects of deviant worship, but at the end of his life he relies on a political alliance rather than trusting in God. The Book of Kings and Chronicles differ in angle of presentation, allowing for the study of historical memory and interpretive theology. The initial success does not cancel out the weakness of the end, nor does the mistake cancel out all the previous honesty. The disease of the feet in Chronicles is not a call to interpret every disease as a punishment, but rather part of a criticism of dependence. The introduction links personal reform to fear management, politics, and resources.

Key Evidence: 1 Kings 9:15-24; 2 Chronicles 14-16.

references.author: Sara Japhet, I & II Chronicles, Old Testament Library

entries.title: Ahaz
entries.content:
Ahaz, King of Judah, faces a military threat and chooses to protect the Assyrian Empire, but his decision links political security with religious dependency. In Isaiah, God offers the king a sign, but he rejects it outwardly with humility and inwardly with distrust. Then Emmanuel comes as a sign of God’s continued presence despite the ruler’s failure. The Book of Chronicles describes harsh cult practices, while the Chronicles of Kings situates reforms within international politics. The image of Ahaz should not be built from a single source or foreign policy turned into an abstract spiritual matter. His character reveals the danger of seeking salvation from a stronger power while losing freedom of conscience.

Basic evidence: 2 Kings 16; 2 News 28; Isaiah 7.

references.author: John N. Oswalt, The Book of Isaiah 1-39, NICOT

entries.title: Hezekiah
entries.content: Hezekiah from חִזְקִיָּהוּ (Ḥizqiyyahu), meaning the Lord strengthens. The king of Judah, who was associated with reforming worship and confronting Assyria, but his end reveals that reform does not exempt from the danger of pride. The place is Jerusalem, the Temple, and Lachish, and the most famous events are the breaking of the bronze serpent and prayer during the siege of Sennacherib, then displaying the kingdom’s treasuries to Babylon. His contemporaries Isaiah, Micah, Sennacherib, and Manasseh. Biblical witness: 2 Kings 18-20; 2 Chronicles 29-32; Isaiah 36-39. Theologically, the introduction links trust, prayer, and reform, and presents the different narratives of Kings, Chronicles, and Isaiah without forcibly merging them.

originalLanguage.meaning: The meaning and derivation are mentioned along with the degree of certainty.

entries.title: Ayalon
entries.content:
Elon is the name of a valley and a city in the geography of the highlands and the Shephelah, and it appears in stories of battles and in the Song of Joshua about the stopping of the sun. The poetic expression should not be read as an astronomical proof divorced from the function of the text to glorify God's work, nor ignore the geography that made Aijalon a military corridor. The different locations bearing the name require adjusting the context and lineage. Ayalon's study helps to understand the difficulty of biblical maps and to see how poetry preserves the memory of victory. The spiritual value is that power is not attributed to the leader alone, while avoiding turning the text into a war slogan.

Key Evidence: Joshua 10:12-14; Judges 1:35; 1 Samuel 14:31.

references.author: Richard S. Hess, Joshua, Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries
Anson F. Rainey and R. Steven Notley, The Sacred Bridge, Carta

entries.title: Adonai
entries.content:
Adonai is a Jewish form of respect that is traditionally recited in place of the fourfold divine name in the recitation. A distinction must be made between its linguistic meaning, Lord or Master, and the history of its liturgical and translational use. Jewish practice reveals fear of handling the name and sanctity of pronunciation, while Arabic translations often convey the meaning to God. Studying the name requires comparing the Hebrew text, the Masoretic text, the Septuagint, and Jewish traditions, not reducing it to a single word.

Key Evidence: Genesis 15:2; Exodus 3:15; Psalm 8:1.

references.author: Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, Fortress Press

entries.title: Azara
entries.content:
Azara is one of the names that appears in genealogical or masonry lists, and the few evidence does not allow the establishment of an independent biography. The value of the entry is systematic: the lists preserve the names of people who participated in the group even when their actions are not recorded in detail. Hebrew etymology and translations should be compared, and proportions and placement examined before combining similar names. Thus, small names become testimony that the history of the era includes not-so-famous workers as well.

Key Evidence: 1 Chronicles 8:15; Nehemiah 3:23.

references.author: Sara Japhet, I & II Chronicles, Old Testament Library
H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah, Word Biblical Commentary 16

entries.title: Asmon
entries.content:
Ezmon is a place mentioned in the lists of the borders of the Land of Israel, and its importance lies in delineating the area, not in a personal story. The difference in modern definitions reminds the researcher that ancient boundaries are not always fixed geometric lines, but rather descriptions linked to natural routes and centres. Comparing Numbers and Joshua helps in understanding the transfer of geographical memory between the lists. Archaeological hypotheses must be kept as probabilistic, while reading land as a gift and a responsibility, not just political ownership.

Basic evidence: Numbers 34:4-5; Joshua 15:4.

references.author: Richard S. Hess, Joshua, Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries
Anson F. Rainey and R. Steven Notley, The Sacred Bridge, Carta

entries.title: Azmaut
entries.content:
Azmaut is a noun that appears for people and places, and therefore it is necessary to adjust the proportions and context before the plural. One of the bearers of the name appears in lists of David's heroes, while post-exilic texts mention a group or place in the organization of the city. This material reveals that biblical memory preserves both military leadership and local identity. The brevity of the evidence does not allow adding undocumented stories, but rather calls for respecting the limits of knowledge and examining differences in transmission.

Key Evidence: 2 Samuel 23:31; 1 Chronicles 11:33; Nehemiah 12:29.

references.author: Robert Alter, The David Story, W. W. Norton
H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah, Word Biblical Commentary 16

entries.title: Habiq
entries.content: Habiq from חֲבַק (Ḥavaq), the derivation is indefinite, and is traditionally associated with embrace or conflict. The Prophet stands in Judah before the question of the violence of the oppressors and the silence of God, and then he learns that the righteous lives by faith in the midst of an unfinished history. The place is Jerusalem and Judah in light of the rise of Babylon, and its contemporaries Josiah, Jehoiakim, and the Babylonians, according to the proposed dating. Witness: Habakkuk 1-3, with echoes of Romans 1:17 and Hebrews 10:38. The book does not provide a quick explanation for pain, but rather turns complaining into watching, waiting, and praising. Spiritually, faith here is steadfastness in God’s faithfulness, not denial of evil.

references.title: Habakkuk 1-3, with echoes of Romans 1:17 and Hebrews 10:38

references.author: O. Palmer Robertson
references.title: The Books of Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah, NICOT, 1990

entries.title: Hajji
entries.content: Haggai from חַגַּי (Ḥaggai), meaning one who belongs to the holiday or was born on a holiday according to the linguistic suggestion. He addresses the post-exilic community that built their homes and neglected the temple, linking rebuilding to a reordering of priorities. The place is Jerusalem and the Second Temple, and its contemporaries are Zerubbabel, Joshua the priest, Zechariah, and Darius the Persian. Witness: Haggai 1-2; Ezra 5-6. Travel is not reduced to urban success; The temple is a sign of presence and hope, but it does not eliminate the question of obedience and justice. Spiritually, it calls for an examination of what we put first and for a hope that operates within a limited political reality.

references.author: R. K. W. R. Mason
references.title: Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, Old Testament Library, 1977

entries.title: Ham
entries.content: Ham is from חָם (Ḥam), and may be associated with heat or the name of a person, without complete etymological certainty. He is the son of Noah in the Table of Nations and the story of nudity, and his importance appears in how the text builds lineages and moral boundaries after the flood. The place is the ark, then the regions of Egypt and Canaan according to the table of nations, and its contemporaries are Noah, Shem, Japheth, and Canaan. Witness: Genesis 5:32; 9:18-27; 10:6. The Curse of Canaan may not be used to justify slavery or racism; This is a history of misinterpretation, not the result of the text. The entry distinguishes between Ham and Canaan and between the original narrative and subsequent reception.

entries.title: Pub
entries.content: Hanna is a common Arabic name in some translations of Hannah, from חַנָּה (Ḥannah), meaning blessing or favor. Samuel is presented by a woman of prayer in Shiloh, where barrenness and distress are transformed into a cry and then a vow and devotion. The place is Shiloh, and the most famous events are its prayer, its song, and the handing over of Samuel to Eli. Her contemporaries were Elkanah, Peninnah, Eli, and Samuel. Witness: 1 Samuel 1-2. The text does not depict Hannah merely as an instrument of procreation; Her anthem announces the reversal of the standards of power and the uplifting of the poor. Spiritually, the story preserves the right of grief in prayer and warns against reducing women to their family function.

entries.title: Ananias
entries.content: Ananias from חֲנַנְיָה (Ḥananyah), meaning the Lord had compassion, which is a name for several people. In Acts 5, he appears with Sapphira in the Jerusalem community, where the text does not condemn the possession of money, but rather lying to the community and the spirit. The place is Jerusalem and the home of the congregation, and its contemporaries Sapphira, Peter, and the believers. Witness: Acts 5:1-11. This pair should be distinguished from Ananias the high priest and Ananias the prophet. Theologically, the holiness of the community is linked to honesty, money, and conscience, and the story must not be turned into a tool of intimidation that prevents repentance. Spiritually, free giving does not require religious representation.

entries.title: Ananias the high priest
entries.content: Ananias the High Priest of חֲנַנְיָה, the Lord had compassion, a high priest who confronted Paul in the Jerusalem trial. His presence reveals the intertwining of religious authority and Roman politics, and he should not be lumped in with Ananias of Acts 5 or the prophet in Jeremiah. The place is Jerusalem and Caesarea, and its contemporaries Paul, Felix, and the elders. Witness: Acts 23:2-5; 24:1. The novel displays the tension of justice and procedure, as he orders Paul's mouth to be punched before the trial is complete. The entry reads the text in its imperial context, not as an ethnic condemnation of the Jews or the entire priesthood.

entries.title: Ananias the prophet
entries.content: Ananias the prophet from חֲנַנְיָה, the Lord had compassion, the prophet of Gibeon who opposed Jeremiah and announced that the yoke of Babylon would be quickly broken. The place was Jerusalem and its temple in the fourth year of Zedekiah, and his contemporaries were Jeremiah, Zedekiah, and the Babylonians. Witness: Jeremiah 28. The entry does not treat disagreement only as a personal conflict; The problem is to test a comforting word against a word that warns of realistic judgment. Ananias' death leaves open the question of prophetic responsibility, and prevents the transformation of prophecy into a political promise. Spiritually, the right message is not always the most comforting.

entries.title: Hanouk
entries.content: Enoch, from חֲנוֹךְ (Ḥanokh), meaning consecrated or trained, is a name that is repeated in genealogies. Enoch the son of Jared walks with God, and the narrative does not mention his death in the usual way, while Enoch the son of Cain and the grandson of Reuben appears in other contexts. The place is the world before the flood, and its contemporaries are Adam, Seth, Jared, and Methuselah, according to lineage. Witness: Genesis 4:17; 5:18-24; 1 Chronicles 1:3. The entry distinguishes between similar characters and the later Book of Enoch, which is not equal to the text of Genesis. Spiritually, walking with God is an ongoing relationship, not a religious title.

entries.title: Poplar
entries.content: Hur is from חוּר (Ḥur), and its derivation is unclear. It is the name of a leader and the name of other characters. In Exodus 17 he supports Moses with Aaron during the Battle of Amalek, and in Exodus 24 he maintains the administration of the community during Moses' ascension. The place is Rephidim and Sinai, and its contemporaries are Moses, Aaron, and Joshua. Witness: Exodus 8:17-16; 24:14. His story reveals that spiritual leadership is not individual heroism; Raising hands requires a group to support and guard. A biography broader than the text should not be invented, but rather the silence of the source should be respected while reading the partnership function.

entries.title: Hur bin Kaleb
entries.content: Hur bin Caleb, from חוּר (Ḥur), and the name Hur in the text has many uses; As for Kaleb, it is from כָּלֵב (Kalev), and it is traditionally linked to the dog or loyalty without etymological assertion. The genealogy links Judah's leadership to the continuity of memory, his contemporaries Caleb and Joshua, and the builders of later generations. Witness: 1 Chronicles 2:19-20; 2 Chronicles 26:10. Hur bin Kaleb should not be combined with Hur, Musa's companion, without examining the lineage. Spiritually, lineages preserve the value of quiet service.

entries.title: Horon
entries.content: Horon from חוֹרֹן (Ḥoron), a name that appears in Beth Horon and other places, and the derivation is not settled. The place was the region of Benjamin and Ephraim, and was associated with roads, battles, and the distribution of land, and its contemporaries were Joshua and the tribes of Israel in the stage of settlement. Witness: Joshua 10:10; 16:3,5; 18:13-14. The entry distinguishes between the city and the name of the god Horon in some Near Eastern texts without direct equality. Spiritually, geography does not become a property without responsibility.

entries.title: Hebron
entries.content: Hebron is from חֶבְרוֹן (Ḥevron), and is linked to the idea of connection or group according to linguistic research. It is the place of Abraham's residence and the burial of Sarah and the fathers, then a priestly city and the first capital of David. Witness: Genesis 13:18; 23; Joshua 13:14-15; 2 Samuel 2:1-4. Its contemporaries are Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, and David. The introduction balances the sanctity of memory with the complexity of the conflict on the ground, so as not to make history an excuse for violence.

entries.title: Mother-in-law
entries.content: Hamath from חֲמָת (Ḥamath), the name of a northern city whose etymological meaning is inconclusive. It appears in borders, conquests, and prophecies, and was on trade routes between the Levant and the Euphrates. Witness: Numbers 13:21; 2 Samuel 8:9-10; Amos 6:2; 2 Kings 14:25. Her contemporaries are David, Jeroboam II, and the Prophets, depending on the context. The entry explains that the city is not studied merely as a map, but as part of a network of empires, borders, and prophetic responsibility.

entries.title: Homer
entries.content: Hamor, from חֲמוֹר (Ḥamor), meaning a donkey, which is the name of the ruler of Shechem in Genesis 34. The place is Shechem, and the most famous events are his negotiations over Dinah, then deceiving Simeon and Levi and killing the people of the city. His contemporaries are Jacob, Dinah, Shechem, and the sons of Jacob. Witness: Genesis 33:18-34:31. The narrative neither exonerates Hamor nor justifies collective revenge; Rather, it reveals the failure of men to protect the weak and the transformation of marriage into a political deal. Spiritually, the introduction calls for violence to be read honestly, not glorified.

entries.title: Havilah
entries.content: Havilah from חֲוִילָה (Ḥavilah), the name of a region or person, the derivation is unclear. It appears in the description of one of the rivers of Eden, in the Table of Nations, and in the borders of Ishmael, so the places do not prove a single geographical identity. Witness: Genesis 2:11; 10:7; 25:18. The place extends in perception from the geography of Eden to the Arab regions, and its contemporaries Adam and the sons of Noah and Ishmael according to the texts. The entry distinguishes between geographical suggestions and biblical certainty, and links gold to resources and responsibility rather than myth.

entries.title: Hushai
entries.content: Hushai, from חוּשַׁי (Ḥushai), a name traditionally interpreted as speed or haste without certainty. He is a friend of David and an advisor who opposes the advice of Ahithophel during Absalom's rebellion, in the two places Jerusalem and Mahanaim. Witness: 2 Samuel 15:32-37; 16:16-19; 17. His contemporaries are David, Absalom, and Ahithophel. The novel does not present political deception as a general moral rule, but rather as part of a complex civil war. Spiritually, it brings forth the wisdom that protects life at its personal cost.

entries.title: Hoshem
entries.content: Hosham, from חוּשָׁם (Ḥusham), the name of the king of Edom in a brief chronicle, and its meaning is indeterminate. The place is Edom, and the most famous thing that the text preserves is its occurrence in a series of kings before the rise of a king in Israel. Witness: Genesis 36:31-35; 1 Chronicles 1:43-45. His contemporaries are the kings of Edom and Israel in genealogical memory. The lack of news prevents the making of a biography, but it allows studying the function of lists in preserving political memory and identity. Spiritually, a person's value is not measured by the amount of what is written about him.

entries.title: urge
entries.content: Hitt from חִתִּי (Ḥitti), referring to the Hittites, and its meaning varies between the Hittite Empire and local peoples in Canaan depending on the period. The place is Hebron, Jerusalem, and the land of Canaan, and its contemporaries are Abraham, Esau, David, and Uriah the Hittite. Witness: Genesis 23; 26:34; 2 Samuel 11. Each Hittite may not be combined into a single political identity, nor may the name be used to produce ethnic judgments. The entry links history, migration, integration, and injustice, especially in the story of Uriah.

entries.title: Hawi
entries.content: Havi is from חִוִּי (Ḥivvi), the name of the Canaanite people in the lists, and its derivation is not settled. It appears in Gibeon within the story of the treaty and in the lists of the land, and the place is in the middle and north of Canaan. Witness: Genesis 34:2; Exodus 3:8; Joshua 9:1-27. His contemporaries Joshua and the inhabitants of Gibeon and Israel are in the entry stage. The entry distinguishes between the category of name in the list and the specific characters, and reads the covenant with the Gibeonites as a lesson in haste and commitment after it.

entries.title: Hawaila
entries.content: Havilah, from חֲוִילָה (Ḥavilah), the name of a region or lineage, the derivation is unclear. It occurs in Genesis 2 within the Rivers of Eden, in Genesis 10 within the lineage of Cush, and in Genesis 25:18 within the domain of Ishmael; Therefore, the evidence does not support one area. The place extends in perception from the geography of Paradise to the regions of the Arabian Peninsula, and the contemporaries of the texts, Adam and the sons of Noah and Ishmael. Biblical witness: Genesis 2:11; 10:7; 25:18; 1 Samuel 15:7. The study reveals the limits of geographical conformity, and warns against transforming gold and resources into a myth of wealth separated from covenant responsibility.

entries.title: Hourma
entries.content: Hormah, from חָרְמָה (Ḥormah), is associated with prohibition or consecration, and is a place in the Negev. After Israel's defeat in Numbers 14, victory comes in Numbers 21 in the context of a vow and repentance, and then the name appears in the southern judiciary. The place is south of Canaan, and the contemporaries of the events were Moses, Joshua, the Canaanites, and the tribes of Judah and Simeon. Biblical witness: Numbers 14:40-45; 21:1-3; Joshua 12:14; Judges 1:17. The war narrative should not be used to justify contemporary violence; Rather, the introduction reads within the history of the Exodus, the borders of the Earth, and criticism of disobedience.

entries.title: Cornerstone
entries.content: Cornerstone from פִּנָּה (pinnah) or λίθος ἀκρογωνιαῖος (lithos akrogōniaios), the stone that determines the cohesion or position of a building. In the Psalm and Isaiah, the rejected stone turns into a sign of foundation, and the Gospels and New Testament letters reread the image in Christ and the community. Biblical witness: Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 28:16; Matthew 21:42; 1 Peter 2:6-8. The place is the building, the temple, the city, and its contemporaries, the builders, the prophets, Jesus, and the apostles. The entry distinguishes between poetic meaning and Christian rereading.

entries.title: Veil
entries.content: The veil of פָּרֹכֶת (parokhet), a curtain that separates the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies. In the tabernacle and the temple, the veil regulates the approach to God’s presence, so it does not equate the sacred with the ordinary place. The place is the Tabernacle and the Temple, and the most famous events are its entry into the Day of Atonement system and its disruption in the accounts of the Cross, and its contemporaries Moses, Aaron, the High Priest, and Jesus. Biblical witness: Exodus 31:26-37; Leviticus 16:2; Matthew 27:51; Hebrews 9:1-8. The entry reads of sanctity and approach without abrogating the Jewish history of the Temple.

entries.title: Temple veil
entries.content: Temple veil from καταπέτασμα (katapetasma) in Greek, curtain of the sanctuary. Its rupture in Matthew, Mark, and Luke is a narrative and theological reference to the death of Jesus and the opening of the path of approach, but it cannot be reduced to eliminating all meaning of the Temple or Judaism. The place is Jerusalem, the temple, Jesus' contemporaries, the priests, soldiers, and women present. Biblical witness: Matthew 27:51; Mark 15:38; Luke 23:45; Hebrews 10:19-22. The study presents the different narratives and the function of the symbol within each Gospel.

entries.title: War
entries.content: The war is from מִלְחָמָה (milḥamah) or πόλεμος (polemos), which is both a political reality and a theological image. The Torah offers protection and boundaries, the Prophets reveal the violence of empires, while the Gospels place Christ's kingdom on a path different from the sword. The place is Egypt, the wilderness, the land of kings, Jerusalem, and the contemporaries of the events: Moses, Joshua, David, and Jesus. Biblical witness: Exodus 14; Deuteronomy 20; 1 Samuel 17; Matthew 26:52. The entry Texts of War does not provide a contemporary authorization for violence, but rather reads them historically and morally.

entries.title: Freedom
entries.content: Freedom from חֵרוּת (ḥerut) in the later Hebrew tradition, is associated in Scripture with the act of going out and serving God, while Paul uses ἐλευθερία (eleutheria) in the context of Christ and the Spirit. The setting is Egypt, the wilderness, Christian groups, and the concept's contemporaries Moses, Pharaoh, Paul, and the churches. Biblical witness: Exodus 6:6-8; Deuteronomy 15; Galatians 5:1-13. Freedom does not mean separation from every obligation, but rather a transition to love that serves one's neighbor. The introduction distinguishes between political, theological, and moral freedom.

entries.title: Harvest
entries.content: Harvest from קָצִיר (qatsir) or θερισμός (therismos), the season of gathering the seeds and an image of judgment and mission. Levitical law protects the right of the poor and the stranger to the edges of the field, and the Gospels use the harvest to image the kingdom and the workers. The place is the fields of Bethlehem and Galilee, the agricultural villages, and its contemporaries Ruth, Boaz, Jesus, and the disciples. Biblical witness: Leviticus 19:9-10; Ruth 2; Matthew 9:37-38; 13:24-30. Spiritually, agricultural blessing is inseparable from social justice.

entries.title: Field
entries.content: Field from שָׂדֶה (sadeh) or ἀγρός (agros), land of cultivation, ownership, burial, and cultivation. Abraham bought the field of Machpelah, and Jesus used the field as an image of crops and treasure, so the word moves between the economy and the kingdom. The place is Hebron, the villages of Galilee, the proverbial fields, and its contemporaries Abraham, Ephron, Jesus, and the farmers. Biblical witness: Genesis 23; Jeremiah 32; Matthew 3:13-44. The entry distinguishes between land ownership as a responsibility and a sign of possession, and links it to justice and hope.

entries.title: Wheat
entries.content: Spelled from חִטָּה (ḥittah) or σῖτος (sitos), a staple grain for bread and the economy. It appears in the harvest and in the parable of the wheat and the tares, where patience does not allow the final discernment to be canceled but rather postpones it until the time of judgment. The place is Egypt, Bethlehem, and the fields of Galilee, and its contemporaries are Joseph, Ruth, Boaz, and Jesus. Biblical witness: Exodus 32:9; Deuteronomy 8:8; Ruth 2; Matthew 13:24-30. Spiritually, the entry links daily work with waiting on God and not uprooting others with hasty judgment.

entries.title: Dove
entries.content: The dove from יוֹנָה (yonah) or περιστερά (peristera), a bird that appears in the story of Noah and is a sign of the spirit at baptism. The place is the ark, the waters of the flood, the Jordan River, and its contemporaries Noah, Jesus, John, and the disciples. Witness: Genesis 8:8-12; Matthew 3:16; Mark 1:10; Luke 3:22. The entry distinguishes between the natural sign in the flood and the spiritual image in the Gospels, so it does not impose a complete correspondence between the two scenes. Spiritually, the dove carries the meaning of the end of judgment and the beginning of new creation.

entries.title: Pregnancy
entries.content: The lamb, from כֶּבֶשׂ (keves) or ἀμνός (amnos), a Passover animal, a sacrifice, and an image of meekness. The place is Egypt, the altar, and Jerusalem, and the most famous events are the Passover of the Exodus, the hymn of Isaiah, and the testimony of John the Baptist. His contemporaries are Moses, Israel, Isaiah, Jesus, and John. Witness: Exodus 12; Isaiah 53:7; John 1:29; Revelation 5. The entry links the allegory to liberation, substitution, and testimony without reducing each text to a single Christian reading.

entries.title: Copper serpent
entries.content: The copper serpent is from נְחַשׁ נְחֹשֶׁת (neḥash neḥoshet), a phonetic play between serpent and copper. Moses set it up in the wilderness to heal bites, then Hezekiah destroyed it when it became an object of incense. The place is the wilderness and Jerusalem, and its contemporaries are Moses, Israel, Hezekiah, and Jesus. Witness: Numbers 21:4-9; 2 Kings 18:4; John 3:14-15. The story reveals the difference between a symbol that points to God and an idol that takes over worship. Spiritually, even sacred memory needs examination.

entries.title: Wisdom
entries.content: The wisdom of חָכְמָה (ḥokhmah) or σοφία (sophia), a skill for living and discerning before God, not abstract information. The place is the houses of learning, palaces, markets, and communities, and its contemporaries Solomon, Job, Jesus, and Paul. Witness: Proverbs 1-9; Job 28; 1 Kings 3; 1 Corinthians 1:18-25. The study compares the wisdom of creation to the wisdom of the cross, and warns against claiming wisdom that justifies injustice. Spiritually, wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord and manifests itself in justice.

entries.title: Wise
entries.content: The sage from חָכָם (ḥakham) or σοφός (sophos), someone who learns to listen and accept correction. It appears in Proverbs, the Book of Ecclesiastes, and Paul’s dialogue with the wisdom of the world, and the place is the house of wisdom, the city, and the community. Witness: Proverbs 8:9-9; Ecclesiastes 7:5; Matthew 7:24-27; 1 Corinthians 1:20-31. His contemporaries Solomon, the teachers, Jesus and Paul. The book does not equate wisdom with cunning, but rather tests it by its moral fruit. Spiritually, the sage is teachable.

entries.title: Life
entries.content: Life is from חַיִּים (ḥayyim) or ζωή (zōē), a gift of creation, covenant, and resurrection. The place is Eden, the wilderness, the land of promise, the graves, and the villages of the Bible, and its contemporaries: Adam, Moses, the prophets, Jesus, and Lazarus. Witness: Genesis 2:7; Deuteronomy 30:19-20; Ezekiel 37; John 11:25. The introduction rejects the separation of spiritual life from the body and justice, and reads resurrection as a renewal of man’s relationship with God, not a denial of death. Spiritually, choosing life is a choice of honesty.

entries.title: Love
entries.content: Love is of אַהֲבָה (ahavah) or ἀγάπη (agapē), a relationship of loyalty and action and not an isolated feeling. The place is the home, worship, the street, the community, and the contemporaries of the concept: Moses, the prophets, Jesus, and the apostles. Witness: Deuteronomy 6:4-9; Leviticus 19:18; Mark 12:28-34; 1 Corinthians 13. The entry links the love of God with the love of neighbor and stranger, and prohibits the use of love to cover up injustice. Spiritually, biblical love is demonstrated in obedience and compassion.

entries.title: Stone
entries.content: Stone, from אֶבֶן (even) or λίθος (lithos), is a building material, monument, and memory, and it may become an idol. The place is Bethel, the temple, the tomb, and the altar, and its contemporaries Jacob, Moses, Joshua, and Jesus. Witness: Genesis 28:18; Exodus 20:25; Joshua 24:26-27; John 1:20; 1 Peter 2:4-8. The entrance distinguishes between a witnessing stone and a stone that is worshipped, and between a closed tomb and a stone that was removed in the Resurrection narrative. Spiritually, memory requires worshiping God, not matter.

entries.title: God's presence
entries.content: God's presence is from פָּנִים (panim), face or presence, and from Greek παρουσία (parousia) in Advent contexts. The place is the tent, the temple, the wilderness, the community, and its contemporaries Moses, David, the prophets, Jesus, and the disciples. Witness: Exodus 33:12-23; Psalm 139; Matthew 28:20. Presence does not mean possessing God or confining Him to a place, but rather a relationship of holiness, closeness, and mission. Spiritually, the presence anchors the community in fear and calls it to serve the world.

entries.title: A dream
entries.content: The dream is from חֲלוֹם (ḥalom) or ὄναρ (onar), and may be a vision channel or a narrative element that needs to be distinguished. The place is the palaces of Egypt and Babylon, the homes of Matthew, and his contemporaries Joseph, Daniel, Nebuchadnezzar, and Joseph, Mary’s fiancé. Witness: Genesis 40-41; Daniel 2; Matthew 1:20-24; 2:13. The Bible does not grant every dream prophetic authority, nor does it justify basing absolute decisions on individual experiences. Spiritually, interpretation remains a gift and a responsibility.

entries.title: Sadness
entries.content: Sorrow, from יָגוֹן (yagon) or λύπη (lypē), is an experience of pain that the book does not exclude from worship. The place is the homes of loss, the temple, the graves, the roads of exile, and its contemporaries David, Job, Jeremiah, Jesus, Lazarus, and Mary. Biblical witness: Psalms 42-43; Lamentations 3; John 11:33-35; Romans 12:15. The text does not provide a quick explanation for every pain, but rather gives the sufferer a language for complaint and waiting, and puts the community before the duty of weeping with those who weep. Spiritually, hope does not mean erasing the memory, but rather the presence of God within the wound and the possibility of renewal without denying the truth. The study distinguishes between natural sadness and despair, and between comfort that listens and comfort that silences the sufferer.
