entries.title: Babylon
entries.content: Babylon is not just an ancient city, but a historical and theological symbol that develops throughout the Bible. In Genesis 10-11 it is associated with the table of nations and the building of the tower; The narration highlights the human ambition to make a name and reach heaven without obedience, and then it is met with the dispersion of the language. In Kings and Jeremiah, Babylon becomes an empire that is an instrument of judgment against Judah, but being an instrument does not excuse its violence, and therefore the prophecies also announce its judgment. As for Daniel, he places Nebuchadnezzar’s pride before the sovereignty of the God of heaven, while Revelation 17-18 uses Babylon as an image of an economic and political system that tempts nations and persecutes saints. A distinction must be made between historical Babylon and apocalyptic Babylon, and between the description of the empire and its moral criticism. In the Jewish tradition, Babylon is linked to the memory of exile and return, while the Christian reading repurposes it to criticize the worship of power and wealth. Spiritually, the introduction warns against turning civilizational success into a substitute for God, and calls for faithfulness to the community in exile without hatred of peoples.

references.author: John Goldingay
references.title: Daniel, Word Biblical Commentary 30, Word Books, 1989

entries.title: Barak
entries.content: Barak is a leader in Judges 4-5, and his story appears within the cycle of persecution, outcry, and redemption. Barak does not start from an independent heroic initiative, but rather needs the word of Deborah, which combines prophecy, leadership, and wisdom. He agrees to go on the condition of her presence. The text does not simply present this condition as cowardice, but rather places leadership in a network of cooperation between a man and a woman. His victory over Sisera is not attributed to military superiority alone; The song reads the battle as a divine intervention, and the dignity of overthrowing the enemy goes to Jael. Hebrews 11 compares Barak to heroes of faith, showing that biblical faith does not mean the absence of hesitation. Historically the novel reflects a tribal conflict in northern Canaan, and literary it interprets the prose song. Spiritually, it shows the value of listening to the word of God and accepting partnership, while refusing to turn the story of war into a permanent model of violence.

references.author: Barry G. Webb
references.title: The Book of Judges, NICOT, Eerdmans, 2012

references.author: Yairah Amit
references.title: The Book of Judges, Sheffield Academic Press, 1999

entries.title: Barnabas
entries.content: Barnabas, whose name is interpreted in the Book of Acts as the son of exhortation or encouragement, is a bridge figure in the emergence of the church. He sells his field and puts its price at the feet of the apostles, then accepts Saul when the disciples fear him, and goes to Antioch to confirm the believers. His ministry is not limited to encouraging words; He participates in the interpretation of the acceptance of the nations and in the first mission. His disagreement with Paul over Mark reveals that the apostolic church was not without tension, and that disagreement does not negate the faithfulness of individuals. A distinction must be made between Barnabas in Acts and later traditions that attribute writings to him. Theologically, the introduction highlights the role of the mediator who opens the community to a rejected person, the relationship of giving to the mission, and that ecclesiastical encouragement is an act of discrimination and construction, not courtesy. The transmission of the Gospel from Jerusalem to Antioch also reveals that Christian unity is built by crossing cultural boundaries.

references.author: Beverly Roberts Gaventa
references.title: The Acts of the Apostles, Abingdon, 2003

references.author: John Barclay
references.title: Jews in the Mediterranean Diaspora, University of California Press, 1996

entries.title: Peter
entries.content: Peter in the New Testament is a character who moves between confession, fall, and recovery. In Caesarea Philip declares that Jesus is the Christ, but he rejects the way of the cross and Jesus rebukes him; Thus, the text shows that the validity of the title does not guarantee an understanding of the nature of the kingdom. Peter is denied in Passion Night, then recommissioned in John 21 through questions of love and care for the sheep. In Acts he becomes a witness of the Resurrection and a preacher on the Day of Pentecost, but in the story of Cornelius he learns that God does not accept nations on the basis of ritual national discrimination. Peter should not be read as an authority separate from the rest of the apostles, as the texts display his leadership within a community and shared witness. The Jewish interpretation of the background of purity and food is essential to understanding Acts 10, and subsequent Christian reading needs respect for the Jewish context. Spiritually, the entrance links repentance, care, and humility before the breadth of God's grace.

references.author: Oscar Cullmann
references.title: Peter: Disciple, Apostle, Martyr, Westminster Press, 1953

references.author: Raymond E. Brown, Karl P. Donfried, and John Reumann
references.title: Peter in the New Testament, Fortress Press, 1973

entries.title: Paul
entries.content: Paul is an apostle to the Gentiles and a pivotal interpreter of Christ's death and resurrection and the relationship between Jews and Gentiles. His story begins with violent religious zeal, then he reads the road to Damascus test as an invitation and an announcement, not just a psychological transformation. In Romans and Galatians he links justification to Abraham's promise, but does not treat the law as absolute evil; The question is its place in the history of the covenant and in a group that includes nations. The cross is a declaration of God's faithfulness and the victory of grace, and resurrection is the basis of the new creation, not a spiritual idea separate from history. Modern studies differ in understanding “the works of the law” and righteousness, and therefore the disagreement must be presented and Paul should not be reduced to one theological slogan. His Pharisaic, Jewish, and Hellenistic background is part of the explanation for his language. Spiritually, the introduction calls for reading Christian freedom as a service of love, not selfish independence, and for rejecting Paul’s use against the Jews or against the law in an undisciplined, historical manner.

references.author: N. T. Wright
references.title: Paul and the Faithfulness of God, Fortress Press, 2013

entries.title: Boaz
entries.content: Boaz in the Book of Ruth is a rich man from Bethlehem, but his importance is not based on wealth alone. In his field, he meets Ruth, the Moabite widow, and reads her presence within the law of the harvest and the right of the stranger and the poor. Not only does he let her pick, he protects her and orders the workers to leave her a surplus. However, he moves according to the norms of kinship and law, so he goes to the closest guardian before marrying her. The title of Redeemer here should not be transferred directly into Christian doctrine without understanding its social and legal function in the book. The ring of Ruth and Boaz links the family lineage to the history of David, so daily mercy enters the history of kingship and hope. The Jewish reading highlights charity and loyalty, and the Christian reading sees a pattern of salvation without eliminating the original context. Spiritually, Boaz combines strength, boundaries, and generosity, showing that holiness is demonstrated in protecting the weak within the economy and family.

references.author: Robert L. Hubbard Jr.
references.title: The Book of Ruth, NICOT, Eerdmans, 1988

entries.title: Balaam
entries.content: Balaam is a non-Israeli prophet or seer who is summoned by Balak, king of Moab, to curse Israel, but Numbers 22-24 depict the divine word resisting the king’s desire. The text does not present Balaam as an upright hero; He speaks in correct terms, and later texts reveal his connection to the temptation of Israel. The story of the talking donkey mocks the blindness of the Prophet, in which the animal sees what it does not see, and puts the prophetic talent to the test of obedience. Balaam's blessings include a promise to Israel and the image of a star and scepter, and have been received in various messianic ways by the Jewish and Christian tradition. A distinction must be made between the meaning of the prophecy in the context of the number and its subsequent interpretation, and between the written evidence and the known inscription from Deir Alla that clarifies the environment of the seers without proving a complete correspondence. Spiritually, the entry warns against separating religious knowledge from morality, and against turning talent into commerce or influence.

references.author: K. Lawson Younger Jr.
references.title: The Old Testament in Its World, 2002

entries.title: Belqis
entries.content: The Queen of Sheba in 1 Kings 10 and 2 Chronicles 9 is a foreign visitor who comes to Solomon with questions and riddles, to test his wisdom and see the order of his kingdom. The text highlights her ability to discern; She does not believe the news just because she hears it, but rather sees, examines, and then blesses the God of Israel. Yet the scene does not offer unqualified praise of royal wealth, because the abundance of gold and horses in Solomon's context needs to be read alongside Deuteronomy 17's warning against their accumulation. Matthew 12 compares the Queen of the South to a generation that rejects wisdom, and reuses the character as a call to respond to the word greater than Solomon. Historically, the identity of Sheba and the itinerary remain a subject of research, and the commercial similarity is not enough to prove every detail. Spiritually, the Queen represents the model of the seeker who tests, questions, and then responds, and at the same time warns that wisdom may turn into imperial showmanship.

references.author: Tikva Frymer-Kensky
references.title: Reading the Women of the Bible, Schocken, 2002

entries.title: Beersheba
entries.content: Beersheba is a place name and a memory of an era. In Genesis 21 it is linked to the oath of Abraham and Abimelech and the well of water, and in Genesis 26 Isaac renames the wells and establishes the connection to the land. The name is sometimes interpreted as a well and sometimes as an oath, and linguistic and narrative multiplicity should not be abolished. The city also appears as a starting point or residence for the fathers, and then becomes in the prophets a symbol of the network of centers of worship that need moral examination. The geographical location in the Negev demonstrates the value of water in a pastoral society, but wells are not only economic property; They are signs of conflict, loyalty and mutual recognition. Archaeological studies help chart the history of settlement, but they do not alone confirm every formative landscape. Spiritually, the entry links the gift of water with the responsibility of the covenant, and reminds that true peace does not abolish justice in the distribution of resources.

references.author: Anson F. Rainey and R. Steven Notley
references.title: The Sacred Bridge, Carta, 2006

entries.title: Bethlehem
entries.content: Bethlehem is a small city in Judah, but it expands within the narrative from David's homeland to a place of messianic hope. In Ruth, it is associated with bitterness, return, and harvest. Then the book ends by introducing the house of Ruth and Boaz into the lineage of David. In 1 Samuel, David is anointed, and the paradox of choosing a young man from a non-central family appears. Micah 5 links Ephrathah with the emergence of a ruler from a humble position, and Matthew rereads the text about the birth of Jesus within the debate of prophecy and identity. Geography should not be made into a separate proof of literature; The meaning arises from the network of David, Ruth, and the promise. The city reveals that divine action is not measured by the size of a place or its political center. Spiritually, Bethlehem combines poverty and hope, the memory of pain and the possibility of a small place becoming the bearer of a vast story of salvation.

references.author: Raymond E. Brown
references.title: The Birth of the Messiah, Doubleday, 1993

references.author: R. T. France
references.title: The Gospel of Matthew, NICNT, Eerdmans, 2007

entries.title: Bethel
entries.content: Bethel is the place of memory of the fathers and the struggle of worship. In Genesis 28, it is linked to Jacob's dream and the promise of presence and preservation, and then the city returns in the history of the kingdom as a religious center in the north. Therefore, the introduction reads it on two levels: the experience of the divine presence in the story of the fathers, and the transformation of the place into a tool of political legitimacy in the time of the kings. The research distinguishes between the sanctity of memory and the sanctity of the site, as the place does not guarantee the integrity of the community. In the Jewish tradition, Bethel continues within the geography of the fathers, while the Christian reading highlights the principle that God's presence is not confined to a building. Spiritually, the entrance calls for preserving memory while examining worship, so that the symbol that leads to God does not turn into a substitute for Him.

entries.title: Bethany
entries.content: Bethany is the village of friendship, illness, and resurrection in the Gospel of John, and the place where Jesus was received before the Passion. The story of Lazarus, Martha, and Mary reveals that faith does not eliminate sorrow; Martha confesses Christ while she is still facing the death of her brother, and Jesus weeps in front of the tomb before declaring himself resurrection and life. Anointing Mary with perfume adds to the consecration and preparation for burial. Not every detail of Bethany should be combined with other survey narratives without literary comparison. Historically, the village's proximity to Jerusalem helps understand Jesus' final movement. Spiritually, the entrance combines friendship, tears, hope and devotion.

references.author: Raymond E. Brown
references.title: The Gospel According to John I-XII, Anchor Bible 29, 1966

entries.title: Pete Vage
entries.content: Bethphage is a location on the road to Jerusalem in the Entry narratives, and functions geographically and narratively as a threshold between the road and the city. Its association with the Mount of Olives places Jesus' entry within the horizon of Zechariah and royal hope, but the image of the colt interprets royalty in a modest rather than imperial sense. The entry reads the Gospels' variation in scene arrangement without flattening it, and distinguishes between confirmed geography and later traditions that determined the location. Theologically, entry does not offer a quick political victory, but a path through rejection and the cross. Spiritually, the place calls to welcome a king who does not seek the glory of power.

entries.title: Bethsaida
entries.content: Bethsaida, a fishing town and the home of Andrew, Peter, and Philip, appears in the geography of Galilee and in narratives of healing and teaching. The name links maritime work to the local economy and invites students to leave behind the security of their habit. The healing of the blind man in Mark 8 comes gradually, a narrative detail that is consistent with the disciples' gradual understanding of Jesus' identity. Not every geographical difference between the Gospels should be turned into a contradiction before examining the texts and evidence. Spiritually, the introduction shows that seeing a miracle does not mean complete insight, and that discipleship is a path of understanding and obedience.

entries.title: Jerusalem
entries.content: Bayt al-Maqdis is an Arabic name for Jerusalem as the city of the temple, prayers and memory. The entry balances the promises of Zion in the Psalms and Prophets with criticism of the Temple when it is separated from justice. Jerusalem in the Gospels is the city of prophecy, rejection, and resurrection, and in the Revelation of John it is transformed into an image of the new city of God. The city's Jewish history must be respected and not reduced to later Christian use. A distinction must also be made between the promise of a place and political possession that justifies injustice. Spiritually, the city declares that holiness is inseparable from fidelity and mercy.

references.author: J. Gordon McConville
references.title: Exploring the Old Testament, Volume 4, IVP Academic, 2002

entries.title: Well
entries.content: The well in the book is a symbol of water, meeting, conflict, and survival. From the Well of the Patriarchs and Hagar to Jacob's Well and the Samaritan Dialogue, wells are linked to community life, land rights, and relationships between strangers. The name does not have a single fixed symbol; It may be an economic resource, a place for a sermon, or the subject of an advertisement. John 4 makes it clear that Jesus does not cancel the history of the well, but rather shifts the conversation from the necessary water to the inexhaustible gift of life. Historically, wells reveal the fragility of desert communities and their dependence on water management. Spiritually, the entrance combines thirst, hospitality, truth, and grace.

references.author: John H. Walton
references.title: Ancient Near Eastern Thought and the Old Testament, Baker Academic, 2006

entries.title: Orchard
entries.content: The garden is a space of fertility, work and encounter, but it can also become an image of possession and ruin. In Eden it is associated with life and choice, in the Song of Solomon with love and fertility, in the story of Naboth with kingship and injustice, and in John 18-20 with the scene of arrest, burial and resurrection. Therefore, it is not correct to establish a single symbolic meaning. The entry reads the orchard as a place that reveals man's relationship to the land, the body, and power. He also distinguishes between the agricultural background and the Christian interpretation of the Resurrection in the garden. Spiritually, the place links the preservation of creation with the rejection of exploitation and the hope of new life.

references.author: Adele Berlin
references.title: Poetics and Interpretation of Biblical Narrative, Eisenbrauns, 1994

references.author: John H. Walton
references.title: The IVP Bible Background Commentary, Zondervan, 2000

entries.title: Sea
entries.content: The sea in the narrative of Creation, Exodus, and the Gospel represents chaos, unity, and the path to salvation. In Exodus 14, Israel does not triumph through its own strength, but rather discovers that liberation comes from a confrontation with fear and empire. In the Psalms, the sea becomes part of the praise of the Creator, who sets an end to it. As for the Gospels, they use the storm to show the authority of Jesus and to expose the disciples’ fear to confidence. The sea should not be read as a rival god, as the biblical text de-divides it and places it under the authority of the Creator. Spiritually, the entry declares that chaos is not the last word, but faith does not absolve the responsibility of crossing danger with the community.

references.author: William P. Brown
references.title: The Seven Pillars of Creation, Oxford University Press, 2010

references.author: Richard Bauckham
references.title: The Theology of the Book of Revelation, Cambridge University Press, 1993

entries.title: Sea of Galilee
entries.content: The Sea of Galilee is an environment of fishing, storms, and calling, not just a backdrop for Jesus’ miracles. The entry links the fishing economy to the call to the disciples, to power over wind and fear in Mark 4, and to bread and water in John 6. The functions of the sea differ between the Gospels, so each narrative is read within its structure. Geography and sudden winds help understand the realism of the danger, but they do not reduce the miracle to a natural explanation. Spiritually, the sea becomes a school of trust and responsibility, where disciples learn that Christ's presence does not mean the absence of the storm.

entries.title: Sea of Souf
entries.content: The Sea of Suf in the story of the Exodus is a place of crossing, judgment, and the birth of a community. The geographical identification of the name remains a matter of debate, and modern certainty cannot be built from translation alone, but the narrative function of place is clear: a defenseless people confronts Pharaoh's army and then experiences a salvation that the Song of Moses interprets as the work of the Lord. Later texts re-invoke the crossing as a memory of liberation, and Paul reuses it in reading community baptism. The entry distinguishes between event, symbol and subsequent reception. Spiritually, crossing does not mean the end of the road, but rather the beginning of faithfulness in the wilderness.

references.author: Brevard S. Childs
references.title: The Book of Exodus, Westminster Press, 1974

entries.title: Wilderness
entries.content: The wilderness is not only a geographical void, but a school of testing and certification. The entry brings together manna, thirst, rebellion, and the presence of God, then traces how the prophets and the Gospel repurposed the wilderness as a space of renewal and invitation.

references.author: Brevard S. Childs
references.title: The Book of Exodus, Westminster Press, 1974

references.author: John H. Walton
references.title: Ancient Near Eastern Thought and the Old Testament, Baker Academic, 2006

entries.title: Blessing
entries.content: Blessing in the book is a word, a promise, and a relationship, not a magical substance or a guarantee of wealth. The introduction studies the blessing of the fathers, the blessing of the priest, and the blessing of Christ, distinguishing between God’s gift and man’s responsibility toward his neighbor.

references.author: John Goldingay
references.title: Old Testament Theology, Volume 1, IVP Academic, 2003

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright
references.title: Old Testament Ethics for the People of God, IVP Academic, 2004

entries.title: Leprosy
entries.content: In ancient texts, leprosy is a complex ritual and social condition that is not automatically equated with modern sin or disease. The entry presents the system of isolation and purification and then reads Jesus' healing as the restoration of man to the community.

references.author: Christine E. Hayes
references.title: Introduction to the Bible, Yale University Press, 2012

entries.title: Lightning
entries.content: Lightning is an image of appearance, power, and thunder in the language of the book, but it does not make natural phenomena gods. The introduction links the language of the storm in the Psalms and the Prophets with the declaration of God’s sovereignty over creation.

references.author: John H. Walton
references.title: The Lost World of Genesis One, IVP Academic, 2009

entries.title: Incense
entries.content: Incense is an article of worship, prayer, and priestly boundaries. The entry explains that his scent does not buy the divine presence, but rather works within a system of holiness, and then appears in the vision as an image of the prayers of the saints.

entries.title: Trumpet
entries.content: The trumpet is a tool of announcement, mobilization, war, and celebration, and its meaning changes according to the context. The entry combines the feasts of Israel, the fall of Jericho, and the image of the Resurrection, while rejecting the mechanical reading of the symbol.

entries.title: Benjamin
entries.content: Benjamin is a tribe located between the north and the south, and its identity appears between the story of Rachel, the blessing of Jacob, the wars of the judges, Saul, and Paul. The entry examines how lineages create memory without erasing historical tensions.

entries.title: Benhadad
entries.content: Benhadad is a name for the kings of Aram in successive narratives, so they should not be combined without examining lineage and time. The introduction reveals the relationship of war to diplomacy, the limits of the king's victory, and criticism of reliance on alliances.

references.author: Iain Provan
references.title: 1 and 2 Kings, New International Biblical Commentary, 1995

entries.title: Pinhas
entries.content: Pinchas the priest is a jealous character in verse 25, and then his name becomes a sign of lineage and service. The entry presents the tension of covenant jealousy with the danger of justifying violence, and compares the original text with the reception of later tradition.

references.author: Tikva Frymer-Kensky
references.title: Reading the Women of the Bible, Schocken, 2002

entries.title: Babylonian
entries.content: Babylonian describes the language, culture, or exile associated with Babylon, and should not be reduced to a single religious identity. The entry examines the impact of translation, displacement, and the reshaping of Jewish memory under the empire.

references.author: Carol A. Newsom
references.title: Daniel, Old Testament Library, Westminster John Knox, 2014

entries.title: Virgin
entries.content: The firstborn in Sharia law is a sign of priority, responsibility, and redemption, not absolute privilege. The introduction traces the transition of the concept from the multiplication of Egypt's firstborn to the consecration of the firstborn, and then reads it in light of Christ's birth and worship.

entries.title: The sons of Korah
entries.content: The sons of Korah are a priestly group and the name of a group of psalms, and their story shows between rebellion, mercy, and continuity. The introduction shows that family failure does not eliminate the possibility of serving subsequent generations, and that worship preserves memory with criticism and hope.

entries.title: Pharaoh's daughter
entries.content: Bint Pharaoh is a relatively silent figure but crucial to saving Moses' life. Her story reveals that resistance to death can come from within the home of empire, and that God's providence works through one woman's courage and compassion beyond measure.

references.author: Brevard S. Childs
references.title: The Book of Exodus, Westminster Press, 1974

entries.title: Baal
entries.content: Baal is the name of a Canaanite god and religious title, and appears in the book within the struggle for loyalty, fertility, and power. The entry takes advantage of the Ugaritic background without equating the biblical text with it, and reads Elijah's confrontation as a critique of worship and injustice.

references.author: Mark S. Smith
references.title: The Early History of God, Eerdmans, 2002

references.author: John Day
references.title: Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan, Sheffield Academic Press, 2002

entries.title: Baasha
entries.content: Baasha, King of Israel, escalates with violence and then repeats the sin of Jeroboam, his story offering a critique of the cycle of political upheaval. The introduction links prophecy and legitimacy, and shows that changing the ruling family does not mean changing the worship of the kingdom.

references.author: Walter Brueggemann
references.title: First and Second Kings, Smyth & Helwys, 2000

entries.title: Barzilai
entries.content: Barzillai, a Gileadite man, supports David during his time of flight and then refuses the reward of the palace in his old age. The entry reveals the virtue of non-possessive giving, the limits of political loyalty, and the memory of characters who work without seeking glory.

references.author: Robert Alter
references.title: The David Story, W. W. Norton, 1999

entries.title: Praya
entries.content: Praya is a name that appears in genealogical and service lists, and the lack of evidence prevents the construction of an imaginary biography. The introduction explains the value of small names in preserving the history of the group, and the necessity of adjusting the text before concluding.

references.author: Sara Japhet
references.title: I & II Chronicles, Old Testament Library, 1993

entries.title: Good news
entries.content: The good news in written revelation is news of a divine action that demands a response, not fleeting optimism. The entry compares the good news of Isaiah, the good news of birth, and the good news of the resurrection, and connects the news to peace, justice, and hope.

entries.title: Insight
entries.content: Insight into wisdom is the ability to discern the path of life, not an intelligence separated from the fear of the Lord. The introduction examines the relationship of knowledge and obedience, and how insight in the New Testament becomes the fruit of love and spiritual discernment.

entries.title: Blessing of the covenant
entries.content: Covenant blessing is not an isolated, individual promise, but a relationship that includes memory, lineage, justice, and worship. The introduction links the era of Abraham and Sinai with the New Testament, distinguishing between the continuity of the promise and its different historical stages.

references.author: Moshe Weinfeld
references.title: The Promise of the Land, University of California Press, 1993

references.author: F. F. Bruce
references.title: The Epistle to the Hebrews, Eerdmans, 1990

entries.title: Ark of the Covenant
entries.content: The Ark of the Covenant is a sign of the presence of the covenant, not an amulet that guarantees victory. In Exodus 25, it is associated with the mercy seat, the cherubim, and the sanctity of the approach, and in 1 Samuel 4, carrying it into battle reveals the error of turning the sacred into a political tool. Then David places the ark in the heart of Jerusalem, but the story of Azzah reminds us that joy does not cancel the limits of holiness. In the Jewish tradition the ark is associated with memory, the temple, and the Shekhina, while the Hebrews read its symbols in the course of the New Testament. Spiritually, the entrance calls for seeking God's presence, not possessing His symbols.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Terah
entries.content: Terah, Abram's father, in Genesis 11, appears at the point of transition from Ur to Haran. The text does not provide a complete spiritual biography of him, and therefore it should not be burdened with what it does not mention. However, its narrative role links family history to Abraham's calling, and Acts 7 rereads the Exodus as the beginning of God's initiative. The introduction distinguishes between the family's movement before the call and Abraham's movement after it, and between biblical data and geographical hypotheses about Ur. Spiritually, it highlights that God's work may begin within an incomplete family history.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Tabitha
entries.content: Tabitha, or Dorcas, was a disciple in Joppa who was famous for good deeds and making clothes for widows. Her death and resurrection at the hands of Peter in Acts 9 does not cancel the value of her previous service, but rather reveals that the community remembered the faith through its social impact. The difference in the name between Aramaic and Greek explains the multiplicity of linguistic environments in the early church. The story should not be turned into a mechanical promise to abolish death; it is an apostolic sign within a foundational phase. Spiritually, the entrance links piety, tangible giving, and the dignity of widows.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Timothy
entries.content: Timothy is Paul's partner in the mission, and the letters present him as a young man learning to persevere in the midst of pastoral responsibility. His relationship with Paul combines spiritual fatherhood and assignment, but the text does not justify erasing his character or turning him into a copy of his teacher. In 1 Timothy, service is linked to education, conduct, and controlling money and relationships, and in 2 Timothy to endurance and keeping what is entrusted. The research discusses the proportion and history of the pastoral letters, so the opinion must be presented, not hidden. Spiritually, the entry shows that maturity is a long service that requires education and courage.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Titus
entries.content:
Key Evidence: 2 Corinthians 2:12-13; 7:5-16; Galatians 2:1-5; Titus 1:1-5.

Place and context: Corinth, Crete and the apostolic churches.

People associated with the text: Paul, Timothy, the churches of Corinth and Crete.

Theological study: Titus, Paul's international partner in the Corinthian crisis and the organization of the churches of Crete. Paul states that he was not obligated to undergo circumcision, so his presence becomes a living witness to the acceptance of Gentiles without imposing conversion to a Jewish identity. The Epistle to Titus does not reduce it to a list of positions, but rather links sound teaching with behavior that adorns the Gospel and non-profit care.

references.author: The New International Dictionary of Old Testament Theology and Exegesis
references.title: Zondervan, 1997

references.author: The New International Dictionary of New Testament Theology
references.title: Zondervan, 1975-1978

entries.title: Thomas
entries.content: Thomas in the Gospel of John is not just an example of doubt, but a disciple who asks to see the mark of the cross before he professes faith. His absence from the group first, then his confession, “My Lord and my God,” places testimony within a relationship between experience, community, and recognition. The title of skeptic should not be used to dismiss the rest of his character or ignore his appearances in John 11 and 14. The later traditions of Thomas are numerous, but they are not equal to John's text. Spiritually, the entry shows that sincere questioning can become a path to deep worship, provided it does not turn into a permanent rejection of witness.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Tadros
entries.content: Tadros is a name that appears in the lists of the apostles, and is linked in some traditions to Judah, son of Jacob, but the texts do not provide an extensive biography. The biblical name and later church traditions must be distinguished from the letter and the martyrdom. The lists reveal that the apostolic group has many names and backgrounds, and that the importance of the apostle is not measured by the amount of news about him. The entry reads the silence of the text carefully, and prevents the making of history from undocumented myths. Spiritually, it reminds us that honesty may be real even when history does not preserve the details of its owner.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Repentance
entries.content: Repentance in the book is a comprehensive return to God, not just psychological remorse. In the Prophets it is associated with abandoning injustice and idolatry, in the Psalms with a confession seeking a new heart, and in the New Testament with a call to faith and a new life. The introduction distinguishes between remorse, repentance, and the fruits of repentance, and between individual repentance and group reform. He also rejects the use of repentance to condemn the victim or cover up the absence of justice. Spiritually, it is a return to the covenant that appears in behavior and compassion, not a verbal formula separate from changing the path.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Piety
entries.content: Piety in the book is the fear of the Lord and a life before His presence, and it is not a religious appearance or isolation from society. Pious wisdom presents the beginning of knowledge, and links messages to it with contentment, control of greed, and service to others. The introduction needs to distinguish between biblical piety and social religiosity, and between worship that produces mercy and ritual that is used to cover up injustice. In the Jewish context, the fear of God remains linked to Torah and community, and in the Christian reading it appears in following Christ. Spiritually, piety is a daily trust embodied in secret and in public.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Reverence
entries.content: Sanctification in the Torah is a separation of God and an arrangement of life before the Holy, and it does not mean that a person gains independence from grace. Leviticus explains the relationship between purity and closeness, while the Epistles speak of the believer's sanctification in Christ and of a continuing path that extends to the body and relationships. The introduction distinguishes between ritual and moral sanctification, and between divine initiative and human response. It is not right to use holiness to isolate the weak or impose an illusion of perfection; Biblical holiness is associated with mercy and justice. Spiritually, it is transforming daily life into an area of ​​faithfulness to God.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Atonement
entries.content: Atonement in Leviticus is not an automatic erasure of guilt, but a system of approach and restoration within the covenant relationship. The Torah distinguishes between sin, impurity, and sacrifice, and places the Day of Atonement at the center of treatment of communal impurity. Hebrews reads these symbols in light of Christ, but a responsible Christian reading begins with the original priestly meaning and does not eliminate Judaism's ritual history. Spiritually, atonement is linked to confession, holiness, and mercy, not to buying into or manipulating God.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Composition
entries.content: Genesis is the name of a book and the beginning of the act of creation and identity building. Genesis presents Creation, the Flood, and the Patriarchs within the Promise Path, and should not be read as a natural science book separate from its literary and theological genre. The themes of the divine image, the fall, lineage, the earth, and the covenant are repeated in it. Studies compare it with Near Eastern literature while preserving the peculiarity of biblical monotheism. Spiritually, formation places man as a gift and a responsibility before the Creator.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Deuteronomy
entries.content: Deuteronomy is not only a legal repetition, but a covenant renewal speech before entering the earth. Israel calls for hearing, love, and justice, and links blessing to obedience, not mechanical possession. The entry examines the structure of the discourse and its relationship to Josiah's reform and the theology of election, while presenting the controversy over the historical composition of the book. In the Jewish tradition, the centrality of the Shema and the Torah is clear, and in the New Testament Jesus and Paul cite it. Spiritually, remembrance is a condition for faithfulness.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Students
entries.content: Disciples are a group learning to follow Jesus, not a rank that grants immunity from error. The Gospels present their misunderstanding, fear, and then their testimony, while the Book of Acts expands the meaning of Spirit community discipleship and ministry. A distinction should be made between the Twelve and the rest of the disciples, and the later church structures should not be projected directly onto the first century. Spiritually, discipleship is listening, obedience, testimony, and service, not just knowing names.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Education
entries.content: Education in the book is an act of handing over memory and covenant and forming a community. In Deuteronomy 6 it starts from the home, in Ezra and Nehemiah it is linked to reading and understanding the law, and in the early church it is linked to the teaching of the apostles. The introduction distinguishes between teaching and automatic memorization, and between the teacher’s authority and moral responsibility. The Jewish background of the school and the scribes is essential to understanding the texts. Spiritually, education is a trust that liberates the conscience and does not use it to control.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Praise
entries.content: Praise is a response to God’s work, but in the Psalms it includes complaining, waiting, and remembering, not just superficial joy. It is linked in the temple to the liturgy, in Exodus to the memory of liberation, and in the New Testament to a community that expands to the nations. It is not right to separate praise from justice, as the prophets criticize songs that cover injustice. Spiritually, praise preserves the whole truth and realigns fear around God's faithfulness.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Chanting
entries.content: Chanting is a collective practice that preserves faith and memory through language and music. The Psalms of Graduation and Alleluia provide models for worship that moves between uplift, distress, and hope, while the New Testament Epistles situate singing within the encouragement of the congregation. Singing should not be reduced to musical taste; Its function is educational and theological as well. Spiritually, the community becomes one voice without eliminating the diversity of its experiences.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Dust
entries.content: Dust in Genesis is a sign of man's origin and annihilation, but it is not an evil substance. From the dust God forms Adam, and to the dust he returns after the fall, and in the symbols of the prophets he is associated with humility and resurrection. The approach rejects the separation between body and soul in a simplistic philosophical manner, and reads creation within the goodness of matter and human responsibility. Spiritually, dust confronts pride and confirms the hope of renewal.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Heritage
entries.content: The biblical heritage is not a static repetition of the past, but rather a memory that is reinterpreted in new crises. The books recall Exodus, the Patriarchs, and the Temple to ask about faithfulness in the present, while Jesus distinguishes between God's command and human traditions that abolish mercy. It is not permissible to reject every tradition nor sanctify every inheritance; The criterion is its relationship to covenant and justice. Spiritually, heritage preserves memory and requires discernment.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Torah
entries.content: Torah means teaching or guidance before it means abstract law. In the Psalms it is a path of life and joy, in the Covenant it is read within God’s relationship with his people, and in Paul it enters into the debate of promise, faith and the nations. A superficial comparison between Torah and grace should be avoided, with the Mishnah and Talmud serving as a later reception history. Spiritually, the approach links obedience with love and justice rather than legalistic fear.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Translation
entries.content: Translation is an act of interpretation and transfer between languages and cultures, not the mechanical replacement of words. The Septuagint, Syriac and Latin translations reveal the reception history of the text, while comparison of Hebrew and Greek remains essential when constructing the doctrine. The introduction distinguishes between translation differences and manuscript differences, and between the original meaning and subsequent interpretation. Spiritually, translation calls for honesty and humility in the face of multilingualism.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Splatter
entries.content: Tarshish is a name associated with the sea, trade, and long-distance journeys. It appears in the story of Jonah, Solomon’s trade, and prophecies. Its location has not been determined in all places, so the entry distinguishes between several geographical hypotheses and the literary function of the name. Tarshish reveals the vastness of the ancient world and its trade networks, and prophecies warn against reliance on sea power and wealth.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Incarnate
entries.content: The Incarnation in Christian reading is the declaration that the Word became man, but it should be taught through the texts of John, Paul, and the Gospels, not as a separate slogan. The concept preserves the goodness of the body and the realism of history, and refuses to turn salvation into an escape from creation. The entry draws on the background of Jewish monotheism and discussions of the early church, and distinguishes the revealed doctrine from later philosophical formulations.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Transfiguration
entries.content: The Transfiguration is a scene announcing the identity of Jesus in the presence of Moses and Elijah, and places glory within the path of the cross, not an alternative to it. The details of the Gospels vary, but the cloud, the sound, and the mountain recall the language of Sinai and prophecy. Transfiguration should not be separated from teaching disciples about suffering and discipleship. Spiritually, it reveals the glory that leads to hearing and obedience, not to having experience.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Experience
entries.content: The experience in the book is a test that reveals the heart, and it may be a test or a temptation depending on the context. The introduction distinguishes between Israel's experience in the wilderness and Jesus' experience, and between God allowing testing and doing evil. The text does not justify blaming the sufferer or considering every crisis a punishment. Spiritually, testing becomes an area of ​​steadfastness, discernment, and reliance on the Word of God.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Discipline
entries.content: Discipline in wisdom, parenting, and covenant is not uncontrolled revenge, but rather life-oriented correction when exercised justly. The Epistles discuss God's discipline within the filial relationship, but it should not be used to justify domestic violence. The introduction distinguishes between divine discipline and human interpretation of pain, and links maturity with wisdom and mercy.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Meditate
entries.content: Written meditation is not a mental emptiness, but rather a remembrance of God’s word and contemplation of His works. Psalm 1 describes contemplation of the Torah as a path of life, and the wisdom texts link it to behavior, not information. The entry distinguishes between Hebrew meditation and modern practices that may only borrow the name. Spiritually, meditation reshapes desire, decision, and hope.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Offering
entries.content: The offering in the Torah is a gift brought before God within the system of worship, and not a bribe to obtain blessing. Sacrifices differentiate between their functions, and the offering preserves man’s relationship with the land, work, and gratitude. Hebrews reads these symbols into the path of Christ, but does not eliminate their historical meaning. Spiritually, giving is an acknowledgment that what we have is a gift and a responsibility.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Souvenir
entries.content: Commemoration in the book is a present action that restores salvation and forms community, not nostalgia for the past. Easter connects the new generation with the Exodus, monuments preserve the events of the covenant, and the Supper in the Christian tradition recalls the death of Christ and the hope of his coming. The introduction distinguishes between living memory and the glorification of the past, and links remembrance to justice and honesty.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Set
entries.content: Appointment or calling in the biblical texts is linked to God's initiative and to the responsibility of the person and the community. Choice does not mean unaccountable privilege; Prophets and kings are condemned when they betray the covenant. The entry distinguishes between textual vocation and personal vocation, and reads it within gifts, service, and collective distinction. Spiritually, the call is a trust, not a platform for oneself.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: He sets out
entries.content: Westernization in the book is an experience of uprooting and temporary residence, but it is not an absence from God’s care. Abraham, Israel, and the Exiles read the sojourn within the promise, while the Epistles place the believer in the world without assimilation or hatred. The introduction distinguishes between forced and voluntary migration, and between the theology of hope and the justification of injustice. Spiritually, alienation turns into honesty, hospitality, and waiting.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: History of salvation
entries.content: The history of salvation is not a collection of sacred events, but rather a reading of the path of God's initiatives, covenants, judgment, and mercy. It begins with creation and promise, goes through the Exodus, kingship, and captivity, and then the Gospels reformulate it around Christ's death and resurrection. The entry refuses to erase Israel's history or jump beyond the Old Testament, and distinguishes between the event and subsequent theological interpretation.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Crown
entries.content: The crown is a sign of royalty and responsibility, and may appear in the king, the priest, the wedding, and the prophetic image. The crown does not give its owner an absolute right; Kingship is under the covenant, and dignity is tested by justice. The study compares material crowns and the wreath of life in the New Testament, while being careful not to turn the symbol into a promise of worldly success.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Dragon
entries.content: The dragon in apocalyptic literature is an image of the power of chaos and hostility, and the Book of Revelation uses symbolic language associated with the beast, power, and accusation. It should not be transferred to an independent legend or equated with every ancient animal. The entry places the image in the struggle of worship and political loyalty, where God's victory does not eliminate the pain of martyrdom but determines its end.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Fig
entries.content: The fig tree is a tree of food and a sign of fertility and wisdom. It appears in the prophetic parable, the story of the fig tree that does not bear fruit, and in the teaching of Jesus. It is not permissible to reduce every mention of it to one meaning; The context determines whether it is a provision, judgment, or a sign of time. Spiritually, the approach links fruitfulness to responsibility and patience, not to religious appearance alone.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Fig
entries.content: Figs are among the crops of the earth that are associated with peace and abundance, but the destruction of the vines and figs becomes in the prophets a sign of economic and spiritual judgment. The entry examines agriculture and symbolism together, and shows that agricultural blessing is not a moral guarantee. In Christian reading, the tension between tree and fruit continues as an image of faithfulness.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Dregs
entries.content: The dregs or residue in the pictures of the book may refer to what is thrown out or to a trace after the sifting, and therefore needs to adjust the translation and context before constructing a symbol. The introduction distinguishes between material use and a moral image that compares the pure and the bad. Spiritually, it calls for examining what remains of faith after testing without contempt for man.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Pricing
entries.content: Pricing in the ancient world is linked to the valuation of land, labor, and goods, and Sharia law reveals that economics is inseparable from justice and protecting the poor. It is not enough to read prices as numbers; one must understand power, debt, and monopoly. Spiritually, the entrance tests the faithfulness of the community when profit turns into exploitation.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Unification
entries.content: Monotheism in the book is a declaration that God alone is God, but it includes loyalty, worship, and justice, and is not just a philosophical statement. Deuteronomy 6 places love and hearing at its heart, and the prophets criticize the combination of the name of the Lord and injustice. The entry makes use of a comparison of Near Eastern religions without equating biblical monotheism with surrounding systems, and then traces its presence in the Christian faith.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Books of Moses; Prophets; Gospels and Epistles

references.author: Christopher J. H. Wright, The Mission of God, IVP Academic

entries.title: Tamar
entries.content:
Meaning in original: Hebrew תָּמָר (Tamar); Palm or date palm; A feminine name associated with fertility and dignity in the book world.

Tamar in Genesis 38 is not a marginal character, but rather reveals how truth operates within the structure of lineage and kinship. When Judah withholds her rights, she uses available means to seek justice, and Judah then acknowledges that her righteousness is more just than his. Ruth and Matthew reinsert her into the lineage of David and Christ, with her origin story remaining linked to injustice, lineage, and responsibility.

entries.title: Thyatira
entries.content:
Meaning in original: Greek Θυάτειρα (Thyateira); The name of a city in Asia Minor, whose etymological origin is uncertain; Therefore, it is not given a definitive symbolic meaning.

Thyatira is a city in the Book of Revelation and home to Lydia in Acts 16, and is associated with crafts, industry, and trade networks. The message of Revelation to the Church balances love and service with tolerance for deviant teaching, linking economic life with discernment in worship. The image of Jezebel should not be projected onto a contemporary woman; The text deals with leadership and education within a specific group.

entries.content:
Meaning in original: Hebrew פְּרִי (peri), Greek καρπός (karpos); Fruit or crop, used figuratively for the result of behavior or education.

Fruit in the book is the result of life and direction, not external adornment. Wisdom and the prophets use the image of the fruit to judge Israel, and Jesus uses it to judge the false prophet and disciple. Fruit does not mean financial success, but rather appears in justice, repentance, and love of God and neighbor. Paul links the fruit of the Spirit to the formation of a new personality within the community.

entries.title: A dress
entries.content:
Meaning in original: Hebrew בֶּגֶד (beged), Greek ἱμάτιον (himation); clothing or clothing; Contextually, it may indicate identity and dignity or mourning and function.

In the book, clothing is a sign of identity, dignity, mourning, and function. Joseph takes off his robe in the story of betrayal, and the priest's robe appears within the system of holiness, and the Gospels use the robe to ridicule Jesus' kingship and to honor him. Not every garment should be turned into a single symbol; Its meaning is shaped by its owner and the social and ritual scene.

entries.content:
Meaning in original: Hebrew שֶׁלֶג (sheleg); snow; A natural phenomenon and an image of whiteness or purification depending on the context.

Snow is a natural image that is rarely present but rich in meaning: it is mentioned in describing whiteness and purification, and in judging God’s ability to organize creation. In Isaiah, whiteness becomes an image of the forgiveness of sin, and in Job a sign of the forces of nature that man has no control over. The introduction distinguishes between the climatic phenomenon and the poetic image.

entries.title: bull
entries.content:
Meaning in original: Hebrew שׁוֹר (shor), Greek ταῦρος (tauros); ox or cow; An animal for work, wealth, and sacrifice, not a god in and of itself.

The bull is an animal of work, sacrifice, and wealth, and therefore its texts reveal both economy and worship. Sharia law protects the animal from exploitation, and bulls are included in sacrifices and as the golden calf. It is not correct to equate an animal that is permissible for sacrifice with an idol. Context defines the difference between the gift of worship and the replacement of God with an image.

entries.title: Fox
entries.content:
Meaning in original: Hebrew שׁוּעָל (shual), Greek ἀλώπηξ (alōpēx); fox; An image of deception, ruin, or destructive smallness, according to the text.

The fox in the book is an image of ruin, cunning, and destructive weakness. Samson uses it in an act of revenge, Nehemiah uses it to mock a dilapidated wall, while Jesus warns of Herod's cunning in the language of the fox. The entry shows that animal images do not give a comprehensive judgment about animals or people, but rather serve a specific literary scene.

entries.title: Loophole
entries.content:
Meaning in original: Hebrew פֶּרֶץ (perets); A breach or opening in a fence; It is used metaphorically for a place of weakness that needs restoration and guarding.

The vulnerability in the language of war and construction is a place of weakness that allows for penetration, but it also reveals the responsibility of the guard and the group. The Books of Kings and Nehemiah depict walls as political security rather than absolute guarantee, as reliance on God and justice remains more important than stone. The entry reads military language without glorifying violence.

entries.title: Tuck
entries.content:
Meaning in the original: Hebrew מַעֲלֶה (maʿaleh) or דֶּרֶךְ (derekh) depending on the position; An uphill or turning road; There is no single fixed Hebrew equivalent for this Arabic drawing, so it is necessary to specify the witness before confirming.

A fold in the language of biblical geography means a passage or bend between terrain, and appears in place names or road descriptions. Geography should not be invented from a single word; The Hebrew context, translations and maps need to be examined. The value of the entry is systematic: it reminds of the limits of certainty in ancient place names.

entries.title: Trust
entries.content:
Meaning in original: Hebrew בָּטַח (bataḥ), Greek πεποίθησις (pepoithēsis); Reliability, security and stability; An act of relationship, not just an internal feeling.

Trusting the Bible is not unsubstantiated optimism, but rather relying on God’s faithfulness in the midst of danger. It appears in the Psalms as prayer, in Abraham as expectation of the promise, and in the New Testament as faith in Christ. Confidence does not eliminate complaints or questions, but rather prevents fear from becoming the master of the decision.

entries.content:
Meaning in original: Hebrew אָמַן (aman), Greek ὑπομονή (hypomonē); Faithfulness, stability and endurance; The context determines whether what is meant is sincerity of the covenant or patience in distress.

Constancy is a covenantal virtue related to continuing faithfulness, not stagnation. The book links him to patience in distress and preserving learning, while the novels warn of an apparent stability that hides a divided heart. The entry reads fortitude as an act of grace, response, and collective responsibility.

entries.title: Revenge
entries.content:
Meaning in original: Hebrew נָקַם (naqam), Greek ἐκδίκησις (ekdikēsis); revenge or redress; Sharia separates the protection of blood from uncontrolled personal revenge.

Blood feud in the ancient world is a system of kinship to protect blood, but the book sets limits on it and prohibits uncontrolled personal revenge. The stories of David, Saul, and the cities of refuge demonstrate the difference between seeking justice and taking up the sword out of anger. The text may not be used to justify contemporary violence; Rather, the introduction studies the shift of responsibility from revenge to justice and mercy.

entries.title: Price
entries.content:
Meaning in original: Hebrew מְחִיר (meḥir), Greek τιμή (timē); price, value or dignity; The meaning differs between the market, redemption, and consecration.

Price in economic and theological texts reveals the value of land, labor, slavery, and redemption. The book does not present every financial value as evil, but it criticizes the buying of a person, the selling of the poor, and the exploitation of need. In the New Testament, discipleship is linked to cost, not to the purchase of grace. The entry distinguishes between commercial price and the language of consecration and redemption.

entries.title: Wealth
entries.content:
Meaning in original: Hebrew הוֹן (hon), Greek πλοῦτος (ploutos); Money or wealth; A gift, a responsibility, and a test of justice, not an automatic proof of blessing.

Wealth in wisdom is a potential gift and a dangerous responsibility. Deuteronomy links blessing to land, but the prophets expose the injustice of the rich, and Jesus makes money a test of loyalty rather than a criterion of acceptance. The study does not equate poverty with holiness, but rather asks about the source of money, the way it is used, and the rights of the weak.

entries.title: Breast
entries.content:
Meaning in original: Hebrew שַׁד (shad), Greek μαστός (mastós); breast; An image of nutrition, fertility, motherhood or the language of poetic love.

The breast, in the language of the book, is an image of nutrition, fertility, and a maternal relationship, and it may appear in poetry with physical frankness that should not be obscured or turned into vulgarity. Isaiah uses the image to comfort Jerusalem, and the Song of Songs uses the language of love. The introduction distinguishes between the body as a gift and an erotic reading separated from literature and context.

entries.title: The weight of the law
entries.content:
Meaning in the original: not a fixed original expression; It is related, according to the context, to the word Torah: תּוֹרָה (torah); Education or guidance, not necessarily a burden; The title is an interpretive formulation that should not be attributed to a single Hebrew word.

This is an explanatory statement on the concept of Sharia burden and is not a standalone biblical statement, so it is presented with caution. The New Testament discusses the relationship between circumcision, the nations, and the law, while it is not correct to describe the Jewish Torah as a single burden in every context. It is also education, grace and identity. The introduction distinguishes between Pauline criticism of some uses of the law and the abolition of the law.

entries.title: Fruit of the Spirit
entries.content:
Meaning in the original: Greek καρπὸς τοῦ πνεύματος (karpos tou pneumatos); fruit of the spirit; The result of the Spirit's work in the believer's personality and relationships, not a separate list of virtues.

The Fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5 is a comprehensive description of a character formed in freedom and love, not a separate list of virtues. Paul contrasts it with the works of the flesh, placing morality within a collective struggle between ways of life. Fruit does not mean immediate perfection, but growth that appears in relationships, control of desire, and service to one's neighbor.

entries.title: The fruit of righteousness
entries.content:
Meaning in original: Greek καρπὸς δικαιοσύνης (karpos dikaiosynēs); The fruit of righteousness or the result of righteousness; Behavior that arises from a correct relationship with God and appears in love and good deeds.

The fruit of righteousness is an image that combines the moral result and the work of God in man. In Isaiah, righteousness is associated with peace, and in the New Testament letters with the distinction of love and good deeds. The introduction refuses to separate belief from behavior, and it refuses to turn actions into a means of purchasing salvation.

entries.title: Serious
entries.content: Gad in Hebrew גָּד (Gad) is related to the name of happiness or luck, and it is the name of the son of Jacob and a tribe that settled east of the Jordan. Genesis 49 mentions his poetic power and limitations, and Joshua and Judges present his presence in an area vulnerable to invasion. He was contemporary with the rest of the tribes of Jacob, Moses, and Joshua, and characters from his tribe appear later in the time of David. Biblical witness: Genesis 30:11; 49:19; Number 32; Joshua 13:24-28; 1 Chronicles 12:8-15. The introduction links the name to tribal identity and the tribe's responsibility to defend the group, while not turning the meaning of the name into an inevitable judgment on character.

entries.title: Gabriel
entries.content: Gabriel in Hebrew גַּבְרִיאֵל (Gavri'el), meaning the power of God or the man of God, is an angel who interprets visions in Daniel and announces the good news in Luke. He appears in the context of captivity and hope, then in Nazareth in front of Mary, and his textual contemporaries Daniel, Mary, Zechariah, and John the Baptist. The book does not present an independent theology of angels from his biography, but rather makes him a messenger subject to God's initiative. Biblical witness: Daniel 8:15-27; 9:20-27; Luke 1:11-20, 26-38. The research distinguishes between the biblical text and later Jewish and Christian traditions that expanded on its functions.

entries.title: Gideon
entries.content: Gideon, from גִּדְעוֹן (Gid'on), is related to the root of cutting or demolition. His call in Judges 6 begins with the demolition of the altar of Baal, and then God reduces his army so that victory is not attributed to numbers. The place is Ophrah, the Valley of Jezreel, and Midian, and its contemporaries are Deborah and Barak in the earlier memory, and Zebah and Zalmunna in the later battle. The story doesn't end perfectly; His rejection of kingship is met with the making of the ephod, which becomes a trap. Biblical witness: Judges 6-8; Hebrews 11:32. Spiritually, the entrance pits humility against power and the danger of turning a sign of salvation into a center of worship.

entries.title: Gilead
entries.content: Gilead from גִּלְעָד (Gil'ad), a mountainous region east of the Jordan and the name of a person and descendant. The region is associated with balsam, borders, and conflict between Israel, Aram, and Ammon, and Jephthah and Elijah appear in various traditions. Not every use of the name should be lumped into one entity; The context determines whether the target is land, family, or person. Biblical witness: Genesis 21:31-55; Number 32; Judges 10-12; 1 Kings 17:1. His contemporaries were Jacob and Laban, or Jephthah and the elders of Gilead, according to the textual unit. The study reveals that geographical borders become a memory of identity and responsibility.

entries.title: Goliath
entries.content: Goliath, from גָּלְיָת (Golyat), a Palestinian name for which a certain Hebrew derivation is not proven. He stands in the Butm Valley between two armies, and his duel turns into a test of confidence, not the standards of weapons. David is his textual contemporary, and Samuel also mentions other men from Gath in later accounts. Its length numbers differ in some textual evidence, so the study presents the difference in transmission and does not build a belief on the number. Biblical witness: 1 Samuel 17; 2 Samuel 21:19; 1 Chronicles 20:5. Spiritually, the entry does not glorify violence, but rather reads it within a critique of reliance on force.

entries.title: Paradise
entries.content: Paradise is from גַּן (gan), a garden or garden, and from עֵדֶן (Eden), the name of a place or connotation of pleasure according to linguistic discussion. The Garden of Eden is the place of creation, testing, and fall, then its images return in the prophets and Revelation 22. The contemporaries of its events are Adam, Eve, and the serpent, while it later functions as a theological memory and not as a settled archaeological site. Biblical witness: Genesis 2-3; Ezekiel 28:13; 31:8-9; Revelation 22:1-5. The introduction distinguishes between geography and symbolism, and preserves the goodness of creation with the reality of sin and hope.

entries.title: Hell
entries.content: Hell is a translation of several words, the most important of which are גֵּי־הִנֹּם (Ge-Hinnom), the Valley of Ibn Hinnom, and the Greek γέεννα (Gehenna). The name begins geographically south of Jerusalem, then is linked in prophecy to the worship of Moloch and judgment, and in the Gospels to an eschatological warning. It is not correct to combine Hell with all other world concepts in Judaism or Greek philosophy. Biblical witness: Joshua 15:8; 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31-32; Matthew 5:22; Mark 9:43-48. Contemporaries of the texts: Josiah, Jeremiah, Jesus, and his disciples, depending on the context. The research distinguishes between place and semantic development.

entries.title: Gibeon
entries.content: Gibeon from גִּבְעוֹן (Giv'on), a city on a high place, was linked to the resourcefulness of its residents and their reconciliation with Joshua, then to the station of worship and to the struggle of David. The place is in the center of Benjamin, and its most famous events are the era of the Gibeonites, the battle in which the sun was stopped, and the incident of David and Abner. Her contemporaries were Joshua, the Hivite kings, and Zadok at different times. Biblical witness: Joshua 9-10; 2 Samuel 2:12-17; 1 Kings 4:3-15; 1 Chronicles 21:29. Spiritually, the entry warns against decisions without asking the Lord and against turning the covenant into political advantage.

entries.title: Gethsemane
entries.content: Gethsemane, from the Aramaic גת שמני (Gath Shemane), oil press, a garden or place on the Mount of Olives. In it, Jesus prayed before his arrest, and Judas, the soldiers, and the disciples were contemporary with the scene. The text does not mention every detail of the place and every subsequent geographic tradition need not be corroborated. Biblical witness: Matthew 26:36-56; Mark 14:32-52; Luke 22:39-53; John 18:1-11. The introduction links will, obedience, and human weakness, and reads prayer in light of the Way of the Cross, not as spiritual isolation from pain.

entries.title: Jalil
entries.content: Galilee, from גָּלִיל (Galil), a district or district, is a northern region comprising villages and cities around the Lake of Galilee. It became a scene for calling disciples, teaching and healing Jesus, and was a contemporary of Herod Antipas, Pilate, and the Jewish and Gentile villages in the region. Galilee should not be portrayed as a completely non-Jewish region; Evidence and texts reveal social and political diversity. Biblical witness: Joshua 20:7; Isaiah 23:8-9:2; Matthew 4:12-25; John 1:43-46. Spiritually, the entry declares that the centrality of mission is not determined by the center of empire.

entries.title: Embers
entries.content: Coals from גֶּחָלִים (geḥalim), burning embers or coals, appearing in images of purification, judgment, and hospitality. In Isaiah 6, coals touch the lips of the prophet as a sign of purification before mission, and in Proverbs, placing coals on the head carries the meaning of awakening the conscience, not revenge. Witness: Isaiah 6:6-7; Proverbs 25:21-22; Romans 12:20. The place is the temple in Isaiah's vision, the environment of wisdom and the apostolic church, and his contemporaries Isaiah, the angels, Paul, and the Roman community. The entry distinguishes between ritual and moral symbol.

entries.title: Mountain
entries.content: Mountain, from הַר (har), a mountain or a high place, and in the book it is a place of declaration, covenant, and worship. Mountains do not have a single meaning; Fissaina is linked to the covenant, Zion to the temple, and Carmel to the prophetic encounter. Witness: Exodus 19-24; Psalm 48; 1 Kings 18; Matthew 5:1-12. The place determines the nature of the event, and its contemporaries Moses, Elijah, Jesus, and the disciples according to the text. Spiritually, the mountain does not confine God to a terrain, but rather declares that the place becomes holy through the revelation of God and the obedience of the community.

entries.title: Mount of Olives
entries.content: Mount of Olives from הַר הַזֵּיתִים (Har ha-Zeitim), Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem. It is associated with Jesus' entry, prayer, teaching, and ascension according to New Testament traditions, and David crossed it at the time of Absalom's crisis. Witness: 2 Samuel 15:30; Zechariah 14:4; Matthew 21:1; 26:30-46; Acts 1:9-12. The setting links kingship, pain, and otherworldly hope, with its contemporaries David, Jesus, and the disciples. Geography should not be transformed into a material sanctification, but rather a reading of place within the story of Jerusalem.

entries.title: Mount Sinai
entries.content: Mount Sinai, Horeb in some texts, from הַר סִינַי (Har Sinai), the derivation is unclear. It is the place of the covenant, the giving of commandments, and the making of the tabernacle, and in it Israel learns that liberation leads to responsible worship. Witness: Exodus 19-34; Deuteronomy 5; Galatians 4:24-26; Hebrews 12:18-24. His contemporaries Moses and Aaron, the people and the golden calf, are then restored in the interpretation of Paul and Hebrews. Proposals for its location vary, but the theological function is clearer than the coordinates: a liberated people living under the Word of God.
