entries.title: Mount Hermon
entries.content: Mount Hermon, from חֶרְמוֹן (Hermon), may be related to the root of prohibition or consecration, although the derivation remains uncertain. It appears as a northern border, a source of dew, and an image of the greatness of creation, and the Transfiguration traditions invoke it in a later reading without consensus on identifying the mountain. Witness: Deuteronomy 3:8; Psalm 133:3; Matthew 17:1-8. The place is in Bashan and northern Palestine, and its contemporaries are Moses, Joshua, Jesus, and the disciples, according to the text. The entry links geography and symbolism without claiming that every subsequent tradition fixes the location of the event.

entries.title: Tractor
entries.content: Gerar from גְּרָר (Gerar), the name of a city or region in southern Palestine, and its etymological meaning is unclear. Appearing in the stories of Abraham, Isaac, and Abimelech about fear, marriage, and wells, political boundaries test the faithfulness of fathers. Witness: Genesis 20; 26:1-33; 2 Chronicles 14:13-15. The place is in the Negev or the southern plain, according to the proposals, and the contemporaries of the events are Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebeka, and Abimelech. Each Abimelech should not be equated with one person, nor should the site be turned into an archaeological certainty without evidence.

entries.title: Jarjashi
entries.content: The Girgashi are from הַגִּרְגָּשִׁי (Girgashi), a group that appears in lists of the peoples of Canaan, and the book does not provide an extensive independent history of them. Witness: Genesis 10:16; 15:21; Deuteronomy 7:1; Joshua 3:10. They appear on the horizon of entering the land, not on the scene of a specific character, and the contemporaries of the texts are Abraham, Moses, Joshua, and the peoples of Canaan. The entry distinguishes between the theological list and historical details that are not substantiated by the verses. Responsible reading refuses to turn the ancient name into a judgment on a modern group.

entries.title: Jeshur
entries.content: Geshur from גְּשׁוּר (Geshur), a kingdom or territory of Transjordan, whose name has no settled etymological meaning. It was linked to Machir, Talmai's daughter, and Absalom, and then to David's political borders. Witness: Joshua 13:2; 2 Samuel 3:3; 13:37-38; 14:23. The place is northeast of Galilee, or Bashan in geographical research, and its contemporaries are David, Absalom, and Talmai. The study reveals how intermarriage, exile, and return intersect with the legitimacy of the king.

entries.title: Body
entries.content: The body, from בָּשָׂר (basar) and σάρξ (sarx), refers to the tangible human being, weakness, and kinship, not necessarily the evil of matter. In Genesis 2 the body is a human unit, and in Paul the meaning of Sarkes changes according to the context between humanity subject to sin and the created body. Witness: Genesis 2:23-25; Leviticus 17:11; John 1:14; Romans 8. The place is creation, the wilderness, the apostolic community, and the contemporaries of the texts are Adam, Moses, Jesus, and Paul. The entrance preserves the goodness of the incarnation and the dignity of the body and rejects simplistic dualism.

entries.title: Hunger
entries.content: Hunger, in Hebrew רָעָב (ra'av), and in Greek λιμός (limos), is an experience of lack that reveals human fragility and collective responsibility. Joseph links hunger to economic frugality, the prophets reveal that hunger may result from injustice, while Jesus confronts him with giving and teaching. Witness: Genesis 41; Deuteronomy 8:3; Amos 8:4-6; Matthew 4:1-4; 25:35. The place is Egypt, the wilderness, the villages, and his contemporaries Joseph, Moses, Jesus and the poor. Spiritually, the hunger of the needy should not be interpreted as a failure of faith, but rather as a call to mercy and justice.

entries.title: Dryness
entries.content: Drought, from חֹרֶב (ḥorev) or יָבֵשׁ (yavesh), refers to the absence of water or the withering of the earth, but in prophecy it becomes a spiritual sign of the ruin of the covenant. Witness: 1 Kings 17:1; Isaiah 35:1-7; Ezekiel 37:1-14; John 7:37-39. The setting is the wilderness, the Valley of Bones, the Temple, and the contemporaries of Elijah, Ezekiel, and Jesus. The entry distinguishes between climate and symbol, and reads water as a gift and justice, not as a miracle separated from human responsibility.

entries.title: Collection
entries.content: Levy, from τέλος (telos) or τελώνης (telōnēs) in the Greco-Roman setting, refers to the collection of taxes. The book places the tax collector in a network of injustice and social contempt, but it opens the door for him to repent and enter the community. Witness: Leviticus 19:13; Luke 3:12-13; 5:27-32; 19:1-10. The place of Galilee, Jericho, the customs centers, and his contemporaries John the Baptist, Jesus, and Zacchaeus. The approach does not justify the corruption of collection, nor does it reduce the person to his profession.

entries.title: A slave girl
entries.content: Female slave from שִׁפְחָה (shifḥah) or παιδίσκη (paidiskē), a woman in a position of service or slavery depending on the context. Hagar and the slave girl in Galatia present issues of family, freedom, and interpretation, but the text should not be used to beautify slavery. Witness: Genesis 16; 21:8-21; Acts 16:16-18; Galatians 4:21-31. The place is the house of Abraham and Philippians, and the contemporaries of the events are Sarah, Hagar, Paul, and the unknown maid. The entry reads the text with a sensitivity to dignity and power.

entries.title: Jib
entries.content: Pit from בּוֹר (bor), a pit, well, or prison, a place of possible death, waiting, or escape. Joseph was thrown into the pit, Jeremiah was placed in the pit, while the psalm links salvation with the removal of man from the pit. Witness: Genesis 37:22-29; Jeremiah 38; Psalm 40:2; 1 Samuel 24:3. The place is wilderness and prison, and its contemporaries are Joseph and his brothers, Jeremiah, Ebedmelech, and David. Spiritually, deliverance does not eliminate the impact of injustice, but it opens a path to hope.

entries.title: Mountains
entries.content: Mountains are from הָרִים (harim), and appear as borders, shelters, and places of announcement. There are many mountains in the Bible, including Sinai, Zion, Carmel, and Olives, so it is not correct to combine them into one symbol. Witness: Exodus 19; Psalm 121; 1 Kings 18; Matthew 17; 28:16-20. The place identifies the event, and its contemporaries Moses, Elijah, Jesus, and the disciples. The entry declares that creation serves revelation without replacing God, and that climbing the mountain leads to serving the world, not escaping it.

entries.title: Gibeah
entries.content: Gibeah, from גֶּבַע (Gevaʿ), a hill or highland, and the name of a city in Benjamin. It was linked to Saul, the events of the civil war, and the story of the Levite in Gibeah, and therefore geographical memory carries questions of kingship, justice, and violence. Witness: Joshua 18:24; Judges 19-20; 1 Samuel 10:26; 13:2. The place is the Benjamite highlands, and his contemporaries Saul, the Levites and Israel. The introduction distinguishes between the description of the place and the moral justification for the events that occurred there.

entries.title: Swept away
entries.content: Cliff or rock, from צוּר (tsur) or πέτρα (petra) depending on the context, which is a place of protection, a stumbling block, or an image of stability. David took refuge in the rocks, the rock was struck in the wilderness, and Jesus used the image of the rock to build. Witness: Exodus 17:1-7; 1 Samuel 24:1-4; Matthew 7:24-27; 1 Corinthians 10:4. The place is the wilderness and the hideouts of Judah, and his contemporaries Moses, David, Jesus, and Paul. Spiritually, consistency is not a magic stone but obedience to the Word.

The place is the wilderness, the battlefields, the Christian community, and its contemporaries Moses, David, and Paul. entries.title: Create
entries.content:
Hebrew בָּרָא (bara'), a verb describing God's creative work, and Greek κτίζω (ktizō), created or created. Biblical witness: Genesis 1-2; Psalm 33:6-9; Isaiah 40:26; John 1:1-3; Colossians 1:15-17. The place is creation, the garden, and the universe, and the most famous events are the order of creation, human habitation, the fall, and the revelation of the Creator Word. Contemporary persons of the texts: Adam, Eve, Moses, the Prophets, Jesus, and the Apostles, according to the context of each book. Genesis does not provide a modern scientific report, but rather declares the goodness of creation, the sovereignty of God, and the dignity and responsibility of man. Biblical studies compare literary structure to Near Eastern contexts without equating the biblical narrative with the surrounding mythology. Theologically, creation is the basis of covenant and morality; Man does not absolutely own creation, but rather manages it before the Creator. The Christian reading rejects the separation between creation and redemption, because the incarnation and resurrection declare the value of the created world, not its contempt. Spiritually, the entrance brings a person back from consumption to gratitude and care.

The academic reading confirms that Bar' does not alone answer every philosophical question about nothingness, and that the meaning of the text is formed by arranging the days, separating the chaos, and giving man the function of agency. Genesis 1 is therefore examined with Genesis 2 without eliminating the difference of the two literary voices, and with Near Eastern texts without assuming a direct quotation. The theological conclusion remains clear: creation belongs to God, and man is an image and responsible.

entries.title: Bread
entries.content:
Hebrew לֶחֶם (leḥem), bread or food, and Greek ἄρτος (artos). Biblical witness: Exodus 16; Leviticus 24:5-9; 1 Samuel 21:1-6; Matthew 6:11; John 6. The place is the wilderness, the house, the temple, and the tables of Galilee, and the most famous events are the manna, the shewbread, and the feeding of the multitudes. Contemporary persons Moses, David, the priests, Jesus, the disciples and the poor. Bread is not reduced to a spiritual symbol; It is an economic need that reveals the group's responsibility for the hungry. John reads the Bread of Life in light of the Exodus, but he does not eliminate the physical meaning of food. The incident of David also shows that preserving life may explain the application of the ritual in circumstances of necessity. Biblical studies point to the intertwining of hospitality, economics, and worship, while Sharia affirms the right of the poor to the earth's resources. Theologically, the gift of bread links prayer, work, and justice. Spiritually, the entrance asks for a faith that does not separate worship from feeding oneself.

Studies link baking, home economics, hospitality, and structure; Daily bread reminds us that prayer is inseparable from a just production system. In John 6, the physical miracle should not be neglected for the sake of the symbol, as the discourse builds on the memory of the manna and then expands it around the person of Jesus. The researcher compares the showbread and the communal table without settling the ritual differences.

entries.title: Wine
entries.content:
Hebrew יַיִן (yayin), wine, and Greek οἶνος (oinos). Biblical witness: Genesis 9:20-27; Proverbs 20:1; Isaiah 25:6; John 2:1-11; Ephesians 5:18. The place is the vineyards, the houses, the banquets, the temple, and the most famous events are Noah’s drunkenness, the grapes of the Promised Land, and the diversion of water at Cana. Contemporary persons Noah, Jesus, the disciples, and the people of Cana. The book does not present wine in one sense; It is a gift and joy, and it may become a tool of drunkenness and injustice. Therefore, the ethical reading distinguishes between moderate use and enslavement to lust, and does not use Cana to cancel the warnings of wisdom. The Jewish background of the banquet and covenant illuminates the image of the cup, while the issues of the Lord's Supper require respect for different church traditions. Theologically, grace does not justify loss of control. Spiritually, the approach places Joy under the responsibility of loving and protecting the weak.

The Jewish background makes it clear that wine is part of blessing, feasting, and offerings, but it is not morally neutral when associated with drunkenness or injustice. Therefore, Cana is read with the parables of wisdom and the prophets, not in isolation from them. The study distinguishes between the prohibition of drunkenness and the rulings of later Christian sects, while keeping the protection of the weak a moral standard.

entries.title: Tent
entries.content:
Hebrew מִשְׁכָּן (mishkan), dwelling, from the root dwelling, and Greek σκηνή (skēnē), tent or dwelling. Biblical witness: Exodus 25-40; Leviticus 16; John 1:14; Hebrews 8-9. The place is the wilderness and among the tribes of Israel, and the most famous events are the making of the Tabernacle, its filling with glory, and the organization of the priesthood. Contemporary persons Moses, Aaron, Bezalel and the group, then Jesus and the apostles in the rereading. The Tabernacle declares that God dwells among a liberated people, but it sets limits to holiness and closeness. It should not be considered merely an architectural model or reduced to later Christian symbols. Biblical commentaries examine their relationship to creation, the temple, and the incarnation, while respecting the history of Jewish worship. Theologically, presence is a gift over which man has no control. Spiritually, the entrance links divine dwelling with the community's responsibility for holiness and justice.

The tent links liberation and presence; God does not liberate a people to leave them without a collective form, but rather He dwells among a group that learns holiness. The commentaries compare the tabernacle, the temple, and John's images of the tabernacle, while being careful not to reduce the incarnation to an architectural metaphor. The priesthood and the ritual system remain part of the organization of approaching, not possessing, God.

entries.title: Exit
entries.content:
Hebrew יְצִיאָה (yetsi'ah), exodus, is related to the verb exodus, and the Hebrew name for the book שְׁמוֹת (Shemot) means names. Biblical witness: Exodus 1-15; 19-24; Luke 9:31; 1 Corinthians 10:1-4. The place is Egypt, the sea, Sinai, and the wilderness, and the most famous events are the plagues, the Passover, the crossing, and the covenant. Contemporary persons Moses, Aaron, Miriam, Pharaoh, and Israel, and then Jesus and the apostles reclaim the language of Exodus. Biblical liberation does not only equal a political coup; It is a transition from serving Pharaoh to worshiping the Lord and covenant life. Recent studies read narrative, ritual, and law together, and discuss their relationship to collective memory. Theologically, salvation creates a people rather than an isolated individual, and is associated with justice and commandment. Spiritually, the entrance rejects salvation without obedience or freedom without responsibility.

Modern studies read the Book of Exodus as a narrative of liberation, community formation, and legislation, not as a separate story of escape. Passover, crossing over, and covenant are interconnected, so a salvation that does not reshape economy and worship remains incomplete. Research discusses the relationship of historical memory to the final wording of the book, without turning probabilities into certainties.

entries.title: Sin
entries.content:
Hebrew חֵטְא (ḥet'), error or deviation from purpose, and Greek ἁμαρτία (hamartia). Biblical witness: Genesis 3; Leviticus 4-5; Psalm 51; Mark 7:20-23; Romans 3:9-26. The place is Eden, the wilderness, the temple, and the human heart, and the most famous events are the fall, the golden calf, the sin of David, and the crucifixion. Contemporary people: Adam, Eve, Moses, David, Jesus, and Paul. The book does not reduce sin to the breaking of an individual rule; It distorts the relationship with God, neighbors and the community. The Torah distinguishes between types of guilt, impurity, and intentionality, while Paul describes the power of sin as a force that enslaves man. Doctrine should not be used to justify blaming victims or ignoring unjust structures. Theologically, grace does not deny the seriousness of evil but rather addresses it in repentance, redemption, and renewal. Spiritually, true confession leads to reform and justice, not just to self-flagellation.

The research distinguishes between חטא as a deviation, between עון as sin or deviance, and פשע as rebellion in places in the Old Testament, with different translations. This distinction prevents all evil from being reduced to guilt. In Romans, sin becomes a force that enslaves, but the remedy does not eliminate moral responsibility or the need to repair damage.

entries.title: That's it
entries.content:
Hebrew יְשׁוּעָה (yeshu'ah), deliverance or salvation, and Greek σωτηρία (sōtēria). Biblical witness: Exodus 14; Isaiah 52:7; Luke 2:29-32; Ephesians 2:8-10; Revelation 7. The place is Egypt, the wilderness, Zion, the church, the new creation, and the most famous events are the crossing, exile, annunciation, and resurrection. Contemporary persons Moses, Isaiah, Simeon, Jesus, Paul, and the congregation. Salvation in the book is broader than individual escape after death; It includes liberation, forgiveness, reconciliation, and the formation of a people. It is not right to separate spiritual salvation from the physical, poverty, and injustice, nor to reduce it to a political program. Evangelical studies read the Old Testament as a foundation rather than a null background, and differentiate between divine initiative and faith response. Theologically, the cross and resurrection proclaim God's faithfulness and promise. Spiritually, salvation creates new life that produces love and service.

The legal reading emphasizes that salvation is a path that begins with God's promise and includes forgiveness, liberation, resurrection, and renewal of creation. Therefore, it should not be separated from the story of Israel or turned into an individual experience only. Evangelical studies examine the relationship of salvation to faith and works, while refusing to make works a price for grace or making grace an excuse for the absence of work.

entries.title: Lamb
entries.content:
Hebrew כֶּבֶשׂ (keves), sheep or lamb, and Greek ἀμνός (amnos). Biblical witness: Exodus 12; Leviticus 1; Isaiah 53:7; John 1:29; Revelation 5. The place is Egypt, the altar, and Jerusalem, and the most famous events are the Passover of the Exodus, the temple sacrifices, the song of the Suffering Servant, and the announcement of the Lamb of God. Contemporary persons Moses, Israel, the priests, John the Baptist, Jesus, and the apostles. The sheep does not have one meaning in every text; It is food, a sacrifice, and an image of weakness and obedience. The New Testament reads the image of the lamb in light of the Passover and the servant, but the Jewish context of the sacrifice should not be eliminated. The study distinguishes between symbol and history, between the language of worship and the apocalyptic language. Theologically, redemption is not a justification for violence but a declaration of God's initiative to address sin. Spiritually, pregnancy leads to humility and mercy, not coercive force.

Studies differentiate between the Passover lamb, the sin offerings, the servant of the Lord, and the lamb of vision, so do not combine images without context. The Christian reading sees a legal connection between them, but it starts from their Jewish and historical functions. The introduction confirms that the language of sacrifice does not justify violence, but rather announces the treatment of evil and the restoration of communion and holiness.

entries.title: Circumcision
entries.content:
Hebrew מוּל (mul), cut off or circumcised, and Greek περιτομή (peritomē). Biblical witness: Genesis 17; Exodus 4:24-26; Leviticus 12:3; Romans 2:25-29; Galatians 5. The place is the house of Abraham, Egypt, the wilderness, the mixed churches, and the most famous events are the establishment of the sign of the covenant and the controversy over the nations. Contemporary persons Abraham, Moses, Zipporah, Paul, and the Apostles. Circumcision in the Torah is a sign of belonging to the covenant, not a moral guarantee or a substitute for obedience of the heart. Paul addresses the question of the Gentiles within first-century communities, and his polemic should not be read as contempt for the Jews or the Torah. Biblical studies explain the difference between covenantal identity and Gentile entry requirements, while preserving the diversity of Christian positions. Theologically, the sign needs internal honesty. Spiritually, the entry warns against turning a sign of grace into a privilege that cancels out mercy.

The circumcision controversy should be read within the question of the membership of nations in first-century groups, not within a simplistic conflict between Judaism and Christianity. Circumcision is a sign of the covenant in Genesis, while Paul discusses its function in relation to the Gentiles without denying that Israel is a covenant people. Recent studies clarify the difference between criticism of reliance on the sign and criticism of the Torah itself.

entries.title: Servant
entries.content:
Hebrew עֶבֶד (eved), slave or servant, and Greek δοῦλος (doulos), slave or owned depending on the context. Biblical witness: Exodus 21; Isaiah 42:1-9; Mark 10:42-45; Philippians 2:5-11. The place is the houses, the palaces, the temple, the community, and the most famous events are the legislation to protect the slave, the hymn to the servant of the Lord, and Jesus’ teaching about leadership. Contemporary Persons Moses, Isaiah, Jesus, Apostles, and Slaves in the Roman World. Servant language may not be used to beautify slavery or abolish human dignity. The book distinguishes between different historical settings and places limits on exploitation, while the New Testament uses the image of service to critique authoritarianism. In Christ, leadership becomes a gift, not a privilege. Biblical studies read texts within the history of slavery and declare that they should not be dismissed as justification for human trafficking. Spiritually, the true servant protects the weak and seeks the good of the community.

The study of עבד confronts the complex history of slavery and forced labor, so the title of Abd al-Rab cannot be truncated to justify human trafficking. In Isaiah, the servant carries a message of justice and light; In Mark, leadership is measured by giving. The introduction links dignity and servant authority and reads texts within their history, not as complete modern laws.

entries.title: Ruin
entries.content:
Ruin, from חָרְבָּה (ḥorbah) or ἐρήμωσις (erēmōsis), denotes the destruction of a city or land. Biblical witness: Isaiah 1:7; Jeremiah 25:11; Mark 13:14; Revelation 18. The place is Jerusalem, Babylon, and the afflicted cities, and its contemporaries are the prophets, kings, Jesus, and John. The book links ruin with injustice and rebellion, but it does not make every ruin evidence of individual guilt. The entry reads prophecy as a moral warning, distinguishing history from apocalyptic imagery. Theologically, judgment does not eliminate the possibility of renewal, as seen in the hope of rebuilding. Spiritually, devastation calls for repentance and justice, not gloating.

The prophecy does not equate the ruin of the city with the sin of every individual in it; Rather, it talks about the responsibility of kings, regimes, and groups. Hope appears in transforming the wilderness into a road and the collapsed place into a place of life. The study compares the prophecies of exile and apocalyptic images, distinguishing political history from eschatological symbolism.

entries.title: Fear
entries.content:
Fear of יִרְאָה (yirah) or φόβος (phobos), which may mean sacred dread or destructive terror depending on the context. Biblical witness: Exodus 18:20-21; Psalm 23:4; Proverbs 1:7; Mark 4:35-41; 1 John 4:18. The place is Sinai, the wilderness, the sea, the community, and its contemporaries Moses, David, Jesus, and the disciples. The book does not equate the fear of the Lord with panic; The first leads to wisdom, the second requires presence and comfort. Recent studies read fear within the relationship of power, shock, and hope, not as superficial psychological preaching. Spiritually, fear is transformed when man becomes before God and not a slave to terror.

The Psalms make clear that the fear of God is not a terror that depersonalizes, but a terror that reorders loyalty. Pathological fear or fear resulting from oppression requires protection and justice, not religious blame. The introduction compares Sinai, the storm, and the messages of love, where God’s presence does not eliminate the reality of danger, but rather gives the community the ability to confront it.

entries.title: Wood
entries.content:
Wood, from עֵץ (ets) or ξύλον (xylon), a tree or wooden material, and in the New Testament may refer to the wood of the cross. Biblical witness: Genesis 2:9; Exodus 10:25-23; Deuteronomy 21:22-23; Acts 5:30; 1 Peter 2:24. The place is Eden, the Tabernacle, and Jerusalem, and its contemporaries are Adam, Moses, the priests, Jesus, and the apostles. The entrance distinguishes between the tree of life, the woods of worship, and the execution stake, so it does not impose a single symbol. Theologically, the New Testament uses the language of Deuteronomy to read the cross within the story of damnation and redemption. Spiritually, matter is sanctified not by itself but by what it reveals of God's holiness and mercy.

The study traces the transition of wood from a material of creation and construction to an execution stake, with different connotations between the Old Testament and the New Testament. This does not mean that matter carries self-salvation; Meaning arises from God's action and the context of the covenant. The language of the cross and Deuteronomy 21 are read with caution that preserves the dignity of the crucified and does not erase the cruelty of Roman execution.

entries.title: Shame
entries.content:
Shame of בּוּשׁ (bosh) or αἰσχύνη (aischynē), a social disgrace or fall before God. Biblical witness: Psalm 25:2-3; Isaiah 54:4; Mark 8:38; Hebrews 12:2. The place is the gates of the city, the court, the cross, the community, and his contemporaries David, Isaiah, Jesus, and the believers. The Cross reveals the paradox that what the world considered shameful becomes in faith a path of glory, but that does not justify the humiliation of the victims. The entry distinguishes between the shame of sin and a social stigma imposed by the powerful. Spiritually, God restores dignity without denying truth or abrogating the responsibility to repent.

In the book, shame operates socially, judicially, and ritually, and therefore requires a distinction between the shame of crime and a stigma imposed by an unjust society. In Isaiah and Revelation, God overturns the rule of power, and in the cross the paradox of hidden glory appears. The study does not use shame to silence the sufferer, but rather asks who defines dignity and who has the authority to condemn.

entries.title: Eunuch
entries.content:
Eunuch from סָרִיס (saris) or εὐνοῦχος (eunouchos), and may denote a palace official who does not always confirm the meaning of physical castration. Biblical witness: Deuteronomy 23:1; Isaiah 56:3-5; Acts 8:26-39; Matthew 19:12. The place is the Persian palaces, the temple, the road to Gaza, and his contemporaries Isaiah, Philip, and the Ethiopian eunuch. Isaiah highlights the promise of inclusion of those who were excluded, and Acts presents the acceptance of eunuchs into the community of the baptized. The text should not be used to insult people with physical or sexual differences. Theologically, God expands the boundaries of the community without abolishing the sanctity of the covenant.

Research confirms that סריס may mean a palace employee, so it is not permissible to be certain about his physical condition in every situation. The significance of Isaiah 56 and Acts 8 is that the excluded person finds a place in the worship of God, while the covenants and contexts remain different. The entry prohibits the use of the term to insult any contemporary group, and reads inclusion as an act of grace and justice.

entries.title: Seal
entries.content:
Seal from חוֹתָם (ḥotam) or σφραγίς (sphragis), a mark of ownership, authentication, or protection. Biblical witness: Genesis 38:18; Esther 8:8; Daniel 6:17; Ephesians 1:13; Revelation 5. The place: palaces, graves, letters, and visions, and his contemporaries were Judas, the Persian exiles, Paul, and John. Sealing does not always mean protection from pain; The grave may be sealed and then opened, and the message sealed as an authority. The entry links identity, authority, and responsibility, and warns against religious signs without honesty. Spiritually, true belonging appears in covenant life.

In the ancient world, a seal established ownership, authority, and secrecy, so the seal of Paul's letter differs from the seal of a vision or a tomb. The sign does not mean protecting the believer from pain, but rather declares identity and belonging in the midst of conflicting loyalties. The study links the seal and the spirit in Ephesians to the images of sovereignty in Daniel and Revelation without equating the texts.

entries.title: Ring
entries.content:
Seal from חוֹתָם (ḥotam), an inscription and documentation tool, which is close to the meaning of seal. Biblical witness: Genesis 41:42; Esther 3:10-12; Haggai 2:23; Luke 15:22. The place is the palace of Pharaoh and Persia and the home of the returned son, and his contemporaries Joseph, Mordecai, Zerubbabel, and Jesus. The ring confers authority but does not automatically make its owner good; It was used to issue injustice, then it became, in the parable of the son, a sign of restoration of dignity. The entry distinguishes between legal force and familial grace. Spiritually, the ring's return is a declaration of restoration, not a reward for merit.

The story of Joseph reveals that the ring conveyed administrative authority, while the parable of the prodigal son reveals that it restored a lost dignity within the family. This paradox prevents it from being made a symbol of wealth alone. The study compares the seal as a political document and the seal as a sign of reconciliation, noting that authority needs justice so that it does not become a seal of injustice.

entries.title: Tabernacle
entries.content:
The tabernacle from אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד (ohel mo'ed), the tent of meeting or meeting, is the place of God's meeting with the community. Biblical witness: Exodus 33:7-11; Numbers 11:16-30; 12:4-8. The place is outside the camp, then in the middle of it, and its contemporaries are Moses, Aaron, Joshua, and the elders of Israel. Don't reduce the tent to a mobile structure; It regulates the relationship of presence with the word, leadership, and approach. The introduction distinguishes between it and the tabernacle in the functions of the various texts, and reads it within the holiness of the community, not the possession of God. Spiritually, meeting with God leads to hearing and responsibility.

The term “אהל מועד” differs from the description of the tabernacle in some units of exodus and number, and therefore it is necessary not to combine them without examination. The Tabernacle is a place of meeting, hearing, and judgment, and its connection with Moses highlights mediation, not the monopoly of attendance. The study reads the movement of the tent between the outside and the center of the camp as a tension between holiness and proximity.

The entry explains that Easter is a collective memory of the emancipation of slaves, not an individual magical ritual. The New Testament rereads the symbol in light of Christ's death while keeping its Jewish root. Spiritually, salvation requires a new departure, memory, and community.

Easter places family, home, and memory at the center of salvation, and later texts transfer memory to a broader community. Blood is not reduced to protective magic, but rather serves as a sign of obedience and belonging on the night of judgment. The Christian reading remains indebted to the Jewish root of the holiday, although its interpretation of the completeness of the symbol in Christ differs.

Evangelical scholarship reads his psalms within the history of worship and kingship, and discusses his messianic reuse in the New Testament. His contemporaries were Korah, Abiram, Moses, Aaron, and the group. The story does not read as a license to suppress all dissent; It speaks of a rebellion against a specific calling and responsibility within the covenant community. Spiritually, it warns against ambition that uses the language of equality to mask the pursuit of power.

entries.title: Demetrius
entries.content: Demetrius, from Δημήτριος (Dēmētrios), a Greek name associated with the goddess Demeter, is the name of two people in the New Testament. In Acts 19 he was a model maker of Artemis in Ephesus, fomenting economic unrest against Paul when the spread of the Gospel threatened his business. Another Demetrius appears in 3 John as a person praised by all and by the truth itself. Scripture Witness: Acts 23:19-41; 3 John 12. Place Ephesus in Asia Minor and an unspecified local church. His contemporaries were Paul, Artemis, Gaius, and John. The introduction distinguishes between the two people, and reads the story of Ephesus in the relationship of religion to the economy and civil authority, not as hostility to local culture. Theologically, the Bible tests systems that make profit the criterion of truth, but it does not justify chaos. Spiritually, the name combines a negative testimony of one person with a positive testimony of another, reminding that reputation is built by honesty.

entries.title: Sacrifice
entries.content:
Sacrifice of זֶבַח (zevaḥ) or θυσία (thysia), a slaughtered offering offered in worship. Biblical witness: Genesis 22; Leviticus 1-7; Psalm 40:6-8; Mark 12:33; Hebrews 10. The place is the altar, the tabernacle, and the temple, and the most famous events are the sacrifice of Isaac, the Sinai sacrifices, and the Passover. Contemporary persons Abraham, Isaac, Moses, Aaron, Jesus, and the priests. The sacrifice does not function as magic or bribe, but rather within a covenant system that declares sin, thanksgiving, and fellowship. The introduction distinguishes between the types of sacrifices and their functions, and does not equate every sacrifice with atonement. The Hebrews symbols are read in light of Christ while remaining true to their Jewish roots. Theologically, the purpose of the sacrifice is to restore communion and holiness, not to glorify violence. Spiritually, the offering is transformed into gratitude, obedience, and mercy.

Sacrifice appears in the covenant structure as a means of teaching the community that drawing close to God requires confession of sin and thanksgiving for life. Therefore, it should not be interpreted in terms of primitive sacrifice alone, nor transferred to a Christian meaning before understanding the Levitical system and the relationship of the altar to purity and food. The researcher compares between individual and collective sacrifice, and between the sacrifice that treats sin and the sacrifice that celebrates communion. Prophecies also set limits on the ritual when it is separated from justice, so the value of the sacrifice remains linked to the life of the worshiper and his responsibility towards the poor.

entries.title: Sacrifice
entries.content:
Sacrifice from זָבַח (zavaḥ), to slaughter or offer a sacrifice, and it may be a description rather than an independent noun. Biblical witness: Genesis 9:22-13; Isaiah 53:7; Acts 8:32. The place is Mount Moriah, Jerusalem, and the road to Gaza, and its contemporaries are Abraham, Isaac, Isaiah, Philip, and the Ethiopian eunuch. A distinction must be made between the act of slaughter and the identity of the one being slaughtered, and between the story of the test in Genesis and the reading of the servant in Isaiah. The text does not provide justification for human sacrifice; Genesis 22 ends by preventing it and providing an alternative. Theologically, the entry addresses the meaning of substitution and obedience, while not reconciling the various texts. Spiritually, faith does not mean despising life but trusting in God's provision.

The story of Genesis 22 reveals that the commanded act of slaughter is inseparable from its textual conclusion: God prevents the killing of Isaac and provides a ram. Therefore, academic reading refuses to make the story an endorsement of human sacrifice, but rather studies it as a test of promise, obedience, and the alternative. Isaac remains active within the novel despite his silence, while the New Testament reads Abraham's faith from the perspective of resurrection. These levels should be presented in their order, not combined into a single meaning that eliminates history or imposes it on the reader.

entries.title: Wolf
entries.content:
The wolf, from זְאֵב (ze'ev) or λύκος (lykos), is a predator and an image of danger. Biblical witness: Genesis 49:27; Isaiah 11:6; Jeremiah 5:6; John 10:12. The place is the wilderness, the flock, and images of the kingdom, and its contemporaries Benjamin, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Jesus, and the shepherds. The book uses the wolf to depict violence or the hired shepherd fleeing, but it places in Isaiah an image of an afterlife reconciliation between the wolf and the lamb. A zoology should not be constructed from symbol, nor should a human group be demonized. Theologically, the text contrasts predation with care. Spiritually, the call to protection is the standard of leadership.

The image of the wolf in the book operates on two levels: a real danger threatening the flock, and a political or moral image of plunder. In Isaiah 11, eschatological hope overturns predatory relationships, while in John 10, the wolf appears as a test of the shepherd’s faithfulness. This does not mean that nature is absolutely evil, nor that human groups are predators. The entry emphasizes that leadership is measured by protecting the weak in times of danger, not by the power of rhetoric or claims of authority.

entries.title: Gone
entries.content:
Gold from זָהָב (zahav) or χρυσός (chrysos), a precious metal for adornment, power, and worship. Biblical witness: Genesis 2:11-12; Exodus 25:11; 32:2-4; Matthew 2:11; Revelation 21:18. The place is Eden, the Tabernacle, the palaces, the new city, and its contemporaries Abraham, Moses, Aaron, the Magi, and John. The Golden Calf shows that a good material can become an idol when it replaces God, while gold enters into the beauty of worship and gifts. The study does not equate wealth with blessing, but rather examines the source and use of wealth. Theologically, physical beauty is a servant of holiness, not a master of it. Spiritually, freedom from the bondage of gold is an experience of the heart.

Gold carries a clear theological duality: it enters into the beauty of the tabernacle and the temple, but in Exodus 32 it becomes material for an idol that competes with the presence of God. Therefore, its economic, ritual and symbolic value are studied together. The problem is not with the metal, but with transforming the gift into an object of trust and worship. The paradox continues in Matthew and Revelation, where gold can be a gift or an image of a glorious city. The biblical standard is whether gold serves worship and justice or enslaves the heart.

entries.title: Arm
entries.content:
Arm from זְרוֹעַ (zeroaʿ) or βραχίων (brachiōn), an organ of the body and an image of strength. Biblical witness: Exodus 6:6; Deuteronomy 5:15; Isaiah 53:1; Luke 1:51. The place is the body, the exodus, prophecy, praise, and his contemporaries Moses, Isaiah, and Mary. When the book mentions the arm of the Lord, it uses metaphorical human language to declare power and liberation. It does not describe God’s body in a physical way. The study compares the arm of power and the arm of mercy, and the exodus of Israel and the salvation of the nations. Theologically, divine power appears in saving the oppressed, not in display. Spiritually, the entrance confronts man's fear with God's just power.

The language of the arm is a metaphorical language that brings God's power closer to human imagination, but it does not make God a limited body. In Exodus it refers to liberation, and in Isaiah it is associated with the power that is manifested in the suffering servant. This transformation prevents the reduction of power to military superiority. The entry compares the arm of the Lord and the arm of the king, as the former saves the oppressed while the latter may break in the face of judgment. Spiritually, divine power is measured by its faithfulness to the weak, not by the noise of power.

entries.title: Male
entries.content:
Dhikr from זָכַר (zakhar) or μνημονεύω (mnēmoneuō), remembrance and evocation leading to action. Biblical witness: Exodus 12:14; Deuteronomy 8:2; Psalm 103:2; Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24. The place is Passover, wilderness, worship, community, and its contemporaries Moses, David, Jesus, and Paul. Biblical memory is not nostalgia, but a reshaping of the present based on God’s faithfulness. The introduction distinguishes between human remembrance and covenantal remembrance of God, and between remembrance and empty celebration. Theologically, a group that forgets the Exodus may return to new slavery. Spiritually, remembering becomes gratitude, justice, and care for the stranger.

Remembering in the covenant is an act of resistance to the forgetfulness that reproduces slavery and injustice. When Israel mentions the Exodus, it commits itself to giving the stranger, the slave, and the poor a place in the community. When Jesus mentions the bread and the cup, memory becomes a collective practice linked to death and hope. The introduction distinguishes between God's remembrance of the covenant and man's remembrance of God's deeds, as the first is a divine faithfulness and the second is a moral response. Therefore, the memory is not valid if it turns into a celebration that erases the responsibility of the present.

entries.title: Guilt
entries.content:
Guilt, from עָוֹן (avon) or ἀνομία (anomia), iniquity or crookedness and responsibility, with a different connotation than חֵטְא. Biblical witness: Leviticus 5; Psalm 32; Isaiah 53:5-6; Romans 3:23-26. The place is the court, the temple, the heart, the community, and his contemporaries David, Isaiah, and Paul. Guilt is not reduced to a psychological feeling; It is an action, a relationship, and results that need recognition and reform. The Torah distinguishes between intent and error, while the New Testament expands on the power of sin. Guilt should not be used to condemn the sufferer or ignore structural injustice. Theologically, forgiveness does not cancel truth but rather opens the way to reconciliation.

The Hebrew analysis distinguishes between guilt as a state of responsibility and the psychological feeling of guilt. It is not enough for a person to feel remorse without facing the impact of his action. In Leviticus, the treatment of guilt is linked to confession, compensation, and return to the community, while the Psalm extends the language of forgiveness to internal renewal. Romans reads sin as a force, but that does not eliminate the actions of humans or the responsibility of systems. Spiritually, forgiveness does not mean denying the truth, but rather opens a path to justice and reconciliation where damage can be repaired.

entries.title: Humiliation
entries.content:
Humiliation from עָנָה (anah) or ταπεινόω (tapeinoō), subjugation or humility depending on the context. Biblical witness: Deuteronomy 8:2-3; Psalm 22; Isaiah 53; Philippians 2:5-11. The place is the wilderness, the captivity, the cross, the community, and its contemporaries: Israel, the sufferer, Jesus, and Paul. The introduction distinguishes between voluntary humility before God and humiliation practiced by oppressors, so violence or exploitation are not sanctified. The book uses the experience of the oppressed to open up the hope of elevation, not to ask the victim to accept injustice without resistance. Theologically, the logic of power is inverted in the cross. Spiritually, humility is service, not self-loathing.

The word humiliation requires a moral distinction between humility that a person chooses before God and humiliation imposed by the tyrant. The Psalms of the Suffering use the language of humiliation to reveal violence, not to sanctify it, while Philippians uses Christ's humility as a framework for serving others. Therefore, it is not permissible to ask the victim to remain silent in the name of humility. The entry declares that God resists pride, but He also lifts up the oppressed and protects their dignity. Christian humility is not an acceptance of injustice, but a refusal to turn power into privilege.

entries.title: Subservient
entries.content:
The servile, from עָנִי (ani) or πτωχός (ptōchos), poor, broken, or oppressed depending on the context. Biblical witness: Psalm 18:9; 34:6; Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18; James 2:1-6. The place is the gateway to the city, the village, the temple, the community, and its contemporaries David, Isaiah, Jesus, and the poor. The book does not praise poverty as a spiritual condition, but rather declares God's closeness to the oppressed and condemns their exploitation. The law and the prophets place the responsibility of protecting the poor, and the Gospels read the gospel as universal liberation. Theologically, choosing the weak does not mean neglecting the rich, but rather calling him to justice. Spiritually, faith is measured by how we treat those without influence.

The servile appears in the Torah and the Prophets as a person in need of judicial and economic protection, not just a poor figure arousing pity. Therefore, worship is related to leaving the edges of the fields and preventing the bias of the court. When Jesus proclaims good news to the poor, he restores the horizon of Isaiah in the context of the Kingdom of God. The introduction distinguishes between God’s preference for the oppressed and the glorification of poverty, as the goal is to restore dignity and justice. The Church that honors the humble tests the truth of its theology in practice.

entries.title: Disclaimer
entries.content:
Dhimma comes from דָּם (dam) in some forms of responsibility for blood, but the Arabic “dhimma” is not a single fixed equivalent in Hebrew. Biblical witness: Genesis 4:10; Ezekiel 3:18-21; Acts 18:6. The place is the court, the city, the prophetic message, and his contemporaries Cain, Ezekiel, and Paul. The introduction explains the necessity of not imposing a modern Arabic term on a single biblical term, and then examines the responsibility of the witness for blood and right. Responsibility does not mean owning the fate of another, but rather a sincere warning and a refusal to complicity. Theologically, the right is linked to the protection of life. Spiritually, silence in the face of injustice is not always neutrality.

Because the Arabic word is not a fixed equivalent in every text, the research must begin by identifying the Hebrew or Greek word in the witness. The matter may be related to blood, martyrdom, or responsibility for warning the oppressor, and it is not correct to combine them under one meaning. This precision prevents the introduction of modern legal concepts into the book. Yet the theological thread remains clear: the witness cannot be complicit in the waste of life, and the judge cannot use responsibility as an excuse for retaliation.

entries.title: Slaughter
entries.content:
Slaughter from זָבַח (zavaḥ) or σφάζω (sphazō), the act of offering or killing an animal depending on the context. Witness: Genesis 22; Exodus 12; Leviticus 1; Revelation 5. The place is the altar, the house, the Passover, and the apocalyptic scene, and its contemporaries are Abraham, Moses, the priests, and Jesus. The entry distinguishes between ritual slaughter and criminal violence, and does not turn the sacrifice into magic. Theologically, the act relates to worship, covenant, and redemption, while rejecting the glorification of cruelty. Spiritually, he associates sacrifice with obedience and mercy.

The act of slaughter needs a careful historical reading, because the Torah distinguishes between slaughtering for food, slaughtering on the altar, and unlawful killing. In Genesis 22, the story does not end with the completion of the slaughter, but rather with its prevention. At Passover, the slaughter is linked to a collective memory of the Exodus, and in the New Testament, the language of the lamb and sacrifice is repeated within the interpretation of Christ’s death. Therefore, it is not correct to collect all uses in one doctrine or use it to justify violence. The theological question remains how the covenant addresses sin and preserves the sanctity of life at the same time.

entries.title: Offspring
entries.content:
Offspring from זֶרַע (zeraʿ) or σπέρμα (sperma), offspring, transplantation, or continuation. Witness: Genesis 12:7; 15:5; 17:7; Galatians 3:16. The place is the land of the fathers, the wilderness, the community, and its contemporaries Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Paul. The promise is not limited to biology, but includes covenant identity and the blessing of nations. The introduction distinguishes between the singular and plural in Hebrew and Greek, and between the historical meaning and the reading of Christ. Spiritually, the promise demands fidelity, not possession.

The meaning of זרע expands from agricultural seed to offspring and promise, and therefore the context determines whether it is talking about a group, offspring, or a person. In Genesis, posterity is associated with land, blessing, and the responsibility of the family to be a blessing to the nations. As for Galatians, it reads the promise messianically in its own controversy, and this interpretation should not be imposed on every place before understanding Genesis. The entry shows that covenant identity is not a closed ethnic privilege but a calling and a mission.

Same from זֹאת (zot) or αὕτη (hautē), a feminine demonstrative whose meaning changes depending on the sentence, and is not an independent theological noun. Witness: Exodus 12:11; Deuteronomy 6:6; Matthew 26:26. The setting is the text, the teaching, the banquet, and its contemporaries Moses, Jesus, and the disciples. The entry explains that the Arabic translation may make the definite article a title, so the full phrase must be read. Spiritually, the meaning is inseparable from the thing or commandment referred to.

Because it is an Arabic deictic device, it is not permissible to claim a fixed Hebrew meaning for it without specifying the witness. In Hebrew you may encounter זאת, זו, or another expression, and its meaning changes with the noun it refers to. Therefore, the introduction teaches that the study of translation begins with grammar and context, not with the dictionary alone. The theological importance of the word comes from the thing referred to: a commandment, a sign, bread, or a covenant, not from the tool alone.

entries.title: Chin
entries.content:
The chin, from זָקָן (zaqan) or γένειον (geneion), is a part of the face and a symbolic position of dignity and shame. Witness: Leviticus 13:29-30; 2 Samuel 10:4-5; Isaiah 50:6. The place is the body, the city, the captivity, and its contemporaries Moses, David, and Isaiah. Shaving or dishonoring one's beard is associated with mourning and shame, and should not be transferred into contemporary judgments about appearance. Theologically, the entry reveals how violence uses the body to humiliate people. Spiritually, dignity is linked to the work of God and not to the opinion of the aggressor.

In Near Eastern culture, the chin is associated with identity, dignity, and mourning, so shaving or insulting it was a social act, not just a change in appearance. The story of David and the Ammonites reveals that an attack on the face could spark a war and undermine the legitimacy of the king. As for Isaiah 50, it places hair removal within the image of the suffering servant who does not escape from humiliation. The approach distinguishes between patience with pain and justification of the aggressor, and preserves the dignity of the body.

entries.title: Save
entries.content:
Treasure, from אָצַר (atsar) or θησαυρός (thēsauros), treasure or stock. Witness: Deuteronomy 28:12; Proverbs 4:2; Matthew 6:19-21; 2 Corinthians 4:7. The place is the storehouses, the houses, the sky, the community, and its contemporaries Moses, Solomon, Jesus, and Paul. The book does not condemn all saving, but it exposes the danger of turning stock into a security substitute for God. Jesus links treasure to the heart, while the law warns against monopolizing blessing. Spiritually, the value of an asset appears in the way it is used for good.

Wisdom distinguishes between a treasure that is preserved wisely and an asset that turns into a substitute trust in God. In Deuteronomy, stock is linked to the blessing of the earth, but the prophets condemn its accumulation when it is accompanied by the crushing of the poor. In Matthew, Jesus moves the question from the size of the treasure to the direction of the heart. Therefore, the study does not offer romantic poverty nor guaranteed wealth, but rather asks about justice, generosity, and responsibility.

entries.title: Humiliation
entries.content:
Humiliation from עֳנִי (oni) or ταπείνωσις (tapeinōsis), distress, humiliation, or state of brokenness. Witness: Deuteronomy 26:7; Psalm 25:18; Luke 1:48; James 1:9. The place is Egypt, the wilderness, the village, the community, and its contemporaries Israel, Mary, and Jacob. The introduction distinguishes between humility before God and humiliation imposed by the oppressor. The book does not sanctify oppression, but rather it hears the cry of the broken and overturns the standards of power. Spiritually, divine elevation does not erase human dignity, but rather restores it.

Man's humiliation does not mean that God requires him to accept oppression; The texts that describe the humiliation of Israel in Egypt or the humiliation of the poor before the oppressor use it as a basis for cry and rescue. The introduction distinguishes between humility before God and political and social humiliation. In the Song of Mary, God turns the scales of power and exalts the humble, but exaltation is not random revenge but rather establishing truth. Spiritually, hope preserves the dignity of the broken.

entries.title: Ammunition
entries.content:
Ammunition from כְּלִי (keli) or ὅπλον (hoplon), a tool, weapon, or equipment depending on the context; The Arabic title requires a distinction between ammunition and weapons. Witness: 1 Samuel 17:40; 2 Kings 20:13; Ephesians 6:11-17. The place is the battlefields, the palaces, the community, and its contemporaries David, Hezekiah, and Paul. It does not turn the image of God's weapon into a license for human war, but rather presents resistance to evil in the language of its time. Spiritually, true power is associated with truth and righteousness.

Ammunition and equipment in the context of war reveal the kingdoms' dependence on tools of force, but the book does not make weapons a criterion of right. Paul uses the language of God's armor figuratively to describe truth, righteousness, and faith, not to arm the group against humanity. The introduction distinguishes between military description and spiritual metaphor, and places each reading in front of the history of wars and victims. Christian strength is not the ability to harm, but rather steadfastness in the truth.

entries.title: Arm of the Lord
entries.content:
The Arm of the Lord from זְרוֹעַ יְהוָה (zeroaʿ YHWH), a metaphor for God's power to save. Witness: Exodus 6:6; Isaiah 40:10; 53:1; John 12:38. The place is Egypt, Jerusalem, and exile, and the contemporaries of the image are Moses, Isaiah, and Jesus. The expression does not describe God's physical body, but rather uses the language of power and liberation, and Isaiah then reconnects power with the suffering servant. Spiritually, God's power appears in supporting the weak, not in displaying oppression.

The image of the Lord's arm develops from the memory of Exodus to the declaration of power in Isaiah, but it does not remain an image of military power. In Isaiah 53, the arm is associated with the servant who does not impose himself by force, so the image challenges the very definition of strength. John reuses the text in the context of the rejection of some listeners, which links the announcement to response, not just viewing. Theologically, God's power works to save and expose injustice.

entries.title: Two arms
entries.content:
Arms is a dual form of זְרוֹעַ (zeroaʿ), and refers to two physical forces or extensions depending on the context. Witness: Exodus 17:12; Ezekiel 30:22; Daniel 10:10. The place is Rephidim and the arenas of prophecy, and his contemporaries Moses, Aaron, Ezekiel, and Daniel. The image of Moses shows that victory requires the support of the community, while prophecy uses the lever of political power. The introduction distinguishes between physical description and metaphor. Spiritually, the leader does not carry the burden alone.

The image of Moses' arms in Rephidim shows that victory is not the achievement of a single leader; Moses needs Aaron and Hur to keep his hands up. In prophecies, arms may symbolize the power of a king or an empire that can be broken. The introduction distinguishes between a physical function and a political metaphor, and highlights that leadership requires support and accountability. Spiritually, accepting support is part of faithfulness and not a sign of failure.

entries.title: Wolves
entries.content:
Wolves is the plural of wolf from זְאֵב (ze'ev) or λύκος (lykos), and the image appears in the language of prophecy about predation and danger. Biblical witness: Genesis 49:27; Isaiah 11:6; Jeremiah 5:6; John 10:12. The place is the wilderness, the flock, and the images of the kingdom, and its contemporaries Benjamin, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Jesus, and the shepherds. The text does not equate animals with a human group, but rather uses images to reveal violence and meet it with care. Theologically, the Good Shepherd protects the flock and does not flee from the wolf. Spiritually, leadership is tested by how well you protect the weak.

Collecting wolves expands the image of danger from an individual animal to a predatory group, but it should not be transformed into an ethnic or religious description of a human group. In Isaiah 11 God depicts the reconciliation of creation, and in John 10 the wolf appears as a test of the shepherd's faithfulness. Therefore, the study measures leadership by protecting the flock in danger, not by raising slogans. Care is a practical commitment to the weak and threatened.

entries.title: Burnt offering
entries.content: Hebrew עֹלָה (olah), that which is offered, which is the burnt offering. Witness: Leviticus 1; Genesis 8:20; Mark 12:33. The place is the altar and the tabernacle, and its contemporaries are Noah, Moses, Aaron, and the priests. Burning an offering does not mean purchasing God's favor, but rather declares complete consecration within the covenant system. The entry distinguishes between them and peace and sin offerings, and the New Testament reads the symbol without erasing its Jewish root. Spiritually, consecration is obedience and mercy, not just a ritual appearance.

entries.title: The peace offering
entries.content: Hebrew זֶבַח שְׁלָמִים (zevaḥ shelamim), peace or fellowship offering. Witness: Leviticus 3; 7:11-21; 1 Samuel 9:12-24. The place is the altar and the feast, and its contemporaries Moses and Samuel, the priests and the community. Sacrifice is linked to thanksgiving and sharing, so worship is inseparable from shared food and relationships. Sharia sets limits on impurity and time, preventing the feast from turning into chaos. Theologically, peace is organized communion before God. Spiritually, the Holy Table calls for the participation of the poor, not their exclusion.

entries.title: Sin offering

The place is the Tabernacle and the Temple, and its contemporaries are Moses, Aaron, Hezekiah, and the priests. The sacrifice is not offered as an automatic abrogation of responsibility, but as part of the treatment of covenant impurity. The study distinguishes between unintentional error and rebellion, and reads Hebrews within a Christian reinterpretation. Spiritually, reconciliation requires confession, holiness, and reform.

entries.title: The sin offering

The entry highlights that forgiveness does not cancel compensation when reparable harm occurs. The use of the word differs between sin and sacrifice, so it is necessary to adjust the context. Theologically, grace is not antagonistic to justice. Spiritually, mature repentance returns the truth to its owner.

Gratitude is not reduced to an internal feeling, but rather is embodied in offering, recognition and sharing. Sharia law sets a time for eating, linking worship to discipline. Spiritually, gratitude is a memory of salvation and responsibility toward others.

entries.title: Passover sacrifice
entries.content: The Passover sacrifice is from פֶּסַח (pesaḥ), crossing or protection, and from שֶׂה (seh), a head of sheep. Witness: Exodus 12; 2 News 30; John 19:36; 1 Corinthians 5:7. Easter is a collective memory of liberation, not an individual magical ritual. The New Testament rereads the symbol in light of Christ's death, while keeping its Jewish root. Spiritually, salvation is exit, memory, and community life.

The place is the land of Canaan, the wilderness, the Christian groups, and their contemporaries Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Paul. The promise is not limited to the biological number, but rather links it to the blessing and the message. The entry distinguishes between historical Israel and Paul's reading of the Gentiles, without erasing either. Spiritually, offspring are carriers of blessing and responsibility.

entries.content: Guilt is a legend, not a separate Hebrew name, and is used to study David's sin and the king's responsibility. Witness: 2 Samuel 11-12; Psalm 51. The place is Jerusalem, the palace, and the battlefield, and its contemporaries are David, Bathsheba, Uriah, and Nathan. The text reveals that repentance does not prevent the crime from being named, nor does it erase its political and familial effects. The entry rejects the use of the king's fall to justify abuse of power or victim-blaming. Spiritually, true confession accepts judgment and seeks a new heart.

entries.content: Temple Gold is a topical title that combines the use of gold in the Tabernacle and the Temple, and its origin is זָהָב (zahav). Witness: Exodus 10:25-22; 1 Kings 6; 2 Chronicles 3. The place: the Tabernacle and the Temple, and its contemporaries Moses, Solomon, Hiram of Tyre, and the priests. The entry explains that beauty and wealth serve worship and do not guarantee honesty of the heart; The golden calf proves the danger of the symbol. Spiritually, matter becomes sacred by function and does not become God.

entries.title: The anniversary of the Exodus
entries.content: The memory of the Exodus is a compound title based on זָכַר (zakhar), remember, and on יָצָא (yatsa), he went out. Witness: Exodus 12:14; Deuteronomy 5:15; 16:1-12; Luke 22:19. The place is the homes, the wilderness, the feast, and its contemporaries Moses, Israel, Jesus, and the disciples. Memory here is a present action that reshapes justice and identity, not just a celebration of the past. Spiritually, he who remembers liberation protects the stranger, the slave, and the poor.

entries.title: Moses' arm
entries.content: The Arm of Moses is a legend that studies the image of human strength in the face of Pharaoh, and the origin of the arm זְרוֹעַ (zeroaʿ). Witness: Exodus 4:6-9; 6:6; 17:8-13. The place is Egypt and Rephidim, and its contemporaries are Moses, Aaron, Pharaoh, and Joshua. The narrative does not attribute salvation to Moses' physical strength, but rather to the word of God and the support of the community. Spiritually, a leader needs a group to carry the burden with him.

The place: the palaces and courtyards of the empires, and their contemporaries, the kings of Egypt and Babylon, and the prophets. The picture reveals that the political arm can be broken, no matter how strong it appears. Theologically, judgment limits the authority of the emperor. Spiritually, hope is not based on the power of the state alone.

The introduction does not justify modern collective punishment, but rather examines and critiques the perception of responsibility in the ancient world. Spiritually, reform requires collective recognition and justice that protects the weak.

The place is Mount Moriah, and its contemporaries are Abraham, Isaac, and the angel. The entry distinguishes between the test command and the textual consequence that rejects the completion of human sacrifice. Jewish and Christian scholarship reads the story in multiple ways, and it cannot be used to justify harming children. Spiritually, faith does not negate the sanctity of life.

The narrative links sacrifice to the stability of creation and promise, not to the purchase of security. The entry distinguishes between sacrifice and the beginning of the covenant with every living person in Genesis 9. Spiritually, thanksgiving after deliverance leads to the responsibility of preserving life.

The place is Gibeon and the temple, and its contemporaries are Solomon, the priests, and the people. The abundance of offerings reveals the joy of the dedication but also raises the question of wealth and power. The entrance does not equate the abundance of weather with God’s satisfaction, as the king remains under the covenant. Spiritually, worship requires wisdom and justice.

The introduction distinguishes between declaring sovereignty and responsibility for the moral reading of violence. Spiritually, true worship is inseparable from rejection of corruption.

The study distinguishes between the text and later traditions. Spiritually, recognition of the true king counters the fear of authority.

entries.title: Rabbah Ammon
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: rabba from רַבָּה, meaning great or great.

Key Evidence: 2 Samuel 11:1; 12:26-31; Amos 1:13-15.

Place and context: Eastern Jordan, capital of the Ammonites near modern Amman. People contemporary with or associated with the text: David, Joab, Hanun, Ammonites.

Theological study: Rabbah Ammon appears in David's conflict with Ammon, as the narrative juxtaposes the war with David's sin in Jerusalem. The narrative of conquest does not justify violence as an independent value, but rather exposes the intersection of power, desire, and blood. In Amos, the city becomes an example of holding nations accountable for cruelty in war. Interpretation requires distinguishing between the historical city and the prophetic speech of judgment, and not turning these texts into a mandate for a contemporary religious war.

entries.title: Lord / Rabbi
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: from רַבִי rabbi: my teacher or master, from the root רבb denoting greatness.

Key Evidence: John 1:38; 3:2; Mark 9:5; Matthew 23:7-10.

Place and Context: Galilee and Judaism in the Context of First Century Jewish Education. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Jesus, John the Baptist, Nicodemus, the disciples.

Theological Study: The title Rabbi in the Gospels is a sign of respect for a teacher, and does not alone prove that Jesus held a rabbinic position corresponding to the later rabbinic institution. John uses it in discipleship dialogues, while Matthew warns against turning titles into subjective authority. The Jewish background helps to understand Jesus within the world of teachers and the reading of the law, without erasing his messianic uniqueness in the biblical narrative.

entries.title: Rabshaghi
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: From the Akkadian rab šaqê: chief cupbearer, an Assyrian administrative title.

Key Evidence: 2 Kings 17:18-37; 19:1-7; Isaiah 36-37.

Place and context: Jerusalem besieged during the reign of Sennacherib. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Hezekiah, Isaiah, Sennacherib, Eliakim.

Theological study: Rabshakeh is a title, not a personal name, and it shows an Assyrian envoy who fights with language and fear before weapons. His speech targets Judah's trust in God and Hezekiah, and uses political comparison to portray Yahweh as a helpless local god. The narrative is responded to with prayer and the prophetic word, not with nationalist rhetoric. The Assyrian inscriptions help frame Sennacherib's campaign, although their differences from the written presentation remain the subject of historical and literary study.

entries.title: Rahab
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: רָחָב rahav: wide; The derivation is not entirely settled.

Key Evidence: Joshua 2; 6:22-25; Matthew 1:5; James 2:25.

Place and context: Jericho at the entrance to the land of Canaan. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Joshua, the two spies, king of Jericho, Boaz in the genealogical tradition.

Theological study: Rahab, the woman of Jericho, who hides the spies and acknowledges the sovereignty of the Lord. The narrative does not erase her vulnerable position or her past, nor does it make her a mere moral icon; Rather, it places her work within the protection of her home and the transformation of belonging. The New Testament receives her story as an example of working faith, and the Matthew series links it to the memory of the Messianic King. What Yeshua says must be distinguished from the details added by later traditions.

entries.title: Rama
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: רָמָה ramah: high or hill.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 1:1; 7:17; Jeremiah 31:15; Matthew 2:18.

Place and context: the highlands of Benjamin and Ephraim; There are multiple places with this name. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Samuel, Anna, Rachel in the prophetic image, Jesus in Matthew's reading.

Theological study: Ramah is a common geographical name that does not automatically specify a single place. Samuel's Ramah is linked to the judicial and devotional narrative, while Jeremiah's Ramah is used in Rachel's lamentation within the horizon of return from captivity. Matthew cites the text in the context of the killing of the children of Bethlehem, a legal reading that evokes both grief and hope. It is not right to reduce the quote to a simple geographical prediction or to omit its context in Jeremiah.

entries.title: Ramot Gilead
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: רָאמֹת גִּלְעָד: Heights of Gilead.

Key Evidence: Deuteronomy 43:4; 1 Kings 22; 2 Kings 9:1-14.

Place and context: East of the Jordan in Gilead. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Ahab, Jehoshaphat, Micah ben Imlah, Jehu.

Theological study: Ramoth-gilead is a city of refuge and a disputed border site, so the texts around it combine law, war, and prophecy. In 1 Kings 22, its scene displays a conflict between the prophecy of the court and the contradictory word of Micah, so the abundance of advisors is not a criterion for truth. In 2 Kings 9, it becomes the subject of Jehu's anointing. Identification of the archaeological site is probable, not certain, and does not replace the function of place in the narrative.

entries.title: Rebekah
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: רִבְקָה rivqah: It may be related to bondage or families, and the derivation is uncertain.

Key Evidence: Genesis 24; 25:19-34; 27; Romans 9:10-13.

Place and context: Haran, Canaan, and Beer Lahi-Roi. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Isaac, Jacob, Esau, Laban.

Theological study: Rebekah in formation is active in the transmission of the promise within the covenant family: she receives the Book of Abraham, gives birth to the twins, and administers the blessing of Jacob. The narrative does not present her actions as a simple model of deception, but rather reveals the tension of promise, choice, and family. Paul uses her pregnancy to emphasize God's initiative in his debate about Israel, a use that does not negate its original narrative meaning. Readings that justify manipulation in the name of divine purposes must be resisted.

entries.title: Rehoboam
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: רְחַבְעָם reḥav'am: expands the people or expands the neighbor.

Key Evidence: 1 Kings 11:43-12:24; 14:21-31; 2 Chronicles 10-12.

Place and context: Shechem, Jerusalem, and the Kingdom of Judah. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Solomon, Jeroboam, elders, men of the new generation.

Theological study: Rehoboam, son of Solomon, begins his reign by rejecting the advice of the elders and making the yoke of work more difficult, and the king is divided. The narrative does not make the economic decision a secondary detail; The authority that only listens to its own language disintegrates the group. The text also attributes the event to a judgment related to the history of Solomon, without eliminating Rehoboam's responsibility. Chronicles and the novel compare kingship in its depiction, and the reading needs to preserve this tension.

entries.title: Sea trip will
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: יַם־סוּף yam suf: sea of reeds; The Hebrew name “Red Sea” is not literal.

Key Evidence: Exodus 17:13-21:15; Number 14; Psalm 106:7-12.

Place and context: between Egypt and the wilderness, with ongoing discussion about the location. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, Miriam, Pharaoh, the children of Israel.

Theological study: The Sea of ​​Sof is the site of the Exodus crossing, which links salvation from slavery with the formation of a people to worship. The Greek translation “Red Sea” influenced later usage, but the Hebrew text says Sea of ​​Reeds. No single geographical identification is proven from the text alone, and archaeological proposals remain debatable. Theologically, the story does not present nature as an independent enemy, but rather makes the crossing of the water a memory of God's liberation and the responsibility of the community that will later complain.

entries.title: Please rest
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שְׁאֵרִית she'erit: what remains or the survivors.

Key Evidence: Isaiah 20:10-22; Micah 2:12; Romans 11:1-5.

Place and context: Judah and Samaria, then the post-exilic communities. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Isaiah, Micah, Elijah, Paul.

Theological study: The remnant in prophecy is not a superior elite, but rather those who remain through the act of mercy after judgment and call to depend on the Lord. The term carries a historical dimension in surviving disaster and a theological dimension in continuing the promise. Paul invokes the story of Elijah to explain God's faithfulness to Israel. It should not be used to exclude Jews or reduce the church to a group without history. Each text defines the scope and function of the rest.

entries.title: Return and repent
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שׁוּב shuv: to return or return; And μετάνοια metanoia: transformation of thought and direction.

Key Evidence: Joel 2:12-13; Mark 1:15; Luke 15; Acts 2:38.

Place and context: Jerusalem, the wilderness, Galilee, and the apostolic communities. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Joel, John the Baptist, Jesus, Peter.

Theological study: Biblical repentance is a return to God that includes the heart, behavior, and relationships, not emotional regret separate from life. Joel calls for a return based on God's mercy, and Jesus announces the approach of the Kingdom and the call to faith. Proverbs of Luke 15 depict the joy of welcoming, not canceling out the reality of loss, and Acts 2 links repentance with witness and community. It is not right to turn it into a technique for earning forgiveness or into a fruitless feeling.

entries.title: Hope of resurrection
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: ἀνάστασις anastasis: rise or rise; and the Hebrew תְּחִיָּה in later use.

Key Evidence: Daniel 12:2; John 11:25-26; 1 Corinthians 15; Revelation 20-22.

Place and context: the graves in Judah, Jerusalem, and the new creation. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Daniel, Martha, Jesus, Paul, witnesses of the Resurrection.

Theological study: Resurrection is a physical and moral hope, not just the survival of the soul after death. It crystallizes in Daniel within the horizon of divine justice, and John makes it linked to the person and life of Jesus. In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul defends the resurrection of Christ and the resurrected body against denying it, not the restoration of life to the old state. Revelation 21-22 expands hope to a new creation; Therefore, a distinction must be made between resurrection, philosophical immortality, and popular images of heaven.

entries.title: The vision
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: ἀποκάλυψις apokalypsis: revealing or lifting the cover.

Key Evidence: Daniel 7; Mark 13; Revelation 1:1-3; 22:6-21.

Place and Context: Patmos and the Seven Churches of Asia Minor. People contemporary with or associated with the text: John, Christ, angels of the apocalypse, churches.

Theological study: The vision in the book is a divine revelation aimed at testimony and stability, not a secret map for calculating the histories of the world. Revelation is written to real-life churches under political and religious pressure, and makes heavy use of biblical symbols and quotations. Its opening links revelation to Jesus Christ and the blessing of reading and memorizing. There are many approaches to interpreting the book, but any responsible approach must respect its literary genre, its imperial context, and its moral message against the worship of power.

entries.title: Righteousness
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: צְדָקָה tsedaqah: uprightness and justice; And δικαιοσύνη dikaiosyne: righteousness or justice.

Key Evidence: Genesis 15:6; Psalm 72; Isaiah 1:16-17; Romans 3:21-26.

Place and context: Israel's courts, the temple, and apostolic communities. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Abraham, the Prophets, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: Righteousness in the Bible combines uprightness in the relationship with God and justice toward one’s neighbor. It is not reduced to an internal quality or an abstract legal ruling. Genesis 15 links Abraham's faith to the promise, while prophecy makes worship divorced from justice an object of condemnation. Paul explains God's righteousness in Christ within the problem of sin and the promise to Israel. Theological disagreements about justification do not permit separating faith from justice or ignoring the Jewish context of the messages.
