entries.title: Jordan River
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: יַרְדֵּן yarden: slope, from the root yard.

Key Evidence: Joshua 3-4; 2 Kings 5; Mark 1:9-11.

Place and context: The Jordan Valley between the Galilee and the Dead Sea. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Joshua, Elisha, Naaman, John the Baptist, Jesus.

Theological study: Jordan is a water barrier, a land border, and a crossing symbol, but it does not have a single symbolic meaning in every text. In Joshua, his crossing is reminiscent of the crossing of the Exodus and the responsible entry into the land, and in 2 Kings 5 ​​he becomes the subject of Naaman’s humble obedience. John the Baptist accredits the Jordan River for the baptism of repentance, and Jesus is baptized in it. Actual geography is important, but interpretation does not turn water or place into an independent magical force.

entries.title: Rome
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Roma is a Latin name; There is no Semitic biblical derivation for it.

Key Evidence: Luke 1:2; Acts 18:2; Romans 1:7; Revelation 17-18.

Place and context: The capital of the Roman Empire and the churches spread within it. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Caesar Augustus, Paul, Priscilla and Aquila, John the Revelator.

Theological study: Rome is a political and social framework for the New Testament, not a neutral background. Luke mentions the Augustan census and transfers of power, and sends Paul to a multi-ethnic congregation in the capital, while Revelation employs the image of Babylon to critique a city that consumes and oppresses. It does not literally equate every reference to Rome with Babylon, nor does it turn criticism of empire into hostility towards peoples. The theological question is how the church bears witness to Christ under broad authority.

entries.title: Romans
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: πρὸς Ῥωμαίους: to the Romanians.

Key Evidence: Romans 1-16; Acts 18:1-2; 28:16-31.

Place and context: Rome in the middle of the first century. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Paul, Phoebe, Priscilla, Aquila, the community of Rome.

Theological Study: The Epistle to the Romans is a dialectical, pastoral presentation of the Gospel in a community not founded by Paul. It begins with the general problem of sin, explains justification, reconciliation, and life in the Spirit, then addresses the fate of Israel and the unity of Jews and nations, and ends with practical guidance. Do not read its chapters as a system separate from the context of the Roman Church or from Paul's missionary message. Chapters 9-11 warn against any Christian understanding that despises Israel, and chapters 12-15 connect theology with hospitality and peace.

entries.title: Ruth
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: רוּת rut: the origin and derivation are not settled.

Key Evidence: Ruth 1-4; Matthew 1:5.

Place and context: Moab and Bethlehem in Judah. People contemporary with or related to the text: Naomi, Boaz, Orpah, David in the lineage.

Theological study: Ruth a Moabite enters Bethlehem through faithfulness to Naomi and an act of courage within the system of harvest and kinship. Travel is not reduced to a romantic story; It discusses poverty, alienation, land, redemption, and integration into the community. Boaz's relationship with the Redeemer serves a social and legal structure, and Christian connotations should not be projected onto it before reading the story. The genealogies conclude by linking the family to the memory of David, while keeping the foreign woman active at the heart of the narrative.

entries.title: Spirit of God
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: רוּחַ ruach: wind, breath, or spirit; And πνεῦμα pneuma: wind or spirit.

Key Evidence: Genesis 1:2; Ezekiel 37; Joel 2:28-29; Acts 2.

Place and context: creation, exile, Jerusalem and apostolic communities. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Ezekiel, Joel, Jesus, disciples, Peter.

Theological study: The Spirit of God is a multi-faceted term: a life force, a divine presence, and the empowerment of testimony. Genesis 1 alone does not impose a complete definition, nor does it limit the vision of the bones to a physical resurrection without regard to the restoration of the exiles. Joel announces the outpouring of the Spirit to broad categories, and Peter reads this on the day of Pentecost. Christian theology requires relating texts without erasing literary distinctions or making particular experiences the sole criterion for the work of the Spirit.

entries.title: Ruin
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: חָרְבָּה horbah: ruin; And ἐρήμωσις eremosis: ischemia or destruction.

Key Evidence: Isaiah 61:4; Jeremiah 7; Lamentations 1-5; Nehemiah 2.

Place and context: Jerusalem and Judah after the exile. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Jeremiah, the people of Judah, Nehemiah, the returnees.

Theological study: Devastation in exile literature is a political, material, and spiritual reality: burned cities, a destroyed temple, and a wounded memory. Jeremiah interprets the catastrophe within covenant criticism, but elegies do not reduce suffering to an easy equation; It gives the community a language of protest and prayer. Isaiah 61 makes building ruins a sign of social hope, while Nehemiah links building to justice and worship. Devastation should not be used to condemn contemporary disaster victims.

entries.title: Saturday rest
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שַׁבָּת shabbat: stop or stop; And ἀνάπαυσις anapausis: rest.

Key Evidence: Genesis 2:1-3; Exodus 20:8-11; Deuteronomy 5:12-15; Mark 2:23-28; Hebrews 4.

Place and context: the house, the fields, the temple, and Galilee. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Moses, the prophets, Jesus, David in Mark's argument.

Theological Study: The Sabbath rest is a reminder of creation and the Exodus, and therefore inseparable from the liberation of the servant, the stranger, and the animal from exploitation. The Gospels discuss the Sabbath in situations of healing, famine, and discipleship, presenting Jesus not as an opponent of Jewish law but as an authoritative interpreter of its merciful purpose. The Epistle to the Hebrews reads rest within the scope of God's promise, without eliminating the meaning of the commandment in its context. Stereotypes about Judaism should be avoided when reading these arguments.

entries.title: The ram
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: אַיִל ayil: ram; It may also indicate strength.

Key Evidence: Genesis 22:13; Exodus 15:29-32; Leviticus 5:15-16.

Place and context: Mount Moriah, the tabernacle, and the temple. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Abraham, Isaac, Aaron, priests.

Theological study: The ram in the Torah sacrifices is a ritual animal with multiple functions, so it cannot be reduced to one symbol. In Genesis 22, a ram appears caught in the forest instead of Isaac, showing that God is planning the sacrifice and that the promise does not end with death. In Exodus 29 it includes the consecration of priests, and in Leviticus it includes specific sacrifices. The Christian reading sees stereotypical connections to Christ, but is responsible when it first respects the meaning of the Israelite text and rejects human sacrifices.

entries.title: Ransom
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: כֹּפֶר koper: cover or compensation; The λύτρον lytron: ransom or price for liberation.

Key Evidence: Exodus 30:11-16; Job 33:24; Mark 10:45; 1 Timothy 2:6.

Place and context: tabernacle, Roman Judaism, and the apostolic churches. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Moses, Job, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Ransom is a legal, ritual, and social term that changes depending on the context. In Exodus 30, the ransom of the census is linked to the life of the community before the Lord, while Mark 10 uses the service of the Son of Man and his sacrifice for many. One word is not enough to build a complete theory of the atonement; The book also uses reconciliation, sacrifice, exodus, and victory. “Of Many” should be read in light of Isaiah 53 and the ministry of Jesus, while rejecting any notion that makes God thirsty for violence.

entries.title: Reconciliation
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: καταλλαγή catallage: a change from enmity to a relationship of peace.

Key Evidence: Leviticus 16; Romans 5:10-11; 2 Corinthians 5:18-21; Ephesians 2:11-22.

Place and context: the temple and the churches of Corinth and Ephesus. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Paul, Christ, Jews and Gentiles, the Corinthian community.

Theological Study: Reconciliation in Paul is God's initiative in Christ toward a hostile world, and it also appears in the creation of a community that transcends hostilities. 2 Corinthians does not make the apostles arbitrators of forgiveness, but rather ambassadors of the word of reconciliation. In Ephesians, the cross is linked to demolishing the wall of hostility between Jews and Gentiles, without erasing the history of Israel. Contemporary application does not equate reconciliation with bypassing justice or pressuring those affected to avoid the label of evil.

entries.title: Redemption
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: גָּאַל ga'al: undo or recover with a close description; And ἀπολύτρωσις apolytosis: liberation by redemption.

Key Evidence: Exodus 6:6; Ruth 4; Isaiah 43:1; Galatians 4:4-7.

Place and context: Egypt, Bethlehem, exile, and the Galatian communities. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Moses, Boaz, Ruth, Isaiah, Paul.

Theological study: Redemption in the Old Testament is a close image of rights, land, and salvation from slavery, and in the New Testament it is linked to the liberation of man in Christ. In Exodus God appears as a redeemer of his people, and the Book of Ruth explains the responsibility of one's neighbor within a concrete social order. Paul uses the language of redemption to affirm sonship and freedom, not individual independence without community. Therefore, the doctrine of redemption is not separated from justice, mercy, and the restoration of dignity.

entries.title: Renewal
entries.content:
Etymology: παλιγγενεσία palingenesia: new birth or renewal; And חדש hadash: make new.

Key Evidence: Ezekiel 36:25-27; John 3:3-8; Titus 3:4-7.

Place and context: the exile of Israel, Jerusalem, and the apostolic churches. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Ezekiel, Nicodemus, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: Regeneration is the work of God that creates obedience and new life, and combines the language of the heart, spirit, water, and birth. Ezekiel promises purification and a new heart for a people in exile, while Jesus speaks to Nicodemus about being born from above, a phrase that has two meanings in Greek. Titus links salvation to God's mercy and the washing of new birth, not to merited works. Renewal should not be reduced to a single momentary experience or separated from student and community growth.

entries.title: Joy
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שִׂמְחָה simhah: joy; And χαρά chara: joy or joy.

Key Evidence: Nehemiah 8:10; Psalm 16:11; Luke 2:10; Philippians 4:4.

Place and context: The Temple, Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Paul's prison. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Ezra, Nehemiah, shepherds, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Biblical Joy in Response to God's Work and Presence No command to ignore sorrow. In Nehemiah 8, the joy of the Lord becomes strength for a group that hears the law after crying, and in Luke, Christmas announces general joy. Paul writes about joy from prison within fellowship, giving, and prayer, not within comfortable comfort. Therefore, do not use the call to joy to silence those who are suffering; Rather, it is coupled with hope, prayer, and mutual care.

entries.title: Rain
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: מָטָר matar: rain; And ὑετός hyetos: rain.

Key Evidence: Deuteronomy 13:11-17; 1 Kings 17-18; Psalm 65; Matthew 5:45.

Place and context: the agricultural land of Israel and Mount Carmel. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Moses, Elijah, Ahab, Jesus.

Theological Study: Rain is a life resource in a fragile agricultural economy, and therefore writers use it in blessing, judgment, and hope. Deuteronomy links rain to the faithfulness of the covenant, but this connection does not turn into a law that explains every individual drought. In 1 Kings 17-18 drought reveals a struggle against Baal as the storm god, and in Matthew Jesus makes rain a sign of God's goodness to all people. Responsible reading avoids accusing drought victims of sin.

entries.title: Crow
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: עֹרֵב orev: crow.

Key Evidence: Genesis 8:7; 1 Kings 17:4-6; Job 38:41; Luke 12:24.

Place and context: the ark, the valley of Crete, and the wilderness of Israel. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Noah, Elijah, Jesus.

Theological study: The raven is a bird that appears first in Noah's experience of the receding waters, and then in the story of Elijah carrying food in the wilderness. The text does not explain how to feed him or make him an amulet, but rather highlights God's providence in a place of drought and danger. Jesus uses ravens as an argument against anxiety: a creation that does not store up suffers from the Creator. The interpretation does not build a doctrine of purity or impurity from the presence of the bird in one story.

entries.title: rainbow
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: קֶשֶׁת qeshet: bow, which also means weapon bow.

Key Evidence: Genesis 8:9-17; Ezekiel 1:28; Revelation 4:3.

Place and context: Heaven after the flood and in visions of the throne. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Noah, God, Ezekiel, John the Revelator.

Theological study: The rainbow in the formation of a sign of God’s covenant with Noah and all flesh after the flood. The word bow is the same as the weapon bow, and commentators have noted that the image suggests hanging a tool of war, but the text does not explain it in a separate doctrine. Ezekiel and the vision restore the image of the glory of God, so it remains a sign of mercy and sovereignty. The mark should not be transformed into the exclusive property of a group or into a promise that disasters will not occur.

entries.title: The shelter
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: מִקְלָט miqlat: a place for shelter; And καταφυγή kataphyge: refuge.

Basic evidence: Numbers 9:35-34; Deuteronomy 19:1-13; Psalm 46; Hebrews 6:18.

Place and context: Cities of refuge in Israel and the temple in the language of the Psalms. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Moses, the unintentional murderer, the elders, the psalmist.

Theological Study: Cities of Refuge A legal system that distinguishes between intentional and manslaughter, and protects against blood vengeance until the case is heard. Therefore, the recourse is not an elimination of accountability, but rather a protection of fair procedures. The Psalms borrow the language of refuge for trust in God, and Hebrews uses it for hope. The old order should not be romanticized or used to evade justice; Its focus is on saving life and curbing revenge.

entries.title: The rock
entries.content:
Etymology: צוּר tsur and סֶלַע sela: rock; And πέτρα petra: rock.

Key Evidence: Exodus 17:1-7; Deuteronomy 32; Psalm 18:2; Matthew 16:18; 1 Corinthians 10:4.

Place and context: Rephidim, the wilderness, and Caesarea Philippi. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Moses, Israel, Peter, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: The rock is an image of stability, protection, and a gift of water, and its meaning changes according to the context. In Exodus 17, the water crisis is related to the community’s complaint and the Lord’s test, while the Lord is called the Rock of Israel in the Song of Moses. Matthew 16's dialogue about Peter requires a linguistic and contextual reading and cannot be resolved simply by verbal play between Peter and the rock. Paul reads the rock of the wilderness as a symbolic Christian reading, and in doing so does not cancel out the date of the Exodus.

entries.title: The stick
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: מַטֶּה matteh: stick or tribe; The ῥάβδος rhabdos: a stick or rod.

Key Evidence: Exodus 4:1-5; 17:5-6; Number 17; Psalm 23:4.

Place and context: Egypt, the wilderness, and the Tabernacle. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, Korah, David.

Theological Study: The staff is a shepherd's tool, authority, and narrative marker, but it has no power independent of the Word of God. Moses' staff bears the verses of Exodus, Numbers 17 confirms the Aaronic priesthood in a crisis of rebellion, while Psalm 23 combines the shepherd's staff and staff in an image of protection. One must be careful not to read it as a mantra or model of religious domination; The texts place leaders accountable to God and serving the community.

entries.title: Surface
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: גָּג gag: surface; And δῶμα doma: the roof of the house.

Key Evidence: Deuteronomy 22:8; Joshua 2:6; 2 Samuel 11:2; Acts 10:9.

Place and context: The houses of Jericho, Jerusalem and Jaffa. People contemporary with or related to the text: Rahab, David, Peter, Cornelius.

Theological study: The roof in ancient houses is a practical space for sleeping, drying, and praying, and therefore appears in different scenes. Deuteronomy orders a barrier on the roof to preserve life, and Rahab hides spies on it, and from the roof of the palace begins David’s vision that leads to a grave sin. In Jaffa, Peter prays on the roof before a vision expanding the boundaries of the community. These comparisons prevent the transformation of an everyday place into a fixed moral symbol.

entries.title: Rooster
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: ἀλέκτωρ alektor: rooster.

Key Evidence: Mark 14:30; Luke 22:54-62; John 15:18-27.

Place and context: The house of the high priest in Jerusalem. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Peter, Jesus, the doormaid, the high priest.

Theological study: The rooster’s crowing in the Passion narratives is a temporal sign that recalls Jesus’ word to Peter after his denial. The Gospels differ in the order of details and expression of exhortations, and each account must be read before being combined into an artificial sequence. The scene does not stop at Peter's failure; The Gospels also confirm his re-call and ministry. Theologically, the text confronts the illusion of self-consistency and opens the way for repentance and restoration, not defamation of the collapsed.

entries.title: The way
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: דֶּרֶךְ derek: path or behavior; And ὁδός hodos: way.

Key Evidence: Isaiah 40:3; Mark 2:1-3; Acts 9:2; 19:9.

Place and context: the wilderness, Galilee, Judaism, and the Roman roads. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Isaiah, John the Baptist, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: The road in the book is a reality of travel and an image of life’s conduct. Isaiah calls for the preparation of the Lord's way in the context of the return of the exiles, and the evangelists apply it to John's ministry. The first Christian community in the Acts of the Apostles is called “the way,” which indicates an identity of living and witnessing, not just a set of ideas. Don't turn the image into escapist spirituality; Physical travel routes and city networks helped the message spread.

entries.title: Presidency and authority
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: מָשַׁל mashal: ruling; ἄρχων archon: a chief or ruler.

Key Evidence: Deuteronomy 14:17-20; Psalm 72; Mark 10:42-45; Romans 13:1-7.

Place and context: royal Israel, Roman Judaism, and Rome. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Moses, Kings, Jesus, Disciples, Paul.

Theological study: The Torah places the king under the law, and Psalm 72 prays for a ruler who will do justice to the poor. Jesus overturns the logic of sovereignty when he makes greatness service rather than domination, while Paul discusses state power in Romans 13 within the life of a weak group within Rome. Neither text offers carte blanche to the ruler or blind obedience; The book also preserves the tradition of resisting evil and bearing witness to God above humans.

entries.title: Royal priesthood
entries.content:
Etymology: βασίλειον ἱεράτευμα basileion hierateuma: royal priesthood.

Key Evidence: Exodus 19:5-6; 1 Peter 4:2-10; Revelation 1:5-6.

Place and context: Sinai and the groups of Asia Minor. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Moses, Israel, Peter, Christ, churches.

Theological Study: The Royal Priesthood in 1 Peter A quotation and adaptation of the Exodus 19 promise to Israel: a community called to proclaim the works of God among the nations. The text does not eliminate its Israelite roots or transform the church into a political authority. The identity relates to living stones, holiness, and good behavior in the midst of persecution, and the vision presents the king and priests as serving God. Responsible reading rejects privilege and emphasizes witness and compassion.

entries.title: White clothes
entries.content:
Etymology: λευκός leukos: white or shiny; And στολή stole: a long dress.

Key Evidence: Daniel 7:9; Mark 9:3; Revelation 4:3-5; 7:9-14.

Place and context: The Mount of Transfiguration and the heavenly throne in the vision. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Jesus, Moses, Elijah, the elders of the vision, the crowds.

Theological study: The white clothes in the vision are a sign of victory, purity, and worship, and they use visual language, not a simple physical description of the afterlife. It responds to the clothes of the Transfigured One and to the throne scenes in Daniel, but each context gives the image a special function. In Revelation 7, the clothes are washed in the blood of the Lamb, a symbolic paradox that resists the logic of power. No dress code or ethnic preferences should be built from symbolic color.

entries.title: Redemption in the Book of Exodus
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: פָּדָה padah: ransomed or saved; And גאל ga'al: restored as a relative.

Key Evidence: Exodus 12-15; 19:4-6; Deuteronomy 7:6-8.

Place and context: Egypt, the wilderness, and Mount Sinai. People contemporary with or associated with the text: Moses, Pharaoh, Aaron, the Children of Israel.

Theological Study: The Book of Exodus links redemption with the exit from slavery and then entry into a covenant and service. Salvation is not a private goal, as God leads it to a community called to holiness and justice. The language of divine power and the language of immediate redemption juxtapose in the texts, bringing together liberation and belonging. The New Testament recovers this mode of understanding the work of Christ, but it neither erases Israelite history nor makes salvation separate from the liberation of the oppressed.

entries.title: Zechariah the Prophet
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: זְכַרְיָה: The Lord remembers.

Basic evidence: Zechariah 1-14; Ezra 5:1-2; Matthew 21:5.

Place and context: Persian Jerusalem and Judah after the exile. People associated with the text: Haggai, Joshua the priest, Zerubbabel, the returnees.

Theological study: The book links the rebuilding of the temple with visions of purifying leadership and the presence of the Lord and His sovereignty over the nations. Researchers are divided in the history of its units, but the legal reading preserves the unity of hope and accountability.

entries.title: Zakaria Abu Youhanna
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Ζαχαρίας: Greek form of Zechariah, the Lord remembers.

Key Evidence: Luke 5:1-80.

Place and context: The Temple of Jerusalem and Ein Kerem in a later tradition. People associated with the text: Elizabeth, Gabriel, Mary, John the Baptist.

Theological study: Zechariah is a good priest whose silence and then his song become a framework for announcing the birth of John. His song links God's mercy to the promise of Abraham and the house of David, and presents John as a prophet who prepares the way.

entries.title: Zechariah son of Jehoiada
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: זְכַרְיָה: The Lord remembers.

Key Evidence: 2 Chronicles 24:20-22; Matthew 23:35.

Place and context: The temple house in Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Jehoiada, Joash, leaders of Judah.

Theological study: Zechariah confronts the king and the people after the death of his father, and is killed in the temple courtyard. The book links the rejection of the Word with political and spiritual collapse, and the New Testament invokes the memory of the blood of the Witnesses.

entries.title: Smart
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Ζακχαῖος from a Semitic root denoting purity or righteousness.

Key Evidence: Luke 19:1-10.

Place and context: Jericho on the way up to Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Jesus, tax collectors, Jericho crowd.

Theological study: Zaki is a rich chief tax collector, but meeting Jesus transforms money from a sign of isolation into a field of return, compensation, and giving. The story does not make salvation a reward for his work, but rather the fruit of Jesus' presence in the home.

entries.title: Buttery
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Ζεβεδαῖος, and possible Hebrew origin: gift of the Lord.

Key Evidence: Matthew 4:21-22; 20:20-28; Mark 1:19-20.

Place and context: Sea of ​​Galilee. People associated with the text: James, John, Jesus, mother of Zebedee's sons.

Theological study: Zebedee, the father of James and John, is a fisherman, and appears in the background of their vocation. The story reveals that apprenticeship rearranges economic and family ties, but it does not excuse the neglect of family or work as a general rule.

entries.title: Zebulon
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: זְבוּלֻן: dwelling or dignity, and the derivation is subject to debate.

Key Evidence: Genesis 30:20; 49:13; Joshua 19:10-16; Isaiah 9:1.

Place and context: Lower Galilee and northern Israel. People associated with the text: Jacob, Moses, Isaiah, inhabitants of Galilee.

Theological study: Zebulun is a tribe that appears in genealogies, blessings, and geographical division. Isaiah regains his land with Naphtali in the hope of light, and then Matthew reads that at the beginning of Jesus’ ministry in Galilee.

entries.title: He swayed
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: זֶבַח: sacrifice or proper name.

Key Evidence: Judges 4:8-21; Psalm 83:11.

Place and context: eastern Jordan and Karkar. People associated with the text: Gideon, Zalmunna, the men of Sukkot.

Theological Study: Zebah, King of Midian, occurs at the conclusion of Gideon's campaign. The narrative does not present a war without criticism, but rather reveals the spiral of revenge and the refusal of Israeli cities to stand in solidarity in times of danger.

entries.title: Sacrifice and sacrifice
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: זֶבַח: sacrifice, from the verb to slaughter.

Key Evidence: Exodus 12:27; Leviticus 3; Psalm 51:16-17; Hebrews 10.

Place and Context: Tabernacle, Temple, and New Testament Communities. People associated with the text: Moses, the priests, David, Christ.

Theological study: The sacrifice in the Torah is a system of worship and covenant, not a magical mechanism. The prophets offer sacrifice separate from obedience, and the New Testament reads the work of Christ in the light of this symbolic world with an emphasis on the life of faith and obedience.

references.author: John H. Walton, Ancient Near Eastern Thought and the Old Testament

entries.title: Zebul
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Ζεβούλ: prince or lord; His connection to Beelzebub is debated.

Key Evidence: Matthew 10:25; 12:24-28; Mark 3:22-27.

Place and context: Galilee and Judaism. People associated with the text: Jesus, the scribes, the crowds.

Theological study: Zebul appears in Jesus’ opponents accusing him of expelling demons by the power of the prince of demons. Jesus responds with the logic of the division of the kingdom and the declaration of the presence of the Kingdom of God, not by satisfying curiosity about the ranks of evil powers.

entries.title: Jealousy of the Lord
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: קִנְאָה qinah: jealousy or fever.

Key Evidence: Exodus 20:5; Numbers 25:10-13; Zechariah 1:14.

Place and context: Sinai, Shittim, and Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Moses, Phinehas, Zechariah.

Theological Study: Jealousy of the Lord is covenantal language that describes God’s rejection of idolatry and injustice, and is not an imperfect human emotion. Violent texts must be read carefully, and must not be used to justify religious fanaticism or individual revenge.

references.title: Baker Academic

entries.title: Zemmour
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: מִזְמוֹר mizmor: a hymn with instrumental music.

Key Evidence: Psalm 3; 23; 51; 150.

Place and Context: The Temple and Cult Environments in Israel. People associated with the text: David, the singers, and the worship group.

Theological study: The psalm is a poetic text for worship and prayer, not just hymn words. Its types vary between complaint, praise, wisdom, and kingship, and it builds a sincere language of joy, fear, and hope before God.

entries.title: Zimri bin Salu
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: זִמְרִי: May be associated with chanting or power.

Key Evidence: Numbers 6:25-15; Psalm 106:28-31.

Place and context: Shittim in Moab. People associated with the text: Phinehas, Cozbi, Moses, the children of Israel.

Theological study: Zimri appears in the Baal Peor crisis that brings together strange worship and mass chaos. The text records his name and lineage, but the interpretation of Phinehas's act does not give individuals the authority to carry out religious violence outside the text and his covenant.

entries.title: Zimri the king
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: זִמְרִי: proper name; The derivation is uncertain.

Key Evidence: 1 Kings 8:16-20.

Place and context: Tirzah, the capital of the Northern Kingdom. People associated with the text: Elah, Omri, the army of Israel.

Theological study: Zimri reigned for seven days after the assassination of Elah, then his rule ended with suicide at the siege of Omri. The narrative demonstrates the fragility of power built on assassination and the continued judgment of the House of Baasha.

entries.title: Fake
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: זִיף: name of a place or gloss.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 14:23-29; 26:1-4; Psalm 54.

Place and context: The Judah Wilderness, southeast of Hebron. People associated with the text: David, Saul, Zion, Abishai.

Theological study: Zif is a place in which David experiences betrayal and danger before the king. David refuses to kill Saul when the opportunity arises, so the story links survival with controlling power and waiting for God's judgment.

entries.title: The olives
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Zif: attributed to Zif.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 23:19; 26:1; Psalm 54.

Place and context: The Wilderness of Ziph in Judah. People associated with the text: David, Saul, residents of Ziph.

Theological study: Some Zainites deliver news of David to Saul, and local geography turns into a loyalty test. It is not correct to generalize the action of a group in a story to the inhabitants of an entire region or people.

entries.title: Zalfa
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: זִלְפָּה: It may indicate a drop or perfume, and the derivation is not clear.

Key Evidence: Genesis 29:24; 30:9-13; 35:26.

Place and context: Adan Aram and Canaan. People associated with the text: Leah, Jacob, Gad, Asher.

Theological study: Zilpah, Leah’s maid and the mother of Gad and Asher, according to the narrative. Her presence reveals the system of family, procreation, and power in the ancient world, and does not beautify the exploitation of women or transform the description into a moral model.

entries.title: Zelophehad
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: צְלָפְחָד: the derivation is uncertain.

Basic evidence: Numbers 26:33; 27:1-11; 36:1-12.

Place and context: Plains of Moab before entering the land. People associated with the text: daughters of Zelophehad, Moses, Eleazar.

Theological study: The daughters of Zelophehad ask for the right to inheritance after their father died without a son, so Moses listens to the ruling from the Lord. The text shows that Sharia deals with a new situation that preserves the family’s name and rights, and that listening to the aggrieved parties is part of justice.

entries.title: Zalmon
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: צַלְמוֹן: It may be associated with shadow or darkness.

Key Evidence: Judges 9:48; Psalm 68:14.

Place and context: near Shechem or in Bashan, depending on possible identification. People associated with the text: Abimelech, the people of Shechem, the psalmist.

Theological study: Zalmon the mountain is linked to Abimelech's campaign against the tower of Shechem, and the name of a relative appears in poetic form in the psalm. The difference in context prevents the integration of signals into one certain history.

entries.title: Zalmunna
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: צַלְמֻנָּע: The name is of uncertain derivation.

Key Evidence: Judges 4:8-21; Psalm 83:11.

Place and context: eastern Jordan and Karkar. People associated with the text: Gideon, Zebah, Jether, the people of Nobah.

Theological study: Zalmunna is Zebah’s partner in the narrative of Gideon, and the chapter on their killing embodies the difficulty of moving from defending the group to revenge. The narrative calls for a critical reading of power, not its glorification.

entries.title: Zion
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: צִיּוֹן: name of a place; The origin of the word is debated.

Key Evidence: 2 Samuel 5:7; Psalm 48; Isaiah 2:1-4; Hebrews 12:22.

Place and context: Jerusalem and the Temple Mount. People associated with the text: David, the prophets, the community of Hebrews.

Theological study: Zion is a fortress, a city, and a symbol of God’s presence and kingdom. Prophecy criticizes Zion's confidence when it is separated from justice, then makes it a horizon of peace in which nations learn the ways of the Lord.

entries.title: Olive oil
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: זַיִת zayit: olive.

Key Evidence: Exodus 27:20; Deuteronomy 8:8; Zechariah 4:1-14; Romans 11:17-24.

Place and context: the Land of Israel and the Temple. People associated with the text: Aaron, Zechariah, Paul.

Theological study: Oil is a source of nourishment, light, and anointing, and it appears in Zechariah as an image of the spirit’s help in rebuilding. Paul uses the olive tree to warn the nations against pride and to call for hope for Israel.

entries.title: Anointing oil
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שֶׁמֶן הַמִּשְׁחָה: anointing or anointing oil.

Key Evidence: Exodus 30:22-33; Leviticus 8:10-12; James 5:14.

Place and context: tabernacle, temple, and church communities. People associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, priests, elders.

Theological study: Anointing oil designates things and people for the service of God, so it does not become a magical substance or private property. The Church uses oil in prayer for the sick, while keeping hope in God and not in the tool.

entries.title: Zerubbabel
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: זְרֻבָּבֶל: the seed of Babylon or the descendants of Babylon.

Basic evidence: Ezra 3-6; Haggai 1-2; Zechariah 4; Matthew 1:12-13.

Place and context: Jerusalem in Persian Judah. People associated with the text: Joshua the priest, Haggai, Zechariah, Darius.

Theological study: Zerubbabel, a leader of the descendants of David, leads the returnees in establishing the temple. His name bears the memory of exile, but his message does not restore an independent king but rather builds a communal cult under Persian rule.

entries.title: Zerah
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: זֶרַח: sunrise or dawning.

Key Evidence: Genesis 38:27-30; Joshua 7:1; Matthew 1:3.

Place and context: Canaan and Judah. People associated with the text: Tamar, Pharez, Achan, Judah.

Theological study: Zerah, son of Judah and Tamar, and the genealogies preserve his role alongside Pharez. The story of Achan, attributed to Zerah, distinguishes between lineage and individual responsibility; The grandson does not automatically bear the guilt of his person.

references.author: John H. Walton, Ancient Near Eastern Thought and the Old Testament

entries.title: Zarephath
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: צָרְפַת: place of smelting metals.

Key Evidence: 1 Kings 8:17-24; Luke 4:25-26.

Place and context: The coast of Phenicia between Tire and Sidon. People associated with the text: Elijah, the widow, her son, Jesus.

Theological Study: At Zarephath, Elijah lives with a Gentile widow during a drought, and the narrative reveals God's providence that crosses borders. Jesus brings up the story in Nazareth to confront the monopoly of grace, not to despise Israel.

entries.title: Field lily
entries.content:
Etymology: κρίνον krinon: lily or wild flower.

Key Evidence: Matthew 6:28-34; Luke 12:27.

Place and context: The Galilee Hills. People associated with the text: Jesus, the disciples, the crowds.

Theological study: The lily of the field in Jesus' sermon is not a lesson in botany, but an argument against prevailing anxiety. The text does not glorify laziness; It calls for trusting the Father of Heaven and putting the kingdom and righteousness first.

entries.title: Hyssop
entries.content:
Etymology: אֵזוֹב ezov: aromatic plant; Its botanical identification is uncertain.

Key Evidence: Exodus 12:22; Leviticus 14; Psalm 51:7; John 19:29.

Place and context: Egypt, the Temple, and Golgotha. People associated with the text: Moses, priests, David, Jesus.

Theological Study: Hyssop is used for sprinkling blood or purifying water, associating a familiar plant with a transition from impurity to approachability. One should not be certain about the modern identity of the plant or construct a magical ritual based on its uses.

references.author: John H. Walton, Ancient Near Eastern Thought and the Old Testament
references.title: Baker Academic

entries.title: Adultery
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: נָאַף na'af: adultery; And πορνεία porneia: sexual indecency.

Key Evidence: Exodus 20:14; Hosea 1-3; Matthew 5:27-30; 1 Corinthians 6:12-20.

Place and context: ancient Israel and the churches of Greek cities. People associated with the text: Moses, Hosea, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: The prohibition of adultery protects the marital covenant and the dignity of the body and the neighbor. The prophecy uses the language of adultery to describe idolatry, but the metaphor should not turn into stigmatization of women or survivors of abuse.

references.title: NIBC

references.title: Baker Academic

entries.title: Marriage
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: בְּרִית berit: covenant; And γάμος gamos: marriage.

Key Evidence: Genesis 2:18-25; Malachi 2:13-16; Matthew 19:3-12; Ephesians 5:21-33.

Place and Context: The Home in Israel and Roman Judaism. People associated with the text: Adam and Eve, the prophets, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: Marriage in the book is a covenantal relationship related to loyalty, kinship, physicality, and hospitality. Its texts are discussed in different patriarchal and economic contexts, so they are not used to perpetuate abuse or control; The New Testament places mutual love at the center.

references.author: Craig S. Keener, The Gospel of Luke
references.title: NIBC

entries.title: Time and times
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: עֵת et: time or season; And καιρός kairos: a good time.

Key Evidence: Ecclesiastes 3:1-8; Daniel 7:25; Mark 1:15; Acts 1:7.

Place and context: Israel, exile and Galilee. People associated with the text: Ecclesiastes, Daniel, Jesus, the Apostles.

Theological study: The texts distinguish between daily time and God’s timings, so they do not lead to inevitability or calculations of the end of the world. Jesus declares the fullness of time with a call to repentance, and the Acts of the Apostles forbids turning times into knowledge possessed by the disciples.

entries.title: An earthquake
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: רָעַשׁ ra'ash: trembling; And σεισμός seismos: earthquake.

Key Evidence: Exodus 19:18; 1 Kings 19:11-12; Matthew 27:51-54; Revelation 6:12.

Place and context: Sinai, Horeb, Jerusalem, and the visions of the apocalypse. People associated with the text: Moses, Elijah, Jesus, the centurion.

Theological study: The earthquake is an image of divine presence and cosmic transformation in multiple texts, but it is not an automatic explanation for every natural disaster. Horeb emphasizes that God is not reduced to violent phenomena, and the Gospel places the earthquake near Jesus' death.

entries.content:
Linguistic origin: זְמוֹר: recited; The Psalms are an Arabic name for the Psalms.

Key Evidence: Psalm 1; 19; 23; 51; 150.

Place and Context: Israel, the Temple, and Collective Worship. People associated with the text: David, the psalmists, and the community of Israel.

Theological Study: The Psalms of David is a common Arabic name for the Book of Psalms, although the titles do not attribute all of the Psalms to David. The book provides a language of prayer that includes praise, complaint, repentance, and trust, and should not be used to silence sadness.

entries.title: Structure angle
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: κεφαλὴ γωνίας kephale gonias: the head of the corner.

Key Evidence: Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 28:16; Matthew 21:42; 1 Peter 2:4-8.

Place and context: the temple, Jerusalem, and church communities. People associated with the text: Psalmist, Isaiah, Jesus, Peter.

Theological study: the cornerstone image of construction, rejection, and choice. The New Testament uses it in light of Jesus' rejection and resurrection and the building of a living community, without making the community a justification for despising Israel.

entries.title: Olive Mountain
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Ὄρος Ἐλαιῶν: Mount of Olives.

Basic evidence: Zechariah 14:4; Luke 19:29-44; 22:39-46; Acts 1:9-12.

Place and context: east of Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Jesus, the disciples, Zechariah.

Theological study: The Mount of Olives, the scene of Jesus’ entry and prayer before his Passion and ascension. The Gospels invoke his geography and prophecies, but his importance is not reduced to political predictions or end-time maps.

entries.title: Daughter of Zion
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: בַּת־צִיּוֹן: Daughter of Zion, a poetic personification of the city.

Key Evidence: Isaiah 1:8; Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 21:5.

Place and context: Jerusalem. People associated with the text: prophets, townspeople, Jesus.

Theological study: The Daughter of Zion is a metaphor for the city and its people in weakness, joy, and a call to repentance. Matthew invokes it in Jesus' meek entry, maintaining the tension of humble kingship and prophetic hope.

entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שִׁירֵי צִיּוֹן: Songs of Zion.

Key Evidence: Psalm 137; Isaiah 52:7-10; Revelation 14:1-3.

Place and context: Babylon, Jerusalem, and vision. People associated with the text: exiles, singers, people of God.

Theological study: Hymns of Zion combine longing, pain, and hope. Psalm 137 does not hide the wound of exile, and therefore its harsh language should be read as poetry of complaint, not as a practical call for violence.

entries.title: Zenas
entries.content:
Etymology: Ζηνᾶς Zenas: Greek name, often shortened from Zenodoros.

Key Evidence: Titus 3:13.

Place and Context: Crete and Apostolic Travel Networks. People associated with the text: Titus, Apollos, Paul.

Theological study: Zenas is an expert in the law. Paul asks Titus to help him in his travel with Apollos. The text does not provide an extensive biography of him, but it reveals the churches' interest in practical hospitality and supporting workers in education and mission.

entries.title: The tares of the field
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: ζιζάνια zizania: tares or wheat-like grass.

Key Evidence: Matthew 13:24-30; 13:36-43.

Place and context: The fields of Galilee in the parable. People associated with the text: Jesus, the disciples, the owner of the field, the reapers.

Theological Study: The Parable of the Tares explains the patience of the Kingdom in a world where good and evil mix until harvest time. The parable does not give the group a mandate to uproot people in the name of purity, but rather warns against hasty judgment that also harms the wheat.

entries.title: The adornment of holiness
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: הֲדַר־קֹדֶשׁ hadar-qodesh: the splendor of holiness.

Key Evidence: Psalm 29:2; 96:9; 1 Peter 3:3-4.

Place and Context: Temple and Worship Communities. People associated with the text: the psalmists, the worship people, Peter.

Theological study: The adornment of holiness in the Psalms is a language of worship that sees the beauty of God coupled with His holiness, not with a showy appearance. Peter's message calls for rearranging the value of adornment in the light of gentleness and hope, not to despise the body or impose a single cultural standard.

entries.title: New Zion
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Σιών Sion: Greek translation of Zion.

Key Evidence: Isaiah 62; Hebrews 12:22-24; Revelation 21-22.

Place and Context: Prophetic Jerusalem and the New Creation. People associated with the text: Prophets, Jesus, the community of Hebrews, John.

Theological study: Zion moves from a historical city to the language of eschatological hope for God's presence and peace. This does not abolish land and history, nor does it allow for the claim of ownership of the City of God against others; The vision ends with an image of the healing of nations.

entries.title: Samaria
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שֹׁמְרוֹן: a place of guarding or surveillance.

Key Evidence: 1 Kings 16:24; John 4; Acts 4:8-25.

Place and context: The highlands of Samaria between Galilee and Judea. People associated with the text: Omri, Ahab, the Samaritan woman, Philip.

Theological study: Samaria is a northern capital and then a region that carries the memory of division, mixing, and hostility. Jesus crosses its borders through dialogue, thirst, and revelation of the truth, and the Acts of the Apostles continue to bear witness to it.

entries.title: Good Samaritan
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Σαμαρείτης: Samaritan, from Samaria.

Key Evidence: Luke 10:25-37.

Place and context: The road between Jerusalem and Jericho. People associated with the text: Jesus, a lawyer, a priest, a Levite, a Samaritan.

Theological study: The parable turns the question of who is the relative into the question of who has become a relative of the sufferer. He does not make the Samaritan an abstract symbol, but rather confronts the limits of religious and ethnic identity with the costly practice of mercy.

entries.title: Samson
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שִׁמְשׁוֹן: May be associated with the sun or service.

Key Evidence: Judges 13-16; Hebrews 11:32.

Place and context: Saraa, Wadi Suriq, and Gaza. People associated with the text: Manoah, Delilah, the Philistines.

Theological study: Samson is a Nazirite called to begin the salvation of Israel, but the narrative reveals a contrast between the gift of power and the weakness of desire and revenge. His mention in Hebrews does not turn his errors into a model.

entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שְׁמוּאֵל: He heard God or the name of God.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 1-16; 25:1; Acts 3:24.

Place and context: Shiloh, Ramah, and Mizpah. People associated with the text: Anna, Eli, Saul, David.

Theological study: Samuel considers Israel's transition from judges to kingship, and combines prayer, judgment, and prophecy. He places the king under the word of God and refuses to make authority a substitute for obedience.

entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שָׂרָה: princess.

Key Evidence: Genesis 11:29-23:20; Romans 4:19; Hebrews 11:11.

Place and context: Haran, Canaan, and Gerar. People associated with the text: Abraham, Hagar, Isaac.

Theological Study: Sarah experiences the long wait for a promise, the laughter of impossibility, and family conflicts. Faith reading does not eliminate her voice or her pain, but rather sees God’s faithfulness in the midst of human fragility.

entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שָׂרַי: my princess; Then Sarah is a princess.

Key Evidence: Genesis 12:10-20; 16; 17:15-21.

Place and context: Egypt and Canaan. People associated with the text: Abram, Hagar, Ishmael.

Theological Study: Changing Sarai's name is part of an expansion of the covenant promise, but it does not erase the complexity of her relationship with Hagar or what the narrative reveals about the strength and weakness of the patriarchal household.

entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שְׁלֹמֹה: associated with peace or perfection.

Basic evidence: 1 Kings 1-11; 2 Chronicles 1-9; Matthew 6:29.

Place and context: Jerusalem, Israel and trade routes. People associated with the text: David, Hiram, Queen of Sheba, Rehoboam.

Theological Study: Solomon builds the temple and seeks wisdom, but wealth, alliances, and strange worship rip through his image. The narrative refuses to reduce the king to a discrete urban success or moral failure.

Linguistic origin: Σιλωάμ: the sender; From the Hebrew Shiloh.

Key Evidence: John 1:9-41; Luke 13:4.

Place and context: The Pool of Siloam in Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Jesus, the man born blind, the Pharisees.

Theological study: The man washes in Siloam at Jesus' command, and the story progresses from healing to a question of insight and faith. Jesus refuses to link the disaster in the tower to any specific personal guilt.

entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Σιλᾶς: a form of Silvanus, the derivation is unclear.

Key Evidence: Acts 22:15-5:18; 1 Peter 5:12.

Place and context: Antioch, Philippi, and Thessalonica. People associated with the text: Paul, Barnabas, Timothy, Lydia.

Theological study: Silas is a witness, prophet, and companion of Paul in the mission. He appears in prison worship and in the founding of churches. His role highlights that martyrdom is a team work, not an individual heroism.

entries.content:
Etymology: Σιλουανός: Latin or Greek form of Scylla.

Key Evidence: 2 Corinthians 1:19; 1 Thessalonians 1:1; 1 Peter 5:12.

Place and context: Corinth, Thessalonica, and Asia Minor. People associated with the text: Paul, Timothy, Peter.

Theological study: Silvanus is a link between the Pauline and Petrine mission networks. The few references do not allow the construction of a complete biography, but they show the value of trust, writing, and transmission between churches.

entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Σίμων: hearing; Πέτρος: rock.

Key Evidence: Matthew 13:16-20; Luke 1:5-11; John 21; Acts 2.

Place and context: Galilee, Jerusalem and Caesarea. People associated with the text: Jesus, Andrew, James, Cornelius.

Theological study: Peter is a disciple who advances in confession, then stumbles, denies, and is restored to service. The Book of Acts links his testimony to the Spirit and the community’s opening to the nations, so his character is not read as an unaccountable authority.

Place and context: Galilee and Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Jesus, the Twelve.

Theological study: The text does not know about Simon except his position among the Twelve and his title. The surname may refer to religious zeal or a political movement, and the shortness of the witness does not allow for a detailed biography.

Key Evidence: Luke 2:25-35.

Place and context: The Jerusalem temple. People associated with the text: Mary, Joseph, the child Jesus, Anna.

Theological study: Simon awaits the consolation of Israel and receives Jesus in the temple. His song links God's salvation with light for the nations and glory for Israel, recognizing that Christ's message reveals the thoughts of hearts.

Linguistic origin: Σίμων Κυρηναῖος: Simon of Cyrene.

Key Evidence: Matthew 27:32; Mark 15:21; Luke 23:26.

Place and context: The Way of the Cross in Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Jesus, soldiers, Alexander, Rufus.

Theological study: The soldiers force Simon to carry the cross, so the question remains open about his internal response. Luke uses the scene to depict the carrying of the cross behind Jesus, without turning Roman coercion into a romantic ideal of suffering.

Theological study: Susanna, one of the women who served Jesus and his disciples with their money. This witness refuses to reduce women to a marginal presence, while respecting the limited details provided by the text.

entries.title: Sodom
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: סְדֹם: the name of a place, its derivation is unclear.

Key Evidence: Genesis 13-19; Ezekiel 16:49-50; Luke 17:28-32.

Place and context: the Jordan Valley and the Dead Sea. People associated with the text: Lot, Abraham, angels.

Theological study: Sodom is a city whose story is read in the light of violence, aggression, refusal of hospitality, arrogance, and neglect of the poor. It is not permissible to use it to justify hatred of a human group or to reduce the message of the prophets.

entries.title: Sinai
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: סִינַי: the name of a mountain, its derivation is unclear.

Key Evidence: Exodus 19-24; 32-34; Galatians 4:24-31.

Place and context: Mount Sinai in the wilderness. People associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, Israel.

Theological study: Sinai is the place of declaring the covenant, law, and worship, as well as the place of making the calf and breaking and renewing the covenant. The story reveals that freedom emerging from Egypt learns its form in the service of God and justice.

entries.title: God's dwelling place
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שָׁכַן shakan: residence; Shekhinah is a later Jewish term.

Key Evidence: Exodus 25:8; 40:34-38; John 1:14; Revelation 21:3.

Place and context: tabernacle, temple, and new creation. People associated with the text: Moses, Israel, Jesus, John.

Theological study: The word Shekhinah itself does not appear in the Hebrew text, but it is a later designation for the indwelling presence of God. Exodus describes the glory of the Lord in the tabernacle, and John uses the verb to dwell in reference to the incarnate Word.

entries.title: Saturday
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שַׁבָּת: stop or stop.

Key Evidence: Genesis 2:1-3; Exodus 20:8-11; Deuteronomy 5:12-15; Mark 2:23-28.

Place and context: the house, the fields, the temple. People associated with the text: Moses, David, Jesus, disciples.

Theological study: The Sabbath links creation to the Exodus and limits the exploitation of the worker and the stranger. Jesus' arguments about mercy and the purpose of the commandment do not make Judaism a superficial opponent of grace.

entries.title: Saturday year
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שַׁבַּת שַׁבָּתוֹן: Saturday of rest.

Key Evidence: Exodus 23:10-11; Leviticus 25:1-7.

Place and context: the agricultural land of Israel. People associated with the text: Moses, the poor, strangers.

Theological study: The Sabbath year leaves the earth to rest, and the poor and the animals eat of its fruit. Sharia law places ownership and work within God’s ownership of the land, not within an absolute right to depletion. The association of the comfort of the land with the food of the poor and the strange highlights that the will is not an agricultural technique divorced from social justice. The text alone does not prove a complete history of application in every age, but it reveals a strong critique of the monopoly of fruit and makes human and animal welfare part of the covenant's fidelity.

entries.title: Samaritans of the Torah
entries.content:
Linguistic Origin: The Samaritans are a group associated with the Samaria region and the Books of Moses.

Key Evidence: Deuteronomy 27:4; John 4:20-22.

Place and context: Samaria and Mount Gerizim. People associated with the text: Samaritans, Jews, Jesus.

Theological study: The Samaritans preserved a text of the Torah that differs in places from the Masoretic text and focuses on Gerizim. This helps to understand the difference in worship in John 4, while avoiding describing the congregation in pejorative terms. Textual differences reveal that ancient groups read Sharia law within a contested spatial and religious memory, not outside history. In Jesus' dialogue with the Samaritan woman, the question about worship is not abolished, but rather is transferred to worshiping the Father in spirit and truth while recognizing the roots of salvation in the history of Israel.

entries.title: Ambassador
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: סַפִּיר sappir: often a blue gemstone.

Key Evidence: Exodus 24:10; Ezekiel 1:26; Revelation 21:19.

Place and context: Sinai and visions of the throne. People associated with the text: Moses, elders, Ezekiel, John.

Theological Study: The sapphire is an image of brilliance, throne, and glory, not conclusive evidence of a modern metallic definition. Its significance changes between the Testament scene and the vision, and the nature of the figurative language must be preserved.

entries.content:
Linguistic origin: חֶרֶב herev: sword; μάχαιρα machaira: sword.

Key Evidence: Genesis 3:24; Isaiah 4:2; Matthew 26:52; Ephesians 6:17.

Place and context: Aden, Israel, Galilee and the churches. People associated with the text: Adam, the Prophets, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: The sword is a tool of war and judgment and an image of the word in various contexts. Jesus' statement about the sword in Gethsemane prohibits the use of violence in defense of his message, and Isaiah turns the horizon to peace among the nations.

entries.title: Hello
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שָׁלוֹם shalom: peace and safety; εἰρήνη eirene: Peace.

Basic evidence: Numbers 6:24-26; Isaiah 9:6; John 14:27; Ephesians 2:14.

Place and Context: Israel and the Apostolic Churches. People associated with the text: Aaron, Isaiah, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: Peace is the completion of a relationship, well-being, and justice, not just the absence of conflict. Jesus proclaims a peace unlike the peace of the world, and Paul describes Christ as the peace of two hostile groups.

entries.content:
Linguistic origin: נַעַל na'al: sole; ὑπόδημα hypodema: shoe.

Key Evidence: Exodus 3:5; Ruth 4:7; Mark 1:7; Ephesians 6:15.

Place and context: Sinai, Bethlehem, and the wilderness. People associated with the text: Moses, Boaz, John the Baptist.

Theological study: The sandal is a sign of sacred land, legal treatment, and travel preparation. John declares that he is not worthy of untying the straps of Jesus' sandals, thus making Christ's status clear without the insult to manual labor.

Linguistic origin: σπείρω speiro: to plant; σπόρος sporos: seed.

Key Evidence: Mark 1:4-20; Matthew 1:13-23; Luke 4:8-15.

Place and context: the fields of Galilee. People associated with the text: Jesus, the disciples, the crowds.

Theological study: The parable of the sower explains the reception of the word of the Kingdom with the land of the heart, the path, tribulations, and worries. He does not place easy blame on those who suffer, but rather calls for fruitful listening and patience.

entries.title: Sefra Samuel
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Σαμουήλ: name of the book of Samuel.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 1-31; 2 Samuel 1-24.

Place and context: Israel, Ramah, and Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Samuel, Saul, David, Nathan.

Theological study: The two books present the emergence of kingship under the word of prophecy, the rise and fall of David, and the promise of the Davidic house. They do not hide the corruption of leaders, so they become a theological criticism of power.

entries.title: Seraphim
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שְׂרָפִים seraphim: flaming or burning.

Key Evidence: Isaiah 6:1-7; Numbers 21:6-9.

Place and context: The Jerusalem temple and the Sinai wilderness. People associated with the text: Isaiah, Uzziah, Seraphim.

Theological study: Seraphim are visionary beings who proclaim the holiness of the Lord and touch the lips of Isaiah for purification. The text does not provide a detailed system of the ranks of angels, but rather directs attention to the holiness of God and the mission of the Prophet.

entries.title: The fall of man
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: חַטָּאת hatta't: sin; ἁμαρτία hamartia: failure or sin.

Key Evidence: Genesis 3; Psalm 51; Romans 3:9-26; 5:12-21.

Place and context: Aden, Israel and Rome. People associated with the text: Adam and Eve, David, Paul.

Theological Study: The Fall of Genesis 3 tells of disobedience and a rupture in relationship, not just abstract theory. Paul reads Adam and Christ within the horizon of sin and grace, while maintaining human responsibility and the hope of reconciliation.

entries.title: Scythians
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Σκύθης: Scythian, one of the peoples of the northern Black Sea.

Key Evidence: Colossians 3:11.

Place and Context: The Greco-Roman World. People associated with the text: Paul, the Colossians community.

Theological study: Paul mentions the Scythians among a list of cultural and social differences that he says Christ overcomes in the community. This does not erase the diversity of identities, but rather refuses to make them a basis for privilege or exclusion.

entries.title: Ambassadors of Christ
entries.content:
Etymology: πρεσβεύω presbeuo: He works as an ambassador.

Key Evidence: 2 Corinthians 5:18-21; Ephesians 6:20.

Place and context: Corinth, Rome, and the prison. People associated with the text: Paul, the Corinthian community.

Theological study: Paul calls the apostles ambassadors for Christ in the service of reconciliation. Embassy is not about possessing people or controlling their forgiveness, but rather faithfulness to the message that calls for reconciliation with God.

entries.title: Sun
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שֶׁמֶשׁ shemesh: sun; ἥλιος helios: sun.

Key Evidence: Genesis 1:14-18; Psalm 19; Malachi 4:2; Matthew 5:45.

Place and context: Heaven and the Land of Israel. People associated with the text: the psalmist, Malachi, Jesus.

Theological study: The sun is a creation that gives light and time, and poetry uses it as a symbol of justice and splendor. The Bible rejects its worship and Jesus makes its rising over the wicked and the righteous an example of the goodness of the Father.

entries.title: Sky
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שָׁמַיִם shamayim: heavens; οὐρανός ouranos: sky.

Key Evidence: Genesis 1:1; Psalm 19:1; Matthew 6:9; Revelation 21:1.

Place and Context: Creation and the New Jerusalem. People associated with the text: the psalmist, Jesus, John.

Theological study: Heaven in the book is the domain of God’s creation and glory, not necessarily a place far from history. Revelation uses a new heaven and new earth to emphasize the renewal of creation, not its abandonment.

entries.title: The good shepherd
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: רֹעֶה ro'eh: shepherd; ποιμήν poimen: shepherd.

Key Evidence: Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34; John 1:10-18; 1 Peter 5.

Place and context: the pastures of Israel and Judaism. People associated with the text: David, Ezekiel, Jesus, the Apostles.

Theological study: Ezekiel criticizes the shepherds who devour the flock, and John presents Jesus as the good shepherd who gives himself. The image places leadership at the service of the weak, not above them.

entries.title: Samaritan
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Σαμαρῖτις: a woman from Samaria.

Key Evidence: John 1:4-42.

Place and context: Jacob's Well near Sychar. People associated with the text: Jesus, the disciples, the townspeople.

Theological study: The Samaritan woman transforms from a conversation about water and worship into a witness calling for her city. The text does not present her as an object of shame, but rather as an interlocutor capable of questioning and testifying.

entries.title: Sukkot
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: סֻכּוֹת: tents or huts.

Key Evidence: Leviticus 23:33-43; John 7-8.

Place and context: the wilderness and Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Moses, Jesus, pilgrims.

Theological study: The Feast of Tabernacles recalls Israel’s dwelling in the wilderness and links the harvest with joy and dependence on God. John puts Jesus' sayings into context to proclaim the water of life and the light of the world. The holiday combines the fragile memory of temporary residence with general joy before the Lord, and therefore does not turn into a celebration of prosperity divorced from dependence on God. The Gospel uses symbols of water and light within the days of the holiday to declare that Jesus fulfills hope, while the background of Jewish worship remains necessary to understand his power.

entries.title: The sword of the spirit
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: μάχαιρα τοῦ πνεύματος: the sword of the spirit.

Key Evidence: Ephesians 6:10-20; Hebrews 4:12.

Place and context: The Church of Ephesus and images of the Roman soldier. People associated with the text: Paul, the Ephesian community.

Theological Study: The sword of the Spirit is the Word of God in the form of spiritual armor, not a weapon against humans. The paragraph places wrestling within the framework of steadfastness, prayer, truth, and righteousness, thus preventing the militarization of faith.

entries.title: Captivity
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: גָּלוּת galut: evacuation or exile; The αἰχμαλωσία aichmalosia: captivity.

Key Evidence: 2 Kings 24-25; Jeremiah 29; Ezekiel 1; Ezra 1.

Place and context: Babylon, Judah, and Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Nebuchadnezzar, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Cyrus, the returnees.

Theological study: Captivity is a political and religious catastrophe that destroys the city and the temple, but in prophecy it is a place of prayer, accountability, and a promise of return. The text does not explain the suffering of the exiles on an easy charge, but rather preserves the hope of God in the midst of the loss of land and familiar worship.

entries.title: The Book of Passion
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: πάσχω pascho: to suffer.

Key Evidence: Isaiah 52:13-53:12; Mark 8:31-38; 1 Peter 2:21-25.

Place and context: Jerusalem, the cross, and the churches of Asia. People associated with the text: Jesus, disciples, servant of the Lord.

Theological Study: The Passion narratives link Jesus' rejection to his death, resurrection, and call to bear the cross. The texts are not used to beautify abuse or force the injured person to remain in danger, but rather reveal God’s solidarity with the suffering person and the judgment of evil.

entries.title: Saul
entries.category: King and the beginnings of monarchy
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שָׁאוּל: required or borrowed.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 9-15; 31; Acts 13:21-22.

Place and context: Gibeah, Benjamin, and Israel. People associated with the text: Samuel, Jonathan, David.

Theological study: Saul is the first king of Israel in the narrative of Samuel, and his choice appears in response to the request of a people who wanted a king like the nations. Travel does not reduce his downfall to one personal flaw; Rather, it highlights his fear of people, his tension with the word of the Prophet, and his inability to use authority in obedience. David's elegies for him and Jonathan preserve the dignity of the murdered king, and therefore his story does not turn into a celebration of the opponent's failure.

entries.title: Shmr
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שַׁמְגַּר: The derivation of the name is unclear.

Key Evidence: Judges 3:31; 5:6.

Place and Context: Israel's Ways in the Age of Judges. People associated with the text: Anath, Deborah, Jael.

Theological study: The text does not mention anything about Shamgar other than his killing of six hundred Palestinians with a cow prick and his contribution to the salvation of Israel. This limitation prevents building an imaginary biography for him or turning him into a model of individual violence. The Song of Deborah places it in a time of turmoil, confirming that salvation in the Book of Judges comes in a fragile social reality, not in a simple, heroic world.

entries.title: Shavan
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שָׁפָן: rock or hyrax rabbit.

Key Evidence: 2 Kings 3:22-14; Jeremiah 26:24.

Place and context: Jerusalem during the reign of Josiah. People associated with the text: Josiah, Hilkiah, Ahikam, Jeremiah.

Theological study: Shaphan, a royal scribe, mediates between discovering the Book of the Law and reading it before Josiah. His role makes it clear that religious reform requires a public reading and faithful transmission of the text, not just political enthusiasm. His family also later appears in Jeremiah's protection, revealing a network of scribes and officials who helped the prophetic word survive in times of crisis.

entries.title: A straw
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שָׁפָט: ruling or ruling.

Basic evidence: Numbers 13:5; 1 Chronicles 3:22.

Place and context: The wilderness of Paran and Judah. People associated with the text: Moses, the spies, the tribe of Simeon.

Theological study: Shaphat ben Hori is one of the spies sent to explore the land. His presence on the list indicates that the group’s negative decision was not news without names or distributed responsibilities. But the text does not record his individual position, so the entry remains committed to the limits of the witness rather than inventing later positions or history.

entries.title: Ambassador
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Σάπφειρα: Aramaic or Greek name, its meaning is uncertain.

Key Evidence: Acts 1:5-11.

Place and context: Jerusalem in the first community. People associated with the text: Ananias, Peter, the Apostles.

Theological Study: Sapphira and her husband test the congregation with a lie regarding the gift of the land. Peter does not condemn their possession or retention of part of the money, but rather claims a complete donation to achieve a spiritual reputation. The difficulty of the death scene is not hidden; It emphasizes the danger of lying in a group that shares its resources, and does not give today's leaders the right to pass harsh judgments on consciences.

entries.title: Sharia
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: תּוֹרָה torah: teaching or guidance; νόμος nomos: law.

Key Evidence: Exodus 20; Deuteronomy 6; Psalm 119; Matthew 5:17-20.

Place and context: Sinai, Israel and Galilee. People associated with the text: Moses, the psalmist, Jesus.

Theological study: Sharia in the book is a covenant teaching that includes worship, justice, and daily life. It is not equal to a list of rulings stripped of its story. Psalm 119 exalts the Word as a way of life, and Jesus declares that he does not abolish the law but fulfills it. The superficial comparison between law and grace does not work; Grace itself calls for a life faithful to God and neighbor.

entries.title: Sharon
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שָׁרוֹן: plain or flat land.

Key Evidence: Isaiah 35:2; 65:10; Song 2:1.

Place and context: The coastal plain between Carmel and Jaffa. People associated with the text: Isaiah, the shepherds, the bride.

Theological study: Sharon is a fertile plain used by the prophets as an image of the return of fertility after devastation, and it appears in the hymn within a poetic language of love. The description of “Narcissus of Sharon” does not mean a definitive botanical definition; Translations of ancient plant names vary. The theological value of the image lies in the promise of renewal of the land and the people, not in proving the identity of a modern flower.

entries.title: Shalmanasr
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Šulmanu-ašared: The god Sulmanu is advanced.

Key Evidence: 2 Kings 17:3-6; 18:9-12.

Place and context: Samaria and Assyria. People associated with the text: Hosea, King of Israel, Sargon II.

Theological study: Shalmaneser V is associated with the siege of Samaria before the fall of the Northern Kingdom, while later Assyrian inscriptions attribute the conquest of the city to Sargon II. Resources should not be settled by force; The biblical text focuses on the meaning of captivity in the history of the era, and the Assyrian materials draw the context of imperial policy. The two sources combine to remind the reader of the reality of violent displacement.

entries.title: Shalom
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שָׁלוּם: complete or intact.

Key Evidence: 2 Kings 22:14; Jeremiah 32:7; Colossians 4:11.

Place and context: Jerusalem, Judah and the churches of Paul. People associated with the text: Huldah, Jeremiah, Paul.

Theological study: Shalom is a name given to different people, most notably the husband of Huldah the prophetess in the days of Josiah, the uncle of Jeremiah in the context of the truth of the field, and a person in the company of Paul. The common name does not allow these characters to be combined. The distribution reveals that everyday names are involved in networks of prophecy, kingship, kinship, and church service.

entries.title: Shalom and peace
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שָׁלוֹם shalom: integrity and completeness; εἰρήνη eirene: Peace.

Basic evidence: Numbers 6:24-26; Isaiah 9:6; John 14:27; Ephesians 2:14.

Place and context: Israel, Galilee and the apostolic churches. People associated with the text: Aaron, Isaiah, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: The peace of the book is broader than the absence of war; It is wellness, justice, and a right relationship with God, neighbors, and creation. Jesus proclaims a peace unlike the peace of the empire, and Paul describes Christ as the peace of Jews and Gentiles. Therefore, the greeting of peace is not used to cover up injustice, but rather to affirm reconciliation that destroys hostility and seeks truth.

entries.title: Candles
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שַׁמּוּעַ: heard or news.

Basic evidence: Numbers 13:4; 2 Samuel 5:14.

Place and context: The Paran Wilderness and Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Moses, David, the tribe of Reuben.

Theological study: Shammua bears two names in two contexts: a leader from Reuben among the spies, and a son of David in Jerusalem. The lists do not provide more than a name and lineage, but they preserve the responsibility of the tribes and the memory of the royal house. An honest reading recognizes the smallness of the material and does not build a relationship between the two characters on the name alone.

entries.title: Shmuel I and II
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שְׁמוּאֵל: He heard God or the name of God.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 1-31; 2 Samuel 1-24.

Place and context: Ramah, Shiloh, and Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Samuel, Saul, David, Nathan.

Theological Study: The Books of Shmuel recount the rise of kingship under the supervision of prophecy: the people's demand for a king, Saul's failure, David's rise and fall, and the promise to his house. The narrative does not hide the sins of the leaders, the Davidic promise does not become a blank check for power. Stories of prayer, justice, family, and war are linked in one assessment: the king's faithfulness to God's word.

entries.title: Smell
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שַׁמָּה: devastation or astonishment according to the root.

Key Evidence: 2 Samuel 23:11-12; 1 Chronicles 11:12-14.

Place and context: A lentil field in Palestinian land. People associated with the text: David, warriors, Philistines.

Theological study: Shammah, one of David’s heroes, defends a field when the people flee. The text does not make heroism a constant invitation to violence; Rather, it presents a military memory within a turbulent history. The transmission of the name and the details differs between Samuel and the chronicles, which draws attention to the need for the researcher to compare the narratives instead of building certainty from a single formula.

entries.title: Shamjar Streets
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: The noun appears in a poetic phrase without a reliable derivation.

Key Evidence: Judges 5:6.

Place and Context: Israel's Ways in the Song of Deborah. People associated with the text: Shamgar, Jael, villagers.

Theological Study: The Song of Deborah says that the roads were deserted in the days of Shamgar, and fear affected travel, the economy, and village life. The statement need not be a statistical report; It is a poetry of triumph that uses collective memory to magnify transformation. The entry highlights that salvation in Judges includes people's ability to move around and live without fear.

entries.title: Shamson
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שִׁמְשׁוֹן: It may be related to the sun.

Key Evidence: Judges 13-16; Hebrews 11:32.

Place and context: Saraa, Suriq, and Gaza. People associated with the text: Manoah, Delilah, the Philistines.

Theological study: Shamson is a Nazir from the womb and his call is to begin the salvation of Israel from the Palestinians. But his story does not glorify raw power; As desire, division, and revenge recur, the vow appears as a sign, not a substitute, for fidelity. The New Testament mentions him among the witnesses of faith without erasing the tragedy of the narrative or making moral failure secondary.

entries.title: Saul of Tarsus
entries.content:
Etymology: Σαῦλος: Greek form of Saul, required.

Key Evidence: Acts 9; 22; 26; Galatians 1:11-24.

Place and context: Jerusalem, Damascus, and Antioch. People associated with the text: Ananias, Barnabas, the Apostles.

Theological study: The Book of Acts presents Saul’s transformation from persecuting the community of Jesus to an apostle to the Gentiles, while Paul affirms in Galatians that the Gospel is a call by God’s grace. Paul's use of his Latin name need not mean that he replaced it at the time of conversion; Both names are part of a multilingual world. Conversion links the encounter with Christ, reconciliation with the community, and long service.

entries.title: King Saul
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שָׁאוּל: required.

Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 10; 13; 15; 28.

Place and context: Gibeah, Gilgal, and En-dor. People associated with the text: Samuel, Jonathan, Agag.

Theological Study: King Saul's scenes focus on the test of obedience when pressured by war and public opinion. In Gilgal he acts before Samuel arrives, and in Amalek he keeps what he was ordered to remove, then resorts to the Oracle of En Dor. These scenes do not explain his psychological disorder in a modern medical way, but rather read it within the question of the king who wants to preserve his position instead of listening to the word of the Lord.

entries.title: Satisfied
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שֶׁבַע: seven or section; A name may have more than one origin.

Key Evidence: 2 Samuel 1:20-22.

Place and context: Northern Israel and the city of Abel-Beit Maacah. People associated with the text: David, Joab, the wise woman.

Theological study: Sheba bin Bikri leads a rebellion after Absalom’s revolt, so the story turns to Abel Beth Maacah. A wise woman ends the siege by negotiating and handing over the rebel's head, revealing that the narrative does not limit the solution to military force. However, the cruelty of the ending remains part of a criticism of a world in which stability is governed by violence and threats.
