entries.title: Queen of Sheba
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שְׁבָא: the name of a southern people or region.

Key Evidence: 1 Kings 10:1-13; 2 Chronicles 9:1-12; Matthew 12:42.

Place and context: South Arabia or the Horn of Africa in historical debate. People associated with the text: Solomon, Queen of Sheba.

Theological study: The Queen of Sheba visits Solomon to test his wisdom and exchange gifts. The story places the Israeli king on a broad international and commercial horizon. The text does not specify the queen's name or her modern home with certainty. Jesus uses her visit to confront a generation that rejects greater wisdom than Solomon, not to justify later myths about her.

entries.title: Shechem
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שְׁכֶם: shoulder or slope.

Key Evidence: Genesis 12:6-7; 34; Joshua 24; Judges 9.

Place and context: Between Ebal and Gerizim in Samaria. People associated with the text: Abraham, Jacob, Joshua, Abimelech.

Theological study: Shechem is an early site of promise, then a scene of aggression, revenge, covenant renewal, and royal conflict. This accumulation prevents it from becoming a sacred place without history; The city holds promise, sin, violence, and collective decision. In Joshua 24 the memory is summoned to choose to serve the Lord, while Judges 9 exposes the kingship that grows from Abimelech's ambition.

entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שְׁכֶמִי: attributed to Shechem.

Key Evidence: Judges 9:1-57.

Place and context: Shechem in the highlands of Samaria. People associated with the text: Abimelech, Gaal, Jotham.

Theological study: The people of Shechem ally themselves with Abimelech, and then the conflict turns against them and their city. The text does not make the population a single moral bloc, but it reveals the price of partnering with a rule based on money and violence. Yotam's Parable of Trees uses political satire to expose a leader who promises protection and then devours those around him.

entries.title: Lamb sheep
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שֶׂה seh: sheep or kid; ἀμνός amnos: pregnancy.

Key Evidence: Exodus 12; Isaiah 53:7; John 1:29; Vision 5.

Place and context: Egypt, the Temple, Galilee, and Revelation. People associated with the text: Moses, the servant of the Lord, John the Baptist, Christ.

Theological study: The lamb at Passover is a sign of domestic salvation within the liberation of Exodus, and in Isaiah there is an image of a servant in pain, then John uses language about Jesus. These connections cannot be reduced to a single metaphor: Passover, sacrifice, innocence, and victory each have their context. The vision makes the slaughtered lamb the center of the throne, changing the definition of power from oppression to subjugation.

entries.title: Shepherd
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: רֹעֶה ro'eh: shepherd; ποιμήν poimen: shepherd.

Key Evidence: Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34; John 10; 1 Peter 5.

Place and context: the pastures of Israel and Judaism. People associated with the text: David, Ezekiel, Jesus, church elders.

Theological study: The image of the shepherd begins with the life of shepherds and moves to God, the king, and the leaders. Ezekiel exposes shepherds who feed themselves, and John declares Jesus the good shepherd who knows his sheep and gives himself. This is why the image does not grant the leader the privilege of control, but rather measures it by protecting the weak, seeking the lost, and holding oneself accountable.

entries.title: blade
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שִׁפְרָה: beautiful or good.

Key Evidence: Exodus 1:15-21.

Place and context: Egypt at the time of Israel's enslavement. People associated with the text: Puah, Pharaoh, mothers of the Hebrews.

Theological study: Shifra and her midwife, Puah, reject Pharaoh’s order to kill male newborns. The text describes them as fearing God, placing obedience to God above the state’s order that violates life. It does not explain all the details of their ethnic identity or function, but mentioning their names as opposed to not naming Pharaoh honors women's resistance and preserves the value of life in the face of authority.

entries.title: Shiloh
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שִׁלֹה: the name of a place, its derivation is uncertain.

Key Evidence: Joshua 18:1; 1 Samuel 1-4; Jeremiah 7:12-15.

Place and context: The highlands of Ephraim, north of Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Eli, Samuel, Anna, Jeremiah.

Theological study: Shiloh was the location of the Tabernacle in the beginnings of settlement, and is linked to the prayers of Hannah, the invitation of Samuel, and the loss of the ark. Jeremiah invokes its desolation to warn Jerusalem against trusting the temple unjustly. Therefore, place does not become an automatic guarantee of the divine presence; Worship is tested by obedience and mercy.

entries.title: Shimon
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שִׁמְעוֹן: He heard or responded.

Key Evidence: Genesis 29:33; 34; 49:5-7; Joshua 19:1-9.

Place and context: Canaan and Judah. People associated with the text: Jacob, Levi, Dinah.

Theological study: Simeon, son of Jacob and a tribe within Israel. Shechem's account links his anger with Levi to violence, Jacob's blessing criticizes him, and then the tribe appears with land within Judah. Texts should not be transformed into fixed ethnic judgements; Rather, it reveals how lineages preserve the memory of wounds and violence and restore the place of the tribe in the life of Israel.

entries.title: Shimon Peter
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Σίμων: listener; Πέτρος: rock.

Key Evidence: Luke 1:5-11; Matthew 13:16-20; John 21; Acts 2.

Place and context: Sea of Galilee, Jerusalem and Caesarea. People associated with the text: Jesus, Andrew, Cornelius.

Theological study: Shimon Peter moves from the call during the hunt to confession, then denial, and restoration. The Gospel does not hide its fragility, and thus his leadership becomes a testimony to a grace that reassigns those who cried, not to heroism without failure. In the Acts of the Apostles, his speech on the Day of Pentecost links the opening of the promise to the Spirit, and the story of Cornelius reveals the expansion of the community to the nations.

entries.title: Shimon the jealous
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Σίμων ὁ ζηλωτής: Simon the Zealot.

Key Evidence: Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13.

Place and context: Galilee and Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Jesus, the Twelve.

Theological study: The New Testament does not record anything about Simeon the Zealot except his title and his presence among the Twelve. The title may indicate religious zeal or political affiliation, but the evidence is not enough to make a determination. This entry teaches the integrity of indexing: not to turn the silence of the source into an interesting biography, noting that Jesus gathered disciples from disparate backgrounds.

entries.title: Simeon of Cyrene
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Σίμων Κυρηναῖος: Simon of Cyrene.

Key Evidence: Matthew 27:32; Mark 15:21; Luke 23:26.

Place and context: The Way of the Cross in Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Jesus, soldiers, Alexander, Rufus.

Theological study: The soldiers force Simon of Cyrene to carry the cross of Jesus, and Mark adds the names of his two sons, which may indicate the church’s knowledge of them. The text does not tell us whether his choice was voluntary, so Roman coercion should not be embellished. But Luke uses the scene to explain the discipleship behind Jesus, where faithfulness is inseparable from the reality of suffering.

entries.title: Shimon Sheikh
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: Συμεών: Greek form of Simon.

Key Evidence: Luke 2:25-35.

Place and context: The Jerusalem temple. People associated with the text: Mary, Joseph, Jesus, Anna.

Theological study: Simeon awaits the consolation of Israel and takes the child Jesus into the temple, so he sings of God’s prepared salvation before all peoples. His song brings together the light of the nations and the glory of Israel, so it is not right to separate them. He also predicts a sword for the mother and the exposure of hearts, thus preserving that messianic hope is not a victory without pain or resolution.

entries.title: Shane
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שׁ shin: the name of a Hebrew letter; It may indicate age depending on the context.

Key Evidence: Deuteronomy 6:4; Psalm 119:161-168.

Place and Context: The Hebrew Language and the Worship of Israel. People associated with the text: scribes and singers.

Theological study: The Shin is a letter from the Hebrew alphabet, and its importance appears in the study of the text, not as an independent theological symbol. The Shin section of Psalm 119 uses the arrangement of the letters to frame a meditation on God's Word. It is necessary to be careful not to build hidden meanings from the shape or sound of a letter without the support of the text, while appreciating the value of language in transmitting revelation and worship.

entries.title: Shame
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: בּוּשׁ bush: shyness; αἰσχύνη aischyne: shame.

Key Evidence: Genesis 2:25; 3:7-10; Isaiah 54:4; Romans 10:11.

Place and context: Aden, exile, and the churches of Rome. People associated with the text: Adam and Eve, Isaiah, Paul.

Theological study: Shame in a formation that appears after a broken relationship and fear of the divine presence, but it is not a definition of the body or nudity in itself. Isaiah promises that Zion will not remember the shame of her youth, while Paul declares that whoever believes will not be ashamed. The text can help those suffering from humiliation, but it does not become a tool for intensifying shame or blaming the victims.

entries.title: Thanks
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: יָדָה yadah: praise or acknowledge; εὐχαριστία eucharistia: thanks.

Key evidence: Psalm 100; Luke 11:17-19; 1 Thessalonians 5:18.

Place and context: Temple and border between Samaria and Galilee. People associated with the text: the psalmist, Jesus, the Samaritan leper, Paul.

Theological study: Thanksgiving is an acknowledgment of God’s gift, not a denial of sadness or injustice. In Luke, the purified Samaritan returns to give thanks, revealing that gratitude goes beyond benefit into a relationship. Paul calls for thanksgiving in all circumstances, not for every evil; The context links the call to hope, prayer, and discerning God’s will.

entries.title: Devil
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: שָׂטָן satan: opponent or opponent; διάβολος diabolos: slanderer.

Basic evidence: Job 1-2; Zechariah 3:1-5; Matthew 4:1-11; Revelation 12.

Place and context: a heavenly council, the wilderness, and the churches of the apocalypse. People associated with the text: Job, Yeshua the priest, Jesus.

Theological study: The use of Satan changes between the adversary in Job, the opponent in Zechariah, the tempter in the Gospels, and the adversary in Revelation. The book does not call for curiosity about hidden worlds as much as it calls for steadfastness in the truth and resistance to lies. The experience of Jesus refuses to turn sonship into a display of power or possession, and the vision preserves the hope that evil is not the master of history.

entries.title: Certificate
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: עֵד ed: witness; μαρτυρία martyria: testimony.

Key Evidence: Isaiah 43:10; John 1:6-8; Acts 1:8.

Place and Context: Israel, Judaism, and the Extension of Mission. People associated with the text: Isaiah, John the Baptist, the Apostles.

Theological study: The testimony in the book is word and deed that declare what the people saw of God’s faithfulness. Isaiah describes Israel as a witness of the Lord among the nations, and John the Baptist refers to the light and does not replace it. In the Acts of the Apostles, testimony is linked to the power of the Spirit and the extension from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. It is not a means of pressure, but loyalty to truth and love.

entries.title: Healing
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: רָפָא rapha: healed; ἴασις iasis: healing.

Key Evidence: Psalm 103:1-5; Mark 2:1-12; Luke 4:18-19; James 5:13-16.

Place and context: Galilee and community homes. People associated with the text: Jesus, the paralytic, friends, elders.

Theological study: Healing in the ministry of Jesus is a sign of mercy and the approach of the Kingdom, and is not reduced to proof of the faith of the sick person or a technical result of prayer. In Mark 2, the forgiveness of sins and the healing of the paralytic are linked to the authority of the Son of Man and to the carrying of his friends. James calls the Church to prayer, care and confession, without promising that every illness ends in the same way.

entries.title: Compassion and mercy
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: רַחֲמִים rahamim: mercies; σπλαγχνίζομαι splagchnizomai: compassion.

Key Evidence: Exodus 34:6-7; Hosea 11:8; Matthew 9:36; Luke 10:33.

Place and context: Israel, Galilee and the Jericho Road. People associated with the text: Moses, Hosea, Jesus, Samaritan.

Theological Study: God’s mercy in the Torah and the Prophets is not leniency toward evil, but rather faithfulness that moves toward the broken. Jesus' compassion before the crowds and the sick is repeated, and the Samaritan embodies mercy when he approaches, treats, and risks his money. Therefore pity does not remain a private feeling; It is a practice that restores the neighbor to life and dignity.

entries.title: Fishing net
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: δίκτυον diktyon: network.

Key Evidence: Matthew 4:18-22; Luke 1:5-11; John 1:21-14.

Place and context: Sea of ​​Galilee. People associated with the text: Peter, Andrew, James, John, Jesus.

Theological study: The net appears in the call of the fishermen and in a miraculous catch after the resurrection. The image of people being hunted does not remove their humanity or make the message about forced hunting; It constitutes a call to leave the profession to follow Jesus and serve others. John 21 reveals that abundance does not exempt the disciples from work, and that Jesus welcomes them to the communion table.

entries.title: Tree of life
entries.content:
Linguistic origin: עֵץ הַחַיִּים: tree of life.

Key Evidence: Genesis 2:9; 3:22-24; Proverbs 3:18; Revelation 22:1-5.

Place and context: Eden and the New Jerusalem. People associated with the text: Adam and Eve, Al-Hakim, John.

Theological Study: The Tree of Life frames the book between Eden and Revelation, where he guards the way to it after disobedience, and then the River of Life and its tree return in the new creation. Proverbs of the image are used about wisdom, so it is forbidden to limit it to only a missing plant. The text does not draw a biological diagram, but rather declares that life is a gift from God and that the end includes the healing of nations.

entries.title: Church elders
entries.content:
Etymology: πρεσβύτερος presbyteros: old or older.

Key Evidence: Acts 14:23; 20:17-38; 1 Timothy 3; 1 Peter 5.

Place and Context: The Churches of Asia and Ephesus. People associated with the text: Paul, Peter, elders of Ephesus.

Theological study: Elders in the early church are servants of care, education, and oversight, not a class above the group. Paul asks the elders of Ephesus to watch over themselves first and then over the flock, and Peter forbids control over those in charge. Later church structures vary, but the text establishes standards of service: honesty, humility, and protection of the weak.

entries.title: Officer
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 37:36; 39:1-23; Acts 8:26-39.

Place and Context: Egypt in Potiphar's house and Gaza in the Book of Acts.

Persons Associated with the Text: Joseph, Potiphar, the Ethiopian eunuch, Philip.

Theological Study: The officer appears in the stories of Joseph within the Egyptian state apparatus, where a false accusation turns into imprisonment and then into a path of wider service. In the Book of Acts, the Ethiopian eunuch holds a high financial position but reads Isaiah and seeks understanding. The position itself does not provide spiritual value; the text reveals that authority and office are subject to justice, truth, and the capacity to learn.

entries.title: Frogs
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 25:7-15:8; Psalm 78:45; 105:30.

Place and context: Egypt in the days of Pharaoh.

People associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, Pharaoh, Egyptians.

Theological study: The frogs are the second plague in the Exodus narrative, confronting Pharaoh within the religious and political world of Egypt. The text does not explain all the natural mechanisms of the event, but rather places the plague in a conflict between the God of Israel and Pharaoh's claim to control. The frogs became afraid at Pharaoh’s request, then his heart hardened, and the intention of warning, reprieve, and disobedience was repeated. The vision uses the image of frogs in a different symbolic way, so the Exodus story does not dissolve into the subsequent symbol.

entries.title: Hospitality
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 1:18-15; 19:1-11; Luke 10:38-42; Hebrews 13:2.

Place and context: The tents of Abraham and Sodom and the house of Martha and Mary.

People associated with the text: Abraham, Sarah, Lot, Martha, Mary, Jesus.

Theological study: Hospitality in the book is welcoming and protecting the stranger, not just a social duty. Abraham receives his visitors in Mamre, while the story of Sodom makes the violation of guest protection a sign of the city's corruption. In the house of Martha and Mary, Jesus does not insult service, but rather places it alongside listening to His word. Hebrews calls on the people not to forget strangers, without making hospitality an abolition of borders or an exploitation of the hosts.

entries.title: Distress
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Psalm 46:1; 120:1; Romans 8:35-39; 2 Corinthians 4:8-10.

Place and context: Jerusalem in the language of the Psalms and the churches of Paul.

People associated with the text: the psalmist, Paul, the Romans and the Corinthian communities.

Theological study: The distress in the Psalms is a field of shouting and confidence, not automatic evidence of abandonment from God. Paul describes believers as pressed but not abandoned, and emphasizes that distress does not separate them from the love of Christ. These texts are not used to silence those who suffer or deny the causes of injustice; Rather, a language of prayer and community provides hope and mutual responsibility.

entries.title: Conscience
entries.content:
Key References: Romans 2:14-16; 1 Corinthians 8:7-13; 10:23-33; 1 Timothy 1:5.

Place and Context: Rome and Corinth.

Persons Related to the Text: Paul, the Corinthian community, the weak in faith.

Theological Study: Conscience in Paul's letters is an inner witness that needs to be shaped by truth and love, not an infallible authority or an isolated personal standard. Regarding food, Paul refuses to let freedom become a stumbling block and calls for the edification of others. Therefore, the believer is not judged based on cultural or intellectual strength but connects freedom with responsibility, love, and worship of God.

entries.title: Weakness
entries.content:
Key Evidence: 2 Corinthians 7:12-10; Romans 8:26; 1 Corinthians 1:26-31.

Place and context: the churches of Corinth and Rome.

People associated with the text: Paul, the Corinthian community, the Holy Spirit.

Theological study: Paul does not define weakness as a virtue in suffering itself, but rather as a place in which the apostle refuses to rely on himself. In 2 Corinthians the text does not explain the nature of Paul's thorn, so it cannot be diagnosed. Paul asks for it to be lifted and then receives the promise of sufficient grace. Strength in weakness does not mean glorifying illness or abusing others; It is a criticism of self-pride and a declaration of dependence on the grace of Christ.

entries.title: Astray
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Isaiah 53:6; Ezekiel 34:1-16; Matthew 18:10-14; 1 Peter 2:25.

Place and Context: Israel, Judaism, and the Churches of Asia Minor.

People associated with the text: Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jesus, Peter.

Theological study: The book uses the image of straying from the path to describe people's distance from God and justice. In Ezekiel, the Lord rebukes shepherds who abandon the lost, and in the parable of the lost sheep, Jesus highlights the joy of seeking and recovering. The image does not make a group of people an object of contempt; Everyone is invited to return, and the leaders themselves are asked how they care for the weak.

entries.title: Shrine
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Isaiah 53:9; Matthew 27:57-61; John 19:38-42; 20:1-18.

Place and context: near Golgotha ​​in Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: Jesus, Joseph of Arimathea, Nicodemus, Mary Magdalene.

Theological study: Jesus' new tomb is part of the Gospels' testimony to the reality of his death before the announcement of the resurrection. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus provide a dignified burial in a dangerous political situation, and Mary arrives at the tomb at dawn on Sunday. The text does not confirm the form of the archaeological shrine or all subsequent site traditions; Its focus is that the one who was crucified died and was buried, and then the grave did not imprison Christ.

entries.title: Tax
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Matthew 15:22-22; Mark 13:12-17; Luke 20:20-26; Romans 13:6-7.

Place and context: the Temple, Roman Judaism, and Rome.

People associated with the text: Jesus, Pharisees, Herodians, Caesar, Paul.

Theological study: The tribute question is an attempt to trap Jesus between a political and a religious accusation. He asks for the dinar and returns to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s. He does not grant the state absolute sanctity and does not allow the dinar to be used to hide the worship of money. Paul discusses taxes in Romans within a broader call to love and non-retaliation. The entry asks for a distinction between true civic responsibility and the limits of loyalty that only God has.

entries.title: Dia
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Psalm 27:1; Isaiah 60:1-3; John 1:4-9; Ephesians 5:8-14.

Place and context: Zion, Galilee, and the churches of Ephesus.

People associated with the text: Isaiah, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: Light is an image of life, guidance, and the presence of God, and it does not have a single meaning in every place. Isaiah calls Zion to rise up because her light has come, and John declares that the life of the Word is the light of people. In Ephesians, the metaphor moves to the behavior of the children of light. Therefore, light does not become a privilege for one group over another, but rather a call for truth and goodness and exposing the works of darkness.

entries.title: Flood
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 6:5-9:17; Isaiah 54:9-10; Matthew 24:37-39; 1 Peter 3:20-21.

Place and context: The world before the flood and the mountains of Ararat.

People associated with the text: Noah, his family, the sons of men, Peter.

Theological Study: The Flood links the corruption and violence of the Earth with God's judgment, but it ends with a covenant with Noah and all flesh. It cannot be reduced to a story of individual rescue or material for geographical debate alone; The covenant includes creation, the sanctity of blood, and human responsibility. The Gospels use it to warn against people's negligence, and Peter reads it in connection with baptism with the resurrection of Christ, while keeping in mind the difference between the original story and the apostolic reception.

entries.title: Obey
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Deuteronomy 4:6-9; 1 Samuel 15:22-23; John 14:15; Philippians 2:5-11.

Place and context: Sinai, Israel, Atticism, and Philippi.

People associated with the text: Moses, Saul, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: Obedience in the Torah is a response of love and covenant, not just external compliance. Samuel matches the sacrifice that conceals disobedience with hearing the word of the Lord, while John links love for Jesus with keeping his commandments. Paul describes Christ's obedience to the point of death in the context of his humility. Christian obedience does not turn into a tool of control or justification for abuse. Its standard is Christ who serves and gives himself.

entries.title: Purity
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Leviticus 11-15; Psalm 51:7-12; Mark 1:7-23; Acts 9:10-16.

Place and context: Tabernacle, Israel, Roman Judaism, and Joppa.

People associated with the text: Moses, David, Jesus, Peter.

Theological Study: Purity in Leviticus is a ritual system that determines the possibility of approaching the sacred, and does not automatically equate to moral guilt or human deficiency. David asks for a pure heart in the psalm, and Jesus rearranges the discussion about what comes from the heart. This does not allow for the portrayal of Jewish law as a failure or the conclusion that patients are morally impure. Peter's vision in Acts 10 opens the way for the Gentiles to be welcomed into the community.

entries.title: Food
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 1:16-36; Deuteronomy 8:1-10; Mark 6:30-44; 1 Corinthians 1:8-13.

Place and context: the Sinai wilderness, Galilee, and Corinth.

People associated with the text: Moses, Israel, Jesus, disciples, Paul.

Theological study: Food in the book is a gift of creation and a sign of dependence and communion, not just a material need. The manna teaches Israel that life is not based on controlled hoarding, and the feasts in Jesus' ministry reveal mercy that satisfies the multitudes. Paul treats food sacrificed to idols with the rule of love and the building of conscience. These texts do not turn into a single diet, but rather place eating in a relationship with gratitude, justice, and the other.

entries.title: Tarsus
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Acts 9:11; 9:30; 11:25; 21:39; 22:3.

Place and context: Cilicia in southeastern Asia Minor.

People associated with the text: Saul/Paul, Barnabas, the Antioch community.

Theological study: Tarsus, the city Paul mentions in his defense before the crowds. He goes out to her after threats in Jerusalem, then Barnabas comes to look for him and takes him to Antioch. The New Testament does not provide a complete account of its culture or Paul's teaching there, so historical information is separated from textual testimony. Its importance lies in the network of cities through which the message was transmitted and in the identity of a messenger who combines a Jewish background and Roman citizenship.

entries.title: Tiberius
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Luke 3:1-2; Matthew 22:17-21.

Place and Context: The Roman Empire and Judaism.

People associated with the text: Tiberius Caesar, Pilate, Herod, John the Baptist.

Theological study: Luke dates the appearance of John the Baptist to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, linking the good news to the dates of known rulers. The name does not offer political salvation or make Roman rule neutral; The scenes of taxation and trial reveal the tension between the Kingdom of God and the authority of Caesar. The entry helps distinguish between fixing a time frame and turning the Gospel into an imperial biography.

entries.title: Blessed are you
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Psalm 1:1-3; Matthew 5:1-12; Luke 6:20-26; Revelation 1:3.

Place and Context: The Galilee and Visionary Communities.

People associated with the text: the psalmist, Jesus, the disciples, John.

Theological study: The formula of blessedness is a declaration of blessing and wisdom, not a superficial congratulation. Psalm 1 describes the path of man who rejects the counsel of the wicked and meditates on the law of the Lord, while the Beatitudes inaugurate a kingdom that revalues ​​poverty, sorrow, meekness, and hunger for righteousness. The Beatitudes do not glorify misery or persecution, but rather promise God's presence and justice and call the community to mercy and peacemaking.

entries.title: Mud
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 2:7; Job 10:9; John 1:9-12.

Place and context: Eden, the image of creation, and the pool of Siloam.

People associated with the text: Adam, Job, Jesus, the man born blind.

Theological study: Clay links the fragility of man made of dirt to the hand of the Creator in the language of Genesis and Job. In John 9, Jesus makes clay and wipes the eyes of the blind man and then sends him to Siloam, and the miracle turns into a question about insight and faith. The text does not teach a prescription or associate blindness with personal sin; Rather, it reveals the works of God and confronts the stubbornness of those who claim insight.

entries.title: Darkness
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 2:1-5; Exodus 10:21-29; Psalm 139:11-12; John 1:4-9.

Place and context: Creation, Egypt, and the Johannine Church.

People associated with the text: Moses, Pharaoh, Psalmist, Jesus.

Theological study: Darkness in Genesis is a state before the season of light, and the plague of Egypt is a sign of judgment on a system that enslaves. But the psalm declares that darkness is not hidden from God, and John confronts it with the light of the Word. Darkness does not have a single meaning: it may be a physical description, a language of fear, or a symbol of evil. Therefore, it is not used to evaluate a color or a people, but rather to understand the revelation of God who creates, liberates, and guides.

entries.title: Shadow
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Psalm 17:8; 36:7; 91:1; 121:5; Colossians 2:16-17.

Place and context: the temple, the wilderness, and the churches of Colossae.

People associated with the text: the psalmist, Moses, Paul.

Theological Study: The shadow in the Psalms is a metaphor for protection in closeness to God, not a guarantee that the believer does not face danger. In Colossians, Paul uses shadow to describe some practices in relation to what he sees as completion in Christ. This metaphor does not mean disdain for the Torah or Israel; Rather, you need to read the apostolic argument in its entirety and refuse to use it to cancel the history of the Old Testament.

entries.title: Nail
entries.content:
Key Evidence: 1 Corinthians 15:50-58; Hosea 13:14.

Place and Context: The Church of Corinth and the Memory of Hosea.

People associated with the text: Paul, the Corinthian community, Christ.

Theological study: Paul asks: “O death, where is your sting?” At the conclusion of a long argument about the resurrection of the body, he invokes the language of Hosea. The victory here is not the denial of the reality of death or the promise of earthly success, but rather the victory of Christ, which establishes the hope of resurrection. Therefore, the Apostle concludes with a call to persevere and work in the Lord, linking the afterlife hope with daily fidelity.

entries.title: Unjust
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Psalm 10; Isaiah 1:15-17; Luke 18:1-8; 1 Corinthians 6:9-11.

Place and context: Israel, Judaism, and the churches of Corinth.

People associated with the text: the psalmist, Isaiah, the widow, the judge, Paul.

Theological study: The book cries out in the face of injustice and is not satisfied with calling for mere patience. Isaiah asks for justice for the oppressed, and Luke presents a widow who insists on seeking justice from an unjust judge. Paul’s warning about the oppressors in Corinth mentions that some believers were like this and then were purified, so that the judgment does not turn into despair or constant stigma, but rather into a call to repentance and justice.

entries.title: The appearance of Christ
entries.content:
Key Evidence: 2 Timothy 1:9-10; Titus 2:11-14; Hebrews 9:24-28.

Place and context: the apostolic churches.

People associated with the text: Paul, Titus, the writer of Hebrews, Christ.

Theological study: The appearance of Christ in the Epistles refers to his salvific appearance in history and to the hope of his glorious appearance. Titus links apparent grace to raising a people who reject immorality and do good, so hope is not a passive expectation. The writer of Hebrews places the appearance in the context of Christ's unique sacrifice and the hope of salvation, not in calculating promises or inciting fear.

entries.title: External and internal
entries.content:
Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 16:7; Psalm 139:1-4; Matthew 6:1-18; 2 Corinthians 4:16-18.

Place and context: Bethlehem, Israel, Galilee, and Corinth.

People associated with the text: Samuel, David, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: The book contrasts looking at the outward with God's knowledge of the heart. This does not mean contempt for the body or public life, but rather criticism of religiosity that seeks people's praise. In Matthew, Jesus teaches almsgiving, prayer, and fasting in secret, while Paul distinguishes between the outer man, who is corrupted, and the inner man, who is renewed. The approach calls for complete honesty, not concealing injustice or escaping accountability.

entries.title: Noon
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 18:1; John 4:6; Acts 22:6.

Place and context: Mamre, Jacob's Well, and the Damascus Road.

People associated with the text: Abraham, Jesus, the Samaritan woman, Saul.

Theological study: Noon is a specific time that appears in different encounters: Abraham’s visit at Mamre, Jesus’ dialogue with the Samaritan woman, and the appearance of light to Saul on the road. The book does not make the clock a fixed symbol, but the chronology anchors the events in a human reality. In John, fatigue and thirst at noon increase the power of dialogue over the water of life and worship, and in Acts 22, the powerful light links Saul’s conversion to a concrete invitation.

entries.title: Noon
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 33:18-23; John 13:4-5; 2 Corinthians 12:7.

Place and context: Sinai, Attica and Corinth.

People associated with the text: Moses, Jesus, disciples, Paul.

Theological study: In Exodus 33, the text uses human language about Moses seeing the Lord “appear” while emphasizing that he does not see his face. The phrase is not an anatomical description of God, but a language of appearance that preserves the holiness of God and the limits of human understanding. In the upper room, Jesus bends down to wash the disciples' feet, and authority appears in the form of service. The introduction combines careful language about God with the dignity of the body in serving one’s neighbor.

entries.title: Antelope
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Proverbs 6:5; Song of Solomon 2:9; 8:14.

Place and context: The Judah wilderness and the language of the Song of Songs.

People associated with the text: the sage, the two lovers in the song.

Theological study: The deer in Proverbs is an image of speed in escaping a trap, and in the Song of Songs it is an image of beauty and movement in love poetry. The text does not provide a scientific zoological definition or a fixed theological symbol. The introduction teaches that poetic images are read according to genre: an aphorism that warns of a trap, and an anthem that celebrates love and the body within its literary language.

entries.title: The thoughts of the heart
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 6:5; Psalm 139:23-24; Mark 7:20-23; Hebrews 4:12-13.

Place and Context: The World Before the Flood, Israel, and Judaism.

People associated with the text: Noah, the psalmist, Jesus, the writer of Hebrews.

Theological study: The texts describe the thoughts of the heart when they turn into evil, anxiety, or a request for examination before God. God's knowledge of thoughts does not mean that humans are able to read each other's consciences or make a final judgment about them. Jesus reveals that evil comes from within, while the psalm calls for examination and leadership on the eternal path. The entrance combines moral responsibility and humility before the depth of the heart.

entries.title: Shadow of the Most High
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Psalm 91:1-16; Ruth 2:12; Luke 13:34.

Place and context: the wilderness, Bethlehem, and Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: the psalmist, Boaz, Ruth, Jesus.

Theological study: The believer dwells in the cover of the Most High and the shadow of the Almighty in Psalm 91, which is a language of trust, not a formula of mechanical immunity. Boaz blesses Ruth because she has taken refuge under the wings of the Lord, and Jesus likens his desire to gather Jerusalem to a bird protecting its chicks. This hope does not negate the suffering or death of believers; Rather, it places fear within a relationship of trust and care and calls on the group to be an object of protection, not exploitation.

entries.title: Injustice
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Isaiah 15:1-17; Amos 5:21-24; Micah 6:6-8; James 1:5-6.

Place and Context: Judah, Israel, and the Diaspora Churches.

People associated with the text: Isaiah, Amos, Micah, Jacob, the rich and the workers.

Theological study: The prophets link worship with justice and reject sacrifices and festivals that conceal the deprivation of the poor. Amos and Micah do not offer a modern economic program, but they delegitimize a piety that coexists with worker exploitation and a biased judiciary. Jacob continues to criticize when the rich withhold wages from workers. Therefore, injustice is not a political issue external to faith, but rather a decisive test for the sincerity of worship.

entries.title: A branch
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Isaiah 11:1-5; Jeremiah 23:5-6; Zechariah 3:8; 6:12; Revelation 22:16.

Place and context: Bethlehem and Jerusalem in prophetic hope.

People associated with the text: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zechariah, Christ.

Theological study: The branch is a botanical image of the seed and the king coming from the house of David. In Isaiah, a branch emerges from the trunk of Jesse after a scene of cutting and collapse, and in Jeremiah and Zechariah, the image is associated with a just king and rebuilding. The term alone does not confirm all the details of Christology, but it contributes to building the biblical hope that Revelation reads in the light of Christ. Its context prevents the promise from being transformed into a national authority separate from justice and the spirit.

references.author: John N. Oswalt
references.title: The Book of Isaiah, Chapters 1-39, NICOT, Eerdmans, 1986

entries.title: Forgiveness
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 34:6-7; Psalm 32:1-5; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Mark 2:1-12; Ephesians 1:7.

Place and context: Sinai, Jerusalem, Galilee, and the churches of Ephesus.

People associated with the text: Moses, David, Jeremiah, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: Forgiveness in the Bible is a divine act that removes guilt and restores the relationship, not ignoring evil or absolving of responsibility. Exodus 34 declares both the mercy and justice of the Lord, and in Psalm 32 David arrives at confession, not concealment. Jeremiah promises not to remember sin in the New Testament, and Jesus' healings demonstrate the power of forgiveness in the community. Forgiveness does not ask the offended person to deny the harm or undo the justice; Rather, he confronts evil in the name of grace and truth.

entries.title: God's wrath
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 32:7-14; Psalm 11:7; Hosea 11:8-9; Romans 1:18; 2:1-11.

Place and context: Sinai, Israel and Rome.

People associated with the text: Moses, Hosea, Paul.

Theological Study: God's wrath is biblical language about His opposition to evil, violence, and idolatry, and is not equal to a human whim or an uncontrolled emotion. In Exodus 32, anger intersects with Moses’ intercession and God’s return from the announced doom, and in Hosea, mercy stands within the discourse of judgment. Paul explains anger as revealing human corruption, so believers should not use it as an excuse for their anger at their opponents. Justice and mercy remain intertwined in the theological reading.

references.author: Douglas J. Moo
references.title: The Epistle to the Romans, NICNT, Eerdmans, 2018

entries.title: Strangeness
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Jeremiah 29:4-14; Psalm 137; 1 Peter 1:1; 2:11-12.

Place and context: Babylon and Asia Minor.

People associated with the text: Jeremiah, exiles, Peter, churches.

Theological study: Exile is the experience of losing the land, the temple, and the familiar language in the time of exile, then an image of the identity of the church in the letter of Peter. Jeremiah asks the exiles to seek peace in the city and build their lives there, so that exile does not turn into isolation or hatred for the place. Peter uses the description of strangers and inmates to free the loyalty of believers from the harmful values ​​of society, not to remove them from civic responsibility or the common good.

references.author: John J. Collins
references.title: Introduction to the Hebrew Bible, Fortress Press, 2018

entries.title: Prevail
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Romans 8:31-39; 1 Corinthians 15:50-58; 1 John 5:4-5; Revelation 12:10-11.

Place and context: the churches of Corinth and Asia Minor.

People associated with the text: Paul, John, Christ, witnesses.

Theological Study: Victory in the New Testament does not mean political success or immunity from suffering. Paul concludes the argument for resurrection by declaring victory over death, and links it to steadfastness and work in the Lord. In the vision, the witnesses are defeated by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, so the image inverts the logic of victory based on oppression. Therefore, victory is read as a faithful hope in the face of evil, not as a claim of superiority over others.

references.author: G. K. Beale
references.title: The Book of Revelation, NIGTC, Eerdmans, 1999

entries.title: Sheep
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 2:4-4; Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34:1-16; John 1:10-18.

Place and context: the pastures of Israel and Judaism.

People associated with the text: Abel, David, Ezekiel, Jesus.

Theological study: The sheep is a pastoral and sacrificial animal, then an image of the people and leaders in the book. The Lord accepts Abel's offering without the text explaining the reason for acceptance in all its details. Psalm 23 depicts the Lord as a shepherd, while Ezekiel exposes leaders who devour the flock. John rereads the image in Jesus, the good shepherd who knows his sheep and gives his life for them. Image does not give leaders the power to own people; Rather, you measure them by caring and searching for what is lost.

references.author: Daniel I. Block
references.title: The Book of Ezekiel, Chapters 25-48, NICOT, Eerdmans, 1998

entries.title: Gar
entries.content:
Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 22:1-5; 24:1-22; 1 Kings 9:19-18; John 11:38-44.

Place and context: Adullam, En Gedi, Horeb, and Bethany.

People associated with the text: David, Saul, Elijah, Jesus, Lazarus.

Theological study: The cave is a place of refuge and danger in the stories of David, then a place of question and revelation to Elijah in Horeb. It does not make the laurel a magical space or an invitation to perpetual escape; David goes out to shepherd a troubled group, and Elijah goes out with a new message. In John, Lazarus' grave is associated with grief and Jesus' power over death. Places combine human fragility and God's call to him in places of fear and loss.

references.author: David G. Firth
references.title: 1 & 2 Samuel, Apollos Old Testament Commentary, IVP Academic, 2009

entries.title: Gaza
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Judges 16:1-3; Amos 1:6-7; Acts 8:26-40.

Place and context: the southern coastal plain and historical Palestine.

People associated with the text: Samson, Amos, Philip, the Ethiopian eunuch.

Theological study: Gaza is an ancient Palestinian city that appears in the story of Samson, and in the judgment of Amos on the prisoner trade, and then on the road where he meets Philip, the Ethiopian eunuch. The name's ancient connections do not mean that every story about Gaza takes place in the same city; Acts 8 mentions a way down to it. The entry links geography with justice: Amos condemns the sale of captives, and Acts shows the Gospel reaching a Gentile traveler reading Isaiah.

references.author: John D. W. Watts
references.title: Isaiah 34-66, Word Biblical Commentary 25, Word Books, 1987

entries.title: Galatians
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Galatians 1:1-9; 2:1-10; 3:1-14; 5:1-15.

Place and context: The province of Galatia in central Asia Minor.

People associated with the text: Paul, Peter, Barnabas, Titus, Galatian churches.

Theological study: Galatia is the name of the region and churches addressed in Paul's letter in a dispute over circumcision and the membership of Gentiles in the people of God. Paul does not attack the Torah or Judaism per se, but rather rejects the obligation of Gentiles to have signs of Jewish identity as a condition for belonging to Christ. He draws on Abraham, the promise, and the Spirit to show that freedom is not freedom, but love that serves one's neighbor. The audience and date of the message remain a matter of debate, but it does not change the center of the argument.

references.author: James D. G. Dunn
references.title: The Epistle to the Galatians, Black's New Testament Commentary, Hendrickson, 1993

entries.title: He sang
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Deuteronomy 8:11-18; Proverbs 11:4; Mark 10:17-31; 1 Timothy 6:6-19.

Place and context: Israel, Galilee, and the churches of Timothy.

People associated with the text: Moses, the wise man, Jesus, the rich man, Paul.

Theological study: Riches in Scripture are a gift that can serve as gratitude and generosity, but it is dangerous when it becomes a source of security and privilege. Deuteronomy warns against forgetting God in prosperity, and Jesus confronts the rich man with a question of dependency, not a prohibition of property for every person. Paul asks the rich not to be arrogant and to be generous in giving. Therefore, the introduction does not glorify poverty or justify greed, but rather places money under the sovereignty of God and the right of one's neighbor.

entries.title: Easter
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 12:1-28; Leviticus 23:4-8; Luke 7:22-20; 1 Corinthians 5:7-8.

Place and context: Egypt, Jerusalem, and the houses of Israel.

People associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, Jesus, disciples, Paul.

Theological study: Passover commemorates the liberation of Israel from Egypt, and places the sacrifice of the lamb, blood, and family food within the night of the Exodus. The text does not interpret blood as a talisman, but rather a sign of obedience in a historical event of salvation. Jesus celebrates the Supper in the context of Passover, and Paul uses the language of the lamb and leaven to discipline the Corinthian community. The Christian reading does not erase the Jewish meaning of Passover or turn it into an accusation against the Jews; Rather, you read it in the path of covenant, salvation, and worship.

references.author: Nahum M. Sarna
references.title: Exodus, JPS Torah Commentary, Jewish Publication Society, 1991

entries.title: Pharaoh
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 1-14; Ezekiel 29:1-16; Romans 9:14-18.

Place and context: Egypt and the Red Sea in the Exodus narrative.

People associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, the children of Israel, Pharaoh.

Theological study: Pharaoh is the title of the kings of Egypt, not the name of a single person in the book. In Exodus, the head of a regime that enslaves Israel and resists the demand for worship appears, and the plagues reveal a struggle with the deification of authority, not just a personal disagreement. Romans 9 discusses the story of Pharaoh's crucifixion within the question of God's mercy and sovereignty, and does not make it a justification for eliminating human responsibility. The text does not specify the historical identity of the Pharaoh with sufficient certainty, so modern identification attempts are divorced from the meaning of the narrative.

entries.title: Palestine
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 10:13-14; Exodus 13:17; 1 Samuel 4-7; Amos 9:7.

Place and context: The southern coastal plain and the cities of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, and Gath.

People associated with the text: Philistines, Samson, Samuel, David.

Theological study: In the Arabic translation, the name Palestine or the land of the Palestinians appears, while the Hebrew text uses Flesht. It is not permissible to project modern political terminology directly onto the geography of the ancient text. Palestinian cities appear in conflicts, alliances, and a coastal economy, and the book does not describe the people with a single moral quality. Amos reveals that God holds both Israel and the nations accountable, and rejects the use of biblical history to justify contemporary hostility.

references.author: Aren M. Maeir
references.title: The Philistines and Aegean Migration at the End of the Late Bronze Age, Cambridge University Press, 2012

entries.title: Pharisees
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Matthew 1:23-36; Mark 1:7-23; Luke 9:18-14; Acts 23:6-9.

Place and context: Galilee, Judea and Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: Jesus, Paul, Pharisees, scribes.

Theological study: The Pharisees are a multi-voiced Jewish group concerned with the law and its interpretation, and the New Testament does not describe them as a homogeneous bloc. The Gospels criticize certain attitudes about appearance, mercy, and authority, while Paul declares that he was a Pharisee and in Acts 23 shows their difference from the Sadducees in the resurrection. The use of “Pharisee” as an insult or as a tool of hostility toward the Jews should be rejected. The entry reads the debates within the diversity of first-century Judaism and Jesus' call for justice, mercy, and faithfulness.

references.author: E. P. Sanders
references.title: Judaism: Practice and Belief 63 BCE-66 CE, SCM Press, 1992

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Acts 11:16-40; Philippians 1:1-30; 2:1-11; 4:10-20.

Place and context: Roman colony in Macedonia.

People associated with the text: Paul, Silas, Lydia, the jailer, Epaphroditus.

Theological study: Philippi is the first Macedonian city that Paul reaches in Acts 16, where the community forms around Lydia and then within the prison experience and meeting the jailer. The Epistle of Philippians combines joy with imprisonment, giving and humility, and Song 2 preserves the memory of Christ who emptied himself and did not cling to privilege. Joy here does not represent a denial of distress, but rather the fruit of mutual partnership and evangelical work between the Apostle and the Church.

references.author: Gordon D. Fee
references.title: Paul's Letter to the Philippians, NICNT, Eerdmans, 1995

entries.title: Phoenician
entries.content:
Key Evidence: 1 Kings 1:5-18; Isaiah 23; Matthew 15:21-28; Acts 11:19; 21:2-7.

Place and context: The eastern coast of the Mediterranean, especially Tire and Sidon.

People associated with the text: Hiram, Solomon, the Canaanite woman, Paul.

Theological study: Phoenicia is a region of coastal and commercial cities, associated in the kings with Hiram and cedar wood to build the temple. Isaiah criticizes Tire's pride and wealth, while Matthew places Jesus' encounter with the Canaanite woman in the regions of Tire and Sidon within the question of faith and mercy. The apostolic message passes through Phoenicia to Antioch, and the region appears in a network of roads, seas, and communities. The approach does not reduce trade to evil, nor does it sanctify it. Rather, he reads it in the light of justice and worship.

references.author: K. Lawson Younger Jr.
references.title: A Political History of the Arameans, SBL Press, 2016

entries.title: Paradise
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 2:8-10; Luke 23:39-43; 2 Corinthians 12:1-4; Revelation 2:7.

Place and Context: Eden, Golgotha, and Visions of the Church.

People associated with the text: Adam and Eve, Jesus, the thief, Paul.

Theological study: Paradise is a Greek word used in the Septuagint translation to mean paradise, and then appears in Luke, the letters of Paul, and Revelation. Jesus, crucified with him, promises to be with him in paradise, but the text does not provide a detailed schedule of the stages of the afterlife. In the vision, Paradise is linked to the Tree of Life and the restoration of what was lost in Eden. Therefore, the entrance combines the hope of presence with Christ and the hope of renewing creation, while avoiding popular images that separate paradise from the resurrection of the body.

references.author: N. T. Wright
references.title: The Resurrection of the Son of God, Fortress Press, 2003

entries.title: Noah's ark
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 6:9-9:17; Isaiah 54:9; Hebrews 11:7; 1 Peter 3:18-22.

Place and context: the pre-Flood world and the mountains of Ararat.

People associated with the text: Noah, his family, animals, Peter.

Theological study: Astronomy is a means of preservation in the midst of a flood that Genesis describes as a response to the earth being filled with violence. The narrative does not present a contemporary engineering model or an individual survival story; The covenant that follows the flood includes all flesh and establishes the sanctity of blood and the responsibility of humans. Isaiah refers to Noah's waters to emphasize God's faithfulness, and Peter reads water in connection with the baptism and resurrection of Christ. A distinction should be made between the text and later traditions about the location and size of the ark.

references.author: Gordon J. Wenham
references.title: Genesis 1-15, Word Biblical Commentary 1, Word Books, 1987

entries.title: unleavened
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 14:12-20; Leviticus 23:5-8; Matthew 5:16-12; 1 Corinthians 6:5-8.

Place and context: Egypt, Jerusalem, and the Church of Corinth.

People associated with the text: Moses, Jesus, disciples, Paul.

Theological study: Unleavened bread, the bread of the Feast of the Exodus, which reminds of the hasty departure from Egypt. Khmer does not become evil in every text; It may appear in Jesus' parables as a picture of the growth of the kingdom. But in the context of Passover and Corinth, Leaven uses an image of the evil seeping into the community. Therefore, the context determines the meaning of the symbol, and Paul links unleavened bread to sincerity and truth, not to a food system separate from moral life.

references.author: Anthony C. Thiselton
references.title: The First Epistle to the Corinthians, NIGTC, Eerdmans, 2000

entries.title: Redemption
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 6:6; Ruth 4:1-10; Isaiah 43:1; Mark 10:45; Galatians 4:4-7.

Place and context: Egypt, Bethlehem, exile, Galilee, and Galatia.

People associated with the text: Moses, Boaz, Ruth, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: Redemption in the Old Testament is liberation from slavery and restoration of responsibility for neighbor and land, not an abstract financial concept. God appears as a Redeemer in Exodus, and the Book of Ruth makes neighborly rights and family safety the realm of redemption. Jesus uses the language of redemption in serving the Son of Man, and Paul uses redemption in his talk about sonship and freedom. These images are not reduced to a single theory; Rather, they meet in the work of God, who liberates to raise up a people to serve Him with love.

entries.title: Cain
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 1:4-16; Hebrews 11:4; 1 John 3:11-15.

Place and context: Eden and the land of Nod.

People associated with the text: Adam, Eve, Abel.

Theological Study: Cain, Abel's brother and the first murderer in the Genesis account. The text does not explain all of the reasons why Abel's offering was accepted and his was rejected, but it confronts Cain with a warning about sin lying at the door and the responsibility of controlling it. After the murder, he asks God about his brother, so the story makes the brother's responsibility a basis for justice. The mark of Cain does not mean a license to take revenge on him; Rather, it limits the cycle of violence after His judgment.

entries.title: Kadesh
entries.content:
Basic evidence: Numbers 13:26; 20:1-13; 27:12-14; Deuteronomy 1:19-46.

Place and context: The wilderness of China near the borders of Edom.

People associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, Miriam, Israel.

Theological study: Kadesh is a pivotal place in the wilderness journey, linked to the sending of spies, the water crisis, the death of Miriam, and the judgment of Moses and Aaron. The text does not specify its final archaeological site, but its narrative function is clear: at the border the group's fear and mistrust appear. Moses hitting the rock instead of speaking to it cannot be reduced to a technical error. The text links it to the sanctification of God before the people.

entries.title: Cana of Galilee
entries.content:
Key Evidence: John 1:2-12; 4:46-54; 21:2.

Place and context: Galilee, and researchers suggest multiple locations to locate it.

People associated with the text: Jesus, Mary, the disciples, Nathaniel, the king's servant.

Theological study: Cana is the location of the first verse in the Gospel of John, where Jesus turns water into wine at a wedding. The narrative does not offer a showy miracle or a promise of well-being; It proclaims glory and calls for faith. In Cana, Jesus heals the son of the king’s servant from a distance, and the place turns into a context of trust in the word before the vision. The definition of the modern village remains a matter of debate, and this does not change its theological function in the Bible.

entries.title: Korah
entries.content:
Basic evidence: 16; 26:9-11; Psalm 42-49; 84-85.

Place and context: The wilderness near Kadesh.

People associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, Dathan, Abiram, the sons of Korah.

Theological study: Korah leads a rebellion that challenges the leadership of Moses and Aaron, and the narrative places the question within the sanctity of the community and proximity to the sacred. The story does not grant leaders immunity from criticism, but it also rejects the appropriation of service in the name of abstract equality. The verse states that the sons of Korah did not die, and the titles of later psalms are linked to them, so memory prevents reducing the family to the sin of its father.

entries.title: Cyrus
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Ezra 1:1-4; 6:3-5; Isaiah 44:28-45:7; 2 Chronicles 36:22-23.

Place and context: Persia, Babylon, and Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: Cyrus, the returnees, Zerubbabel, Isaiah.

Theological study: Cyrus, king of Persia, who allows the return of the groups of Judah and the rebuilding of the temple. Isaiah calls him “the Lord’s anointed” in the sense of an instrument dedicated to a divine purpose, not in the sense that he shares Israel’s faith or Christ’s place in the New Testament. The texts reveal that God's sovereignty operates through a non-Israelite emperor, and that the return requires the building of worship and community rather than a mere political transition.

entries.title: Caiaphas
entries.content:
Key Evidence: John 11:47-53; 18:13-28; Matthew 26:57-68; Acts 4:5-12.

Place and context: Jerusalem and the house of the high priest.

People associated with the text: Jesus, Annas, the chief priests, Peter, John.

Theological Study: Caiaphas the High Priest in the Accounts of the Trial of Jesus. In John, he utters a political argument about the death of one man for the sake of the people, and the narrator reads his words with prophetic irony, not with an acknowledgment of the justice of the trial. The reference to him does not justify accusing all the Jews of killing Jesus; The Gospels show the intersection of priestly and Roman authorities, crowds, and disciples. The introduction focuses on the responsibility of authority when it makes maintaining order a reason for sacrificing rights.

entries.title: Resurrection
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Daniel 12:2-3; John 11:23-27; 1 Corinthians 1:15-58; Revelation 20:11-15.

Place and context: The tombs in Judah, the churches of Corinth, and the Apocalypse of John.

People associated with the text: Martha, Jesus, Paul, witnesses of the Resurrection.

Theological study: Resurrection in the Bible is a hope for the body and creation, not just the survival of the soul after death. John links the resurrection to the person and life of Jesus, and Paul defends it in 1 Corinthians 15 as the foundation of the gospel and the hope of the dead. The resurrected body does not describe a return to the old state, but rather a transformation under the authority of Christ. Therefore, the resurrection prevents contempt for the body or despair over death, and calls for steadfast work in the Lord.

entries.title: Caesar
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Luke 1:2; Matthew 15:22-22; John 19:12-15; Acts 25:10-12.

Place and Context: The Roman Empire and Judaism.

People associated with the text: Augustus, Tiberius, Jesus, Pilate, Paul.

Theological Study: Caesar is an imperial title that places the New Testament within the de facto authority of Rome. In the question of tribute, Jesus rejects the trap that wants to turn him into a rebel leader or a religious follower of Rome, and returns to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s. This does not give the state absolute loyalty, because the image of God in man and the authority of Christ define its limits. Paul's appeal to Caesar is an available legal use, not a sanctification of the empire.

entries.title: Guitar
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Psalm 33:2; 57:8; 150:3; Revelation 5:8; 14:2-3.

Place and Context: The Temple and Visions of Patmos.

People associated with the text: the psalmists, the elders, John the Revelator.

Theological study: The harp is a stringed instrument that appears in the praise of the Psalms, then in the Revelation of John, next to the prayers and hymns of the saints. The texts do not define the modern instrument form or make music the sole test of spirituality. Its function in the Psalms is to involve the body, voice, and skill in thanking God, and in the vision to depict a worship that resists the noise of divinized powers. The introduction links art to worship, not to consumption or ostentation.

entries.title: An offering
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Leviticus 1:1-17; Mark 7:9-13; Hebrews 1:10-18.

Place and Context: Tabernacle, Temple, and Controversies in Galilee.

People associated with the text: Moses, priests, Jesus, scribes.

Theological study: Qurban is a word derived from the Arabic translation of the sacrifice or gift dedicated to God. The Levites offer sacrifices in a system of holiness and fellowship, so they are not a purchase of the divine presence. Jesus criticizes the use of “sacrifice” to bypass the responsibility to honor one’s parents, and in doing so rejects a piety that uses vows to escape family justice. Hebrews reads Christ's sacrifice in light of sacrifices, emphasizing that new worship is inseparable from obedience.

entries.title: The word of God
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Deuteronomy 8:3; Isaiah 55:10-11; John 1:1-18; Hebrews 4:12.

Place and context: Sinai, exile, Galilee, and churches.

People associated with the text: Moses, Isaiah, Jesus, writer of Hebrews.

Theological study: The word of God in the Torah is a declaration that nourishes and guides the people, and in the prophets is an effective word that fulfills God’s purpose. John declares that the Word became flesh in Jesus, so not every use of the word equates to the person of Christ. Hebrews describes the Word as living and searching, not a weapon to condemn others. The entry combines written revelation, the incarnate Christ, and practical obedience.

entries.title: Church
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Matthew 13:16-20; Acts 2:42-47; 1 Corinthians 12; Ephesians 2:11-22.

Place and context: Galilee, Jerusalem, Corinth, and Ephesus.

People associated with the text: Jesus, Peter, the Apostles, Paul.

Theological study: The church in the New Testament is a group called around Christ, not an abstract building or institution. The Acts of the Apostles describe its teaching, its table, its prayers, and the sharing of its resources, and Paul explains that it is a diverse body. The image does not give an unaccountable leadership or a group the right to exclude others; Christ is the head, and the unity of Jews and nations is the fruit of reconciliation.

entries.title: Canaan
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 12:5-7; Numbers 13-14; Joshua 1:1-9; 24:1-28.

Place and context: The eastern Mediterranean between Egypt and Syria.

People associated with the text: Abraham, Moses, Joshua, the peoples of Canaan.

Theological study: Canaan is the name of a land and peoples in the narratives of the Patriarchs, Exodus, and Joshua. The promise of land is linked to covenant and justice, and is not reduced to justifying a modern political takeover. The story of the spies reveals Israel's fear and Joshua reveals the difficulty of transitioning to a new life. The texts do not describe the Canaanites with one voice, as the example of Rahab and her inclusion in Israel highlights.

entries.title: Capernaum
entries.category: Cities and the Ministry of Jesus
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Matthew 4:13-17; 8:5-17; Mark 1:21-39; John 6:24-59.

Place and context: The northwestern shore of the Sea of ​​Galilee.

People associated with the text: Jesus, Peter, the centurion, the townspeople.

Theological study: Capernaum is an important center for Jesus' ministry in Galilee, where teachings, healings, and controversies appear. A city's proximity to Jesus does not automatically make it a faith; When does he mention her responsibility for refusing to repent despite the verses? The entrance brings together the house, the synagogue and the sea, where Jesus proclaims the Kingdom and confronts sickness, power and the search for bread.

entries.title: Corinth
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Acts 1:18-18; 1 Corinthians 1-16; 2 Corinthians 1-13.

Place and context: Achaia in Roman Greece.

People associated with the text: Paul, Priscilla, Aquila, Crispus, Titus.

Theological Study: Corinth is a multicultural commercial city and its church community suffers from divisions and moral and liturgical questions. The two letters are not written to a corrupt group without hope, but to saints called to grow. Paul treats the body, the table, giving, and resurrection as communal issues, and refuses to turn freedom or knowledge into a privilege that hurts the weak.

entries.title: Cornelius
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Acts 1:10-48; 11:1-18.

Place and context: Caesarea on the coast.

People associated with the text: Peter, Cornelius, the angel of the Lord, the people of Caesarea.

Theological study: Cornelius, a God-fearing Gentile centurion, is brought to him by Peter after a vision that challenges the limits of food and community. The story does not erase the roots of the gospel in Israel, but rather reveals that God is no respecter of persons and that the Spirit is given to the nations. Peter corrects his interpretation before the Church of Jerusalem, so the message shows a process of collective discernment rather than an individual, transcendent decision.

entries.title: Colossians
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Colossians 1:1-29; 2:6-23; 3:1-17; 4:7-18.

Place and context: Phrygia in Asia Minor.

People associated with the text: Paul, Timothy, Epaphras, Philemon.

Theological study: Colossae is a city and a church addressed by a message that emphasizes the sovereignty of Christ over creation and the church. The treatise confronts teachings that mix austerity, visions, angels and ceremony, and do not allow us to reconstruct specific adversaries with complete confidence. Paul links the fullness of Christ to a practical life of forgiveness, love, and thanksgiving, not elitist knowledge.

entries.title: Kush
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 10:6-7; Isaiah 18; Zephaniah 3:10; Acts 8:26-39.

Place and context: Southern Egypt and Nubia in ancient usage.

People associated with the text: Cush, Isaiah, the Ethiopian eunuch, Philip.

Theological study: Kush is the name of the region of southern Egypt in biblical geography, and does not automatically equal a modern state. It appears in the Table of Nations and the prophecies of Isaiah and Zephaniah, then the eunuch of Kendace comes from Cush, reading Isaiah in the Acts of the Apostles. The story does not make the man merely a distant symbol; He is a reader who asks, relies, and returns with joy, so the message appears to cross borders.

entries.title: Priests
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 28-29; Leviticus 8-10; Malachi 2:1-9; Hebrews 4:14-16.

Place and context: the tabernacle, the temple, and the communities of the Hebrews.

People associated with the text: Aaron, his sons, Malachi, Jesus.

Theological Study: Priests in the Torah serve in a system of sanctity, teaching, and sacrifice, and have no privilege separate from obedience. The story of Nadab and Abihu reveals the limits of approaching the sacred, and Malachi criticizes the corruption of the teachings of the priests. Hebrews reads Jesus as a great high priest, not to abolish Israel's history but to explain his unique work and open hope to those who draw near to God.

entries.title: Vine
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Isaiah 5:1-7; Psalm 80:8-19; John 1:15-17.

Place and context: Israel, Galilee, and Atticism.

People associated with the text: Isaiah, the psalmist, Jesus, the disciples.

Theological Study: The Vine is an image of Israel in Isaiah and the Psalm, revealing God's expectation of justice rather than bloodshed. In John, Jesus declares himself to be the true vine and calls his disciples to persevere, love, and be fruitful. Fruit is not a measure of success or productivity, but rather a life that is formed in a relationship with Christ and remains in His love.

entries.title: Lot
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 11:27-32; 13:1-13; 19:1-29; 2 Peter 2:6-8.

Place and context: Haran, Canaan, and Sodom.

People associated with the text: Abraham, angels, inhabitants of Sodom.

Theological study: Lot, Abraham's nephew, and his story reveals the tension of kinship, choice, and survival. He chooses the Jordan plain near Sodom, then Abraham rescues him from captivity and leaves the city before its judgment. His survival does not justify his choices, and his description in 2 Peter does not make the reading of Genesis uncritical. The story asks for intercession, justice and mercy without reducing his person to a single image.

entries.title: Luke
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Luke 1:1-4; Acts 1:1-8; Colossians 4:14; 2 Timothy 4:11.

Place and context: Antioch, the Mediterranean and Rome in the service tradition.

People associated with the text: Paul, Theophilus, the Apostles.

Theological Study: Luke relates to the Gospel, Acts, and Paul's fellowship in the Epistles. He opens his Gospel with the investigation and arrangement addressed to Theophilus, and Acts continues the story of the spread of the testimony from Jerusalem. The New Testament does not resolve all the details of the author's identity or profession, so later church traditions must be separated from the textual evidence.

entries.title: Lazarus
entries.content:
Key Evidence: John 1:11-44; 12:1-11.

Place and context: Bethany near Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: Mary, Martha, Jesus, the disciples.

Theological study: Lazarus' illness and death place Jesus before the grief of the two sisters and the grave of a friend. Jesus does not postpone coming until he has banished the pain, but rather weeps and then calls Lazarus out. The verse is a sign in the Gospel of John that leads to the belief of some people and the conspiracy of others. It does not equate the resurrection of Lazarus with the final resurrected life. Lazarus returns to his previous life.

entries.title: Levi
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 29:34; 34:25-31; Exodus 32:25-29; Numbers 3:5-13.

Place and context: Canaan, Egypt, and the wilderness.

People associated with the text: Jacob, Simeon, Moses, Aaron.

Theological study: Levi, Jacob's son, and the story of Shechem links his anger with Simeon to the violence that Jacob's blessing criticizes. In Exodus and Numbers, the group of Levites appears in the service of the tabernacle, with the distinction of priests from the descendants of Aaron. Subsequent service does not make the sin of Shechem irrelevant, nor turn lineage into a privilege without responsibility; The prophets also hold the priests and Levites accountable.

entries.title: Laban
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 24:29-61; 29:1-30; 31:1-55.

Place and context: Haran and Gilead.

People associated with the text: Rebekah, Jacob, Leah, Rachel.

Theological study: Laban, Rebekah's brother and Jacob's uncle, and his stories reveal the economy of family, marriage, and work in the world of the patriarchs. He changes the wage agreement and deceives Jacob into marrying Leah, but Jacob himself enters the story with a prior deception. The conflict ends with a covenant in Gilead that sets boundaries between the two sides. It is not appropriate to use the story to sanctify labor exploitation or forced marriage; It describes a complex family world and situates it within God's promise.

entries.title: Lydia
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Acts 11:16-15; 16:40.

Place and context: Philippi in Macedonia.

People associated with the text: Paul, Silas, Luke, Philippians.

Theological Study: Lydia, a purple seller from Thyatira, worships God and hears Paul by the river in Philippi. The Acts of the Apostles describes the Lord as opening her heart to listen, and then receiving the apostles into her home. The text does not make her verse merely a household detail; Hospitality became the basis for an emerging group after prison. Her professional or family life should not be filled with details that the source does not mention.

entries.title: Lystra
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Acts 6:14-23; 16:1-3; 2 Timothy 3:10-11.

Place and context: Lycaonia in Asia Minor.

People associated with the text: Paul, Barnabas, Timothy, the townspeople.

Theological study: In Lystra, Paul heals a man. People think he and Barnabas are gods, so the two apostles tear their clothes and refuse to worship. Then, after incitement from other cities, the crowd turns and stones Paul. The story reveals the fickleness of the masses and the fragility of the message, and the city later becomes associated with Timothy. No glorification of miracle or suffering is separate from calling people to the living God.

entries.title: Lebanon
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Deuteronomy 1:7; 1 Kings 5:1-18; Psalm 92:12; Isaiah 2:13; Ezekiel 31:3.

Place and context: The mountain range north of the Land of Israel.

People associated with the text: Solomon, Hiram, the Prophets.

Theological study: Lebanon is a mountainous region famous for its cedars, and in the kings it is linked to Hiram and the wood for building the temple. The Psalms and Prophets use the cedar as an image of splendor and power, but Isaiah makes his very exaltation an object of humility before the Lord. Matter or mountain are not understood as intrinsic sanctity; The texts collect resources for trade and construction, and images of pride and fertility.

entries.title: The two tablets of testimony
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 24:12; 31:18; 32:15-20; 34:1-4; Deuteronomy 9:9-17.

Place and context: Mount Sinai.

People associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, Israel.

Theological study: The two tablets of the testimony bear the words of the covenant in the Sinai narrative. Moses breaks them in front of the golden calf as a sign of the people’s breaking of the covenant, and then new tablets come after intercession and renewal. The narrative does not provide a technical description of the form of the tablets so much as it links the written word to the presence of God and the responsibility of the community. The entrance combines the holiness of the law and the mercy of the renewed covenant.

entries.title: Night
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 3:1-5; Psalm 4:8; 121:5-8; John 3:19-21; 13:30.

Place and context: Creation, Jerusalem, and the Johannine Church.

People associated with the text: the psalmist, Jesus, Judas.

Theological study: Night in Genesis is part of the rhythm of creation and does not equal evil in itself. The Psalms use night as a language of protection and peace, while John employs darkness and night within the drama of faith and rejection. Judas' departure at night has a narrative function in the Gospel, but it does not allow for the transformation of natural time into a comprehensive moral judgment. The entry balances the night as a created reality with symbolic images in its context.

entries.title: Moses
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 2-20; number 12; Deuteronomy 34; Hebrews 11:23-29.

Place and context: Egypt, Midian, Sinai, and the plains of Moab.

People associated with the text: Aaron, Miriam, Pharaoh, Joshua.

Theological study: Moses, the leader of the Exodus and the mediator of the covenant in the Torah, and his story begins with the survival of a child in the house of Pharaoh and then an invitation at the bush. The texts do not place him above criticism; Verse 20 relates the crisis of Miriam and Aaron, and verse 20 links his failure to enter the land with his inability to sanctify God. The New Testament rereads Moses as a witness to God's faithfulness, not a substitute for Christ or the responsibility of the people.

entries.title: Mary, mother of Jesus
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Luke 1:26-56; 2:1-35; John 2:1-12; 19:25-27.

Place and context: Nazareth, Bethlehem, and Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: Gabriel, Joseph, Elizabeth, Jesus.

Theological Study: Mary receives the Annunciation in Nazareth and responds with faith that places herself at the service of God's purpose. Her hymn recalls the language of Anna and the Psalms and proclaims God's mercy and justice to the poor. The text does not provide all the details of her later life, and a responsible reading remains distinctive among the biblical evidence and later traditions. Her presence at Cana and the Cross links motherhood to discipleship and trust in the word of Jesus.

entries.title: Mary Magdalene
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Luke 8:1-3; John 19:25; 20:1-18.

Place and context: Galilee, Jerusalem, and the tomb.

People associated with the text: Jesus, Mary the mother of Jesus, Peter, the disciples.

Theological study: Mary Magdalene is one of the women who accompanied and served Jesus, and the Gospels witness her presence at the cross and the tomb. In John 20 she meets the risen Lord and is sent to tell the disciples. The New Testament does not describe her as a sexual sinner or confuse her with the woman of Bethany; Those are later traditional additions. The entry confirms the centrality of women's testimony in announcing the Resurrection.

entries.title: Martha
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Luke 10:38-42; John 1:11-44; 12:1-8.

Place and context: Bethany near Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: Mary, Lazarus, Jesus.

Theological study: Martha welcomes Jesus into her home, and Luke addresses the tension of serving and listening, not despising domestic work. In John 11, she declares her faith in the resurrection of her brother and in Christ, and then stands in front of the tomb of Lazarus.
