It is not right to make her a simple opposite of Mary; Both texts present a woman who serves, asks, and confesses in the midst of grief.

entries.title: When
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Matthew 9:9-13; 10:3; Mark 2:13-17; Luke 5:27-32.

Place and context: Capernaum and Galilee.

People associated with the text: Jesus, tax collectors, Pharisees, the Twelve.

Theological study: Jesus invites Matthew from the tax office and then eats with tax collectors and sinners. The invitation shows a grace that goes beyond reputation. The Gospels differ in naming the tax collector between Matthew and Levi, and the text does not resolve all the details of the relationship between the two names. As for the Gospel of Matthew, it directs the reading of Jesus within the law of Israel and its prophets, and emphasizes mercy, not sacrifice separate from the people.

entries.title: Mark
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Mark 1:1; 8:27-38; 10:35-45; 15:33-39.

Place and Context: Galilee, Judaism and Rome in the Ecclesiastical Tradition.

People associated with the text: Jesus, Peter, the disciples, the centurion.

Theological Study: The Gospel of Mark begins with the proclamation of the Gospel of Jesus Christ and moves quickly toward the cross. It reveals the weakness of the disciples and their misunderstanding of the kingdom, and makes the path of Christ a path of service and giving, not control. The book does not specify the name of the author or the place of writing, but the voice of the Gospel invites the reader to acknowledge Christ in the face of the mystery of his passion and resurrection.

entries.title: Melchizedek
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 17:14-24; Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 5-7.

Place and context: Salem in the time of Abraham.

People associated with the text: Abraham, Melchizedek, writer of Hebrews.

Theological study: Abraham meets Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the Most High God, after the war. He blesses him and gives him tithes. Genesis does not provide a complete genealogy or biography of him, and Hebrews uses this literary silence to explain Christ's different priesthood from Levi's. The portal does not turn the character into a mythical being; He distinguishes between the bildungsroman and the exegetical reading of the message.

entries.title: Malachi
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Malachi 1-4; Matthew 11:10; Mark 1:2.

Place and context: Judah after the exile and the Second Temple.

People associated with the text: the priests, the people of Judah, John the Baptist in the evangelical reception.

Theological study: Malachi criticizes flawed sacrifices, priests who neglect education, and threatened social justice. Travel is not enough to fix the temple ritual; It links worship to fidelity in marriage, fairness, and fear of the Lord. The New Testament uses the apostle's promise to prepare the way in the context of John the Baptist, preserving the function of the book in a post-exilic society.

entries.title: Micah
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Micah 1-7; Matthew 2:5-6; 6:6-8.

Place and context: Moreshet in Judah, Jerusalem, and Samaria.

People associated with the text: Micah, leaders of Judah, inhabitants of Samaria.

Theological Study: Micah speaks against the exploitation of the land, judicial corruption, and false confidence in Zion, but he also proclaims the hope of a shepherd coming from Bethlehem. His phrase about doing what is right, showing mercy, and behaving humbly is inseparable from criticizing sacrifices. Sincere worship is embodied in justice. Matthew welcomes Bethlehem into the Christmas story without eliminating Micah's prophetic context.

entries.title: Psalm
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Psalm 1; 23; 42; 51; 137; 150.

Place and context: temple, exile, and cult community.

People associated with the text: David, the sons of Korah, Asaph, the psalmists.

Theological study: The Psalms are a diverse poetic collection that includes complaint, praise, wisdom, royalty, and repentance. Each title should not be read as a historical proof of David's authorship, nor as turning poetry into a doctrine divorced from its context. The Psalms give honest language to joy, fear, and protest, and connect worship to covenant memory, hope, and justice.

entries.title: Migrate
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 16:1-16; 21:8-21; Galatians 4:21-31.

Place and context: Wilderness of Shur and Beer-lahi-roi.

People associated with the text: Sarah, Abraham, Ishmael, the angel of the Lord.

Theological study: Hagar, an Egyptian slave, bore Ishmael after the initiative of Sarah and Abraham. The composition does not beautify its exploitation or expulsion; The Lord hears her humiliation and sees her crying in the wilderness. Galatians uses her story in a symbolic argument, and this does not negate the history of women and their suffering in formation.

entries.title: Herod the Great
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Matthew 1:2-18; Luke 1:5.

Place and context: Judea, Bethlehem and Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: Magi, Joseph, Mary, Jesus.

Theological study: Herod is the king of Judea in Matthew's birth narrative, and his fear of a rival king reveals the nature of authority that protects itself through violence. The text does not confirm the number of children or details of later traditions, but it places the birth in a real political context. Luke mentions Herod in the chronicle of the priesthood of Zechariah.

entries.title: Abel
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 1:4-16; Hebrews 11:4; 12:24.

Place and context: outside Aden.

People associated with the text: Cain, Adam, Eve.

Theological study: Abel, Cain's brother, and his offering are accepted in the Genesis account, then his brother kills him. His blood cries out from the ground, and the story makes violence against a brother an issue before God. The text does not explain all the reasons for accepting the offering; Therefore, a human differentiation system cannot be built on it. Hebrews reads his blood next to the blood of Christ which speaks best.

entries.title: Holiness
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 19:3-6; Leviticus 19:1-18; Isaiah 6:1-8; 1 Peter 1:13-16.

Place and context: Sinai, Jerusalem, and the groups of Asia Minor.

People associated with the text: Moses, Isaiah, Peter, the people of Israel.

Theological study: Holiness in the book belongs first to God, then it becomes a call to His people in worship and behavior. Leviticus 19 links the phrase “be holy” to justice toward one’s neighbor and the weak, and is not limited to rituals. Isaiah's vision reveals that approaching God's holiness exposes sin and sends the prophet to ministry. Peter regains the call within the hope of Christ, bringing together a new identity and responsible living.

entries.title: Holy of holies
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 31:26-35; Leviticus 16:1-34; 1 Kings 6:19-28; Hebrews 1:9-14.

Place and context: the tabernacle in the wilderness, then the temple in Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, the high priest, the writer of Hebrews.

Theological study: The Holy of Holies is the inner space in the tabernacle and temple, and is associated with the Ark of the Covenant and the Day of Atonement. The text does not describe it as a magical place owned by the priest, but rather regulates the approach to God's presence within the framework of atonement and holiness. Hebrews reads the arrangement of the Tabernacle as a sign that needs to be interpreted in light of Christ's work. Therefore, the symbol does not eliminate the history of Israelite worship, nor does it make the place an abstract geometric detail.

entries.title: Judges of Israel
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Judges 6:2-23; 4:4-10; 6:11-16; 13:1-5; 21:25.

Place and context: the land of Canaan and the Israelite tribes.

People associated with the text: Deborah, Gideon, Samson, Samuel.

Theological Study: The Judges are leaders who rise in crises before kingship, and the book does not provide a stable system or completed moral model. The cycle of distress, cry, survival, and then apostasy is repeated, revealing the fragility of the people more than the heroism of individuals. Deborah features leadership, judgment, and prophecy, while the stories of Gideon and Samson display the limits of human power. The conclusion does not uncritically justify ownership, but rather describes the chaos of a time in which the community lost a common reference for justice.

entries.title: rainbow
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 8:9-17; Ezekiel 1:26-28; Revelation 4:1-3.

Place and Context: After the Flood and the Visions of Ezekiel and John.

People associated with the text: Noah, his sons, Ezekiel, John the Revelator.

Theological study: The bow is placed in formation as a sign of the covenant between God and every living thing after the flood. The sign does not turn into a promise that life will not know disasters or judgment, but rather confirms God's commitment to preserving the order of creation and not destroying the earth with a total flood again. Ezekiel's visions and apocalypse conjure up the arc of divine glory. The symbol thus links covenant mercy with God's sovereignty without separating them.

entries.title: Heart
entries.category: A human being and a covenant
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Deuteronomy 4:6-6; Psalm 51:10; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Mark 7:20-23.

Place and Context: Israel and Judaism in Prophetic and Biblical Teaching.

People associated with the text: Moses, David, Jeremiah, Jesus.

Theological study: The heart, in the language of the book, is the center of thought, will, and emotion, not feelings alone in the modern sense. The Law calls for loving God with all the heart, and the Psalm calls for a pure heart after sin. Jeremiah promises to write the covenant on the inside, while Jesus confronts what comes from the heart as a source of moral impurity. The entrance combines the grace that renews man and his practical responsibility before God and his neighbor.

entries.title: Wheat
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 9:31-32; Ruth 1:2-23; Matthew 13:24-30; John 12:20-26.

Place and context: Egypt, Bethlehem, Galilee, and Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: Ruth, Boaz, Jesus, disciples.

Theological study: Wheat is an essential crop in the economy of the book, and appears in the plagues, the harvest, and the right of the poor to glean. In Ruth, the field becomes a field of honesty, generosity, and protection of the stranger. Jesus' parables of the wheat and the tares are used to teach patience and judgment, not to mandate the group to hastily root out those it deems evil. In John, Jesus' death and fruit are explained by the image of a seed falling into the ground.

entries.title: Restrictions
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Acts 1:12-17; 16:22-34; 21:27-36; Ephesians 6:18-20.

Place and context: Jerusalem, Philippi, Caesarea, and Rome.

People associated with the text: Peter, Paul, Silas, the prison guard.

Theological study: The restrictions in Acts show an effect of the confrontation of testimony with the authorities, and do not make imprisonment an automatic proof of the validity of every position. Peter comes out of prison in a story, while Paul remains in long chains that lead him to testify before the rulers. Philby's story does not neglect the wounds of the imprisoned or turn the earthquake into a show of strength; The scene ends with everyone's protection and the guard's hospitality. Paul writes about the boldness of the gospel from within the context.

entries.title: God's power
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 1:15-18; Isaiah 40:25-31; 1 Corinthians 1:18-25; 2 Corinthians 12:7-10.

Place and Context: Exodus, Exile, and the Churches of Corinth.

People associated with the text: Moses, Isaiah, Paul, the church.

Theological study: The Exodus hymn proclaims the power of God that liberates an oppressed people, and Isaiah comforts the exiles with a Creator whom nothing faints. As for Paul, he puts the power of God in the message of the cross, upending the prevailing standards of wisdom and prestige. This is not the same as glorifying weakness or denying pain; The power of Christ appears in a messenger who seeks help and serves with real limits. Therefore, power is measured by faithfulness to Christ, not by control.

entries.title: A ram
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 22:1-14; Exodus 15:29-32; Leviticus 5:14-16; Hebrews 1:10-14.

Place and context: the land of Moriah and the dwelling.

People associated with the text: Abraham, Isaac, Moses, Aaron.

Theological study: The ram appears in Genesis 22 as a substitute provided by God in place of Isaac, and in the law of the priesthood as part of the sacrifices of consecration and reparation. The story does not mean that God requires human sacrifice; He stops the slaughter and gives an alternative. Subsequent sacrifices help to set the scene within the language of the covenant and draw closer to God. Hebrews reads this system in light of Christ's unique sacrifice, with the biblical context remaining essential to understanding the allegory.

entries.title: He lied
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 20:16; Zechariah 8:16-17; John 8:31-47; Ephesians 4:25.

Place and context: Sinai, Jerusalem, and the churches of Asia Minor.

People associated with the text: Moses, Zechariah, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: The commandments prohibit false testimony within the framework of justice and the protection of one's neighbor, and then the prophetic and apostolic texts extend this commitment to the life of the community. Zechariah links honesty to the peace of the city after the exile. In John, lying stands against steadfastness in the word of Jesus, not against honest questions or weakness in knowledge. Paul asks the church to speak the truth because its members are connected to each other, so honesty becomes a structural act and not just an individual virtue.

entries.title: Canaanites
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 15:10-19; Joshua 1:9-27; Judges 1:27-36; Matthew 15:21-28.

Place and context: Canaan, Phenicia, and the tribal regions.

People associated with the text: Joshua, the Gibeonites, the Canaanite woman, Jesus.

Theological study: Canaanites is a collective name for the peoples of the earth in a number of texts, and it should not be used as a simple or unified ethnic designation. Joshua exposes the Gibeonites within a complex covenant, and Judges describes the continued presence of multiple groups in the land. In Matthew, a Canaanite woman insists on Jesus’ mercy, showing her capacity for faith in the context of the message of Israel and the nations. These texts resist any reading that makes identity a justification for contemporary contempt or annihilation.

entries.title: Book of life
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 32:30-35; Psalm 69:28; Philippians 3:4; Revelation 3:5; 20:11-15.

Place and context: Sinai, the prayers of the Psalms, Philippians, and the visions of Patmos.

People associated with the text: Moses, David, Paul, John the Revelator.

Theological study: The Book of Life is a written image of divine knowledge and belonging to His people, and its function varies according to the literary genre. Moses intercedes for the people in the language of the record, while the psalm uses the image of erasure within adversarial prayer. In the vision, the image stands in a scene of judgment and hope, and does not present a human record that can be controlled or whose content can be secretly known. The introduction stresses the responsibility of faith and God's justice and mercy together.

entries.title: Clerks
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Ezra 6:7-10; Matthew 5:17-20; 23:1-12; Mark 12:28-34.

Place and context: Babylon, Jerusalem, and Galilee.

People associated with the text: Ezra, Jesus, Pharisees, writer of the law.

Theological study: The writer in the Old Testament and later Judaism is an expert in writing and the law, and it is not permissible to reduce him to a fixed negative image. Ezra provides a model for studying, working with, and teaching the law. Jesus criticizes some writers when they separate religious authority from justice and mercy, but he responds to a writer in Mark with a positive statement about the greatest of the commandments. The introduction distinguishes between criticism of hypocrisy and rejection of education or Judaism in general.

entries.title: Cup
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Psalm 23:5; Isaiah 51:17; Mark 10:35-40; 14:22-24; 1 Corinthians 10:14-22.

Place and context: the Temple, Jerusalem, and Corinth.

People associated with the text: David, James, John, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: The cup is an image with multiple meanings: hospitality, blessing, and sometimes judgment in the language of the prophets. Jesus asks the two sons of Zebedee what cup he should drink, and then gives the cup at supper as part of his blood covenant. Letters do not separate the table from fellowship and moral discernment; Paul links the cup of blessing to participation in the body of Christ. The entry reads the symbol in its context and does not turn it into a talisman or just an empty souvenir.

entries.title: Canaanite
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Matthew 21:15-28; Mark 7:24-30.

Place and context: Tire and Sidon districts.

People associated with the text: Jesus, the disciples, the woman's daughter.

Theological study: The Canaanite woman asks for the healing of her daughter in the region of Tire and Sidon, and Matthew presents the dialogue within the tension of Jesus’ message to Israel and the breadth of mercy to the nations. Her persistence is not a verbal examination separate from her daughter's pain, but a plea for mercy from the Son of David. The story ends with praise for her faith and the daughter's recovery. Therefore, metaphorical expressions in dialogue are not suitable to justify insulting people, but rather reveal the movement of the Gospel that transcends borders.

entries.title: Kochi
entries.content:
Key Evidence: 2 Samuel 19:18-33.

Place and context: Ephraim and Mohannaim in the context of the War of Absalom.

People associated with the text: David, Joab, Ahimaaz, the Cushite, Absalom.

Theological study: The Cushite is a messenger sent by Joab to David with news of the end of the battle and the death of Absalom. The text does not give a personal name or details of his origin beyond description, so filling his biography with speculation should be avoided. The scene highlights the tragedy of the civil war: the messenger brings news of victory, but the king hears the news of the loss of his son. The story reveals that military success does not erase the cost of family and political conflict.

entries.title: The district of the Gadarenes
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Matthew 8:28-34; Mark 1:5-20; Luke 8:26-39.

Place and context: The eastern bank of the Sea of ​​Galilee at the Decapolis.

People associated with the text: Jesus, the possessed man, the people of the area, the disciples.

Theological study: The Gospel manuscripts differ in naming the region between the Gadarenes, the Gerasenes, and the Gerasenes, a difference that calls for geographical caution. The accounts agree on Jesus crossing into a Gentile or mixed area and healing a man isolated among the graves. Jesus returns him to his family as a witness of mercy instead of keeping him a follower in the boat. One should not base a blanket judgment on the people of the area based on their fearful reaction in the story.

entries.title: Leviticus
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Leviticus 1:1-17; 16:1-34; 19:1-18; 25:1-55; Matthew 22:34-40.

Place and context: The dwelling in the Sinai wilderness.

People associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, priests, Jesus.

Theological Study: Leviticus regulates sacrifices, purity, priesthood, and holiness within the covenant of Israel. The holiness of travel is not reduced to the ritual season; Chapter nineteen links it to honesty, fair wages, and love of one’s neighbor. The Day of Atonement places a collective treatment of sin within the worship of the people. Jesus quotes love for one's neighbor from the book, and it becomes clear that there is a moral continuity that does not contradict worship and justice.

entries.title: Damn
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 3:14-19; Deuteronomy 27:11-26; Jeremiah 17:5-8; Galatians 3:10-14.

Place and context: Eden, Moab, Judah, and the churches of Galatia.

People associated with the text: Adam, Eve, Moses, Jeremiah, Paul.

Theological Study: The curse in Scripture is a judicial and covenantal language describing the effect of disobedience and God's judgment, not a tool possessed by individuals to harm their opponents. In Genesis, land and work are among the consequences of the fall, and in Deuteronomy the group declares its responsibility before the covenant. Jeremiah contrasts trust in man with trust in the Lord. Paul reads Galatians in light of the work of Christ, so he does not justify contempt for the law or the Jewish people.

entries.title: Tongue
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Psalm 34:12-14; Proverbs 19:10; 18:21; James 3:1-12.

Place and context: Israel and the communities of Jacob.

People associated with the text: David, the wise men, Jacob, the teachers.

Theological study: The tongue in wisdom literature is a symbol of speech capable of benefit or harm. Proverbs do not call for cowardly silence, but rather for honest, disciplined speech that preserves life. James likens the tongue to a small organ that directs big things and alerts teachers to a higher responsibility. The difficulty of controlling it does not mean despair of change, but rather placing the statement under the worship of God and reconciliation with one’s neighbor.

entries.title: Laodicea
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Colossians 2:1; 4:13-16; Revelation 3:14-22.

Place and context: Lycus Valley in Asia Minor.

People associated with the text: John the Revelator, the Church of Laodicea, the Church of Colossae.

Theological study: Laodicea is a city in the Lycus Valley linked to the churches of Colossae and Hierapolis, and a message criticizing apathy and self-sufficiency appears in the vision. The metaphor of lukewarm, hot, and cold addresses a group that believes they are rich and need nothing. The message is not final humiliation, because Christ calls for repentance and communion. The interpretation makes use of the geography of local waters without making it the sole key to the meaning of the text.

entries.title: Lachish
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Joshua 3:10-27; 2 Kings 13:18-17; 19:8; Jeremiah 34:6-7.

Place and context: The plain of Judah, southwest of Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: Joshua, Sennacherib, Hezekiah, Jeremiah.

Theological study: Lachish is a fortified city in Judah. ​​It appears in the Joshua War and then in the Assyrian campaign of Sennacherib. The Book of Kings shows its siege to be part of a broader threat to Jerusalem, while Jeremiah invokes its stay with Azekah in late Judah. Archaeological evidence confirms the presence of destruction and siege, but it does not replace a careful reading of the texts. The entry reveals the fragility of cities in the face of empires and the question of political and religious trust.

entries.title: Leah
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 15:29-35; 30:9-21; 35:16-26; 49:1-28.

Place and context: Haran and Canaan.

People associated with the text: Jacob, Rachel, Laban, her sons.

Theological study: Leah, daughter of Laban and Jacob's first wife, in the account of the formation of the tribes of Israel. The narrative does not excuse the deception in her marriage or the painful rivalry between her and Rachel. The novel records her children's naming and prayers as an attempt to find acceptance and love within a tense family. Her descendants include Judah and Levi, but her place in the story is not limited to her relative function; The text preserves her voice and her suffering.

entries.title: Refugees
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Mark 1:5-20; Luke 8:26-39.

Place and context: The eastern bank of the Sea of ​​Galilee.

People associated with the text: Jesus, the possessed man, the people of the area, the disciples.

Theological study: Legion is the name with which the unclean spirit responds in the story of the tormented man among the graves, and in Roman usage it means a large military unit. The text does not impose a single political interpretation of the name, even though the scene takes place in a world penetrated by the authority of Rome. The narrative focuses on the man regaining his sanity and returning to his family. Therefore, the story does not become a guide to diagnosing every disease or disorder as a spiritual possession.

entries.title: Luke and the Gospel
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Luke 1:1-4; 4:16-21; 9:51-56; 24:44-53; Acts 1:1-8.

Place and context: Galilee, Jerusalem and the Mediterranean.

People associated with the text: Jesus, Theophilus, the disciples, the apostles.

Theological study: Luke's Gospel arranges the account of Jesus from birth to ascension, presenting it as an investigation based on what the witnesses received. Jesus' road to Jerusalem gives narrative and theological weight, highlighting the poor, women, strangers, prayer, and the work of the Spirit. The dedication to Theophilus does not need to resolve all questions of authorship or history. The Book of Acts completes the movement from Jerusalem to the broader testimony.

entries.title: Lucius
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Acts 13:1-3; Romans 16:21.

Place and context: Antioch and the context of the Epistle to the Romans.

People associated with the text: Barnabas, Saul, Simon, Lucius, Timothy.

Theological Study: The Acts of the Apostles mentions Lucius of Cyrene among the prophets and teachers in the Church of Antioch when sending Barnabas and Saul. Paul mentions Lucius among his relatives or colleagues in the Romans greetings. The text cannot prove that the two names are for the same person, so the entry separates possibility from confirmation. Both references reveal a geographically and ethnically diverse leadership network in early Christian communities.

entries.title: Baptism
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Matthew 3:13-17; 28:18-20; Acts 2:37-42; Romans 6:1-11.

Place and context: the Jordan River, Jerusalem, and Rome.

People associated with the text: John the Baptist, Jesus, Peter, Paul.

Theological study: Baptism in the New Testament is linked to the repentance of John, the baptism of Jesus, and then the formation of the group of disciples. The Acts of the Apostles does not present it as a private ritual separate from faith and teaching, but as a public response to the Gospel and joining the community. In Romans 6, Paul explains the believer’s union with Christ in his death and resurrection, not as an automatic mechanism for salvation. The texts preserve their connection with water, the body, and new life together.

entries.title: Altar
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 8:20-22; Exodus 20:24-26; 1 Kings 18:30-39; Hebrews 10:13-16.

Place and context: the land of Noah, Sinai, Carmel, and the Temple.

People associated with the text: Noah, Moses, Elijah, priests of Israel.

Theological study: The altar is a place where sacrifices are offered in the narratives of the fathers, the law, and the temple, and it is linked to remembering the presence of God and the covenant. Elijah rebuilds the ruined altar of the Lord in opposition to the worship of Baal, so the site becomes a critique of division rather than a tool for personal superiority. Hebrews uses the language of the altar to explain the work of Christ and the new worship. The book does not sanctify stones in and of themselves, but rather judges worship by whether it is faithful to God and just.

entries.title: Kingdom of God
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Daniel 7:13-14; Mark 1:14-15; Luke 4:43; Matthew 6:9-13; 1 Corinthians 15:20-28.

Place and context: Galilee, Judaism and the churches of Paul.

People associated with the text: Jesus, Daniel, the disciples, Paul.

Theological Study: The Kingdom of God is the effective rule of God, not merely a geographical territory nor a human political program. Jesus announces the nearness of the Kingdom and calls for repentance and faith, and healings, the table, and forgiveness appear as signs of him. Prayer keeps the request for His coming open, while Paul places its fulfillment in the submission of all power to Christ. This tension between the present and the future prevents the transformation of the Kingdom into a national success or an escape from the responsibility of the world.

entries.title: Christ
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Psalm 1:2-12; Isaiah 61:1-3; Mark 8:27-38; John 20:30-31.

Place and context: Israel, Galilee and Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: David, Isaiah, Peter, Jesus.

Theological study: Christ is a title that means the Anointed One in the traditions of the king and the priest, and his expectations are formed within multiple texts, not in a single model. Peter confesses Jesus Christ and then Jesus corrects expectations of power by speaking of suffering and discipleship. Luke reads Isaiah 61 in his ministry, and John writes for the reader to believe that Jesus is the Messiah. Therefore, it does not separate the title from Israel and does not turn it into a slogan without the cross and resurrection.

entries.title: Loving
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Leviticus 19:17-18; Hosea 11:1-9; Mark 12:28-34; John 13:34-35; 1 Corinthians 13.

Place and context: Israel, Galilee, Attica, and Corinth.

People associated with the text: Moses, Hosea, Jesus, disciples, Paul.

Theological study: Love for God and neighbor meet in the law and the teaching of Jesus, so love is not a feeling separated from truth and justice. Hosea depicts God's love in the midst of the judgment of his people, and Jesus makes love the greatest of the commandments and the sign of the disciples. In Corinthians, Paul criticizes gifts that seek status without building others up. Biblical love is an act that seeks the good of one’s neighbor and accepts discernment and accountability.

entries.title: Forgiveness
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 34:6-9; Psalm 103:8-14; Matthew 18:21-35; Luke 23:32-34; Ephesians 4:31-32.

Place and context: Sinai, Jerusalem and the churches of Ephesus.

People associated with the text: Moses, David, Peter, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Forgiveness in the Bible is linked to God’s mercy and covenant, and does not mean calling evil good or abolishing justice. Exodus 34 proclaims God's forgiveness while not ignoring the consequences of wrongdoing, and Jesus' parables teach that those who receive mercy do not withhold it from their debtors. The Gospel does not ask the hurting person to deny the harm or drop legal protections, but rather to reject revenge and work for reconciliation where it is honest and safe. Paul places forgiveness within the life of a new community.

entries.title: Who
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 1:16-36; Numbers 11:4-9; Deuteronomy 8:1-5; John 6:25-59.

Place and context: the Sinai wilderness and the Galilee.

People associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, Israel, Jesus.

Theological study: Manna is food that God provides to Israel in the wilderness day after day, teaching them dependence and obedience, not anxious hoarding. The complaint of the number reveals that the gift does not prevent complaining or longing for slavery. Deuteronomy interprets experience as education that man does not live by bread alone. In John, Jesus uses manna to talk about himself as the bread of life, without denying the date of the Exodus or turning it into a metaphor without real hunger.

entries.title: Moab
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 19:30-38; Numbers 22-25; Ruth 1:1-22; Deuteronomy 34:1-8.

Place and context: East of the Dead Sea and the plains of Moab.

People associated with the text: Balak, Balaam, Ruth, Naomi, Moses.

Theological study: Moab is a land and people east of the Dead Sea, and its texts combine conflict, kinship, and migration. The story of Balaam deals with Balak's attempt to curse Israel, and then Ruth the Moabitess appears within David's lineage with a loyalty that transcends national boundaries. The plains of Moab are the scene of Moses' speeches and death before entering the land. Therefore, the diversity of evidence does not allow for creating a fixed picture of an entire people or transforming geography into a moral judgment.

entries.title: Mercies
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 34:6-7; Psalm 136; Micah 7:18-20; Luke 1:46-55.

Place and context: Sinai, the Temple, Judah, and Nazareth.

People associated with the text: Moses, the psalmist, Micah, Miriam.

Theological study: God’s mercies declare in the covenant formulas that He is merciful, compassionate, and slow to anger, and His mercy is not separated from His faithfulness and justice. Psalm 136 reiterates this truth within the memory of creation and Exodus, while Micah concludes with the hope of forgiveness of sin. The Song of Mary invokes this language to announce a revolution that lifts up the humble and recalls the promise of Abraham. Mercy is not tolerance of injustice, but rather a divine initiative that establishes the covenant and calls for tangible justice.

entries.title: Structure
entries.content:
Key Evidence: 1 Kings 1:8-30; Jeremiah 7:1-15; Ezra 3:10-13; John 2:13-22.

Place and context: Jerusalem in the First and Second Temples.

People associated with the text: Solomon, Jeremiah, the returnees, Jesus.

Theological study: The temple is the center of Israel's worship in Jerusalem, but it does not confine God to a building or grant the city moral immunity. Solomon acknowledges that the heavens cannot contain him, and Jeremiah criticizes people’s confidence in the phrase “the temple of the Lord” while the injustice continues. The returnees celebrate the founding of the Second Temple amid mixed tears and joy. John interprets Jesus' action in the temple and his reference to his body within the question of worship and presence, not as a disdain for Israel's history.

entries.title: Aaron
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 4:10-17; 28:1-43; 32:1-35; Numbers 12:1-16; 20:22-29.

Place and context: Egypt, Sinai, the wilderness, and Mount Hor.

People associated with the text: Moses, Miriam, Israel, Eleazar.

Theological study: Aaron, Moses’ brother and the first high priest in the priestly narrative, and his presence combines service and weakness. He is appointed to support Moses in speaking and then wears priestly robes, but he is also associated with the making of the golden calf. His story reveals that religious office does not eliminate accountability, and that intercession does not excuse sin. His death on Mount Hor ends with the transfer of the priesthood to Eleazar within the continuity of the community.

entries.title: Hosea
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Hosea 1:1-11; 2:14-23; 6:1-6; 11:1-9; 14:1-9.

Place and context: Northern Kingdom of Israel.

People associated with the text: Hosea, Gomer, Ephraim, Judah.

Theological Study: Hosea confronts northern Israel with marriage and family analogies that reveal idolatry and political and religious injustice. His symbolic marriage should not be used to justify control or harm in contemporary relationships; The focus of the book is God’s faithfulness and criticism of the people’s betrayal. The language of mercy amounts to a promise to restore the relationship and change the name from “You are not my people” to God’s people. The book combines judgment and tenderness within a sincere invitation to return.

entries.title: Herod Antipas
entries.category: The Kings and Ministry of Jesus
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Mark 6:14-29; Luke 3:1-20; 9:7-9; 23:6-12.

Place and context: Galilee, Berea, and Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: John the Baptist, Herodias, Jesus, Pilate.

Theological study: Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Berea at the time of Jesus’ ministry, differs from Herod the Great in the Christmas story. He imprisons John the Baptist and then kills him after a rash oath and the pressure of a feast, showing the intertwining of power, fear, and the desire to save face. He wants to see Jesus but receives no answer from him in Luke's account. The text does not present its curiosity as a search of faith, but rather judges an authority that treats the truth as a threat.

entries.title: Herodias
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Matthew 14:1-12; Mark 6:17-29.

Place and context: Galilee and Makhawar Castle in the historical background.

People associated with the text: Herod Antipas, John the Baptist, her daughter.

Theological study: Herodias appears in the account of the killing of John the Baptist within a marriage that the prophet criticizes. Mark attributes her hostility to John, but the account does not justify turning her into a general symbol of the evil of women or holding her solely responsible for the ruler’s decision. Herod swears an oath and orders the killing, knowing John's status. The scene reveals how court power, irresponsible oaths, and fear of the public conspire against the voice of prophecy.

entries.title: Hormone
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Deuteronomy 3:8-9; Joshua 11:3; Psalm 42:6; 133:3.

Place and context: The northern border of the Land of Israel and the eastern Lebanon Mountains.

People associated with the text: Moses, Joshua, the psalmists.

Theological study: Harmon is a prominent mountain range in the north of the region, and Deuteronomy mentions it with different names among the neighboring peoples. The psalm uses it within the memory of distance and longing for God, and Psalm 133 likens its blessing to the dew of a hormone. The Bible does not designate the Mount of Transfiguration by name, so this connection should not be confirmed as a textual identification. Geography here serves poetry, political borders, and hope in a blessing that descends to the community.

entries.title: Hadsa
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Esther 5:2-11; 4:12-17; 7:1-10.

Place and context: Susa in the Persian Empire.

People associated with the text: Mordecai, Esther, Ahasuerus, Haman.

Theological Study: Hadassah is the Hebrew name mentioned in the Book of Esther for the girl known as Esther, Mordecai's adopted cousin. The narrative takes place in a Persian court and does not explicitly mention God's name, but the decisions, fasting, and risks craft a story of collective survival. The novel does not make Esther a fearless character; She asks for the support of her people before she enters the kingdom. The introduction combines identity in exile, political courage, and saving the group from extermination.

entries.title: Hermas
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Romans 16:14.

Place and context: Rome in greetings letter.

People associated with the text: Paul, Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas.

Theological study: Hermas appears in Romans' greetings among a group of brothers in Rome, and the New Testament does not provide any other details about his person. This is why it is not certainly valid to equate him with the later Christian author of “The Shepherd,” although there is a tradition that discusses this. The value of the reference is that it reveals that the Epistle to the Romans is linked to a real network of people, not to an abstract theological discussion. The limitations of the witness prevent us from building an imaginary biography around the name.

entries.title: Herodion
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Romans 16:11.

Place and context: Rome in greetings letter.

People associated with the text: Paul, the people of Narcissus, Herodion.

Theological study: Paul greets Herodion at the end of Romans and calls him his relative, a word that may refer to family or national kinship depending on the context. The name alone does not establish a definite connection to the House of Herod or a specific social location. However, the greetings reveal the breadth and diversity of the network of believers in Rome. The introduction teaches that responsible historical reading distinguishes between what the name states and what speculation suggests.

entries.title: Promise
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 12:1-3; 2 Samuel 8:7-16; Isaiah 55:1-5; Galatians 6:3-18.

Place and context: Canaan, Jerusalem, exile, and the churches of Galatia.

People associated with the text: Abraham, David, Isaiah, Paul.

Theological Study: The Promise in Scripture is God's initiative that establishes the covenant and opens a future for his people and for the nations. The promise to Abraham begins with land, descendants, and blessing, and then takes the form of a royal hope in the covenant of David. A promise does not equal unconditional possession or an exemption from justice; The prophets face betrayal within the people of promise. Paul reads the promise in Christ and the breadth of blessing to the nations without erasing the context of the Old Testament.

entries.title: Valley
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 14:17; 1 Samuel 17:1-3; Psalm 23:4; Ezekiel 37:1-14.

Place and context: Wadi Shuwa, Wadi Al-Butam, and Wadi Al-Ru’ya.

People associated with the text: David, Goliath, Ezekiel, the Psalmist.

Theological study: The valley in the book's geography is a low-lying stream that may be fertile in season or a military and dangerous passage. David and Goliath stand in the terebinth valley between two rows facing each other, while the psalm makes the valley an image of man's journey under God's care. Ezekiel sees the Valley of Bones in a vision that speaks of hope for the politically and spiritually dead Israel. The meaning of the valley changes with the type and context, so it is not limited to one negative symbol.

entries.title: Revelation
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Deuteronomy 15:18-22; Isaiah 1:1; Galatians 1:11-17; Revelation 1:1-3.

Place and context: Sinai, Judah, Damascus, and Patmos.

People associated with the text: Moses, Isaiah, Paul, John.

Theological study: Revelation in the book is God’s revelation that calls for obedience and discernment, not secret knowledge that grants its possessor unaccountable authority. Deuteronomy sets a test for the prophet, and Isaiah presents his vision against the reality of Judah. Paul describes his gospel as accepted by the revelation of Jesus Christ, while Revelation begins with the revelation of Jesus to his servant John. The introduction distinguishes between the authority of the biblical text and contemporary claims of revelation that need to be examined.

entries.title: Birth of Jesus
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Matthew 1:18-25; 2:1-12; Luke 1:26-38; 2:1-20.

Place and context: Nazareth and Bethlehem.

People associated with the text: Mary, Joseph, Gabriel, shepherds, Magi.

Theological Study: Matthew and Luke narrate the birth of Jesus with two different emphases that complete the picture of the incarnation within Israel's history. Matthew highlights Joseph, Bethlehem, the Magi, and the symbol of Emmanuel, while Luke highlights the Annunciation, Mary, the shepherds, and the hymn of glory. The two accounts do not provide details for every year of Jesus' childhood, and should not be filled with unstated traditions. Christmas declares that salvation comes in a body, a history, and a family under the power of the Empire.

entries.title: Feast
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 18:1-8; Isaiah 25:6-9; Luke 7:14-24; Revelation 19:6-9.

Place and context: Mamre, Jerusalem, and the Revelation of John.

People associated with the text: Abraham, Jesus, the called, John.

Theological study: The banquet in the Bible is a place of hospitality, joy, and covenant, and it may also become a place of exposing pride and exclusion. Abraham's tent receives guests with food, and Isaiah depicts a feast of hope for all peoples. In Luke, Jesus confronts the quest for the first seats and calls for the reception of those who cannot respond. The vision uses the wedding of the Lamb as an image of a fulfilled hope, not a closed social privilege.

entries.title: Commandments
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 20:1-17; Deuteronomy 6:4-9; Psalm 119:1-16; Matthew 22:34-40; John 14:15.

Place and context: Sinai, Moab, and Judea.

People associated with the text: Moses, Jesus, Pharisees, disciples.

Theological study: The commandments in the covenant are a framework for a liberated people’s relationship with God and their neighbor, and not a means to buy acceptance. The Ten Commandments begin by mentioning the Exodus, making obedience an answer to grace. Jesus summarizes the law in love for God and neighbor, and this summary does not isolate justice and mercy. His commandment to his disciples links love to memorizing the word, thus showing that discipleship is a faithful collective practice.

entries.title: Agent
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 15:2; Luke 12:35-48; 16:1-13; 1 Corinthians 4:1-2.

Place and context: Abram's house, Judaism, and Corinth.

People associated with the text: Abram, Jesus, the disciples, Paul.

Theological study: A steward is a person who manages a house or money that is not his own, and therefore his role is linked to honesty and accountability. Luke's parables use the image of the steward to address waiting on the master and the use of resources, and the parable of the unjust steward needs to be read as a warning against the worship of money, not as an endorsement of deception. Paul calls the apostles stewards of God's mysteries and asks them to be faithful. The entrance rejects the transformation of management into ownership or privilege into an exemption from accountability.

entries.title: Meekness
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Numbers 12:1-15; Psalm 37:1-11; Matthew 5:5; 11:28-30; Galatians 5:22-23.

Place and context: the wilderness, Galilee, and the churches of Galatia.

People associated with the text: Moses, Jesus, disciples, Paul.

Theological study: Meekness is not weakness or silence in the face of injustice, but rather a disciplined strength that relies on God. Verse describes Moses in a family dispute, and the psalm places the meek within the hope of divine justice. Jesus calls the meek blessed and describes himself as meek and lowly in heart. Then Paul mentions meekness among the fruits of the Spirit. Therefore, meekness is associated with truth, patience, and reform, not with surrender to abuse.

entries.title: Fig leaf
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 3:1-21; Mark 12:11-14; 20-25.

Place and context: The Garden of Eden and the road to Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: Adam, Eve, Jesus, disciples.

Theological study: Adam and Eve make themselves aprons of fig leaves after realizing their nakedness, thus showing shame and trying to cover up after disobedience. The paper text does not offer a cure for guilt; God confronts them with the consequences of their actions and covers them. The scene of the fig tree in Mark differs in type and context, as it occurs within a prophetic act linked to the temple and does not explain the story of Eden. The introduction refuses to connect the two texts with an automatic symbolic reading that goes beyond their differences.

entries.title: Jesus
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Matthew 1:18-25; Mark 8:27-38; John 1:1-18; Philippians 2:5-11.

Place and context: Nazareth, Galilee, Jerusalem, and the churches of Philippi.

People associated with the text: Mary, Joseph, John the Baptist, the disciples, Paul.

Theological study: Jesus is the focus of the Gospels and the testimony of the Apostles, and his name appears in Matthew in connection with the salvation of his people from their sins. The Gospels reveal his ministry of teaching, healing, table, and cross, and do not separate his messianic identity from the path of suffering. John declares that the Word became flesh, and Philippians describes his humiliation and exaltation. The entry reads these witnesses together without reducing Jesus to a moral teacher or abstract religious symbol.

entries.title: John the Baptist
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Isaiah 40:3; Malachi 3:1; Matthew 3:1-17; Mark 1:1-11; John 3:22-36.

Place and context: The Judean wilderness and the Jordan River.

People associated with the text: Zechariah, Elizabeth, Jesus, Herod Antipas.

Theological study: John the Baptist is a prophet calling Israel to repentance and baptism in the wilderness, and the Gospels present his ministry as preparation for the way of the Lord. Jesus baptizes, but he does not equate him with himself, but rather points to the stronger coming. He criticizes Herod and pays for it with his life. This does not make his testimony a worthless introductory stage; It places repentance, justice, and waiting for Christ at the heart of the story.

entries.title: Jacob
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 25:19-34; 27:1-45; 28:10-22; 32:22-32; 35:9-15.

Place and Context: Beersheba, Haran, Paddan-aram, and Canaan.

People Related to the Text: Isaac, Rebekah, Esau, Laban, Rachel.

Theological Study: Jacob, son of Isaac and Rebekah, moves the story between promise, deception, flight, and return. His choice within the lineage does not grant immunity for his actions; his deception of Esau and Isaac returns to him in Laban's house. In Paddan-aram, he receives the name Israel after a mysterious struggle that leaves him limping and blessed. The introduction links the covenant with personal transformation and complex family history, not with inherited moral superiority.

entries.title: Joseph
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Genesis 37:1-36; 39:1-23; 45:1-15; 50:15-26.

Place and Context: Canaan and Egypt.

People Related to the Text: Jacob, his brothers, Potiphar's wife, Pharaoh.

Theological Study: The story of Joseph narrates his transition from the favored son to a servant and prisoner, then to a person of responsibility in Egypt. Joseph's statement about God's intention does not cancel out the evil done by his brothers or the weakness of the authority structures in the palace and prison. The story reaches its peak in the revelation of identity, reconciliation, and securing life during the famine. Divine providence is shown working within responsible human decisions, not as a reason to justify injustice or to wait for salvation without action.

entries.title: Jonah
entries.content:
Key references: Jonah 1:1-17; 3:1-10; 4:1-11; Matthew 12:38-41.

Place and context: Jaffa, the sea, and Nineveh.

People related to the text: Jonah, the sailors, the king of Nineveh, the people of the city.

Theological study: God sends Jonah to Nineveh, but the prophet flees and then finally arrives at a city that repents. The story is not only about the whale; the conclusion confronts Jonah's anger at God's mercy toward the enemies of his people. The book places mercy and justice together, as it declares a potential judgment that the city responds to with repentance. Jesus uses Jonah as a sign for his generation, while preserving the critical tone of the book regarding the prophet's national limitations.

entries.title: Joshua
entries.content:
Background Evidence: Numbers 15:27-23; Joshua 1:1-9; 1:6-27; 1:24-28. 

Location and context: The plains of Moab, Jericho, and Shechem. 

People associated with the text: Moses, Rahab, Caleb, the tribes of Israel. 

Theological Study: Joshua succeeds Moses in leading Israel to the land, and his book combines the promises of the land, difficult wars, and renewed covenants. The text does not provide all the details of modern military history, nor does it allow it to be used to justify contemporary settler violence. Rahab and the Gibeonites show the complexity of the borders within the narrative itself. In Shechem, Joshua renews the covenant, making the worship of God and the rejection of idols the center of the people's identity, not the control of the land alone.

entries.title: Judas
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 29:31-35; 49:8-12; 2 Samuel 5:1-5; Matthew 1:1-6; Revelation 5:1-5.

Place and Context: Canaan, Jerusalem, and New Testament communities.

Persons Related to the Text: Jacob, Judah son of Jacob, David, Jesus.

Theological Study: Judah is the name of Jacob's son, a tribe, and a later southern kingdom; therefore, its meaning changes according to context. Jacob's blessing gives the tribe a leadership role, then David and his lineage are associated with Jerusalem. Matthew uses the genealogy to trace Jesus back to the promised history, and Revelation evokes the lion of the tribe of Judah in the scene of the slain Lamb. This does not turn the tribal identity into an ethnic privilege, but places it within a story of covenant and responsibility.

entries.title: The Lord's Day
entries.content:
Background evidence: Joel 1:2-32; Amos 18:5-24; Zephaniah 7:1-18; 1 Thessalonians 1:5-11; 2 Peter 8:3-13. 

Place and context: Judah, Israel, and the Churches of Thessalonica. 

People associated with the text: Joel, Amos, Zephaniah, Paul, Peter. 

Theological Study: The Lord's Day is a prophetic language about God's intervention in judgment and salvation, and is not limited to a calculable timeline. Amos shocks those who wait for the day as a national privilege as injustice continues, while Joel opens the door to repentance and pouring out the Spirit. Paul calls the Church of Thessalonica to awaken and console, and Peter places waiting within a holy life. The entrance combines fear, hope, and responsibility rather than calculational excitement.

entries.title: Hand of God
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 13:3; Ezra 7:6-10; Psalm 118:15-16; John 10:27-30; Acts 11:19-24.

Place and Context: Egypt, Jerusalem, Galilee, and Antioch.

People associated with the text: Moses, Ezra, Jesus, Barnabas.

Theological Study: The hand of God is a metaphorical expression of His power, protection, and work in history, and the scripture does not depict a limited body for God. The Torah mentions the strong hand in Exodus, and Ezra sees the hand of his good God in the success of his journey and his reforms. John uses the hand of the Father and the Son in the language of the safety of the flock, while Acts describes the hand of the Lord with the missionaries in Antioch. The expression of divine care is connected to the call to obedience and witness.

entries.title: Jairus
entries.content:
Key References: Mark 5:21-43; Luke 8:40-56.

Location and Context: Capernaum or the vicinity of the Sea of Galilee.

People Related to the Text: Jairus, his daughter, the woman with the bleeding, Jesus, Peter.

Theological Study: Jairus, a synagogue leader, seeks Jesus' healing for his dying daughter, and his story interweaves with the healing of the woman with the bleeding. Mark does not allow religious status to be a barrier to humble request, nor does he depict Jesus' delay as ignoring the suffering of the family. Jesus calls the father to faith in the midst of news of death, then restores the girl to her family. The narrative connects faith with fear, bodily compassion, and the restoration of family life.

entries.title: Jaffa
entries.content:
Key References: Joshua 19:40-48; Jonah 1:1-3; Acts 9:36-43; 10:1-23.

Location and Context: The Mediterranean coast west of Jerusalem.

People Related to the Text: Jonah, Peter, Tabitha, Cornelius.

Theological Study: Jaffa is a port on the Mediterranean coast appearing on the border of the tribe of Dan, from which Jonah departs fleeing his mission to Nineveh. In Acts, Peter stays at a tanner's after the resurrection of Tabitha, where the vision occurs that leads him to the house of Cornelius. The location combines fleeing from the calling and the expansion of witness to the nations, without making the city itself the holder of religious power. Hospitality, work, and the sea remain a tangible backdrop for the transformation of the message.

entries.title: Jeremiah
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Jeremiah 1:4-19; 7:1-15; 31:31-34; 36:1-32; 52:1-34.

Place and Context: Anathoth, Jerusalem, and Egypt.

Persons related to the text: Josiah, Baruch, Zedekiah, the people of Judah.

Theological Study: Jeremiah is called to prophetic service in the late period of Judah before and after the fall of Jerusalem, confronting false confidence in the temple and misleading political alliances. The book does not portray the prophet as a person without fear or objection; he weeps, argues, and faces persecution. It promises a new covenant written on the heart within the context of destruction and exile. His prophecy preserves both judgment and hope, resisting the reduction of the covenant to an inward experience without collective justice.

entries.title: Isaiah
entries.content:
Background evidence: Isaiah 1:6-13; 9:1-7; 40:1-11; 52:13-53:12; 58:1-12. 

Place and context: Jerusalem, Judah, and the prospects of exile. 

People associated with the text: Isaiah, Uzziah, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Abd al-Rab. 

Theological Study: The book of Isaiah combines Judas' judgment, visions of the kingdom, consolation of the exiles, and a call to practical justice. The vision of the temple begins with the proclamation of God's holiness and the sending of the prophet, and later books address political fear, messianic hope, and the return of the people. The breadth of the book does not allow it to flatten its voice into prophecies that are out of context. The Gospels receive some of his texts in the light of Jesus, while his original message of worship, justice, and hope remains essential.

entries.title: Snake
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 3:1-15; Numbers 21:4-9; John 3:14-15; Revelation 12:9.

Place and Context: Eden, the wilderness, and Revelation.

Persons Related to the Text: Adam, Eve, Moses, Jesus, John.

Theological Study: The serpent in Eden is associated with deception and questioning trust in God’s word, while the bronze serpent in the wilderness becomes a sign of healing by God’s command. John reads the lifting of the serpent in light of the cross, and Revelation restores the image of the ancient serpent within its symbolic struggle against God’s people.

entries.title: Bronze Serpent
entries.content:
Key references: Numbers 21:4-9; 2 Kings 18:4; John 3:14-15.

Place and context: The wilderness of wandering and Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: Moses, the Israelites, Hezekiah, Jesus.

Theological study: The bronze serpent illustrates the difference between a sign that leads to God's mercy and something that becomes an idol. Hezekiah smashed it when it became a subject of incense, while John uses the event to understand the lifting up of the Son of Man without re-sanctifying the object itself.

entries.title: The price of blood
entries.content:
Key References: Zechariah 11:12-13; Matthew 26:14-16; 27:3-10; Acts 1:18-19.

Place and Context: Jerusalem during Holy Week.

People Related to the Text: Judas Iscariot, the chief priests, Jesus, Peter.

Theological Study: The price of blood is an expression connected to the money of betrayal and the tragedy of Jesus’ betrayal. The Gospels do not attribute guilt to an ethnic group, but present a specific collusion between Judas and the religious leaders and authority, and reveal that money cannot atone for the death of an innocent person.

entries.title: Thirty pieces of silver
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 21:32; Zechariah 11:12-13; Matthew 26:15; 27:9-10.

Place and Context: Jerusalem and the Temple.

Persons Associated with the Text: Judas Iscariot, the chief priests, Matthew.

Theological Study: The thirty pieces of silver carry a compensatory value in the law, then Zechariah uses it in a symbolic scene about the rejection of the shepherd. Matthew links this amount to the betrayal of Jesus, highlighting the contrast between the insignificant value placed by humans and the innocence of Christ and the weight of the salvific event.

entries.title: Weight of Glory
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 40:34-38; 2 Corinthians 4:16-18; 1 Peter 5:10.

Place and Context: The Tabernacle and the churches of Corinth and Asia Minor.

People Associated with the Text: Moses, Paul, Peter.

Theological Study: The weight of glory in Paul's language places present suffering before an eternal hope that neither cancels nor trivializes it. The expression evokes the backdrop of divine glory in the Old Testament, but it directs believers toward inner renewal and faithfulness amid weakness.

entries.title: Sin
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 4:7; Psalm 51; Romans 3:21-26; 1 John 1:8-10.

Place and Context: Eden and the worship of Israel and the New Testament churches.

People Related to the Text: Cain, David, Paul, John.

Theological Study: Sin in Scripture is not just a legal fault, but a breaking of relationship and a distortion of justice and worship. The Psalms provide the language of confession, Paul explains the universality of the problem and the grace of justification, while John rejects the denial of sin or despair over forgiveness.

entries.title: Khemir
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 12:14-20; Matthew 13:33; 16:5-12; 1 Corinthians 5:6-8.

Place and Context: Egypt, Galilee, and Corinth.

People Related to the Text: Moses, Jesus, the disciples, Paul.

Theological Study: Yeast changes its meaning according to the context; in the Passover it recalls the haste of the Exodus and the purity of the community, and in the Parable of the Kingdom, it becomes an image of hidden spread. Therefore, the introduction teaches that the biblical symbol is not interpreted outside its text and function.

entries.title: Hope
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 130:5-8; Jeremiah 29:11; Romans 5:1-5; 1 Peter 1:3-9.

Place and Context: Israel and the exile, and the churches of Rome and Asia Minor.

Persons Connected to the Text: The psalmist, Jeremiah, Paul, Peter.

Theological Study: Biblical hope is not general optimism, but an expectation founded on the faithfulness of God. In exile, hope does not mean denying devastation, and in the New Testament, it is based on the resurrection of Christ, which creates patience and love amid trials.

entries.title: Shepherd
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34:1-16; John 10:1-18; 1 Peter 5:1-4.

Place and Context: The pastures of Israel, Judaism, and the churches.

People Related to the Text: David, Ezekiel, Jesus, Peter.

Theological Study: The shepherd is a symbol of leadership that feeds, protects, and seeks the lost. Ezekiel condemns exploitative shepherds, and John proclaims Jesus as the good shepherd who lays down his life, showing that leadership is measured by service, not possession.

entries.title: Shepherds
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 46:31-34; Luke 2:8-20; Ephesians 4:11-13.

Place and Context: Egypt, Bethlehem, and the churches.

People Associated with the Text: Jacob and his sons, the shepherds, angels, Paul.

Theological Study: The shepherds appear in the old economy and in the nativity story as the first hearers of the message in Luke. The text does not make their simplicity a romantic virtue, but rather reveals that God's revelation reaches those working on the margins just as it reaches the leaders.

entries.title: Robe
entries.content:
Essential evidence: 1 Kings 19:19-21; Mark 46:10-52; Luke 15:22. 

Place and context: Apple Converter, Jericho and Father's House. 

People associated with the text: Elijah, Elisha, Bartimaeus, the prodigal son. 

Theological Study: The robe in the Bible may proclaim a calling, dignity, or abandonment of the old life. The robe of Elijah touches the call of Elisha, the Bartimaeus throws it out to follow Jesus, and the returning son puts on the robe of restoration.

entries.title: ash
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 18:27; Job 42:6; Jonah 3:6; Matthew 11:21.

Place and Context: Mamre, Nineveh, and Galilee.

People Associated with the Text: Abraham, Job, the King of Nineveh, Jesus.

Theological Study: Ashes remind of human fragility and serve as a sign of repentance in certain contexts. The Bible does not make ashes an automatic ritual, but links it to the breaking of the heart, returning to God, and rejecting pride.

entries.title: Sand
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 22:17; 32:12; Hosea 1:10; Hebrews 11:12.

Location and Context: The seashore and the memory of the fathers.

People Related to the Text: Abraham, Jacob, Hosea, the author of Hebrews.

Theological Study: Sand is a symbol of the countless multitude in God's promise to the fathers. The image does not function as a literal count, but as poetic language about God's faithfulness and the vastness of offspring and blessing.

entries.title: Rock
entries.content:
Essential evidences: Exodus 1:1-7; Psalm 2:18; Matthew 24:7-27; 1 Corinthians 4:10. 

Place and context: wilderness, images of wisdom and community. 

People associated with the text: Moses, David, Jesus, Paul. 

Theological Study: In the Bible, the rock is a place of water, protection, and an image of immortality. The image does not sanctify matter, but rather refers to God's faithfulness, and Jesus makes building on the rock a practical obedience to His Word rather than an abstract hearing.

entries.title: Images
entries.content:
Key References: 1 Kings 5:1-12; Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26-28; Mark 7:24-30.

Place and Context: The Phoenician coast and trade routes.

Persons Related to the Text: Hiram, Solomon, Ezekiel, Jesus, the Syrian Phoenician woman.

Theological Study: It depicts a major coastal city combining trade, alliances, and prophetic critique of economic pride. The appearance of Jesus in its areas opens the scene of mercy to the nations without erasing the prophetic warning against haughty wealth.

entries.title: Sidon
entries.content:
Key References: Joshua 11:8; 1 Kings 17:8-24; Matthew 15:21-28; Acts 27:3.

Place and Context: The Phoenician coast and Sidon.

Persons Associated with the Text: Elijah, the widow, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Sidon appears in the geography of the nations and the coast, with its subordinate city, Zarephath, highlighted in the story of the widow who welcomed Elijah. The Gospels recall this horizon when Jesus speaks of mercy and faith beyond the borders of Israel.

entries.title: Zephaniah
entries.category: Prophecy and the Day of the Lord
entries.content:
Key Passages: Zephaniah 1:1-18; 2:1-3; 3:14-20.

Place and Context: Judah during the days of Josiah.

Persons Related to the Text: Zephaniah, Josiah, the people of Judah.

Theological Study: Zephaniah announces the Day of the Lord as a near judgment and hope for the humble remnant. The book does not use the day to provoke temporal fear, but to confront pride and injustice and to open the door to seek the Lord before the judgment comes.

entries.title: Sincere
entries.content:
Essential evidences: Genesis 9:6; Proverbs 25:10; Habakkuk 4:2; Romans 1:17. 

Place and context: The world of Noah, Judas, and the Church of Rome. 

People associated with the text: Noah, Habakkuk, Paul. 

Theological Study: The righteous or righteous in the Bible lives in a relationship of faithfulness rather than transcendent self-perfection. Habakkuk uses the phrase in the midst of political turmoil, and Paul reads the text in the Gospel's declaration of God's righteousness.

entries.title: Peace
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 33:1-11; Matthew 5:9; Romans 5:1-11; Ephesians 2:13-18.

Place and Context: Penuel and Galilee, and the churches in Rome and Ephesus.

Persons Related to the Text: Jacob, Esau, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Reconciliation in the Bible is not a cover-up of evil, but a movement to restore a relationship based on truth and grace. The reconciliation of Jacob and Esau reveals the fragility of the encounter, and Paul makes the peace of Christ the foundation for a new community that transcends enmity.

entries.title: Patience
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 37:7; Luke 21:19; Romans 5:3-5; James 5:7-11.

Place and Context: Israel, Judaism, and the churches of the New Testament.

People Associated with the Text: David, Jesus, Paul, James.

Theological Study: Biblical patience is faithful endurance rather than passive acceptance of injustice. It arises from hope in God’s work and calls for perseverance, prayer, and good deeds while the believer awaits the fulfillment of justice.

entries.title: crying out
entries.content:
Main References: Exodus 2:23-25; Psalm 22:1-5; Mark 10:46-52; Revelation 6:9-11.

Place and Context: Egypt, the Psalms, Jericho, and Revelation.

People Related to the Text: The Israelites, David, Bartimaeus, the martyrs.

Theological Study: Crying out in Scripture is the language of pain and seeking justice, not of lack of faith. God hears the cries of the oppressed, the psalm allows for a suffering prayer, and Bartimaeus' cry becomes a path to mercy despite people's attempts to silence him.

entries.title: Astonishment
entries.content:
Key References: Joshua 19:41; Judges 13:2-25; 16:31.

Place and Context: The land of Dan in the Shephelah.

Persons associated with the text: Manoah, Manoah's wife, Samson.

Theological Study: The setting of Samson's home in the Book of Judges, linking his birth to a Nazarite calling amid Philistine pressure. The importance of the place is not only geographical but also reveals the beginning of a story of great strength that will remain dependent on obedience and self-control.

entries.title: Hunting
entries.content:
Key References: Ezekiel 47:10; Matthew 4:18-22; Luke 5:1-11; John 21:1-14.

Place and Context: Sea of Galilee and the waters of prophetic vision.

Persons Associated with the Text: Peter, Andrew, James, John, Jesus.

Theological Study: Fishing, as a daily profession, becomes in the Gospels the backdrop for the calling of the disciples. Jesus does not cancel their work but redirects their lives toward a mission, and the miracle in John 21 reveals that fruitful service depends on the word of Christ and His presence.

entries.title: Fishermen
entries.content:
Key passages: Mark 1:16-20; Luke 5:1-11; John 21:1-14.

Place and context: Sea of Galilee.

Persons associated with the text: Peter, Andrew, James, John, Jesus.

Theological study: The first fishermen in the Gospels are not just symbols of poverty, but workers within a real maritime economy. Their calling reveals that discipleship changes the direction of work and relationships, without erasing their expertise but rather putting it to use for testimony.

entries.title: Soffer
entries.content:
Key References: Job 2:11; 11; 20; 42:7-9.

Location and Context: The land of Uz and the assembly of Job’s friends.

Persons Associated with the Text: Job, Eliphaz, Bildad, Zophar.

Theological Study: Zophar is one of Job’s friends, and his words represent a stream that rushes to interpret suffering as punishment. The conclusion of the book rejects the sufficiency of this reasoning, teaching the careful reader to be cautious about instructing the suffering with systems that are outwardly correct but practically harsh.

entries.title: Peacemakers
entries.content:
Key References: Matthew 5:9; Romans 12:18; James 3:17-18.

Place and Context: Galilee and the churches of the New Covenant.

Persons associated with the text: Jesus, Paul, James.

Theological Study: The peacemakers in the Beatitudes are not equal to passive pacifists, but rather those who work to restore justice and relationship. Biblical peace goes beyond the absence of conflict to goodness that resists revenge and enmity.

entries.title: Fasting
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Isaiah 58:3-12; Matthew 6:16-18; Acts 13:1-3.

Place and Context: Judea, Galilee, and Antioch.

Persons Related to the Text: Isaiah, Jesus, Barnabas, Paul.

Theological Study: Fasting is a practice of repentance and discernment, but it is not acceptable when it covers up injustice. Isaiah rejects a fast that neglects restraints and hunger, and Jesus teaches that fasting is directed to the Father, not for human praise.

entries.title: Prayer
entries.content:
Key References: 1 Samuel 1:9-18; Matthew 6:5-15; Philippians 4:4-7.

Place and Context: Shiloh and Galilee, and the church of Philippi.

People Related to the Text: Hannah, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Prayer in the Bible involves a relationship that encompasses complaint, request, thanksgiving, and obedience. It does not work as a technique to pressure God, but rather as a formation of the heart and the community before the name of the Father and His kingdom.

entries.title: Cross
entries.content:
Key References: Mark 8:34-35; 15:21-39; 1 Corinthians 1:18-25; Galatians 6:14.

Place and Context: Jerusalem, Golgotha, and Corinth.

People Related to the Text: Jesus, Simon of Cyrene, Paul.

Theological Study: The cross, a Roman execution tool, becomes in the Gospel a place for declaring God's wisdom. Carrying the cross does not justify imposing suffering on others, but calls for following Christ in love and self-giving.

entries.title: Almsgiving
entries.content:
Key References: Deuteronomy 15:7-11; Matthew 6:1-4; Luke 19:1-10; 2 Corinthians 8:1-15.

Place and Context: Israel, Galilee, Jericho, and Corinth.

People Associated with the Text: Moses, Jesus, Zacchaeus, Paul.

Theological Study: Charity is giving that preserves the dignity of the needy and does not buy reputation or God's favor. Zacchaeus shows that repentance touches money and restitution, and Paul calls for giving that builds equality and mutual care.

entries.title: Sadducees
entries.content:
Key references: Matthew 22:23-33; Acts 23:6-10.

Location and context: Jerusalem and the Sanhedrin council.

Persons related to the text: Jesus, the Sadducees, the Pharisees, Paul.

Theological study: The Sadducees were a Jewish group connected to the priestly leadership in Jerusalem, and the New Testament presents them particularly in discussions about the resurrection. They should not be turned into a caricature or considered representative of all Judaism.

entries.title: The voice of the Lord
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 19:16-19; Psalm 29; John 5:24-29; Revelation 1:10-18.

Place and Context: Sinai, the Temple, and Patmos.

Persons Related to the Text: Moses, the Psalmist, Jesus, John.

Theological Study: The voice of the Lord is an image of the authority of the Word in creation, covenant, and judgment. The voice is not limited to an auditory phenomenon but points to a revelation that seeks to be heard and obeyed and gives life.

entries.title: Image of God
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 1:26-28; 9:6; Colossians 1:15; James 3:9.

Place and Context: Eden, the world, and the churches.

Persons Associated with the Text: Adam and Eve, Noah, Paul, James.

Theological Study: The image of God establishes human dignity and responsibility in creation and does not grant humans the right to exploit. The New Testament links the image to Christ and to controlling the tongue toward the neighbor, who is created in God’s likeness.

entries.title: Stumbling Block
entries.content:
Key References: Isaiah 8:14; Romans 9:30-33; 1 Peter 2:6-8.

Place and Context: Judea and the churches of Rome and Asia Minor.

People Associated with the Text: Isaiah, Paul, Peter.

Theological Study: The stumbling stone combines both steadfastness and danger depending on a person's attitude toward the word of God. Paul and Peter recall Isaiah to explain the acceptance and rejection of Christ, without turning the text into contempt for Israel or a justification for superiority.

entries.title: Truthful
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 15; Zechariah 8:16-17; Ephesians 4:25.

Place and Context: Zion, Jerusalem, and the churches.

Persons Associated with the Text: David, Zechariah, Paul.

Theological Study: Truthfulness in Scripture is a covenantal practice that preserves both the neighbor and the community, not merely an individual virtue. Zechariah links truthful speech to the peace of the city, and Paul urges speaking the truth because believers are members of one another.

entries.title: Silence
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 39:1-9; Isaiah 53:7; Mark 14:60-61; James 1:19.

Place and Context: The temple, the court, and diaspora communities.

Persons Associated with the Text: David, the servant of the Lord, Jesus, James.

Theological Study: Silence may be wisdom in the face of evil, deep pain, or refraining from a futile defense. The Scripture does not call to silence the oppressed, but distinguishes between silence that relies on God and silence imposed by an unjust authority.

entries.title: The Firstborn Strike
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 11:1-10; 12:29-32; Psalm 78:51; Hebrews 11:28.

Place and Context: Egypt on the night of Passover.

Persons Related to the Text: Moses, Aaron, Pharaoh, the Israelites.

Theological Study: The death of the firstborn is the culmination of the confrontation with Pharaoh in Exodus, and comes after a series of warnings and repeated refusals. The text connects judgment with the liberation of the enslaved and with Passover, so it should not be read as violence separate from the context of slavery, warning, and covenant.

entries.title: Adam's rib
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Genesis 2:18-25; Ephesians 5:28-33.

Place and Context: The Garden of Eden and Paul's reading on marriage.

People related to the text: Adam, Eve, Paul.

Theological Study: Adam's rib in Genesis 2 serves the narrative of creating woman as a suitable partner, not as an arrangement of contempt or possession. Paul uses the language of one body in teaching about marriage, and it should be read in light of self-giving love, not control.

entries.title: Sheep
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 4:2-4; Exodus 12:3-6; Psalm 23; John 10:1-18.

Place and Context: Pastures, houses of Passover, and Galilee.

Persons Related to the Text: Abel, Moses, David, Jesus.

Theological Study: The sheep are part of the economy of grazing and sacrifices, then become an image of the people in need of care. The texts combine daily provision, worship, and leadership, and they measure the shepherd by his protection of the flock, not by his benefit from it.

entries.title: Narrow Gate
entries.content:
Key References: Matthew 7:13-14; Luke 13:22-30.

Place and Context: Galilee and Judea in Jesus' teaching.

People Associated with the Text: Jesus, the disciples, the listeners.

Theological Study: The narrow gate in Jesus' teaching does not advocate an elitist attitude, but rather calls for serious discipleship that is not satisfied with mere outward affiliation. The text links entry to the response to Christ's word and living in righteousness.

entries.title: Very Narrow
entries.content:
Key References: Daniel 12:1; Matthew 24:21-31; Revelation 7:13-17.

Place and Context: Judaism and Revelation.

People Associated with the Text: Daniel, Jesus, John the Revelator.

Theological Study: The great tribulation is language referring to an extreme crisis in the horizon of judgment and hope. Do not use the texts to incite time calculations, but rather to encourage perseverance, discernment of evil, and reliance on God who preserves His people.

entries.title: The Lost Son
entries.content:
Key References: Luke 15:11-32.

Place and Context: The father's house in Jesus' parable.

People Related to the Text: Jesus, the younger son, the older son, the father.

Theological Study: The son's loss in Luke 15 is not only a spatial dimension but a severing of relationship and dignity. The parable expands the meaning of loss to include the older son who is close to the house, revealing the father's mercy and his call to rejoice in reconciliation.

entries.title: The Deception of False Prophets
entries.content:
Key References: Deuteronomy 13:1-5; Jeremiah 23:16-32; Matthew 7:15-20; 2 Peter 2:1-3.

Place and Context: Israel, Judaism, and the churches.

People Related to the Text: Moses, Jeremiah, Jesus, Peter.
