Theological Study: Prophetic deception is not measured solely by religious form but by the fruit of teaching and its faithfulness to God and justice. The texts warn against speech that falsely reassures people or exploits them and call for collective discernment rather than blind doubt.

entries.title: Self-control
entries.content:
Key References: Proverbs 25:28; Galatians 5:22-23; 2 Peter 1:5-8.

Place and Context: The wisdom of Israel and the churches of Galatia and Asia.

People Related to the Text: The wise, Paul, Peter.

Theological Study: Self-control in Scripture is not repression without grace, but a fruit of the Spirit and wisdom that protects a person from the slavery of desire and anger. It is connected to true freedom that serves love, not to proving moral superiority.

entries.title: Promise Guarantee
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Genesis 15:1-6; 2 Corinthians 1:20-22; Ephesians 1:13-14; Hebrews 6:13-20.

Place and Context: Canaan and the churches of the New Covenant.

Persons Associated with the Text: Abraham, Paul, the author of Hebrews.

Theological Study: The assurance of the promise appears in God's faithfulness, which does not depend on human ability to secure the future. Paul uses the language of pledge and seal about the Spirit, linking hope to new life rather than anxious possession.

entries.title: Molar
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 21:23-25; Proverbs 25:19; Matthew 5:38-42.

Place and Context: Ancient Israel and Galilee.

Persons Related to the Text: Moses, the wise men, Jesus.

Theological Study: The tooth or eye appears in the law of retaliation to regulate vengeance, not to unleash it. Jesus redirects the audience away from the logic of personal revenge, placing justice within the horizon of mercy and not responding to evil with evil.

entries.title: blow
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 9:14; 2 Samuel 24:15-17; Acts 12:21-23.

Place and Context: Egypt, Jerusalem, and Caesarea.

Persons Associated with the Text: Pharaoh, David, Herod, the angel of the Lord.

Theological Study: The strike in the Scripture may indicate judgment, a plague, or divine intervention, and it should not be generalized to every illness or disaster. Each account requires its moral and historical context, with a rejection of gloating or claiming to know all of God's hidden purposes.

entries.title: Victim
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 22:21-24; Psalm 10; Luke 10:30-37; James 5:1-6.

Place and Context: Israel, the road to Jericho, and the churches of the diaspora.

People Associated with the Text: the stranger, the orphan, the Samaritan, James.

Theological Study: The victim in the Scripture is not the object of fleeting pity, but a person seeking God's justice. The law, psalms, and parables reveal that true worship is shown in protecting the harmed and restoring justice, not in blaming them or silencing their voice.

entries.title: Hatred
entries.content:
Key References: Leviticus 19:17-18; Proverbs 10:12; Matthew 5:21-26; Ephesians 4:31-32.

Place and Context: Israel, Galilee, and the churches of Ephesus.

People Associated with the Text: Moses, the wise men, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Hatred severs the relationship with a neighbor even before it manifests in an outward act. The Scriptures call for confronting wrongdoing, forgiving, and seeking reconciliation, not for burying hatred under formal religiosity.

entries.title: Noise
entries.content:
Key References: Amos 5:21-24; 1 Corinthians 13:1; Revelation 19:6.

Place and Context: Israel, Corinth, and Revelation.

People Related to the Text: Amos, Paul, John.

Theological Study: Noise can be the sound of worship that is rejected when separated from justice, and it can become in Revelation the sound of a crowd praising God. The context distinguishes between an empty sound that covers injustice and a joyful sound that proclaims the reign of the Lord.

entries.title: Loss of the sheep
entries.content:
Key References: Ezekiel 34:11-16; Matthew 18:10-14; Luke 15:3-7.

Place and Context: The pastures of Israel and the teaching of Jesus.

Persons Related to the Text: Ezekiel, Jesus, the disciples.

Theological Study: The lost sheep is an image of loss of protection and direction, and the scripture places the responsibility of searching on the shepherd rather than blaming the weak alone. In Jesus' teaching, finding the lost becomes a cause for joy and a measure of the Father's heart.

entries.title: The weak
entries.content:
Key Passages: Romans 14:1-15:7; 1 Corinthians 8:7-13; 1 Thessalonians 5:14.

Place and Context: Rome, Corinth, and Thessalonica.

Persons Related to the Text: Paul, Christian communities.

Theological Study: The weak in Paul's letters are not objects of contempt, but brothers to be received and built up. Paul limits the freedom of the strong when it harms conscience, making love the standard of knowledge and practice.

entries.title: Necessity
entries.content:
Background evidence: Luke 24:25-27; Acts 9:15-16; 1 Corinthians 9:16. 

Place and context: Jerusalem, Damascus, and Corinth. 

People associated with the text: Jesus, Paul, the disciples. 

Theological study: Necessity in the Apostolic Texts does not imply an irresponsible fatalism, but rather an awareness of God's purpose in the way of Christ and the mission. Paul associates the necessity of evangelization with the grace to which he is called, not to personal glory.

entries.title: Laughter
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 18:9-15; 21:1-7; Luke 6:21.

Place and Context: Corridor and the house of Abraham and Galilee.

People Associated with the Text: Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, Jesus.

Theological Study: Laughter in Sarah's story combines doubt and amazement, then joy at the birth of Isaac. The text does not condemn all laughter but reveals the promise's ability to turn impossibility into joy, while Luke places laughter in the horizon of the reversal of the kingdom.

entries.title: Assurance
entries.content:
Key References: 2 Timothy 1:12-14; 1 Peter 4:19.

Place and Context: The apostolic churches.

Persons Related to the Text: Paul, Timothy, Peter.

Theological Study: The guarantee or deposit in the letters refers to what God preserves and what the servant is entrusted with regarding teaching and life. It does not give its owner the authority to possess the truth, but rather calls him to preserve it with spirit and faithfulness amid suffering.

entries.title: Doctor
entries.content:
Key References: Jeremiah 8:22; Mark 2:17; Luke 4:23; Colossians 4:14.

Place and Context: Gilead, Galilee, and the churches.

People Associated with the Text: Jeremiah, Jesus, Luke, Paul.

Theological Study: The doctor appears in the book in connection with the question of physical and spiritual healing. Jesus declares that he came for the sick, not for the healthy, and this does not imply contempt for medicine but rather reveals the sinners' need for mercy that heals the relationship with God and neighbor.

entries.title: Greed
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 20:17; Luke 12:13-21; Colossians 3:5; Hebrews 13:5.

Place and Context: Sinai, Galilee, and the churches.

Persons Related to the Text: Moses, Jesus, Paul, the writer of Hebrews.

Theological Study: Greed is a desire that seizes the heart and turns the neighbor into a means. Jesus places the parable of the rich fool against reliance on stores, and the epistles connect greed with false worship because it gives money the place of God.

entries.title: Taher
entries.content:
Key References: Leviticus 11; Psalm 51:10; Matthew 5:8; Titus 1:15.

Place and Context: The tabernacle, Galilee, and the churches.

Persons Related to the Text: Moses, David, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: The term 'pure' in the Scriptures may refer to a ritual state or a pure heart depending on the context. Purity should not be confused with social contempt, because Jesus and the apostles redirect the discussion toward the heart, mercy, and communal life.

entries.title: Long-suffering
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 34:6; Romans 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9.

Location and Context: Sinai, Rome, and the churches.

Persons Related to the Text: Moses, Paul, Peter.

Theological Study: The long-suffering of God means His patience that opens the door to repentance, not tolerance of evil. The epistles rely on this attribute to interpret the delay of judgment as mercy that calls for practical return.

entries.title: Child
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 2:1-10; Mark 10:13-16; Matthew 18:1-6.

Place and Context: Egypt, Galilee, and Judea.

Persons Related to the Text: Baby Moses, Jesus, the disciples, children.

Theological Study: The child in the Scripture is not a socially marginal, worthless figure; God protects Moses as an infant, and Jesus receives children and makes them a sign of welcoming the kingdom. Therefore, the text warns against causing the little ones to stumble or misusing them for power.

entries.title: Childhood of Jesus
entries.content:
Key References: Matthew 2:13-23; Luke 2:21-52.

Place and Context: Bethlehem, Egypt, Nazareth, and Jerusalem.

People Associated with the Text: Mary, Joseph, Herod, Jesus.

Theological Study: The childhood of Jesus in Matthew and Luke presents selected cues rather than a complete biography. The narratives combine the true vulnerability of the child with God's protection, and situate Nazareth and the Temple as a framework for Christ's identity within the history of Israel.

entries.title: Bird
entries.content:
Background evidence: Genesis 20:1-22; Psalm 3:84; Matthew 26:6; Luke 6:12-7. 

Place and context: Creation, Temple, and Galilee. 

People associated with the text: psalmis, Jesus, disciples. 

Theological Study: The bird in the Bible is part of the goodness of creation and may become an example of God's care. Jesus' teaching about birds does not eliminate work, but rather addresses the anxiety that forgets the value of man before the Father.

entries.title: Carcass
entries.content:
Essential evidence: Leviticus 14:1-17; 7:5-10; Luke 2:22-24. 

Place and context: The tabernacle and temple in Jerusalem. 

People associated with the text: Moses, Mary, Joseph, priests. 

Theological Study: The Sacrifice Birds reveals that the law provides an offering to the poor within the system of worship. The offering of Mary and Joseph in Luke places the birth of Jesus within the humility of a family subject to the law and living in real economic limitations.

entries.title: OK
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 34:8; Matthew 7:11; Luke 6:45; Ephesians 4:29.

Place and Context: Israel, Galilee, and the churches.

Persons Related to the Text: David, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: The good in the Scripture may describe the goodness of God or good words and deeds. The good does not stop at courtesy but is manifested in the fruit of the heart and in speech that builds up others according to need.

entries.title: Ointment of blessing
entries.content:
Key Passages: Exodus 30:22-33; Mark 14:3-9; John 12:1-8.

Place and Context: The dwelling and the house of Bethany.

Persons Related to the Text: Moses, Mary, Jesus, the disciples.

Theological Study: The anointing oil in Exodus pertains to the consecration of the sacred and the priesthood, and in Bethany, the pouring of the oil on Jesus becomes a sign of love and readiness for His burial. The distinction between the ritual recipe and the gospel event must be preserved without turning them into a magical practice.

entries.title: Edge of the garment
entries.content:
Background Evidence: Numbers 15:37-41; Mark 5:25-34; Matthew 5:23. 

Place and context: Israel, Galilee, and Judea. 

People associated with the text: Moses, the bleeding woman, Jesus, the Pharisees. 

Theological study: The tip of the garment is attached to fringes that remind us of the Lord's commandments, and then the bleeding woman touches it in faith in the story of healing. Jesus criticizes the enlargement of the fringes to pretend that he does not condemn the sign itself but rather its use of hypocrisy.

entries.title: table
entries.content:
Primary References: Psalm 23:5; Luke 14:7-24; 1 Corinthians 10:16-22.

Place and Context: The home, banquets, and Corinth.

Persons Associated with the Text: David, Jesus, Paul, the invited.

Theological Study: The table or meal is a place of hospitality, fellowship, and distinction. In the Psalms, it is a sign of care; in Jesus' teaching, it reveals the arrangement of guests and the heart; and in Corinthians, it becomes a test of communion with Christ rather than with idols.

entries.title: Scroll
entries.content:
Key References: Jeremiah 36:1-32; Ezekiel 2:8-3:3; Revelation 5:1-10.

Place and Context: Jerusalem, exile, and the vision.

Persons Related to the Text: Jeremiah, Baruch, Ezekiel, John.

Theological Study: The scroll carries a written word that resists attempts to erase it or control it. The burning of Jehoiakim on the steps does not nullify the word of the Lord, and in the vision, only the Lamb opens the scroll, so knowledge is subjected to divine revelation.

entries.title: Good Tree
entries.content:
Key References: Matthew 7:15-20; 12:33-37; Luke 6:43-45.

Place and Context: Galilee in the teaching of Jesus.

Persons Associated with the Text: Jesus, the disciples, the crowds.

Theological Study: The good tree in Jesus' teaching is a picture of a life that bears fruit according to its inner nature. The image is not used for hasty classification of people, but to examine teaching, behavior, and speech in the light of the fruit of repentance.

entries.title: The Lord's Request
entries.content:
Key References: Deuteronomy 4:29; Isaiah 55:6-7; Zephaniah 2:3; Matthew 7:7-11.

Place and Context: The wilderness, Judah, and Galilee.

Persons Related to the Text: Moses, Isaiah, Zephaniah, Jesus.

Theological Study: Seeking the Lord involves the turning of the heart and action toward God, not a vague religious search. The prophets call for seeking the Lord in times of danger, and Jesus teaches seeking with confidence in the good Father and the responsibility of obedience.

entries.title: Divorce
entries.content:
Key References: Deuteronomy 24:1-4; Malachi 2:13-16; Matthew 19:1-12; 1 Corinthians 7:10-16.

Place and Context: Israel, Judaism, and Corinth.

Persons Associated with the Text: Moses, Malachi, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Divorce is a sensitive subject addressed in the Scriptures within a social reality that protects the vulnerable and condemns cruelty. Jesus brings the discussion back to the intention of creation and the faithfulness of the covenant, while Paul addresses the conditions of the community with pastoral wisdom, not with harmful oversimplification.

entries.title: Purity Rituals
entries.content:
Key References: Leviticus 11-15; Mark 7:1-23; Acts 10:9-16.

Place and Context: The dwelling, Judaism, and Jaffa.

People Related to the Text: Moses, Jesus, Peter.

Theological Study: Purity rituals organize Israel's life around the sacred and distinction, and not every impurity equals a moral sin. The New Testament reads these rituals in light of Christ and the reception of the Gentiles, while avoiding portraying the law as a meaningless burden.

entries.title: Reassurance
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 4:8; Isaiah 26:3; John 14:27; Philippians 4:6-7.

Place and Context: Israel, the Upper Room, and Philippi.

People Related to the Text: David, Isaiah, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Biblical reassurance is not the absence of problems, but peace that arises from trust in God. John links the peace of Christ with the hour of trouble, and Paul situates prayer and thanksgiving in facing anxiety without denying its reality.

entries.title: Spiritual Ecstasy
entries.content:
Background Evidence: 2 Samuel 14:6-22; Psalm 150; Luke 46:1-55. 

Place and context: Jerusalem, the Temple, and Nazareth. 

People associated with the text: David, Mary, and the Marinathons. 

Theological Study: Spiritual music appears in physical joy and singing before God, but it needs to distinguish between sincere worship and display. David's dance and Mary's hymn associate joy with God's humility and exaltation of the weak.

entries.title: The Poor
entries.content:
Key References: Deuteronomy 15:7-11; Luke 6:20-26; James 2:1-7.

Place and Context: Israel, Galilee, and the churches in the diaspora.

Persons related to the text: Moses, Jesus, James.

Theological Study: The class of the poor in Scripture is not a social subject outside of theology, but a place for testing covenant faithfulness. The law requires openness of hand, and Jesus and James resist favoritism that makes wealth the standard of dignity.

entries.title: Weather
entries.content:
Essential Evidences: Exodus 12:24-27; Leviticus 16; Luke 14:22-20; Hebrews 1:9-14. 

Place and context: Egypt, the dwelling, and Jerusalem. 

People associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, Jesus, the writer of the Hebrews. 

Theological Study: The ritual in the Bible is an act of memory and covenant, no empty movement and no mechanism of salvation. The Passover, the Day of Atonement, and the Dinner reveal that the signs need a word, repentance, and an honest communal life.

entries.title: Shadows of Death
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 23:4; Job 10:21-22; Luke 1:78-79.

Place and Context: The pastures of Israel, houses of mourning, and Luke's hope.

People Related to the Text: David, Job, Zechariah.

Theological Study: Shadows of death as a picture of walking in deep danger not negated by faith. The psalm proclaims the presence of the shepherd in the valley, and Luke uses the image to declare the light of mercy for those sitting in darkness.

entries.title: Thirst
entries.content:
Primary References: Psalm 42:1-2; Isaiah 55:1; John 4:7-15; 7:37-39.

Place and Context: The wilderness, Jacob's well, and Jerusalem.

People Related to the Text: The psalmist, Isaiah, the Samaritan woman, Jesus.

Theological Study: Thirst in the Bible is both a physical need and a symbol of longing for God and life. Jesus starts from real thirst at the well, then opens the conversation to living water and the Spirit, thus not separating the symbol from human tangible need.

entries.title: External darkness
entries.content:
Background evidence: Matthew 11:8-12; 1:1-14-22; 25:14-30. 

Place and context: Jesus' teaching in Galilee and Judea. 

People associated with the text: Jesus, the hearers, the invited. 

Theological Study: The Outer Darkness in Proverbs of Matthew Picture of Judgment on Refusal of Invitation or Betrayal of Trust. It does not provide a detailed map of the other world, but rather a moral warning against trusting in excellence without a response befitting of the kingdom.

entries.title: Shadows of Sharia
entries.content:
Key References: Colossians 2:16-17; Hebrews 10:1-10.

Place and Context: The churches of Colossae and the communities of Hebrews.

Persons Associated with the Text: Paul, the author of Hebrews, Christ.

Theological Study: The shadows of the law in the letters speak of the relationship of ritual symbols to what the author sees as fulfillment in Christ. They should not be used to disparage the Torah or Judaism, but to understand the Christian argument within the context of covenant history.

entries.title: The Appearance of the Lord
entries.content:
Key references: Exodus 16:10; Leviticus 9:23-24; Isaiah 40:5; 2 Thessalonians 2:8.

Place and context: the wilderness, the tabernacle, and prophetic and apostolic hope.

Persons related to the text: Moses, Aaron, Isaiah, Paul.

Theological study: The manifestation of the Lord announces His presence in worship, judgment, and hope. In the tabernacle, the glory appears connected with holiness, while in the prophets and epistles, the manifestation becomes a horizon for revealing truth rather than a tool for temporal curiosity.

entries.title: Faith assumption
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 50:20; 1 Corinthians 13:7; Philippians 1:6.

Place and Context: Egypt, Corinth, and Philippi.

Persons Related to the Text: Joseph, Paul, the churches.

Theological Study: Goodwill is not naivety that denies evil, but trust shaped by love and wisdom. Joseph sees the hand of God not to justify his brothers' sin but to preserve reconciliation, and Paul places love within the horizon of hope and action.

entries.title: The outward appearance of man
entries.content:
Background Evidence: 1 Samuel 7:16; Matthew 23:25-28; 2 Corinthians 16:4-18. 

Place and context: Bethlehem, Judea, and Corinth. 

People associated with the text: Samuel, Jesus, Paul. 

Theological Study: Man's appearance is not sufficient to judge before God who looks to the heart. Jesus criticizes religiosity that shines on the outside and neglects the inside, while Paul does not despise the flesh but distinguishes between the present annihilation and the inner renewal.

entries.title: oppressed
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 22:21-24; Psalm 146:7-9; Luke 18:1-8.

Place and Context: Israel and Judaism.

Persons Related to the Text: The stranger, the orphan, the widow, Jesus.

Theological Study: The oppressed in Scripture has a voice before God, not merely a subject of human pity. The Law, Psalms, and Proverbs make taking the side of the weak a standard of worshiping God, and the parable of the widow calls for seeking justice without despair.

entries.title: Jealousy
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 20:5; Numbers 25:10-13; John 2:13-17; 2 Corinthians 11:2.

Place and Context: Sinai, the wilderness, the temple, and Corinth.

People Associated with the Text: Moses, Phinehas, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Jealousy in the Bible may describe God's faithfulness to a covenant that does not tolerate rival worship, and it can become dangerous in humans if separated from justice and mercy. John links Jesus' jealousy to the temple, and Paul uses pastoral language not to justify control.

entries.title: Planting
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Genesis 2:8; Isaiah 61:3; Matthew 15:13; 1 Corinthians 3:6-9.

Place and Context: Eden, Zion, and Corinth.

People Associated with the Text: Adam, Isaiah, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Planting is a metaphor for creation, settlement, and God's work in the community. Paul distinguishes between the one who plants and the one who waters, preventing the service from being turned into personal glory because growth comes from God.

entries.title: cloud
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 13:21-22; 40:34-38; Matthew 17:5; Acts 1:9.

Place and Context: The wilderness, the Mount of Transfiguration, and Jerusalem.

Persons Associated with the Text: Moses, Jesus, the disciples.

Theological Study: The cloud is associated with the presence of God, which guides and conceals glory at the same time. In the Transfiguration, the cloud comes with the voice to demand listening to the Son, so it does not become a weather sign but a language of proclamation and holiness.

entries.title: Gihon
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 2:13; 1 Kings 1:33-40; 2 Chronicles 32:30.

Place and Context: Eden and Jerusalem.

People Related to the Text: Adam, Solomon, Zadok, Hezekiah.

Theological Study: Gihon is the name of a river in the description of Eden and the name of an important spring in Jerusalem, and it is not necessary to geographically merge the two locations. In the story of Solomon, the spring is associated with the announcement of the king, and in the days of Hezekiah, it appears as part of the water management in the face of danger.

entries.title: Upper Room
entries.content:
Key references: Mark 14:12-16; Acts 1:13-14; 20:7-12.

Place and context: Jerusalem and Troas.

Persons related to the text: Jesus, the disciples, Mary, Paul.

Theological study: The upper room is a place for meeting, prayer, and breaking bread in the New Testament. The text is less concerned with its architectural form than with its function as a place of fellowship, waiting, and listening to the word of God.

entries.title: West
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 103:12; Isaiah 43:5; Matthew 8:11.

Place and Context: Israel and the nations in the form of directions.

Persons Associated with the Text: The psalmist, Isaiah, Jesus.

Theological Study: The West as a geographical direction sometimes becomes an image of the breadth of mercy or the removal of guilt. When Jesus speaks of those coming from the east and the west, he opens the horizon of the kingdom to the nations without canceling Israel's call.

entries.title: Sunset
entries.content:
Key references: Deuteronomy 24:13; Mark 1:32; Ephesians 4:26.

Place and context: Israel, Capernaum, and the churches.

Persons associated with the text: Moses, Jesus, Paul.

Theological study: Sunset is a time limit in the law to preserve the dignity of the poor by returning a pledge, and in the Gospels, it is the time when the sick came after the Sabbath. Paul uses sunset to teach the urgency of reconciliation and controlling anger before it takes root.

entries.title: Dust
entries.content:
Essential Evidences: Genesis 19:3; Job 12:2; Matthew 14:10; Acts 51:13. 

Place and context: Eden, the land of Aws, and the ways of the message. 

People associated with the text: Adam, Job, Jesus, Paul. 

Theological Study: Dust reminds us of man's origin and fragility, and may become a sign of grief or a testimony to the rejection of the message. Dusting does not call people to despise, but rather sets limits on witness when stubbornly rejected.

entries.title: The Coffin Cover
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 25:17-22; Leviticus 16:11-17; Romans 3:25; Hebrews 9:5.

Place and Context: The Tabernacle and the Holy of Holies.

Persons Related to the Text: Moses, Aaron, Paul, the author of Hebrews.

Theological Study: The cover of the Ark is associated with the place of sprinkling on the Day of Atonement and the presence of God between the cherubim. The New Testament uses the language of atonement in the light of Christ, and it cannot be understood without the background of the tabernacle and holy approach.

entries.title: Atoned
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 32:1; 85:2; Romans 4:6-8.

Place and Context: Prayers of Israel and the church of Rome.

People Related to the Text: David, Paul.

Theological Study: In biblical language, forgiveness is associated with lifting guilt and hiding it before God. Paul uses Psalm 32 in his discussion about justification by faith, linking forgiveness with grace and confession, not with falsely covering up evil.

entries.title: Covered
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 6:12; Leviticus 26:41; Jeremiah 9:25-26; Romans 2:25-29.

Place and Context: Egypt, Judah, and Rome.

Persons Related to the Text: Moses, Jeremiah, Paul.

Theological Study: The term 'covered' in the texts may describe the body, lips, or heart, depending on the context. The law and prophets criticize a heart that is not subject to God, and Paul returns the discussion to internal obedience without disregarding the Jewish bodily sign.

entries.title: Anger
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 32:7-14; Hosea 11:8-9; Romans 1:18; James 1:19-20.

Place and Context: Sinai, Israel, Rome, and the churches.

People Related to the Text: Moses, Hosea, Paul, James.

Theological Study: Divine anger is a holy opposition to evil, not a human whim. James distinguishes between human anger, which does not produce the righteousness of God, and God's call to repentance, justice, and mercy.

entries.title: Rich
entries.content:
Key References: Mark 10:17-31; Luke 16:19-31; James 5:1-6; 1 Timothy 6:17-19.

Place and Context: Galilee, Judaism, and the Churches.

People Associated with the Text: Jesus, the rich man, James, Paul.

Theological Study: The rich person in the Scriptures is not condemned simply for ownership, but for relying on wealth and neglecting the needy. The letters call on the rich to be generous and humble, and Jesus' parables reveal the danger of blindness toward the poor at the door.

entries.title: Servant
entries.content:
Key References: 1 Samuel 3:1-10; Matthew 8:5-13; John 4:46-54.

Place and Context: Shiloh, Capernaum, and Cana.

People Associated with the Text: Samuel, the Roman officer, Jesus.

Theological Study: The term 'servant' in the texts may refer to a child or a servant depending on the context, which requires caution in translation. Samuel's calling of a servant reveals that God speaks to a young generation, and Jesus' healings reveal His mercy toward the weak within households.

entries.title: Covering the wings
entries.content:
Key References: Ruth 2:12; Psalm 36:7; Matthew 23:37.

Place and Context: Bethlehem and Jerusalem.

People Associated with the Text: Ruth, Boaz, David, Jesus.

Theological Study: The covering of the wings is an image of protection and covenant, not ownership or nullification of human responsibility. Boaz blesses Ruth because she sought refuge in the Lord, and Jesus weeps over Jerusalem, which rejected its protective gathering.

entries.title: Washing
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 30:17-21; John 13:1-17; Titus 3:5.

Place and Context: The dwelling and the upper room and the churches.

People associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, Jesus, the disciples, Paul.

Theological Study: Washing in Scripture may be a purification ritual, an act of service, or a symbol of renewal. Jesus washing the disciples' feet reverses the meaning of greatness, so that purity is not a distant separation but loving service.

entries.title: Membrane
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 34:29-35; 2 Corinthians 3:12-18.

Place and Context: Sinai and Corinth.

People Related to the Text: Moses, Paul, the Corinthian community.

Theological Study: The veil in the story of Moses preserves the awe of glory, and Paul uses it in a difficult argument about reading and transformation. The text should be read without contempt for Judaism, with attention to the fact that its purpose is to announce the freedom of the Spirit and the renewal of vision.

entries.title: Silver
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 23:16; Exodus 30:11-16; Zechariah 11:12-13; Matthew 26:15.

Place and Context: Hebron, the Tabernacle, and Jerusalem.

People Related to the Text: Abraham, Moses, Zechariah, Judas.

Theological Study: Silver is a medium of exchange and offering and can become the price of betrayal. Therefore, the Bible reads its value according to usage: buying Sarah's tomb preserves a legal right, the ransom of the Tabernacle serves worship, and thirty pieces of silver reveal the cheapness of betrayal.

entries.title: Mouth
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 19:14; Isaiah 6:5-7; Matthew 15:10-20; James 3:1-12.

Place and Context: The Temple, Galilee, and the Diaspora churches.

People Associated with the Text: David, Isaiah, Jesus, James.

Theological Study: The mouth is an organ of praise and testimony and can become a tool of harm. The cleansing of Isaiah's lips precedes the mission, and James warns of a tongue that blesses and curses, linking speech to the worship of the heart.

entries.title: Trap
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 91:3; Proverbs 29:25; Luke 21:34-36; 1 Timothy 6:9.

Place and Context: Israel, Judaism, and the churches.

Persons Associated with the Text: The psalmist, the wise, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: The trap is a symbol of a hidden danger that a person falls into through pride, fear, or love of money. The texts do not call for constant terror, but for alertness, wisdom, and trust in God who delivers from the snare.

entries.title: Traps
entries.content:
Key References: Isaiah 29:16; Jeremiah 18:1-12; Romans 9:20-24.

Place and Context: The potter's house, Judah, and Rome.

Persons Associated with the Text: Jeremiah, Isaiah, Paul.

Theological Study: The potter is a symbol of God's sovereignty over His people, but it does not negate the call to repentance in Jeremiah. Paul uses the image in the debate about mercy and judgment, and the reader needs to keep in mind the tension between sovereignty and responsibility.

entries.title: Lethargy
entries.content:
Key Evidences: Revelation 3:14-22.

Place and Context: Laodicea in the Lycus Valley.

People Related to the Text: Christ, the church of Laodicea, John.

Theological Study: The lukewarmness in the message to Laodicea reveals a self-sufficient wealthy community that does not see its poverty. The message is not a final rejection, as Christ calls for repentance and opens the door of fellowship to those who hear His voice.

entries.title: Temptation
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 22:1-19; Matthew 4:1-11; James 1:12-15.

Place and Context: Mount Moriah, the wilderness, and the churches in the diaspora.

People Related to the Text: Abraham, Jesus, James.

Theological Study: Temptation may mean a test that reveals faithfulness or a lure toward evil, and the context is judgment. James rejects attributing evil temptation to God, and Jesus appears in the wilderness as faithful where human trials fail.

entries.title: Poor
entries.content:
Key References: Deuteronomy 15:7-11; Psalm 72:12-14; Luke 6:20; James 2:1-7.

Place and Context: Israel and Galilee, and the churches of the diaspora.

People Associated with the Text: Moses, the Psalmist, Jesus, James.

Theological Study: The poor in Scripture are persons with dignity and rights, not rhetorical devices. The law calls for an open hand, the epistles condemn favoritism, and Jesus proclaims good news to those crushed by want without glorifying poverty itself.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
Key References: John 1:43-46; 6:5-7; 12:20-22; Acts 8:4-40.

Place and Context: House of Bethsaida, Samaria, and the road to Gaza.

People Related to the Text: Philip the Apostle, Philip the Evangelist, Nathanael, the Ethiopian eunuch.

Theological Study: Philip is a name for two individuals in the New Testament, and a distinction should be made between the Apostle and the Evangelist in Acts. The two names bring together calling, questioning, and witnessing, and in Acts 8 they highlight the spread of the gospel to Samaria and to a Gentile traveler.

entries.title: Felix
entries.content:
Key References: Acts 23:23-35; 24:1-27.

Place and Context: Caesarea Maritima.

Persons Related to the Text: Paul, Felix, Drusilla, Tertullus.

Theological Study: Felix, the Roman governor, listens to Paul's defense but delays his decision, awaiting political or financial gain. His story reveals that authority may recognize the truth yet postpone it, and that Christian testimony stands before the court without abandoning conscience.

entries.title: Festus
entries.content:
Key References: Acts 25:1-27; 26:24-32.

Place and Context: Caesarea and Jerusalem.

People Related to the Text: Paul, Festus, Agrippa, Bernice.

Theological Study: Festus succeeds Felix and faces Paul's case amid pressure from Jewish leaders and Roman law. Paul's appeal to Caesar redirects the course of testimony toward Rome, showing that political procedures themselves are also part of God's providence over the mission.

entries.title: Holiday Ordinances
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 23:14-17; Leviticus 23; Deuteronomy 16:1-17.

Place and Context: Jerusalem and the land of Israel.

People Associated with the Text: Moses, the priests, the people of the covenant.

Theological Study: The commandments of the festivals organize the memory of the exodus, the harvest, and the covenant, so that worship is not separate from time, work, and justice. The seasonal gathering calls for thanksgiving and generosity, especially toward the stranger, the orphan, and the widow.

entries.title: Euphrates
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 2:14; 15:18; Jeremiah 13:4-7; Revelation 16:12.

Place and Context: Mesopotamia and the borders of the promise and the vision.

People Related to the Text: Abraham, Jeremiah, John.

Theological Study: The Euphrates is a great river that sometimes defines the horizon of the land and imperial powers. It moves between the description of Eden, the borders of the promise, and the symbol of judgment, and therefore requires a distinctive geographical and prophetic reading.

entries.title: Dismay and Persecution
entries.content:
Key Evidences: Israel, Galilee, and the churches.

Place and Context: David, Jesus, Paul, Timothy.

Persons related to the text: The fear in the face of persecution is present in the scripture, but it is not the final word. Jesus teaches not to fear those who kill the body, and Paul reminds of the spirit of power, love, and self-discipline, not a spirit of cowardice.

Theological Study: undefined

entries.title: Separation
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 13:1-18; Acts 15:36-41; 20:36-38.

Place and Context: Canaan, Antioch, and Miletus.

People Related to the Text: Abraham, Lot, Paul, Barnabas, elders of Ephesus.

Theological Study: Separation in the Bible may result from conflict, invitation, or a shift in ministry. The text does not make every separation a failure; the separation of Abraham and Lot preserves peace, and the disagreement between Paul and Barnabas reveals the realism of ministry and the limits of leaders.

entries.title: Understanding
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Nehemiah 8:1-12; Luke 24:44-49; Acts 8:30-35; Ephesians 1:17-19.

Place and Context: Jerusalem, the road to Gaza, and the churches.

People Related to the Text: Ezra, Jesus, Philip, the eunuch, Paul.

Theological Study: Understanding in Scripture is linked to explaining the Word and the response of the heart. Ezra reads the Law and interprets it, Jesus opens the minds of the disciples, Philip asks the eunuch: Do you understand what you are reading?

entries.title: The Vine Field
entries.content:
Key References: Isaiah 5:1-7; Matthew 21:33-46; John 15:1-8.

Place and Context: The vineyards of Judah and Galilee.

Persons Related to the Text: Isaiah, Jesus, the vineyard owners, the disciples.

Theological Study: The vineyard in the texts represents care, responsibility, and fruitfulness. Isaiah's vineyard exposes the absence of justice, the parable of the vineyard condemns the monopolization of gifts, and John links fruitfulness to abiding in Christ.

entries.title: Tomb
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 23; Isaiah 53:9; John 19:38-42; 20:1-18.

Place and Context: Hebron and Jerusalem.

Persons Associated with the Text: Abraham, Joseph of Arimathea, Nicodemus, Mary Magdalene.

Theological Study: The tomb in Scripture preserves the reality of death and the dignity associated with burial. Jesus' new tomb testifies to His real death, and then the empty tomb becomes a place proclaiming the resurrection, not denying the pain.

entries.title: Kairouan
entries.content:
Background evidence: Matthew 27:32; Acts 2:10; 11:20; 13:1. 

Venue and context: North Africa, Jerusalem, and Antioch. 

People associated with the text: Simon of Cyrene, Lucius, Barnabas, Saul. 

Theological Study: Kairouan reveals the presence of Diaspora and North African Jews in the New Testament story. Simon holds the cross of Jesus, and Lucius appears among the leaders of Antioch, and the map of the message expands early.

entries.title: caravan
entries.content:
Background evidence: Genesis 25:37-28; Job 18:6-20; Luke 2:44. 

Place and context: Trade routes between Gilead, Egypt, and Judea. 

People associated with the text: Joseph, his brothers, the Ismailis, Mary and Joseph. 

Theological Study: The Caravan in the book provides an economic background for movement, trade, and travel. Joseph's sale of a caravan does not justify the evil of his brothers, but it enters the path of God's providence, which operates amid responsible human decisions.

entries.title: Offerings
entries.content:
Key References: Leviticus 1-7; Mark 12:33; Hebrews 10:1-14.

Place and Context: The tabernacle, the temple, and the churches.

Persons Associated with the Text: Moses, the priests, Jesus, the writer of Hebrews.

Theological Study: The sacrifices in the Law regulate thanksgiving, atonement, and fellowship before God, and do not function as magic or bribery. The New Testament reads the sacrifices in the light of Christ, while understanding the Levitical system remains necessary to avoid oversimplification.

entries.title: Hard heart
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 7:13; Psalm 95:7-11; Mark 3:5; Hebrews 3:7-15.

Place and Context: Egypt, the wilderness, Galilee, and the churches.

Persons Related to the Text: Pharaoh, Moses, Jesus, the author of Hebrews.

Theological Study: Hardness of heart is a repeated rejection of the word of God and mercy, not just intellectual incapacity. The New Testament uses the wilderness of Israel to warn the community against hearing without obedience and against a religion that becomes insensitive to human healing.

entries.title: Judgment
entries.content:
Key References: Deuteronomy 16:18-20; Psalm 82; John 5:22-30; Revelation 20:11-15.

Place and Context: City gates and revelation.

Persons Associated with the Text: Judges, the singer, Jesus, John.

Theological Study: Judgment in the Bible calls for justice and the elimination of evil before God, not human revenge. The Torah calls on judges to be impartial, and John declares that the final judgment reveals the truth and returns responsibility to God.

entries.title: Qumran
entries.content:
Key References: Isaiah 40:3; Habakkuk 2:4.

Place and Context: The Judean wilderness in the background of the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Persons Related to the Text: The Qumran community, the manuscript scribes.

Theological Study: Qumran is not mentioned in the Bible, but it is important for understanding a Jewish textual environment that preserved biblical and interpretive manuscripts. The introduction clearly states this so that Qumran does not become a direct biblical entry, but rather a historical context for understanding the transmission of the text.

entries.title: Priest
entries.content:
Essential evidences: Exodus 1:28-43; Leviticus 16; Luke 10:31; Hebrews 23:7-28. 

Place and context: The dwelling, the temple, and the Jericho Road. 

People associated with the text: Aaron, the priests, Jesus, the writer of the Hebrews. 

Theological Study: The priest serves in the system of sacrifices and sacrifices, but the office does not spare its holder from the failure of mercy as seen in the Samaritan parable. Hebrews read the priesthood of Christ as unique without abolishing the meaning of the ancient priesthood.

entries.title: Priesthood
entries.content:
Essential Evidence: Exodus 6:19; Numbers 18; 1 Peter 9:2; Revelation 6:1. 

Place and context: Sinai, the dwelling, and the churches. 

People associated with the text: Moses, Aaron, Peter, John. 

Theological Study: The priesthood in the Bible is a sacred function and a collective responsibility depending on the context. Israel is described as a kingdom of priests, and 1 Peter restores language to the church as an identity of worship and witness rather than as a privilege of control.

entries.title: Pride
entries.content:
Essential evidences: Proverbs 18:16; Isaiah 11:2-17; Daniel 4; James 6:4. 

Place and context: Jerusalem, Babylon, and the churches of the diaspora. 

People associated with the text: Isaiah, Nebuchadnezzar, Jacob. 

Theological Study: Pride elevates oneself above God and the neighbor, and therefore stands under the criticism of wisdom and prophets. The story of Nebuchadnezzar shows the fall of transcendent power, and James asserts that God resists the arrogant and gives grace to the humble.

entries.title: Mercy
entries.content:
Primary References: Exodus 25:17-22; Leviticus 16:14-16; Romans 3:25; Hebrews 9:5.

Place and Context: The Holy of Holies in the tabernacle.

Persons Associated with the Text: Moses, Aaron, Paul, the author of Hebrews.

Theological Study: The mercy seat or the cover of the ark is associated with the place of sprinkling and God’s presence between the cherubim. The epistles use the language of atonement in the light of Christ, and understanding the Day of Atonement remains key to avoiding superficial interpretation.

entries.title: Atonement
entries.content:
Background Evidence: Leviticus 16; Isaiah 4:53-6; Romans 21:3-26; Hebrews 11:9-14. 

Place and context: the tabernacle, Jerusalem, and the churches. 

People associated with the text: Aaron, Isaiah, Paul, the writer of the Hebrews. 

Theological Study: Atonement is a treatment of sin and impurity within the covenant relationship, not a bribe to an angry God. The New Testament links the Atonement to the work of Christ, with its roots in Leviticus and the Day of Atonement.

entries.title: evangelism
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Jonah 3:1-10; Mark 1:14-15; Acts 2:14-41; 2 Timothy 4:1-5.

Place and Context: Nineveh, Galilee, Jerusalem, and the churches.

People Associated with the Text: Jonah, Jesus, Peter, Paul, Timothy.

Theological Study: Preaching is a proclamation that calls for repentance and faith, and is not limited to conveying information. From Nineveh to Jerusalem, the word reveals that God seeks the return of the hearers and that the servant is not the owner of the message.

entries.title: Cherubim
entries.content:
Essential evidence: Genesis 24:3; Exodus 18:25-22; Ezekiel 10; Hebrews 5:9. 

Place and context: Eden, the tabernacle and the visions of Ezekiel. 

People associated with the text: Adam and Eve, Moses, Ezekiel, the writer of the Hebrews. 

Theological Study: Cherubim are beings associated with the guardianship of the sanctuary and the symbol of the divine throne. The text does not provide a biological description of them, but rather uses them in the language of presence and the boundaries between God's holiness and man's approach.

entries.title: The King's Chair
entries.content:
Key References: 2 Samuel 7:12-16; Psalm 89; Luke 1:32-33; Revelation 3:21.

Place and Context: Jerusalem, Nazareth, and Revelation.

People Related to the Text: David, Nathan, Mary, Jesus.

Theological Study: The throne of the king symbolizes authority and covenant and is inseparable from the responsibility of justice. David's promise is read in the New Testament in light of the kingship of Christ, which does not resemble the domination of kingdoms but passes through the cross and resurrection.

entries.title: flesh
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 16:8-13; Ezekiel 11:19; John 6:51-58; Romans 8:3.

Place and Context: The wilderness, Galilee, and the churches.

Persons Related to the Text: Moses, Ezekiel, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Flesh in Scripture may mean food, the human body, or weak nature depending on the context. The people ask for meat in the wilderness, and John uses the language of the body of Christ in the discourse on life, which requires distinguishing between the literal and theological meaning.

entries.title: Pearl
entries.content:
Key References: Matthew 7:6; 13:45-46; Revelation 21:21.

Place and Context: The teaching of Jesus and the vision.

Persons Related to the Text: Jesus, the merchant, John the revelator.

Theological Study: The pearl in Jesus’ parable is a symbol of the value of the kingdom that is worth selling everything for. In Revelation, pearls are included in the description of the new city, serving the language of beauty and hope rather than earthly luxury.

entries.title: Bridle
entries.content:
Key Evidences: Psalm 32:9; James 3:2-5.

Place and Context: Israel and the churches of the diaspora.

People Related to the Text: The psalmist, James, the teachers.

Theological Study: The bit is a tool of control used by the Scriptures to teach wisdom about guiding the self and the tongue. James warns that a small member directs the whole life, so speech is not separate from spiritual maturity.

entries.title: The Repentant Thief
entries.content:
Key References: Luke 23:39-43.

Place and Context: Golgotha in Jerusalem.

People Involved in the Text: Jesus, the two thieves, the soldiers.

Theological Study: The repentant thief in Luke testifies to Jesus' innocence and asks to be remembered in His kingdom. Jesus' response proclaims immediate mercy at the heart of the cross, without turning the story into a trivialization of repentance or justice.

entries.title: City of David
entries.content:
Key References: 2 Samuel 5:6-10; 1 Kings 8:1; Luke 2:4-11.

Place and Context: Jerusalem and Bethlehem according to the context.

Persons Related to the Text: David, Solomon, Joseph, Mary.

Theological Study: The City of David may refer either to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem or to Bethlehem in Luke's language, and therefore the context determines the meaning. The phrase combines the memory of the king and the Messianic promise without mixing the locations.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 1; 22; 23; 51; Luke 24:44.

Place and Context: The Temple of Israel and the life of prayer.

Persons associated with the text: David, Asaph, the singers, Jesus.

Theological Study: The Psalms are a book of prayer, wisdom, kingship, and hope, containing praise, lamentation, and repentance. The New Testament cites the Psalms in Christ's reading, yet they also remain the voice of a community praying in pain and joy.

entries.title: The Lord's Table
entries.content:
Background evidence: Luke 22:14-20; 1 Corinthians 10:16-22; 11:17-34. 

Place and context: Attic and Corinth. 

People associated with the text: Jesus, the disciples, Paul, the Corinthian church. 

Theological study: The Lord's table is a communion of the body and blood of Christ, not a social feast that reproduces division. Paul rebukes Corinthians for insulting the poor, associating the sacrament with discernment and love.

entries.title: manger
entries.content:
Key References: Luke 2:1-20.

Place and Context: Bethlehem at the time of the census.

People associated with the text: Mary, Joseph, Jesus, the shepherds.

Theological Study: The manger in Luke is a tangible sign of the humility of birth and limited hospitality conditions. The text does not need excessive emotional embellishment; its power lies in the fact that the announcement of glory comes to a child placed in a manger.

entries.title: Money
entries.content:
Key References: Proverbs 30:8-9; Matthew 6:19-24; Luke 16:1-13; 1 Timothy 6:6-10.

Place and Context: Israel, Galilee, and the churches.

People Related to the Text: The wise man, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Money in the Bible is a tool that can serve mercy or become a master rivaling God. Jesus rejects the worship of money, and the letters call for contentment and generosity that free a person from the love of wealth.

entries.title: Perdition
entries.content:
Essential evidences: Proverbs 12:14; Matthew 13:7; John 16:3; 2 Peter 9:3. 

Place and context: Israel, Galilee, and the churches. 

People associated with the text: The Wise, Jesus, Peter. 

Theological Study: Destruction in the Bible is the result of a path that rejects life with God, and is not a separate threat from the call to repentance. John places it in front of God's love for the world, and Peter connects it to the length of God's patience that no one wants to perish.

entries.title: Heba
entries.content:
Key References: Ecclesiastes 3:13; John 4:10; Romans 6:23; James 1:17.

Place and Context: Israel, Samaria, and the churches.

Persons Related to the Text: Ecclesiastes, Jesus, Paul, James.

Theological Study: The gift in Scripture reminds that life and salvation are a gift, not an achievement. Jesus proclaims God's gift to the Samaritan woman, and Paul contrasts the wages of sin with God's gift, preserving the distinction between grace and merit.

entries.title: Calm
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 46:10; Isaiah 30:15; Mark 4:39; 1 Thessalonians 4:11.

Place and Context: Zion, the sea, and the churches.

Persons Related to the Text: Isaiah, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Calmness in the Scriptures is not passivity, but trust that stops panic and control. Jesus quiets the storm, and Paul requests a safe and quiet life, linking inner peace to responsible conduct.

entries.title: Shout
entries.content:
Key References: Joshua 6:5; Psalm 47:1; Zechariah 9:9; Revelation 19:1-6.

Place and Context: Jericho, Zion, and the vision.

Persons Associated with the Text: Joshua, the singers, Zechariah, John.

Theological Study: The shout may be a proclamation of worship, joy at God's victory, or the reception of the king. The sincerity of worship is not measured by the volume of sound alone, but by its direction toward God and its connection to justice and repentance.

entries.title: Flight to Egypt
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Matthew 2:13-15; Hosea 11:1.

Place and Context: Bethlehem, Egypt, and Nazareth.

People Associated with the Text: Joseph, Mary, Jesus, Herod.

Theological Study: The family's flight to Egypt reveals the vulnerability of the child Jesus under oppressive power, and God's protection over him through Joseph's obedience. Matthew uses Hosea in reading the path of the Son, linking the story of Jesus to the memory of Israel's exodus.

entries.title: Guidance
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 23:3; 119:105; John 16:13; Romans 8:14.

Place and Context: Israel, the highlands, and the churches.

Persons Related to the Text: David, Jesus, the Spirit, Paul.

Theological Study: Guidance in the Scripture is God's leading of His people in the way and the truth, without abolishing human discernment. The Word of God is a lamp, and the Spirit guides into the truth and leads the children of God into a new life.

entries.title: Hymn
entries.content:
Key References: 1 Kings 4:31; 1 Chronicles 6:33; Psalm 88.

Place and Context: Jerusalem and the Temple.

Persons Related to the Text: Heman, David, the singers.

Theological Study: Heman is a name associated with wisdom and the service of praise, and Psalm 88, a gloomy psalm, is attributed to him. Its value lies in demonstrating that biblical worship accommodates darkness and crying out, not only joy.

entries.title: Haman
entries.content:
Key Passages: Esther 3-7.

Place and Context: Susa in the Persian Empire.

People Related to the Text: Haman, Esther, Mordecai, Ahasuerus.

Theological Study: Haman embodies the use of power to annihilate a group due to pride and personal rivalry. The story of Esther resists this violence with wisdom, courage, and fasting, without turning the conflict into contemporary racial hatred.

entries.title: Hannah
entries.content:
Key References: 1 Samuel 1:1-2:11.

Place and Context: Shiloh and the house of Elkanah.

Persons Related to the Text: Hannah, Elkanah, Peninnah, Eli, Samuel.

Theological Study: Hannah prays out of the bitterness of her soul before the Lord, and God listens and gives birth to Samuel. Her song is not limited to personal joy, but declares God's reversal that exalts the lowly and opposes the proud.

entries.title: Hanum
entries.content:
Key References: Joshua 15:8; 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31-32; Mark 9:43-48.

Location and Context: Valley of Hinnom, south of Jerusalem.

Persons Associated with the Text: Josiah, Jeremiah, Jesus.

Theological Study: The Valley of Hinnom was associated with condemned practices and severe prophetic criticism, later becoming the background for the concept of hell in the New Testament. A distinction must be made between the historical place and its eschatological semantic development.

entries.title: The Holy City
entries.content:
Key References: Nehemiah 11:1; Matthew 4:5; Revelation 21:2.

Place and Context: Jerusalem and Revelation.

People Related to the Text: Nehemiah, Jesus, John.

Theological Study: The holy city refers to Jerusalem in historical and visionary contexts, but it does not grant its inhabitants immunity from trials or injustice. In Revelation, the new city becomes an image of God's presence with His people and the renewal of creation.

entries.title: Harmony of Praise
entries.content:
Key References: 1 Chronicles 25:1-7; Psalm 150; Revelation 5:8.

Place and Context: The temple and vision.

Persons Related to the Text: David, Asaph, Heman, John.

Theological Study: Praise with music in Scripture serves to proclaim the glory of God and to remember His deeds. Instruments are not an end in themselves, but become part of worship shared by the community before the Lord.

entries.title: The Gift of Hospitality
entries.content:
Essential evidences: Genesis 1:1-8; Hebrews 2:13; 1 Peter 9:4. 

Venue and context: Corridor and churches. 

People associated with the text: Abraham, Sarah, strangers, Peter. 

Theological Study: The gift of hospitality appears when a house is opened to the stranger without complaint or exploitation. From Abraham's tabernacle to the New Testament messages, hospitality is associated with practical faith and the preservation of the dignity of the other.

entries.title: The Glory of the Lord
entries.content:
Key References: Proverbs 1:7; Isaiah 6:1-8; Acts 9:31.

Place and Context: Jerusalem and the early churches.

People Related to the Text: Isaiah, the wise, the church.

Theological Study: The fear of the Lord is not a terror that paralyzes a person, but an awareness of the holiness of God that begins wisdom and sends for service. In the Acts of the Apostles, the fear of the Lord is associated with the encouragement of the spirit and the growth of the community.

entries.title: The Disposition of Piety
entries.content:
Background evidence: Isaiah 11:1-17; Matthew 23; 2 Timothy 3:5. 

Place and context: Judea, Judaism, and the churches. 

People associated with the text: Isaiah, Jesus, Paul. 

Theological Study: The body of piety without justice and a sincere heart is criticized by the prophets, Jesus, and the apostles. The Bible does not reject organized worship, but rather rejects a religious form that obscures injustice or seeks praise.

entries.title: Harvest Rush
entries.content:
Key References: Joel 3:13; Matthew 13:36-43; Revelation 14:14-20.

Place and Context: Judea, Jesus' teaching, and Revelation.

Persons Related to the Text: Joel, Jesus, John.

Theological Study: The imagery of the harvest may refer to either fruit or judgment depending on the context. In eschatological texts, believers are not given authority for vengeance, but it is proclaimed that the final chapter belongs to the Lord who knows the truth.

entries.title: Kidron Valley
entries.content:
Key References: 2 Samuel 15:23; 2 Kings 23:4-6; John 18:1.

Location and Context: East of Jerusalem near the Mount of Olives.

Persons Associated with the Text: David, Josiah, Jesus, the disciples.

Theological Study: The Kidron Valley connects David's flight, Josiah's reform, and Jesus' crossing to the garden. The place reveals the intertwining of royal memory, liturgical purification, and the path of suffering.

entries.title: Valley of Hinnom
entries.content:
Key References: Joshua 15:8; Jeremiah 7:31-32; Matthew 5:22.

Place and Context: South of Jerusalem.

People Related to the Text: Jeremiah, Josiah, Jesus.

Theological Study: The Valley of Hinnom is a historical site associated with criticism of perverted worship, and later became the background for the language of hell. The introduction teaches the distinction between geography and symbolic development without constructing popular images not prescribed.

entries.title: New Commandment
entries.content:
Key References: John 13:34-35; 15:12-17; 1 John 2:7-11.

Place and Context: The upper room and the Johannine communities.

People associated with the text: Jesus, the disciples, John.

Theological Study: The new commandment is to love the disciples as Christ loved them, not to abolish all of God's commandments. It is summarized in the standard of the cross and the community known for practical love.

entries.title: Passover
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Exodus 12:1-28; Luke 22:7-20; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26.

Place and Context: Egypt, Jerusalem, and Corinth.

Persons Related to the Text: Moses, Jesus, the disciples, Paul.

Theological Study: The Passover feast is a memory of family and communal liberation, and Jesus sets his Last Supper within the horizon of covenant and suffering. The Christian reading does not erase the Jewish root of Passover, but understands the supper from within it.

entries.title: Heirs
entries.content:
Essential evidences: Genesis 1:1-6; Romans 14:8-17; Galatians 26:3-29; Hebrews 2:1. 

Place and context: Canaan and the churches. 

People associated with the text: Abraham, Paul, the believers, Christ. 

Theological Study: The heirs in the Bible are associated with promise, sonship, and covenant. Paul extends the concept of inheritance in Christ to include nations by faith, without canceling the date of Abraham's promise.

entries.title: Idol
entries.content:
Essential evidence: Exodus 3:20-6; Isaiah 9:44-20; 1 Corinthians 1:8-13; 1 John 21:5. 

Place and context: Sinai, Babylon, and Corinth. 

People associated with the text: Moses, Isaiah, Paul, John. 

Theological Study: Idolatry in the Bible is a substitute for a creature that takes the place of God, whether made of substance or of the desires of the heart. Paul warns against food associated with idols while taking into account the conscience of the weak, combining monotheism with love.

entries.title: Intermediate
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 32:30-32; Galatians 3:19-20; 1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 8:6.

Place and Context: Sinai and the churches.

Persons Associated with the Text: Moses, Paul, Christ.

Theological Study: The mediator maintains a relationship between God and the people, as seen in Moses' intercession after the calf. The New Covenant announces the unique mediation of Christ, which establishes a better covenant without denying Moses' role in the history of salvation.

entries.title: Time
entries.content:
Key References: Ecclesiastes 3:1-8; Mark 1:15; Galatians 4:4; Ephesians 5:15-16.

Place and Context: Israel, Galilee, and the churches.

People Associated with the Text: Ecclesiastes, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Time in the Bible is not just the passage of hours, but a realm of God's management and human response. Jesus proclaims the fullness of time with the approaching kingdom, and Paul calls for the redeeming of time with wisdom.

entries.title: Woes
entries.content:
Key References: Isaiah 5:8-23; Matthew 23:13-36; Luke 6:24-26; Revelation 8:13.

Place and Context: Judea, Judaism, and Revelation.

Persons Related to the Text: Isaiah, Jesus, John.

Theological Study: The woes are not religious insults, but a prophetic form that reveals danger and judgment over injustice and hypocrisy. In Jesus' teaching, they confront the leaders when they shut the kingdom to the people, and call the listener to repentance.

entries.title: Unity
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 133; John 17:20-23; Ephesians 4:1-6.

Place and Context: Zion, the upper room, and the churches.

Persons Related to the Text: David, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Biblical unity is not an unjustified sameness, but fellowship in God that appears in love, humility, and peace. Jesus’ prayer and Ephesians 4 link unity to testimony and building up the body, not to erasing responsible differences.

entries.title: Meter
entries.content:
Key Texts: Matthew 25:14-30.

Place and Context: Jesus' teaching about the Kingdom.

Persons Related to the Text: The master, the servants, the listeners.

Theological Study: The talents in the parable are large sums entrusted to the servants, thus measuring faithfulness is not only about the size of modern gifts. The parable does not justify economic exploitation, but calls for active responsibility before the master.

entries.title: The Face of God
entries.content:
Key References: Numbers 6:24-26; Psalm 27:8; 2 Corinthians 4:6; Revelation 22:4.

Place and Context: The tabernacle, the temple, the churches, and Revelation.

Persons Associated with the Text: Aaron, David, Paul, John.

Theological Study: The face of God is an expression of presence, favor, and knowledge, not a limited physical description. The priestly blessing asks for the Lord's face to shine, and Revelation concludes with the hope of seeing His face in the new creation.

entries.title: Work
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 2:15; Ecclesiastes 3:13; Colossians 3:23; 2 Thessalonians 3:10-13.

Place and Context: Eden, Israel, and the churches.

Persons Related to the Text: Adam, Ecclesiastes, Paul.

Theological Study: Work in the Bible precedes the Fall as stewardship of creation, but it is affected by toil and injustice. The epistles call for faithful work serving the Lord and neighbor, while rejecting both laziness and exploitation.

entries.title: Revelation of the Scripture
entries.content:
Key References: Jeremiah 36; 2 Timothy 3:16-17; 2 Peter 1:20-21.

Place and Context: Jerusalem and the churches.

Persons Related to the Text: Jeremiah, Baruch, Paul, Peter.

Theological Study: The inspiration of Scripture is linked to the written and proclaimed Word of God, not to secret knowledge without examination. The burning of the scroll in Jeremiah does not nullify the Word, and the epistles connect revelation with teaching, correction, and godliness.

entries.title: Faithfulness
entries.content:
Essential evidence: Ruth 16:1-17; Psalm 1:89-4; 2 Timothy 2:13. 

Place and context: Moab, Bethlehem, and the churches. 

People associated with the text: Ruth, Naomi, David, Paul. 

Theological Study: Faithfulness in the Bible is the righteousness of a relationship based on covenant and mercy. Ruth's faithfulness to Naomi transcends expediency, and Paul proclaims Christ's faithfulness even when He weakens people.

entries.title: Birth
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Genesis 21:1-7; Luke 1:57-66; John 3:1-8.

Place and Context: The house of Abraham, Judaism, and Galilee.

Persons associated with the text: Sarah, Elizabeth, Nicodemus, Jesus.

Theological Study: Birth in the Bible is a gift of life and may be a sign of a promise after infertility and waiting. John uses the language of being born from above to explain spiritual renewal, not to belittle physical birth.

entries.title: Commandment
entries.content:
Key References: Deuteronomy 6:4-9; Psalm 119:9-16; John 14:15; 1 John 5:3.

Place and Context: Moab, the Temple, the upper room, and the churches.

Persons Related to the Text: Moses, the psalmist, Jesus, John.

Theological Study: The commandment in the Scriptures is a way of life within a covenant, not a tool to purchase God's acceptance. Jesus links keeping the commandments with love, and John clarifies that true love for God cannot be separated from practical obedience.

entries.title: Born
entries.content:
Key References: Isaiah 9:6; Luke 2:12; Galatians 4:4-7.

Place and Context: Judah, Bethlehem, and the churches.

People Related to the Text: Isaiah, Mary, Joseph, Paul.

Theological Study: The child in the promise texts carries the hope of the king and peace, and in Luke the sign appears in a wrapped child lying in a manger. Paul links the sending of the Son to the adoption of believers, transforming sonship into grace and responsibility.

entries.title: Vigil Pause
entries.content:
Key References: Mark 13:32-37; 14:37-38; 1 Thessalonians 5:1-11.

Place and Context: Mount of Olives, Gethsemane, and the churches.

Persons Related to the Text: Jesus, Peter, Paul.

Theological Study: Vigilance in Jesus' teaching is faithful watchfulness without keeping track of times. The disciples' failure in Gethsemane shows the weakness of the flesh, and the letters call for spiritual awakening based on hope and love.

entries.title: Awareness and Wisdom
entries.content:
Key Evidences: Israel, Judaism, and the churches.

Place and Context: The sages, Jesus, Paul.

Persons Associated with the Text: Biblical awareness is not intelligence separate from the fear of the Lord, but understanding that leads to justice and love. Jesus praises the writer who discerns the greatest commandments, and Paul prays for knowledge that bears fruit in action.

Theological Study: undefined

entries.title: Inheritance of the land
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 12:1-3; Joshua 13:1-7; Psalm 37:11; Matthew 5:5.

Place and Context: Canaan and Galilee.

People Associated with the Text: Abraham, Joshua, the psalmist, Jesus.

Theological Study: Inheritance of the land in Scripture is a divine promise and a covenantal responsibility, not a license for injustice. Jesus restores the language of the meek who will inherit the earth, linking the promise to humility and justice rather than power.

entries.title: Prophet Jeremiah
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Jeremiah 1:4-19; 7:1-15; 31:31-34; 36:1-32.

Place and Context: Anathoth, Jerusalem, and the exile.

Persons Related to the Text: Jeremiah, Baruch, Josiah, Zedekiah.

Theological Study: The prophet Jeremiah serves during the collapse of Judah, combining judgment on false trust in the temple with the promise of the new covenant. He does not appear without pain, but struggles with rejection and remains faithful to the word.

entries.title: Joshua son of Nun
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Numbers 27:15-23; Joshua 1:1-9; 24:1-28.

Place and Context: Moab, Jericho, and Shechem.

Persons Related to the Text: Moses, Joshua, Rahab, Israelite tribes.

Theological Study: Joshua son of Nun succeeds Moses and leads the people into the land, but his book concludes with a renewal of the covenant, not only with military victory. He calls the people to worship the Lord and reject idols, so the land is defined by obedience, not by possession alone.

entries.title: James the Apostle
entries.content:
Key References: Mark 1:19-20; 5:37; 10:35-45; Acts 12:1-2.

Place and Context: Galilee and Jerusalem.

Persons Related to the Text: James son of Zebedee, John, Jesus, Herod.

Theological Study: James son of Zebedee was among the inner circle close to Jesus, yet he learns that glory comes through service and not by seeking positions. His death in Acts 12 reminds that apostolic witness may face the violence of authority.

entries.title: Judas Iscariot
entries.content:
Background evidence: Matthew 14:26-25; John 18:13-30; Acts 1:15-20. 

Place and context: Jerusalem and the Attic. 

People associated with the text: Judas, Jesus, disciples, high priests. 

Theological Study: Judas Iscariot delivers Jesus from within the circle of disciples, revealing the cruelty of imminent betrayal. The texts do not allow his guilt to be turned into collective condemnation, but rather focus on his responsibility, the complicity of authority, and Jesus' march to the cross.

entries.title: Judas the Apostle
entries.content:
Main References: Luke 6:16; John 14:22; Jude 1:1-25.

Place and Context: Galilee and the apostolic churches.

Persons Related to the Text: Jude the non-Iscariot, Jesus, the churches.

Theological Study: The Apostle Jude must be distinguished from Judas Iscariot. A short letter is attributed to him, urging steadfastness in faith and resistance to corrupt teaching while awaiting the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ.

entries.title: Joel
entries.content:
Key References: Joel 1-3; Acts 2:16-21.

Place and Context: Judah and Jerusalem.

People Related to the Text: Joel, Peter, the Pentecostal congregation.

Theological Study: Joel links the locust plague to the call to repentance and promises the outpouring of the Spirit on all people. Peter cites the text on the day of Pentecost, seeing the coming of the Spirit as the initial fulfillment of a broad prophetic hope.

entries.title: Josiah
entries.content:
Key References: 2 Kings 22-23; 2 Chronicles 34-35.

Place and Context: Jerusalem and Judah.

Persons Related to the Text: Josiah, Hilkiah, Huldah, the people.

Theological Study: Josiah, a reforming king, is associated with the discovery of the Book of the Law and the renewal of the covenant. The text does not present the reform as merely the removal of symbols, but as a return to the word of God and the observance of Passover, while questions of history and politics regarding the end of Judah remain.

entries.title: Jehoshaphat
entries.content:
Key Passages: 1 Kings 22; 2 Chronicles 17-20.

Place and Context: Judah and Samaria.

Persons Related to the Text: Jehoshaphat, Ahab, Micaiah son of Imlah.

Theological Study: Jehoshaphat appears as a king who seeks the Lord but also becomes involved in complex political alliances. The story of Micaiah son of Imlah reveals the danger of ignoring the word of the Lord to please kings, while Chronicles highlights prayer and trust during times of danger.

entries.title: Jehoiakim
entries.content:
Primary References: Jeremiah 22:13-19; 36:1-32; 2 Kings 23:34-24:6.

Place and Context: Jerusalem in the late Judah period.

People Related to the Text: Jehoiakim, Jeremiah, Baruch, Nebuchadnezzar.

Theological Study: Jehoiakim cuts Jeremiah's scroll and burns it, serving as an example of authority attempting to silence the word. The burning does not succeed in nullifying the revelation, but the message is rewritten with additions, demonstrating the steadfastness of God's word in the face of oppression.

entries.title: Jehoiachin
entries.content:
Key Passages: 2 Kings 24:8-17; 25:27-30; Jeremiah 22:24-30.

Place and Context: Jerusalem and Babylon.

People Related to the Text: Jehoiachin, Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-Merodach.

Theological Study: Jehoiachin was a short-reigning king who was exiled to Babylon, and then the book of Kings concludes with the account of his release from prison. This small detail preserves a thread of hope for the house of David amidst the kingdom's collapse.

entries.title: Judahites
entries.content:
Key References: 1 Chronicles 16:41-42; 25:1-6; Psalms 39; 62; 77.

Place and Context: Jerusalem and the service of praise.

Persons Related to the Text: David, Jeduthun, Asaph, Heman.

Theological Study: Jeduthun, a leader of praise, is associated with the titles of Psalms and the temple service. The introduction teaches that music in the Bible is not mere decoration, but an organized remembrance of prayer, complaint, and trust before the Lord.

entries.title: Jebusites
entries.content:
Key References: Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:21; 2 Samuel 5:6-10.

Place and Context: Jerusalem before David.

Persons Associated with the Text: The Jebusites, David, men of Judah and Benjamin.

Theological Study: The Jebusites were the inhabitants of Jerusalem before David captured it, and they are mentioned in the texts within the complexity of land ownership. The entry does not allow the use of the name to justify contemporary conflicts, but rather studies it in the context of the city and property.

entries.title: Jebusites
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 3:1; 18:1-27.  

Place and Context: Midian and Sinai.  

People Related to the Text: Jethro, Moses, Zipporah, elders of Israel.  

Theological Study: Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses' father-in-law, provides administrative advice that saves the leader from exhaustion. His story reveals that wisdom can come from outside the community and that leadership requires a fair distribution of responsibility.

entries.title: Jehoiada
entries.content:
Key References: 2 Kings 11; 2 Chronicles 23-24.

Place and Context: Jerusalem and the Temple.

People Related to the Text: Jehoiada, Athaliah, Joash.

Theological Study: Jehoiada the priest plays a crucial role in preserving Joash and renewing the covenant after Athaliah's violence. The story reveals the intertwining of priesthood and politics and the responsibility of the religious institution in protecting life and worship.

entries.title: Joab
entries.content:
Primary References: 2 Samuel 2-3; 11; 18; 1 Kings 2:28-35.

Place and Context: Hebron and Jerusalem, and the battlefield.

Persons Related to the Text: David, Joab, Abner, Uriah, Absalom.

Theological Study: Joab, David's army commander, combines military competence with political violence. The text does not depict him as simply evil, but it reveals the danger of a man who sometimes protects the king and at other times oversteps justice.

entries.title: Jonathan
entries.content:
Key References: 1 Samuel 18:1-4; 20; 23:15-18; 31:1-6.

Place and Context: Gibeah, the wilderness of Ziph, and Mount Gilboa.

Persons Related to the Text: Jonathan, David, Saul.

Theological Study: Jonathan, son of Saul, chooses the covenant loyalty with David even though it threatens his political interests. His friendship is not merely an emotion but a practical faithfulness that highlights God's purpose amid a troubled royal household.

entries.title: Joiakim the priest
entries.content:
Key References: Nehemiah 12:10-26.

Place and Context: Jerusalem after the exile.

People associated with the text: Joshua the priest, Joiakim, the Levites.

Theological Study: Joiakim the priest appears in post-exilic lists, and the references do not allow for constructing a broad biography about him. The importance of the name lies in maintaining continuity of service and institutional memory after the return from exile.

entries.title: Japheth
entries.content:
Key References: Genesis 5:32; 9:18-27; 10:1-5.

Place and Context: The world after the flood.

People Associated with the Text: Noah, Shem, Ham, Japheth.

Theological Study: Japheth is one of Noah's sons, and his descendants appear in the Table of Nations. Genealogical lists should not be turned into modern racial theories, but rather read as a literary map of the distribution of peoples under God's dominion.

entries.title: Yabīn
entries.content:
Key References: Joshua 11:1-15; Judges 4:1-24.

Place and Context: Hazor and northern Canaan.

Persons Related to the Text: Jabin, Joshua, Deborah, Barak, Sisera.

Theological Study: Jabin is the name of a king associated with Hazor in Joshua and Judges, and it may indicate a royal title or tradition. The two stories reveal different northern conflicts, and they should not be merged without historical distinction.

entries.title: Praise
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 9:1-2; 145:1-7; Hebrews 13:15.

Place and Context: The temple and New Covenant communities.

People Associated with the Text: David, the psalmists, the author of Hebrews.

Theological Study: Praise is the declaration of God's works through speech and life, not a formal compliment separate from obedience. The New Covenant links the sacrifice of praise with the practical acknowledgment of the Lord's name and acts of goodness.

entries.title: Covenant Confirmation
entries.content:
Key References: Deuteronomy 7:9; Psalm 89:28-37; Jeremiah 31:35-37; Hebrews 6:17-19.

Place and Context: Sinai, Zion, and the churches.

People Related to the Text: Moses, David, Jeremiah, the author of Hebrews.

Theological Study: The constancy of the covenant is based on God's faithfulness, not on the power of the people. Therefore, prophets can announce judgment and yet preserve the hope of the promise. The Hebrews use this constancy as an anchor for the soul.

entries.title: Reward
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 19:11; Matthew 6:1-6; 1 Corinthians 3:8-15; Revelation 22:12.

Place and Context: Israel, Galilee, Corinth, and Revelation.

Persons Related to the Text: David, Jesus, Paul, John.

Theological Study: Rewards in the Bible do not buy salvation, but rather declare the justice of God who does not forget faithful work. Jesus warns against seeking human reward, and Paul places work under God's testing, not under boasting.

entries.title: Precious
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Isaiah 43:4; Psalm 116:15; 1 Peter 1:18-19; 2:4-7.

Place and Context: Israel and the churches.

Persons associated with the text: Isaiah, the psalmist, Peter.

Theological Study: The precious in the book describes the value of God's people, the lives of His faithful, and the blood of Christ. Value is not measured by market price, but by God's love and choice, and the cornerstone rejected by men and chosen from them.

entries.title: Absalom's Rebellion
entries.content:
Key References: 2 Samuel 15-18.
