Place and Context: Jerusalem, the wilderness, and the forest of Ephraim.

People Related to the Text: David, Absalom, Ahithophel, Joab.

Theological Study: Absalom's revolt reveals the collapse of the royal house when sins accumulate without justice. The text does not present politics apart from the family, but shows how personal violence wounds the entire kingdom and leaves David between king and father.

entries.title: forefront of justice
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 28:15-30; Leviticus 8:8.

Place and Context: The Tabernacle.

Persons Associated with the Text: Moses, Aaron, the Israelites.

Theological Study: The breastpiece of judgment bears the names of the tribes before the Lord, making the priest a servant who represents the community rather than a holder of personal privilege. The stones and the lot are associated with discerning God's will within a worship system that has limits and holiness.

entries.title: Khalīqah
entries.content:
Key Evidences: Genesis 1:1-31; Psalm 104; Romans 18:8-25; Revelation 1:21-5. 

Place and context: the created world and the vision. 

People associated with the text: Adam, the psalmis, Paul, John. 

Theological study: Creation in the Bible is good and intended by God, not a bad substance to escape. The hope of the New Testament is to liberate and renew creation, not to abolish the world or despise the flesh.

entries.title: New Creation
entries.content:
Key References: Isaiah 43:18-19; 2 Corinthians 5:17-21; Galatians 6:15; Revelation 21:1-5.

Place and Context: Exile, Corinth, Galatia, and Revelation.

People Related to the Text: Isaiah, Paul, John.

Theological Study: The new creation declares that God's work in Christ goes beyond limited internal reform to reconciliation and renewal. The new identity is not separated from the ministry of reconciliation nor from the hope of the new heaven and new earth.

entries.title: Betrayal
entries.content:
Key references: Psalm 41:9; Matthew 26:14-25; John 13:18-30.

Place and context: Jerusalem and the upper room.

People associated with the text: David, Jesus, Judas, the disciples.

Theological study: Betrayal in the scripture is painful because it comes from a circle of trust and intimacy. Judas' betrayal is not used to condemn an entire community, but rather to reveal the corruption of the heart when love is handed over for a price.

entries.title: Quarrel
entries.content:
Key References: Proverbs 17:14; 26:20-21; James 4:1-12.

Place and Context: Israel and the churches of the diaspora.

Persons Related to the Text: The wise, James.

Theological Study: Quarrels are a fire that starts with a word and grows with uncontrolled desires. The texts do not mean to silence justified objection, but they reject turning conflict into wasted honor and revenge.

entries.title: Treasury
entries.content:
Primary References: 2 Kings 12:9-16; Mark 12:41-44; John 8:20.

Place and Context: The Temple of Jerusalem.

People Associated with the Text: Jehoiada, Joash, the widow, Jesus.

Theological Study: The treasury is the place for managing money in worship, and therefore it reveals the relationship of resources with transparency and justice. The story of the widow does not glorify exploiting her poverty, but rather exposes, in the context of Mark, a system that devours the houses of widows.

entries.title: Khabur
entries.content:
Key References: 2 Kings 17:5-6; 18:11; 1 Chronicles 5:26.

Place and Context: Mesopotamia within the Assyrian policy of relocation.

Persons Related to the Text: Kings of Assyria, inhabitants of Samaria, tribes of Israel.

Theological Study: The Khabur is associated with the deportation of the inhabitants of the northern kingdom after the fall of Samaria. Preserving the name places the exile in a real geography, and reminds that historical judgment affected groups and families, not abstract numbers.

entries.title: Five loaves
entries.content:
Key References: Matthew 14:13-21; Mark 6:30-44; John 6:1-15.

Place and Context: The wilderness near Galilee.

Persons Related to the Text: Jesus, the disciples, the crowds, the boy.

Theological Study: Five loaves are enough in the hands of Jesus to feed the multitude, thus the story combines physical compassion with a theological sign. The miracle does not eliminate the organization of the disciples and the service of distribution, but makes them witnesses to the abundance of the kingdom.

entries.title: Covenant Fellowship
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Genesis 17:1-14; Exodus 24:3-8; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Luke 22:20.

Place and Context: Canaan, Sinai, and Jerusalem.

Persons Related to the Text: Abraham, Moses, Jeremiah, Jesus.

Theological Study: The covenant bond unites promise, obedience, and identity, and is not reduced to a legal contract. From Abraham to the Last Supper, the covenant shows a divine initiative that creates a people called to faithfulness and mercy.

entries.title: Rest
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Genesis 2:1-3; Exodus 20:8-11; Matthew 11:28-30; Hebrews 4:1-11.

Place and Context: Creation, Sinai, Galilee, and the churches.

Persons Associated with the Text: Moses, Jesus, the author of Hebrews.

Theological Study: Rest in Scripture is related to creation, the Sabbath, and the promise, and is not laziness or evasion of responsibility. Jesus invites the weary to rest under His yoke, and Hebrews reads rest as the hope of entering God's faithfulness.

entries.title: Compassion
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 34:6; Psalm 103:13; Mark 6:34; Colossians 3:12.

Place and Context: Sinai, Galilee, and the churches.

Persons Associated with the Text: Moses, David, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Compassion is a divine attribute manifested in practical care for the weak. Jesus has compassion for the crowds like a shepherdless flock, and the letters call believers to clothe themselves with compassion within community relationships.

entries.title: Pressure of Authority
entries.content:
Key References: 1 Samuel 8:10-18; 2 Samuel 11; Mark 10:42-45.

Place and Context: Israel, Jerusalem, and Galilee.

People Related to the Text: Samuel, David, Bathsheba, Jesus.

Theological Study: The pressure of power appears when leadership turns into taking and exploiting rather than serving. Samuel warns against the practices of the king, and Jesus redefines greatness through service rather than domination.

entries.title: Apparent Righteousness
entries.content:
Key References: Isaiah 58:1-12; Matthew 6:1-18; 23:27-28.

Place and Context: Judah, Galilee, and Jerusalem.

People Related to the Text: Isaiah, Jesus, The Pharisees.

Theological Study: The appearance of righteousness may hide a heart far from justice and mercy. Jesus rejects almsgiving, prayer, and fasting when they become a display before people, and calls for sincerity that sees God alone as its center.

entries.title: Manifestation of Glory
entries.content:
Key References: Exodus 24:16-17; Isaiah 60:1-3; Luke 2:9; 2 Corinthians 3:18.

Place and Context: Sinai, Zion, Bethlehem, and the churches.

People Related to the Text: Moses, Isaiah, the shepherds, Paul.

Theological Study: The appearance of glory links the divine presence with light, awe, and transformation. From Sinai to the announcement to the shepherds, glory is not a sensory adornment but a revelation that calls for worship and renewed life.

entries.title: Darkness of the yoke
entries.content:
Key References: Isaiah 9:4; 58:6; Galatians 5:1.

Place and Context: Judah and the churches of Galatia.

People Related to the Text: Isaiah, Paul, the Galatian communities.

Theological Study: The oppression of the yoke is a picture of the burden of political or religious enslavement. Isaiah links breaking the yoke with justice, and Paul warns against returning to slavery that destroys the freedom of Christ.

entries.title: Evil intention
entries.content:
Key References: 1 Samuel 1:12-18; 1 Corinthians 13:5-7; James 2:1-4.

Place and Context: Shiloh, Corinth, and the diaspora churches.

People Related to the Text: Hannah, Eli, Paul, James.

Theological Study: Malice appears in Eli's misunderstanding of Hannah, and in the letters' warning against love that suspects evil or favors the rich. The scriptures call for fair discernment that listens before judging.

entries.title: Pumpkin Shade
entries.content:
Key References: Jonah 4:5-11.

Place and Context: Outside Nineveh.

People Related to the Text: Jonah, the people of Nineveh, the Lord.

Theological Study: The shade of the gourd in Jonah is a vivid lesson of a prophet who becomes angry over a plant but shows no mercy to a great city. God uses the shade and its disappearance to reveal the narrowness of the prophet's heart compared to the vastness of divine mercy.

entries.title: Manifestation of Evil
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: 1 Thessalonians 5:21-22; 2 Corinthians 11:13-15; 1 John 4:1.

Place and Context: Churches of the New Covenant.

Persons Related to the Text: Paul, John, the congregations.

Theological Study: The manifestation of evil may disguise itself as goodness or convincing teaching, which is why the letters call for testing and discernment. Vigilance does not mean doubting everyone, but examining the fruit, and acknowledging Christ and love.

entries.title: Victory of Faith
entries.content:
Key References: 1 John 5:4-5; Revelation 2:7; 12:11.

Place and Context: The churches of Asia and Revelation.

People Related to the Text: John, the witnesses, the churches.

Theological Study: The victory of faith in John and Revelation is not based on overpowering others, but on perseverance in Christ and testimony even in the midst of danger. Overcoming is linked to the blood of the Lamb and the word of the testimony, not to violence.

entries.title: Midday Light
entries.content:
Key References: Acts 22:6-10; 26:13-18.

Place and Context: The road to Damascus.

Persons related to the text: Saul, Jesus, companions on the road.

Theological Study: The noon light in the account of Paul's call emphasizes that the encounter with Christ occurred clearly, not in a private vision. The light leads to a mission for the Gentiles and to the transformation of the persecutor's life into that of a witness.

entries.title: Evening Shadows
entries.content:
Key Scriptures: Jeremiah 6:4; Zechariah 14:7; Luke 24:29.

Place and Context: Jerusalem and the road to Emmaus.

Persons Related to the Text: Jeremiah, Zechariah, Jesus, the disciples of Emmaus.

Theological Study: The evening shadows may indicate approaching danger, the end of the day, or the anticipation of new light. In Emmaus, evening becomes a time of hospitality, opening of the Scriptures, and breaking of bread, turning the breaking into understanding.

entries.title: The appearance of the angels
entries.content:
Key Passages: Genesis 18; Luke 1:11-20; 2:8-14; Acts 12:7-11.

Place and Context: corridor, temple, Bethlehem, and prison.

People Related to the Text: Abraham, Zechariah, the shepherds, Peter.

Theological Study: The appearance of angels in Scripture serves God's message and does not call for the worship of the angel itself. The scenes vary between promise, birth, and deliverance, but they all point attention to the work of the Lord rather than curiosity about the beings.

entries.title: The Monster of Isolation
entries.content:
Key References: Psalm 25:16; 68:6; Mark 1:40-45; 2 Timothy 4:16-17.

Place and Context: Israel, Galilee, and Rome.

Persons Related to the Text: David, Jesus, Paul.

Theological Study: Severe isolation appears in the cries of the Psalms, in marginalized patients, and in prison letters. God does not leave the solitary without attention, but rather establishes a home for them and brings them close to a community of mercy and witness.

entries.title: Village
entries.content:
Key Passages: Luke 10:38-42; 17:11-19; 24:13-35.

Place and Context: Villages of Galilee and Judea, and Emmaus.

Persons Associated with the Text: Martha, Mary, the Samaritan, the disciples of Emmaus.

Theological Study: The village in the Gospels is not a small insignificant background, but a place of hospitality, healing, and the opening of the Scriptures. Jesus' ministry appears in ordinary places, proclaiming the kingdom amid homes and roads, not only in major centers.

entries.title: Qaryut
entries.content:
Key References: Joshua 15:25; Jeremiah 48:24; Amos 2:2.

Place and Context: Judah and Moab according to the context.

People Related to the Text: The inhabitants of Judah and Moab, the prophets.

Theological Study: Kirioth is the name of a place that requires contextual adjustment because it appears in different lists and cities. Its value lies in teaching the reader to be careful not to merge locations merely due to name similarity, and to read geography within prophecy and borders.

entries.title: Wild Salwa
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 16:13; Numbers 11:31-34; Psalm 78:26-31.

Place and context: Sinai wilderness.

People associated with the text: Moses, the children of Israel, the mixed group.

Theological study: Quail is food given by God in the wilderness, but in verse 11 it reveals lust and complaint that do not accept the gift. The introduction balances God's providence with the corruption of desire when it forgets liberation and longs for slavery.

entries.title: I was told
entries.content:
Basic Evidence: Ecclesiastes 1:1-11; 3:1-14; 12:9-14.

Place and Context: Israel in Wisdom Literature.

People associated with the text: the university, the wise men, the hearers.

Theological study: Qohlet or university is a judgmental voice that tests the limits of gain and knowledge under the sun. Traveling does not call for despair, but rather for humility that enjoys God’s gifts and fears Him in the midst of the ambiguity of life.

entries.title: Korah
entries.content:
Basic evidence: 16; Psalm 42 is a title; Jude 11.

Place and context: the wilderness and the Levitical ministry.

People associated with the text: Korah, Moses, Aaron, the sons of Korah.

Theological Study: Korah leads a rebellion against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, and his story reveals the danger of turning closeness to service into greed for power. However, the titles of the Psalms preserve the mention of the sons of Korah, thus distinguishing between the condemnation of rebellion and the continuation of grace in the offspring.

references.author: Holy Bible
references.title: Number 16; Psalm 42 is a title; Jude 11

entries.title: beard
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Leviticus 19:27; 2 Samuel 10:4-5; Isaiah 50:6.

Place and context: Israel, Ammon, and the slave texts.

People associated with the text: Moses, David, David's apostles, servant of the Lord.

Theological study: In the ancient world, a beard was a sign of dignity and identity, and therefore shaving half of the beards of David's apostles was a political insult. In Isaiah, the servant of the Lord endures pluck and shame, so physical dignity enters into the language of pain and obedience.

entries.title: Flames
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 3:2; 13:21; Acts 2:3.

Place and context: Horeb, the wilderness, and Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: Moses, the children of Israel, the disciples.

Theological study: The flame appears in the bush, the pillar of fire, and the tongues on the day of Pentecost, but it does not mean that the fire itself is holy in itself. The flame serves to announce presence, guidance, and spirit, not just visual excitement.

entries.title: reed
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Isaiah 42:3; Matthew 12:20; 27:29-30.

Place and context: Judah and Jerusalem.

People associated with the text: servant of the Lord, Jesus, soldiers.

Theological study: The bruised reed in Isaiah is an image of weakness that the servant of the Lord cannot crush. In the Passion of Jesus, the reed turns into a tool of mockery, thus revealing the paradox of the king who does not break the weak and endures the insult of the strong.

entries.title: Building brick
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 11:3; Exodus 6:5-19; Isaiah 9:10.

Place and context: Shinar, Egypt and Judah.

People associated with the text: builders of Babylon, Pharaoh, children of Israel.

Theological study: The bricks appear in the Tower of Babel and in the slavery of Egypt, revealing how work and building can become a tool of pride or oppression. The introduction distinguishes between building as a good deed and building that denies God or enslaves man.

entries.title: Frankincense
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 30:34-38; Leviticus 2:1-2; Matthew 2:11; Revelation 18:13.

Place and context: the tabernacle, Bethlehem and symbolic Babylon.

People associated with the text: Moses, the priests, the Magi, John.

Theological study: Frankincense is an aromatic substance that is included in incense and offerings, and appears in the Magi’s gifts to Jesus. It does not always have one meaning. It may serve worship or engage in trade, which the vision criticizes when it is associated with luxury and injustice.

entries.title: Leprosy
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Leviticus 13-14; 2 Kings 5; Mark 1:40-45; Luke 11:17-19.

Place and context: Israel, Samaria and Galilee.

People associated with the text: the priests, Naaman, Jesus, the lepers.

Theological study: Leprosy in translations covers various skin diseases and is not always equal to Hansen's disease. The law addresses purity and return to community, and Jesus' healings reveal his mercy without morally stigmatizing the sick.

entries.title: Angel
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Genesis 7:16-13; Daniel 6:22; Luke 1:26-38; Hebrews 1:14.

Place and context: the wilderness, Babylon, and Nazareth.

People associated with the text: Hagar, Daniel, Gabriel, Mary.

Theological study: The angel is a messenger who serves God's purpose and is not the center of worship. Angels' messages vary between protection, good news, and interpretation, and the New Testament confirms that they are serving spirits, not substitutes for God.

entries.title: King
entries.content:
Key Evidence: 1 Samuel 8; 2 Samuel 7; Psalm 2; John 18:33-37.

Place and context: Israel, Jerusalem, and Pilate's court.

People associated with the text: Samuel, David, Jesus, Pilate.

Theological study: The king in the book is a subject of promise and criticism at the same time. The people demand a king like the nations, God makes a promise to the house of David, and then Jesus proclaims a kingdom that does not operate according to the logic of imperial violence.

entries.title: He envied the covenant
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Exodus 34:6-7; Ruth 3:10; Psalm 136; Micah 7:18-20.

Place and context: Sinai, Bethlehem, and the Temple.

People associated with the text: Moses, Ruth, Boaz, the psalmists.

Theological Study: Covenant envy is a Hebrew term that refers to steadfast mercy and practical faithfulness. It appears in the proclamation of the name of the Lord and in the loyalty of Ruth and Boaz, and Psalm 136 is sung, for His mercy endures forever.

entries.title: Hallelujah
entries.content:
Key Evidence: Psalm 104:35; 146-150; Revelation 19:1-6.

Place and context: structure and vision.

People associated with the text: the psalmists, John, the heavenly community.

Theological study: Hallelujah is a call to praise the Lord, and many psalms conclude with it as it appears in Revelation 19. It is not reduced to a celebratory expression, but rather a declaration that judgment, salvation, and glory belong to the Lord.

entries.title: Leviticus
entries.content:
Basic evidence: Numbers 3:5-13; 1 Chronicles 23:24-32; Ezra 8:15-20; Luke 10:32.

Place and context: the tabernacle, the temple, and the road to Jericho.

People associated with the text: Moses, David, Ezra, the Levite in the parable of the Samaritan.

Theological study: The Levites serve in worship, teaching, and guarding the sanctuary, and they are not represented by a single sign in all ages. The parable of the Samaritan mentions a Levite who passed by the wounded man, and he judges religiosity when he separates himself from mercy, without reducing all Levites to this scene.
